    1. 22.1 Commands that switch to a major mode

Tuatara Manual

for version 0.90.27, every chapter on one page

This manual is written with modal editing on, first and foremost. Where a command also has a key that works with modal editing off, it is given as well, as the non-modal key.

The screen

What Tuatara shows you, and the name of each part.

When Tuatara starts, its screen is divided into a few parts. Each part has a name, and the rest of this manual uses those names. This chapter goes through them from the large ones to the small ones. For each part it lists the keys that act on it and the settings that change how it looks.

This manual is written with modal editing on, first and foremost. Tuatara has it on until you turn it off, so the keys the manual gives first are those of NORMAL state. Where a command also has a key that works with modal editing off, the manual gives that too.

1.1 Keys and names

Most commands have a key. A key written as C-x means hold down the Control key and press x. A key written as M-x means hold down Alt (called Meta in older manuals) and press x. On a terminal where Alt does not reach the program, press Escape, let go, then press x. S- stands for Shift.

Several keys in a row, as in C-x C-f, are pressed one after the other. You may keep Control held down through the whole sequence. A few keys have names instead of letters: RET is Return (Enter), TAB is Tab, SPC is the space bar, DEL is the Backspace key and ESC is Escape.

Every command also has a name, such as find-file. You can run any command by its name. Press M-x, type a few letters of the name, and press RET. The list of choices that appears shows the keys of each command beside it. A command that has no key can only be run this way, and the tables in this manual say M-x and its name for it.

A setting is a name that starts and ends with a star, such as *mode-line-tuatara*. Settings go in your init file, the file Tuatara reads when it starts, as in (setf *mode-line-tuatara* nil). Each table of settings in this chapter gives the default, the value Tuatara has until you change it. C-h v shows a setting's value, the values it takes and what each does.

Tuatara is a modal editor, which means a key can do different things depending on a state the editor is in. There are two states you will meet first. In NORMAL state, the letter keys are commands: i starts INSERT state. In INSERT state, the letter keys write text. C-g or ESC takes you back to NORMAL state. The mode line, described below, always tells you which state you are in.

The tables of commands have two columns of keys. The Modal column holds the keys of the modal layer, such as the letter keys of NORMAL state. They work only with modal editing on. The Non-modal column holds the keys that work in both states and with modal editing off: those with Control or Alt, the arrow keys and the keys of a major mode. A side with no key says "none". In the text, a key that has a partner of the other kind is followed by it in brackets, as in j (non-modal: C-n) and C-n (modal: j). To turn modal editing off, put (setf *modal-editing* nil) in your init file. Every key of the Non-modal column then does what the table says, and typing inserts text everywhere.

Most letter keys of NORMAL state that have no Control or Alt key of their own are also under C-z, in every state: m w selects a word, and C-z m w does the same with modal editing off. The Non-modal column gives them, as C-z m w. A command that has a key in both states, such as w (non-modal: M-f), is not under C-z a second time.

1.2 The parts of the screen

Figure 1.1 shows the whole editor with two windows and a question open, and Figure 1.2 the same with no question open. Each part is named as this manual, the help and the project's support pages name it, so that a question about a part can say which one it means.

The frame is everything Tuatara draws. In a window of its own it is that window, and in a terminal it is the terminal's screen.

A window is a part of the frame that shows one piece of text. Each window has a mode line under it, a row that describes what the window shows.

The echo area is the last row of the frame. Tuatara says short things there, such as Wrote /home/you/list.txt.

The minibuffer is the row where Tuatara asks you a question. The question is called the prompt, and what you type after it is your answer. While a question is open, the minibuffer and the panel take the bottom of the frame in place of the echo area: the minibuffer on top and the choices under it, or the minibuffer on the last row when *prompt-above-candidates* is nil.

The panel is the rows at the bottom of the frame that list choices while a question is open, and the keys you can press next after a key such as C-x, above the echo area. It is only there when it has something to say.

The cursor is the mark that shows where typed text goes. Other editors call that place the point, and Tuatara's help uses the word too.

The gutter is the narrow strip at the left edge of a window. It can hold line numbers.

1.3 Windows and buffers

A buffer is a piece of text Tuatara holds in memory. When you open a file, Tuatara reads it into a buffer. Your changes go to the buffer, and the file on disk changes only when you save with C-x C-s. Not every buffer has a file. *Messages*, the log of what the echo area said, is a buffer. So is the list of files you get from find-file. Buffers that Tuatara makes itself have their names between stars.

A window is a view of one buffer. Two windows may show the same buffer, each at its own place, or different buffers. Closing a window never closes its buffer, and killing a buffer closes only the windows that were made for it.

Tuatara puts new windows where you would expect. A help buffer opens in another window. The *Messages* log opens across the bottom, 30% of the height, and takes the cursor so that you can read it; q closes it. A window that already holds a buffer is never split into pieces smaller than *window-min-height* rows or *window-min-width* columns.

Try it, with a shopping list and a recipe

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/shopping.txt and press RET. The file does not exist yet, so Tuatara makes an empty buffer with that name.
  2. Press i to start INSERT state. Type eggs, RET, bread, RET, milk. Press C-g to go back to NORMAL state, then C-x C-s to save.
  3. Press C-x 3. The window splits in two, side by side, and both show the shopping list. The left window keeps the cursor.
  4. Press C-x o to move to the right window. Press C-x C-f, type ~/pancakes.txt, press RET, then press i and type a recipe.
  5. Press C-x o to go back to the left window. Press C-x 1. The left window fills the frame again. The pancake buffer is still there: press C-x b, type pan and press RET to bring it back.

noneC-x 3split-window-rightTwo windows side by side. The left one keeps the cursor.

Each of the four keys that make a window larger or smaller says in the echo area what share of the split every window has now, in per cent. Side by side it reads Widths, left to right: 52%, 48%, and one above the other it reads Heights, top to bottom: 55%, 45%. The shares may not add up to exactly 100, as each is rounded. The echo area then lists the keys that repeat the change. Right after one of the size commands, you can press a key alone to go on resizing. } and > make the window wider, { and < narrower, ^ and + taller, and v and - shorter. If the window has no neighbour in that direction, the echo area says that it cannot be made larger or smaller. With the mouse, drag a mode line up or down, or the line between two windows left or right.

1.4 Frames, windows of their own and terminals

Tuatara runs in two ways. Typed as tuatara, it runs in the terminal you started it from. Typed as tuatara --gui, it opens a window of its own on the desktop, drawn with GTK, the toolkit most Linux desktops use. Both have the same keys, the same commands and the same parts. The window of its own has things a terminal does not, such as pictures in every case, a font you can change and ligatures where the font has them.

A frame is one such screen. You can have several frames. In a window of its own each frame is a separate desktop window. A terminal has only one screen, so its frames take turns: the one you work in is shown, and the others wait. When frames take turns, the mode line starts the buffer's name with the frame's name, F1, F2 and so on. Every frame has its own windows and its own echo area. They all show the same buffers, so a change you make in one frame is in the other at once.

Tuatara can also run in the background as a daemon, started with tuatara --daemon, and be reached with tuatara --client, each client with frames of its own. The sign D in the mode line, described below, says that the editor you are in runs as a daemon.

Try it, with two frames

  1. In a terminal, start Tuatara with tuatara ~/shopping.txt.
  2. Press C-x 5 2. A second frame opens showing the same file. In a terminal the new frame replaces the first on the screen, and the mode line now starts the buffer's name with F2.
  3. Press C-x 5 o to go to the other frame, and back again with the same keys. The mode line says F1 in the first.
  4. Press C-x 5 0 in the second frame to close it. Closing the last frame is refused. Quit with C-x C-c.

noneC-x C--text-scale-adjustMakes the font a step smaller.

Font steps are 1.2 times each, from 0.4 to 15 times the starting size. In a terminal the font belongs to the terminal, and these commands say so.

1.5 The mode line

The mode line is the bar under every window. It says what the window shows and in what state. The mode line of the window you are working in is drawn brighter than the others. Here is a typical one.

Read left to right, the parts are these.

  1. The modal state, in square brackets after the word TUATARA.
  2. Up to four signs, P, U, S and D, always in the same place.
  3. The marker that says whether the buffer is saved, [-], [*] or [%].
  4. Words about the buffer itself, such as Safe or Narrow, when they apply.
  5. The buffer's name.
  6. The line and the column of the cursor.
  7. The name of the buffer's major mode, when it has one.
  8. Anything more the buffer has to say, such as CRLF or Page 3 of 10.
  9. The directory the buffer lives in, at the right end.

Only the parts that apply are shown, and a mode line that is too narrow cuts the buffer's name in the middle, with a mark for what is left out.

1.5.1 The modal state

The first part tells you what a key will do. TUATARA[N] is NORMAL state, TUATARA[I] is INSERT state. TUATARA[S] is a support buffer, one that holds a list, help or the *Messages* log. There you can read, move and select but not type. TUATARA[E] is a buffer that holds no modal keys, such as the Lisp prompt (IELM). With *modal-editing* set to nil there is no modal part at all.

With *mode-line-tuatara* set to nil the word TUATARA is left out and only [N] remains. C-x T t switches it while Tuatara runs.

1.5.2 The signs P, U, S and D

Four letters stand before the saved marker, side by side. Each is faint when nothing is going on and bright, in the warning colour, while its work goes on. They never move, so nothing after them jumps when one lights up. A sign stays lit for half a second after its work ends, so that a short job can be seen.

SignSettingWhat it says
P*processing-indicator*Processing. A job is running for this buffer, or waits its turn. Jobs are things done in the background, such as a search through a large file, a sort or a save. C-x j lists them.
U*indexing-indicator*Update. A directory you asked Tuatara to keep read in memory is being read.
S*searching-indicator*Search. A search runs over such a directory.
D*daemon-indicator*Daemon. This editor runs in the background as a daemon.

U and S only appear when *indexed-directories* names some directory, and P and D always appear. Set any of the four settings to nil to hide that sign, or to another piece of text, such as "indexing" or an icon from a font that has one, to show that instead.

1.5.3 Saved or not

Next comes the marker for the buffer's state.

MarkerMeaning
[-]The buffer is as it was saved or read.
[*]You have changed it and not yet saved it.
[%]The buffer is read-only. Typing does not change it. C-x C-q switches that.

1.5.4 Words about the buffer

Just before the buffer's name, Tuatara may add a word that is lit up in a colour of its own.

WordMeaning
SafeThe file was opened safely. Tuatara shows its text and leaves the file untouched.
EvidenceThe file is in a directory listed in *evidence-directories*. It is never written to.
NarrowThe buffer shows only a part of its text (C-x x n, C-x x s). C-x x w shows all of it again.
Look onlyThe buffer belongs to a git repository opened for looking at only. Commands that would change it are refused.

1.5.5 The name, the line and the column

The buffer's name follows. When it is long, it is cut in the middle and a mark stands for what is left out, down to 12 columns. *mode-line-name-limit* sets a shorter limit.

After the name comes L and the line number, then C and the column, which counts from 0. A number above 999 has commas, as in L100,000,001. When Tuatara is still counting the lines of a very large file you see L... instead, and the number appears when the count is done. The same holds for a column on a line too long to measure at once.

After them, if the buffer has a major mode, comes its name, such as Org or Terminal. A major mode is the set of habits Tuatara gives a buffer according to what it holds: how it colours text, which keys it adds, and so on.

1.5.6 Other things the mode line says

While keys are recorded, the word Rec stands before the signs (C-x ( starts recording). While recorded keys play over and over for more than a second, Played 1,200/10,000 says how many plays are done. The words below follow the mode name, each when it applies.

ShowsMeaning
CRLF or CRThe file's lines end the way Windows (CRLF) or old Macintosh files (CR) end them. Plain files with the usual ending show nothing.
FollowingThe buffer follows its file as it grows, like tail -f (follow-file).
Counting lines 40%Tuatara is counting the lines of a large file.
Saving 50%A save is under way. Another buffer's save shows with its name.
Changed on diskAnother program changed the file after you read it.
Deleted on diskThe file was removed.
Stale, read-onlyThe file was rewritten on disk while it was shown, so the buffer is read-only. revert-buffer reads it again.
incompleteA file from another machine stopped arriving before it was all there.
Wrap, CentredThe buffer wraps long lines (C-x T l) or shows its text in a column in the middle (C-x T o).
Rewind a1b2c3dThe buffer shows a file as an older git commit had it (C-x G). The commit's date and its place in the history follow.
Conflicts 3The buffer holds git conflict markers, and says how many.
Hex 0x00000010 digitsThe buffer shows the file's bytes. digits or text says which side the cursor is on.
Page 3 of 10A PDF's page, the number of pages and its zoom.
SandboxedWhat you see was made by a program shut in a sandbox.
Quick editA file opened from a directory list to be edited there.
Filtered by kiwi: 12 of 1,000 recordsA search filter hides some lines of the file.
✘2 ⚠1A language server found 2 errors and 1 warning.
DebugDebug mode is on.
SV<An input method is on, here the one for Swedish.
[0:22] (Task)The Org clock is running on a task.
by time, by nameHow a directory list is sorted.

1.5.7 The directory

The last part is the directory the buffer lives in, written with ~ for your home directory: ~/letters/. A buffer with no file, such as a scratch buffer, shows the directory named by *default-directory*. Files on another machine show their /ssh:pinetree: path.

Try it, with a letter

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/letter.txt and press RET. Look at the mode line: [-], the name, L1 C0.
  2. Press i, type Dear Hana, and press RET. The mode line now says [*], and TUATARA[I], and L2 C0.
  3. Press C-g to leave INSERT state, then C-x C-s. The marker goes back to [-] and the echo area says that the file was written.
  4. Press C-x C-q. The marker becomes [%]. Now C-x C-q again.
  5. Press C-x T t. The word TUATARA disappears from the mode line. Press the same keys to bring it back.
  6. Press M-x, type follow-file and press RET. The word Following appears. Run it again to stop it.

noneC-x C-qread-only-modeMakes the buffer read-only, or editable again.
noneC-x jlist-jobsLists the jobs running or waiting, which P stands for.
noneC-x Jstop-jobStops the job running in this buffer, after asking.

Clicking a window's mode line with the mouse selects that window.

A face is a name for a way of drawing text: a colour, bold, and so on. The theme in force, ao-dark as standard, gives each face its look. Change one in your init file, for example (set-face :mode-line-sign :fg "#e0a33a").

1.6 The echo area and the messages log

The echo area is the last row of the frame. Tuatara writes a short message there after most things you do, such as Wrote /home/you/letter.txt, and the message stays until the next key you press does something. It also shows the keys of a long sequence while you are typing it, and asks questions that one key answers, such as yes or no.

Every message is also kept in the *Messages* buffer. A message said twice in a row is written once with a count, as in Saved [3 times]. The buffer is read-only, and it holds the last 1000 lines. Messages said while a password or other secret was at hand are shown but not kept.

C-h e opens the log across the bottom of the frame, 30% of the height, with the cursor in it. It is a read-only buffer, so q closes it. The log is the place to look when a message went by too fast.

Try it, with a message gone by

  1. Press C-x C-f, open ~/shopping.txt, press i, type tea and press C-g. Then press C-x C-s. The echo area says that the file was written (on a file with no change it says that no changes need to be saved). The message disappears when you press the next key.
  2. Press C-h e. The log opens at the bottom with the message in its last line. Press q to close it.
  3. Press C-h N to read the notifications Tuatara or its packages have given this session, for example when an agenda entry's time came.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-h eview-echo-area-messagesShows the *Messages* log.
noneC-h Nview-notificationsShows the *Notifications* log, each line dated.
noneC-gkeyboard-quitStops what is going on, drops a selection and closes a question.

SettingDefaultWhat it changes

1.7 The minibuffer and its prompt

When a command needs something from you, a file name, a word to search for, a yes or no, it asks in the minibuffer, a row at the bottom of the frame (Figure 1.1). The words that ask are the prompt, such as Find file:, and your answer follows it (Figure 1.3). The prompt is drawn in bold. A frame that has a question open keeps its window text where it was, and its cursor is drawn as an outline there while you type in the minibuffer.

Press RET to give the answer, or C-g or ESC to give up. Before the prompt Tuatara may show a count, such as 3/12, which means the third of twelve choices. A search shows which match the cursor is at and how many there are. */0 means nothing matches but what you typed can be taken, and !/0 means it cannot.

You edit the answer with keys much like the ones in a text buffer. These keys work only while a question is open, so M-x does not list their commands.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneRETminibuffer-finishGives the answer, taking the selected choice if there is one.
noneC-j, M-RETminibuffer-submit-inputGives the answer exactly as typed, whatever is selected.
noneC-g, ESCminibuffer-cancelGives up the question.
noneDEL, C-hminibuffer-backward-delete-charDeletes the character before the cursor.
noneC-b, <left>minibuffer-backward-charMoves the cursor left.
noneC-f, <right>minibuffer-forward-charMoves the cursor right.
noneC-a, <home>minibuffer-beginningMoves to the start of the answer.
noneC-e, <end>minibuffer-endMoves to the end of the answer.
noneC-kminibuffer-kill-lineDeletes the answer after the cursor.
noneC-uminibuffer-clearClears the answer. The prompt stays.
noneC-<backspace>, M-DELminibuffer-backward-kill-wordDeletes the word before the cursor.
noneC-y, C-V, S-<insert>minibuffer-pastePastes the clipboard, or what you cut last.
noneM-pminibuffer-previous-historyBrings back an earlier answer to this question.
noneM-nminibuffer-next-historyGoes to a later answer.

A question the editor thinks is risky, such as deleting a file, needs the whole word yes or no and then RET. A question whose answer is easy to undo takes one key. A password is typed with stars shown, and is never kept.

A question that offers a text to start with selects it, so that typing replaces it and RET takes it.

:cursor-inactivethemeThe cursor in a window that does not get the typing.

1.8 The choices panel

When a question has a list of answers, Tuatara shows them in the panel above the last row, and narrows them as you type. Completing means finishing your answer from that list. Type any part of a name. Several words may be typed, and a choice has to match all of them, in any order. The letters that matched are coloured, one colour for each word.

The selected choice is drawn reversed. C-n or <down> select the next one and C-p or <up> the one before. Above the first one is the line you typed, when what you typed can be taken as it is. TAB puts the selected choice into the answer. For a file name it replaces the part after the last slash, and for a directory it goes into the directory, so that you can walk down a path with TAB. RET gives the selected choice, and C-j gives what you typed.

At most 10 rows are used for the panel, the prompt row included. When there are more choices, M-t makes the panel as tall as the frame allows, and again as usual. A choice may have a note beside it, such as the keys of a command, the mode of a buffer or the permissions of a file. A title with a line beside it begins a group, such as the directory that the files under it are in.

Try it, with a directory of notes

  1. Press C-x C-f. Tuatara starts where you chose last and lists what is there.
  2. Type ~/ and look at the panel. Each choice is a file or a directory.
  3. Type a few letters of a file's name. The list shrinks.
  4. Press C-n twice and C-p once. The marked line moves.
  5. Press TAB. The name is put into the answer. If it was a directory, its contents are listed.
  6. Press M-t. The panel grows. Press it again to shrink it.
  7. Press C-g to give up.

1.8.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-n, <down>minibuffer-next-candidateSelects the next choice.
noneC-p, <up>minibuffer-previous-candidateSelects the previous choice.
noneTAB, C-M-i, M-TABminibuffer-completePuts the selected choice into the answer. In a Lisp question it lists the names that fit the word at the cursor.
noneM-tminibuffer-toggle-tallMakes the panel as tall as it can be, or as usual.

1.9 Key hints

Press C-x and wait. The panel lists every key that can follow, with the name of its command, so you do not have to remember them. Names that start with a plus sign, such as +rectangles and registers, are further prefixes, and pressing their key opens another list. A key whose command cannot run in this buffer is dimmed, and pressing it says why. C-h right after a prefix key lists every key under it in a buffer of its own. C-g closes the hints.

The hints take as many rows as the frame has room for, and the echo area stays under them. If they do not all fit, the last row ends in ... C-h lists all.

Try it, with the keys under C-x

  1. Press C-x and wait a moment. The panel appears with keys such as C-f, C-s and 5.
  2. Press 5. The panel changes to the keys under C-x 5, the ones for frames.
  3. Press C-g. The hints close and nothing was run.
  4. Press C-x and then C-h. A buffer lists all the keys under C-x.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-h after a prefixnoneLists every key under the prefix in a buffer.
noneM-xexecute-extended-commandAsks for a command by name, with its keys beside each choice.

SettingDefaultWhat it changes

1.10 The cursor, the gutter and header lines

The cursor is drawn as a block as standard. A bar or an underline can be chosen, and each modal state may have its own shape and colour, so that you see at once whether you are in NORMAL or INSERT state. In a window that does not get the typing the cursor is drawn as an outline in a window of its own and as an underline in a terminal.

The gutter is on the left edge of a window. It is empty as standard. Line numbers appear in it when you ask: M-x toggle-line-numbers goes through none, absolute and relative, where relative numbers show how many lines away each line is. Where a long line wraps, the gutter shows a mark beside the extra rows.

Tuatara has no tab bar. Buffers are reached by name (C-x b) or from the list (C-x C-b). A window can have a header line at its top. A file of records, such as a CSV, can keep its first row, the header, at the top of the window while the rest scrolls under it.

Moving around

How to put the cursor where you want it.

Before you can change text you have to get to it. This chapter lists every way Tuatara has of moving the cursor: by character, word, line, sentence and paragraph, to the start or end of the text, to a line you name, and back to a place you left. It also covers counts, which repeat a move, and the marks that let you return. For each part it gives the keys and the settings that change how the move behaves. Scrolling and recentring are in chapter 1.

Keys are written as chapter 1 explains: C-x is Control and x, M-x is Alt and x, RET is Return. The tables say "none" for a command that has no key and can only be run by name with M-x.

2.1 Two sets of keys

Tuatara has two sets of keys for moving. They do the same jobs, and you may use either one, or both.

The first set is the letter keys of NORMAL state: h, j, k, l and a few more. They need no Control or Alt, so your hands stay on the letters. They work only in NORMAL state, because in INSERT state a letter is text.

The second set uses Control and Alt, as Emacs does: C-f, M-f, C-a and so on. These work in both states. They are the keys to reach for while you are typing in INSERT state and do not want to leave it. The arrow keys, <home> and <end> work in both states as well. With *modal-editing* set to nil the second set is all there is.

A move never changes the text. If a move cannot go further, such as l (non-modal: C-f) at the very end of the text, the cursor stays where it is.

The mode line shows the line and the column of the cursor, L3 C4, and both count the way chapter 1 describes: the first line is 1 and the first column is 0.

2.2 By character and by line

h and l (non-modal: C-b, C-f) move one character left and right. j and k (non-modal: C-n, C-p) move one line down and up. At the end of a line, l goes on to the start of the next one, and h at the start of a line goes back to the end of the one above.

When you move down or up, Tuatara tries to keep the column you started from. If the next line is shorter, the cursor goes to its end. When you go on pressing j or k (non-modal: C-n, C-p), the cursor returns to the original column as soon as a line is long enough, so a short line in the middle does not pull you off your column. Any other key, even h (non-modal: C-b), forgets the column.

If you have turned on soft wrap (C-x T l), a long line shows as several rows on the screen. j and k (non-modal: C-n, C-p) then move one row, not one whole line.

In the hex view, which shows the bytes of a file, h and l (non-modal: C-b, C-f) move one byte instead of one character.

Try it, with a recipe

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/scones.txt and press RET. Press i and type these five lines, ending each but the last with RET: Scones, 2 cups flour, 4 tsp baking powder, 1 cup milk, Mix well and bake for twelve minutes. Press C-g to go back to NORMAL state.
  2. Press g g (non-modal: M-<) to go to the top. The mode line says L1 C0.
  3. Press j j. You are on line 3 (L3 C0). Press l l l and watch the column go to 3. Press h (non-modal: C-b) once to see it come back to 2.
  4. Press j j to go to the last line, then g l (non-modal: C-e) for its end. The column is 36, the length of that line.
  5. Press k (non-modal: C-p). The line above is shorter, so the cursor goes to its end, at column 10. Press j (non-modal: C-n). The cursor is back at column 36.
  6. Press C-u 3 k. The echo area shows C-u 3- while Tuatara waits for the key, then the cursor moves up three lines at once.

2.2.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
lC-f, <right>forward-charMoves one character on. A count moves that many, or back when it is negative. In the hex view, one byte.
hC-b, <left>backward-charMoves one character back.
jC-n, <down>next-lineMoves down one line, keeping the column when it can. Where long lines wrap, one row.
kC-p, <up>previous-lineMoves up one line, in the same way.
none<down-mouse-1>mouse-set-pointPuts the cursor where you click with the first mouse button, in the window you click.

In a rectangle (chapter 5), l and h (non-modal: C-f, C-b) move the corner of the rectangle at the cursor along the line, and do not run on to the next line.

2.3 By word

w (non-modal: M-f) moves to the end of the next word. If the cursor is in the gap between two words, it first passes the gap and then the next word. b (non-modal: M-b) moves to the start of the word before the cursor. A count does it that many times. A negative count reverses the direction.

W and B (non-modal: C-M-f, C-M-b) move over a whole bracketed group or a quoted piece of text in one step. In a program, they move over one expression as the language reads it. Elsewhere they move over a bracketed group or a symbol. At a closing bracket they stop, because the expression around the cursor ends there. Chapter 13 describes moving over the parts of a program.

Words are looked for no further than 64 MB away, so one stray key in a huge file does not make Tuatara wait. If the limit is reached, Tuatara says so.

2.3.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
wM-fforward-wordMoves to the end of the next word. A negative count moves back.
bM-bbackward-wordMoves to the start of the word before. A negative count moves on.
WC-M-fforward-sexpMoves forward over one balanced expression, a bracketed group, a string or a word.
BC-M-bbackward-sexpMoves back over one balanced expression.

2.4 Within a line

Figure 2.1 shows where the keys for the line and the word land when the cursor is on the f of flour.

g h goes to the start of the line, and g l goes to its end, just before the line break. Where soft wrap shows a long line as several rows, they go to the start and the end of the row the cursor is on, and C-a and C-e do the same.

M-m goes to the first character of the line that is not a space or a tab. This is the place to start when the line is indented.

2.4.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
g hC-a, <home>beginning-of-lineMoves to the start of the line, or of the row where long lines wrap. In the hex view, to the start of the row of bytes.
g lC-e, <end>end-of-lineMoves to the end of the line, before its line break.
noneM-mback-to-indentationMoves to the first character that is not a space or a tab.

2.5 By sentence and paragraph

A sentence ends at a full stop, a question mark, an exclamation mark, an ellipsis (…) or an interrobang (‽) that is followed by a space or the end of a line. Closing quote marks and brackets after the stop belong to the sentence. A full stop after an abbreviation such as Dr. or e.g. does not end it. Tuatara knows a long list of those. You can add your own, or take one away that you would rather have end a sentence.

Some people type two spaces after the end of a sentence. If you do, set *sentence-end-double-space* to t, and a sentence then ends only where two spaces, a tab or a line break follow the stop. A file can say which it uses with a line sentence-end-double-space: t in its Local Variables block, and that wins for that file.

A paragraph ends at a blank line. M-} moves to the start of the blank line after the paragraph, or to the end of the text if there is none, and M-{ moves to the start of the blank line before the paragraph, or to the start of the text.

The sentence and paragraph moves have no letter keys in NORMAL state, but the Alt keys work there. A count does the move that many times, and a negative count goes the other way.

Try it, with a letter

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/letter-to-napier.txt and press RET. Press i and type Dear Napier, and RET RET. Then type Thank you for the weekend. The cake was lovely. We got home at six. and RET RET. Then type Please send the photos when you can. Dr. Taupo says hello. Press C-g.
  2. Press g g (non-modal: M-<). Press M-}. The cursor goes to the blank line after the first paragraph (L2 C0). Press j (non-modal: C-n) to go to the start of the second paragraph.
  3. Press M-e. The cursor moves to just after weekend.. Press M-e again, and it goes after lovely.. Press M-a to go back to the start of that sentence.
  4. Press M-} to go to the blank line after this paragraph. Press M-{ and watch the cursor go back up.
  5. Press g e (non-modal: M->), then M-a. The cursor goes to the start of Dr. Taupo says hello.. The full stop after Dr did not end a sentence.

2.5.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-eforward-sentenceMoves to the end of the sentence, or of the paragraph's text.
noneM-abackward-sentenceMoves to the start of the sentence.
noneM-}forward-paragraphMoves to the start of the blank line after the paragraph.
noneM-{backward-paragraphMoves to the start of the blank line before the paragraph.

2.5.2 Settings

SettingDefaultWhat it changes
*sentence-end-double-space*nilSet to t for two spaces after the end of a sentence. Filling keeps the two spaces too.
*extra-sentence-abbreviations*()Abbreviations of your own whose full stop ends no sentence, as in (setf *extra-sentence-abbreviations* '("Ph.D." "Inc.")).
*removed-sentence-abbreviations*()Abbreviations from Tuatara's list that should end a sentence after all, such as "St.".

2.6 To the start or the end of the text

g g (non-modal: M-<) goes to the very start of the buffer and g e (non-modal: M->) goes to its end. If the buffer is narrowed (C-x x n), they go to the start and end of the part shown. In the hex view, they go to the first and last byte.

These two moves leave the mark behind at the place you left, so that you can go back (see below). They do not do it while a selection is showing, nor when you give a count.

2.6.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
g gM-<beginning-of-bufferMoves to the start of the buffer.
g eM->end-of-bufferMoves to the end of the buffer.

2.7 To a line

: asks for a line number in the minibuffer, and RET takes you to the start of that line. M-g g and M-g M-g do the same, and they work in both states. You may group the digits as the mode line does, 100,000,000. The mark is left where you were, unless a selection is showing.

In a large file whose lines are still being counted, a line in the first 64 MB is found at once. A line further in waits until the count has reached it. In the hex view the same keys ask for a byte offset instead, and a number that starts with 0x is read as hexadecimal.

If the line you ask for is outside the part of a narrowed buffer, Tuatara widens the buffer and says so.

Tuatara has no command that asks for a column. To get to a column, go to the start of the line and press l (non-modal: C-f) with a count, as in C-u 12 l, which works when the line is long enough.

2.7.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
:M-g g, M-g M-ggoto-lineAsks for a line number and goes to the start of that line. In the hex view, asks for an offset.

2.8 Scrolling and recentring

The keys that scroll the window and put the cursor's line in the middle are listed in chapter 1: C-v and M-v scroll by nearly a screenful, C-l and z z recentre, and the mouse wheel scrolls the window it is over. The settings *scroll-margin* and *scroll-recenter* are described there too. They decide how the window follows the cursor when one of the moves in this chapter takes the cursor out of sight.

2.9 Counts

Most moves in this chapter take a count: you say how many times to do the move. Press C-u, type the number, and then press the key of the move. In NORMAL state, C-u 5 j moves five lines down. The echo area shows C-u 5- while Tuatara waits for the key.

C-u with no number means 4, and C-u C-u means 16. A minus sign after C-u makes the count negative, so C-u - 2 w moves back two words, as b (non-modal: M-b) would. A number you type after C-u C-u starts a new count of its own.

. (non-modal: C-x z) runs the last command again, with the count it had. Press . after C-u 3 j and the cursor goes three more lines down.

Other chapters use the same count for other things, such as how many times to insert a character. The count is always taken by the key that follows it.

Try it, with a long letter

  1. Open any file that has more than 30 lines. Press g g (non-modal: M-<) to go to the top.
  2. Press C-u 3 0 j. The cursor is on line 31.
  3. Press C-u C-u k. You have gone 16 lines up, to line 15.
  4. Press C-u - 2 w to move back two words.
  5. Press j (non-modal: C-n), then .. The last command, j, runs once more.

2.9.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-uuniversal-argumentStarts a count. Alone it is 4, twice it is 16, digits give a number and a minus sign negates.
.C-x zrepeatRuns the last command again with its count.

2.10 Marks and going back

The mark is a place that Tuatara remembers, and that stays where it is while the cursor moves on. The text between the mark and the cursor is the region, drawn in the :region face. The jumps in this chapter leave the mark where the cursor was, so a long jump can be taken back.

Each buffer keeps the marks it has had in a mark ring, which holds the last 16. Tuatara also keeps a global mark ring, with the marks of the buffers you set marks in.

Tuatara keeps a second list as well: the places the cursor was at before each move, ten for each buffer. S (non-modal: C-z S) goes back to the place before the cursor's last move, and S again goes further back, round the list. It is meant for taking back a key that jumped to the wrong place. The echo area says Position 2 of 7 so you know how far back you are. A count before S skips that many places.

Registers and bookmarks keep a place for longer. A register (C-x r p, then a character) keeps the place until Tuatara quits, and C-x r j with the same character goes back to it, even after the text above it has changed. A bookmark (C-x m m, then a name) is kept for good, and C-x m b goes to one by its name.

Try it, with a long list

  1. Open a file of more than 30 lines. Press g g (non-modal: M-<), then : (non-modal: M-g g), type 30 and press RET. The echo area says Mark set and you are on line 30.
  2. Press g e (non-modal: M->) to go to the end. Press S. You are on the place before the jump, line 30. Press S again, and you go further back.
  3. Press C-u C-SPC. The cursor goes to the mark, line 30, where you pressed g e. Press C-u C-SPC once more and you are back at line 1.
  4. Press C-x r p, then a. Press g e. Press C-x r j, then a. The cursor goes back to where you set the register.
  5. Press C-SPC at line 1, then j j j, and the region is shown. Press C-x C-x. The cursor and the mark swap places. Press C-g to drop the region.

noneC-SPCset-mark-commandSets the mark at the cursor and shows the region. Pressed again at once, it hides the region, and once more shows it. With C-u, goes back to the mark, as pop-to-mark-command does.
noneC-u C-SPCpop-to-mark-commandGoes to the mark and takes the mark before it from the ring, so the next press goes further back.
noneC-x C-SPCpop-global-markGoes to the newest mark of the global ring, in its buffer, and so back through the buffers where you set marks.
noneC-x C-xexchange-point-and-markSwaps the cursor and the mark.
noneM-x push-mark-commandpush-mark-commandSets the mark and shows the region. When the mark is at the cursor already, only shows the region.
