2.11 Going to the next place in a list

Some commands make a list of places for you to visit: the errors of a program that was built, the lines that a search through files found, the problems that a language server reports, and the errors of a PDF made from Org or LaTeX. Chapters 13, 6 and 14 describe how those lists are made. Two keys take you through the list one place at a time, from any buffer. A place in a file opens that file at the line.

2.11.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-g nnext-placeGoes to the next place of the last list.
noneM-g pprevious-placeGoes to the place before the one gone to last.

2.12 In help, lists and other read-only buffers

The windows that show help, the *Messages* log and similar read-only text are in what the mode line calls SUPPORT state. The reading keys of NORMAL state work there too: h, j, k, l, w, W, b, B, g g, g e, g h, g l, S, : and z z. They move the cursor and change nothing.

A list that a command made, such as the list of buffers or of the files in a directory, may use some of these letters for its own purposes. In a list h closes the window, and g starts a move, so the list is made again with r. The chapter for each list says what its keys do.

Writing and changing text

How to type, correct, undo, repeat and tidy text.

This chapter is about the text itself. It shows how to type it, take it out, change it in place, bring it back after a mistake, and do the same thing again without typing it again. It ends with the commands that tidy a whole block of lines: filling, sorting, spelling and recording keys. Chapter 2 shows how to get to the place you want to change, and chapter 4 shows what happens to the text you cut.

Keys are written as chapter 1 explains: C-x is Control and x, M-x is Alt and x, RET is Return, DEL is Backspace. The tables say "none" for a command that has no key and can only be run by name with M-x.

3.1 The two states

In NORMAL state the letter keys are commands. d deletes, u (non-modal: C-/) undoes, i starts typing. In INSERT state the letter keys write text. Most of your time goes to NORMAL state, where you choose what to change, and you go into INSERT state only to type. Figure 3.1 shows how the two connect.

The mode line says which state you are in. Each buffer keeps its own state, so a buffer you left in INSERT state is still in it when you come back to it.

Everything you type between the key that starts INSERT state and the key that ends it is one step for undo, line breaks included. If you type two lines and press u (non-modal: C-/), both go.

3.1.1 Commands for starting to type

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
inonetuatara-insertStarts typing at the cursor. A selection, if there is one, is dropped first.
anonetuatara-insert-afterStarts typing after the character under the cursor.
Inonetuatara-insert-line-startStarts typing at the start of the line.
Anonetuatara-insert-line-endStarts typing at the end of the line.
ononetuatara-open-belowOpens a new line below this one and starts typing on it. A number first opens that many lines, with the cursor on the first.
Ononetuatara-open-aboveOpens a new line above this one and starts typing on it. A number first opens that many lines.
cnonetuatara-changeCuts the selection, or deletes the character under the cursor, and starts typing. See "Changing text" below.
C-g, ESCnonetuatara-normalIn INSERT state, goes back to NORMAL state. The selection is dropped, and a line you began and left blank loses the blanks that were put in to indent it.
noneC-g, ESCtuatara-quitThe key's command in the global map. In INSERT state it does the same as tuatara-normal, and in NORMAL state it drops the selection.

At the end of a line the cursor stands on the line break, so a types after it, at the start of the next line. A types at the end of the line you are on.

RET, DEL and <delete> change no text in NORMAL state, so you cannot spoil a file by leaning on them. TAB does nothing there either, except in the modes named by *tuatara-normal-tab-modes*, where it does what it does in INSERT state. tuatara-normal-return, tuatara-normal-inert and tuatara-normal-tab are the commands that stand behind those three keys. RET follows a link in an Org buffer and does nothing in a plain text buffer.

Typing the two keys of *insert-escape-keys* quickly one after the other leaves INSERT state too. The first goes into the text as soon as you press it, and is taken out again when the second follows within a fifth of a second. Typed more slowly, both letters stay. It works in ordinary editing buffers, but not in the minibuffer, a terminal or at several cursors.

With *modal-editing* set to nil, there are no states. Every buffer is always typing, letters write text, and all the other keys and commands in this chapter that start with Control or Meta still work.

3.2 Typing

In INSERT state a key that stands for a character puts that character in at the cursor. self-insert-command is the command behind that. A number before such a key puts the character in that many times, so C-u 20 = types a row of twenty equals signs.

Characters you type and delete one after another, in either state, join into one step for undo. After typing "weekend" and deleting the "d" with DEL, one u (non-modal: C-/) takes back all of it.

Try it, with a letter

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/letter.txt and press RET. The file is new, so the buffer is empty. Press i. The mode line shows TUATARA[I].
  2. Type Dear Hana,, press RET twice, then type Thanks for the weekend in Taupo. The weather was kind. Press RET and type Love, Aroha.
  3. Press DEL three times. The last letters of the name go.
  4. Press C-g. The mode line shows TUATARA[N] again. Press DEL once more. Nothing happens, because DEL changes no text in NORMAL state.
  5. Press u (non-modal: C-/). All the typing goes in one step and the buffer is empty again. Press U (non-modal: C-?) and all of it comes back.
  6. Press A to type at the end of the line. Type oha., which finishes the name again. Press C-g.
  7. Press C-x C-s to save.

3.2.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneany character keyself-insert-commandPuts the character in. With a number, that many times. With an input method on and no number, the character goes through its rules.
noneRET, C-jnewlineStarts a new line, indented as the buffer's mode indents it. Spaces left at the end of the line before go. A number gives that many line breaks.
noneC-oopen-linePuts a line break in after the cursor, and the cursor stays before it. The new line is not indented.
noneTABindent-for-tab-commandIn plain text, Org and CSV, goes on to the next tab stop. In code, indents the line.
noneC-z TABtab-to-tab-stopGoes on to the next tab stop in any buffer. A number goes that many stops on.
noneC-qquoted-insertReads one more key and puts in the character it stands for. See "Special characters".
noneM-/expand-wordFinishes the word before the cursor with the nearest word that starts the same way. Press it again for the next one.
noneC-M-/complete-wordLists the words that start like the one before the cursor.

3.2.2 Settings

SettingDefaultWhat it changes
*modal-editing*tnil turns NORMAL and INSERT state off.
*insert-escape-keys*nilTwo characters, "jk" for example, that leave INSERT state when typed quickly together.
*escape-quits*nilt makes ESC do everything C-g does: close a question, stop a wait, stop work in the background.
*indent-new-lines*tnil keeps new lines at column 0 instead of indenting them as the mode does.
*word-completion-keep-case*tWords are found whatever their case and put in with the case you typed. nil finds only words that start exactly as typed.

3.3 Deleting

In INSERT state, DEL deletes the character before the cursor and C-d or <delete> the one after it. A letter with accents, or an emoji with a skin tone, goes as one character. A number first deletes that many, and a negative number deletes the other way. A Windows line end, a carriage return and a newline, counts as one.

In NORMAL state d does the same job and also works on a selection. Without a selection it deletes the character under the cursor. It keeps no copy, because a character under the cursor is a slip being corrected and not a cut. With a selection it cuts the text into the kill ring, which chapter 4 describes. A number before d deletes that many characters.

There is no command that deletes a word in one key. In NORMAL state press m w (non-modal: C-z m w) to select the word at the cursor, which chapter 5 explains, and then d. Press m w again before d to take one more word. M-z cuts up to the next character you name.

3.3.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneDELdelete-backward-charDeletes the character before the cursor. A number deletes that many.
noneC-d, <delete>delete-charDeletes the character after the cursor. A negative number deletes backwards.
dnonedelete-selection-or-charIn NORMAL state. Cuts the selection, or deletes the characters under the cursor. A line selection takes the whole lines.
DC-kkill-lineCuts the rest of the line. At the end of a line, cuts the line break, which joins the next line on. D is for NORMAL state.
noneC-S-<backspace>kill-whole-lineCuts the whole line and its line break. A number cuts that many lines.
noneM-zzap-up-to-charCuts up to, and not including, the next character you type.
noneM-\delete-horizontal-spaceDeletes the spaces and tabs around the cursor. With a number first, only those before it.
noneM-SPCcycle-spacingLeaves one space where there were several. Press it again for none. A third press brings the spaces back.
noneM-x just-one-spacejust-one-spaceLeaves one space, with the cursor after it. A number leaves that many.
noneC-x C-odelete-blank-linesOn a run of blank lines, leaves one. On a lone blank line, deletes it. On a line with text, deletes the blank lines after it.

Where a fold hides text, a delete never removes what you cannot see. The fold opens first, and the same key pressed again deletes.

3.4 Changing text

c is delete and type in one key. With a selection, it cuts the selection and starts INSERT state. Without one, it deletes the character under the cursor and starts INSERT state. A line selection keeps its final line break, so what you type takes the place of the line's words and the line stays a line. The cut and what you type after it are one step for undo, so u (non-modal: C-/) puts back the old text whole.

To replace a word, select it with m w (non-modal: C-z m w), press c, type the new word and press C-g. To replace the end of a line, press D (non-modal: C-k) and then A and type. p with a selection pastes the kill ring over it, and chapter 4 describes it.

Try it, with a recipe

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/pancakes.txt, RET. Press i and type the lines Pancakes, eggs, milk, flour, each ended with RET except the last. Press C-g.
  2. The flour should come before the milk. The cursor is on the last line. Press C-x C-t. The flour line and the milk line trade places.
  3. Press g g (non-modal: M-<) to go to the top, then M-u. The title becomes PANCAKES. Press u (non-modal: C-/) and it is Pancakes again.
  4. Press j (non-modal: C-n) to go to the eggs line. Press d. The first letter goes. Press .. The next letter goes. Press u twice.
  5. Press g h (non-modal: C-a) to go to the start of the line, then C-u 3 d. Three letters go. Press u.
  6. On the eggs line press g j. The flour line joins the eggs line, with one space between. Press u.
  7. Press g g j A, type , large, and press C-g. Press g g and m w c, type Thin pancakes and press C-g. The title changes in one step.
  8. Press C-x C-s to save.

3.4.1 Commands for case

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-uupcase-wordPuts the next word in capitals and moves over it. A number does that many words, and a negative number does the words before the cursor.
noneM-ldowncase-wordPuts the next word in small letters.
noneM-ccapitalize-wordMakes the first letter a capital and the rest small.
noneC-x C-uupcase-regionPuts the selected text in capitals.
noneC-x C-ldowncase-regionPuts the selected text in small letters.

3.4.2 Commands for swapping and joining

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-ttranspose-charsSwaps the two characters about the cursor and moves on past them. At the end of a line, swaps the last two. A number carries the character before the cursor that many characters on.
noneM-ttranspose-wordsSwaps the words about the cursor. A number carries a word that many words on.
noneC-x C-ttranspose-linesSwaps this line with the one before it. A number carries the line that many lines on, and a negative number carries it back.
noneC-M-ttranspose-sexpsSwaps the balanced pieces about the cursor, such as two bracketed groups. Chapter 13 says more about it.
noneM-^join-lineJoins this line to the one before it. The line break goes, and the spaces around it become one space, or none before a closing bracket or after an opening one. With a number first, joins the next line to this one. With a selection, joins all the lines it touches.
g jnonejoin-selected-linesIn NORMAL state. Pulls the next line up onto this one. A number pulls that many. With a selection, joins the lines it touches into one.

A number of 0 given to a transpose command swaps the thing at the cursor with the thing at the mark.

3.5 Undo, redo and repeat

Every change can be undone, back to the file as you opened it. Nothing is let go unless you set *undo-limit*. Undo also covers work Tuatara does in the background. A replacement or a sort of a large file is one step, and it stands where you gave it: while it runs you can keep typing, and u (non-modal: C-/) takes back your edits first and then the background job.

3.5.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
uC-x u, C-/, C-_undoUndoes the last change. In a narrowed buffer a change outside the part shown is undone too, and the echo area says so.
UM-_, C-?, C-M-_redoRedoes the last change you undid. The cursor goes after the text that comes back.
.C-x zrepeatRuns the last command again, with the number it had.
noneC-uuniversal-argumentStarts a number for the next command. See "Repeat counts".

u and U (non-modal: C-/, C-?) work in NORMAL state. The other keys work in both states.

repeat is the key for "do that again". If the last command acted on a selection, the selection is made again first, as large as before, from the cursor. It is the same number of whole lines, or characters, or the same kind of text piece, or the same size of rectangle. After V J d deletes two lines, . deletes the next two. Pressing . again runs the command once more (without the modal layer, z after C-x z does). It repeats one command only, so for a longer run of keys, record them (see "Recording keys").

A number given to . replaces the one the command had. After C-u 3 d, a plain . deletes three characters again, and C-u 5 . deletes five.

3.5.2 Settings

SettingDefaultWhat it changes
*undo-limit*nilThe most memory, in bytes, that one buffer's undo history may hold. nil keeps every change. With a limit, the oldest changes go first, down to about three quarters of it, and never the newest.

3.6 Repeat counts

A number before a command makes it act that many times, or on that many things. Type C-u, then the digits, then the command: C-u 3 d deletes three characters and C-u 12 M-u puts twelve words in capitals. C-u alone means 4, C-u C-u means 16, and C-u - before a command gives it a negative number. While you type the number, the echo area shows it.

Each command in this chapter says what its number does. A command whose entry says nothing about a number does not use one.

3.7 Special characters

C-q reads the next key and puts in the character it stands for, whatever that key does otherwise. C-q TAB puts in a real tab character. C-q C-l puts in a form feed, the character that ends a page, and C-q RET puts in a carriage return. A number first puts the character in that many times.

For letters your keyboard lacks there are three ways. You can type a character by its Unicode name with C-x 8 RET, by a digraph (two keys that stand for one character) with C-x 8 &, or by an input method that changes what keys type while it is on.

Try it, with a card for a friend in Sweden

  1. In ~/letter.txt, press g e to go to the end, then o to start a new line. Type Greetings from Akaroa and press C-g.
  2. Press C-x 8 RET, type em dash and press RET. The dash is put in at the cursor.
  3. Press C-x 8 &, then e and '. An é goes in.
  4. Press C-x RET C-\, type swedish-postfix and press RET. Press i and type smaaland. The word reads småland. Press C-g.
  5. Press C-\ to turn the method off and C-\ again to turn it on.
  6. Press C-x 8 - to turn the method off.

3.7.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-qquoted-insertPuts in the character the next key stands for.
noneM-x insert-tabinsert-tabPuts in a tab character, whatever the tab settings say.
noneC-x 8 RETinsert-charAsks for a Unicode name, such as em dash, or a code in hex such as e9, U+00E9 or #xe9. The names that fit are listed as you type. A number first puts the character in that many times.
noneC-x 8 &insert-digraphAsks for the two keys of a digraph, e' for é, -> for an arrow, << for a guillemet. With a selection, the character wraps it in a pair, such as « ». It works from NORMAL state too.
noneM-x list-digraphslist-digraphsLists every digraph, the common ones first.
noneC-x 8 .digraph-input-modeTurns digraphs on as you type: & and the digraph's keys give the character, so &e' types é.
noneC-x 8 -deactivate-input-methodTurns off whichever input method is on in this buffer.
noneC-\toggle-input-methodTurns this buffer's input method off, or on again. The first time it uses *default-input-method*, or asks.
noneC-x RET C-\set-input-methodAsks for an input method, turns it on, and makes it the one C-\ switches.
noneC-h Idescribe-input-methodShows the rules of the input method that is on, or of one you name.

While an input method is on, the mode line carries its short name after the mode name, SV< for Swedish.

3.7.2 Settings

SettingDefaultWhat it changes
*default-input-method*nilThe method C-\ turns on in a buffer that has had none, such as "swedish-postfix". nil asks.
*input-method-keys*noneMethods of your own, each a key, a label and a method's name. (setf *input-method-keys* '(("s" "swedish" "swedish-postfix"))) makes SPC i s turn it on.

3.8 Indentation and filling in plain text

TAB in plain text goes on to the next tab stop, which is every four columns as standard. Spaces are put in unless you ask for tab characters. In a language mode TAB indents the line as the language does, which chapter 13 describes.

Filling re-flows a paragraph so that no line is longer than the fill column, which is 80 as standard. The words stay in order, and the text that starts each line (an indent, a > for a quotation, a comment mark) is kept. Each item of a list is filled as a paragraph of its own, and its lines go on under its words, past the mark and any check box: - [ ] a task continues six columns in.

3.8.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
g QM-qfill-paragraphFills the paragraph at the cursor. In code, fills the comment there. Asks for the column first, with the buffer's offered. A number first answers the question.
g qC-z g qfill-regionFills the paragraphs of the lines the selection touches. The lines before and after it are left alone.
noneC-x fset-fill-columnSets the fill column of this buffer for as long as Tuatara runs. A number first sets it without asking, as in C-u 72 C-x f.
noneC-z TABtab-to-tab-stopGoes on to the next tab stop.
noneC-M-\indent-regionIndents the selected lines as the mode indents them.
>C-z >indent-selection-or-lineIn NORMAL state. Indents the selected lines, or this line, as the mode does.
noneM-mback-to-indentationMoves to the first character of the line that is not a space or tab.
noneM-x indent-tabs-modeindent-tabs-modeSwitches this buffer between spaces and tab characters. A positive number turns tabs on, and zero or less turns them off.
noneM-=count-wordsCounts the lines, sentences, words and characters of the selection, or of the whole buffer.

Filling takes prose only. In an Org file, headlines, tables, property drawers, comment lines and the inside of source blocks are left as they are. In Markdown, tables and the lines between code fences stay. So g q (non-modal: C-z g q) over a whole note re-flows its paragraphs and leaves its tables and code alone.

A paragraph larger than *fill-paragraph-limit* is left and the echo area says so, so filling never holds the editor up. A sentence ends at ., ?, ! or … followed by a space or a line end, or at a blank line. Short forms such as Dr. end no sentence.

In your init file two functions set the tab habits for one kind of file. (set-tab-width 'c-mode 8) makes tab stops 8 columns apart in C files, and (set-indent-tabs-mode 'bash t) puts tab characters in shell scripts. Their first argument is a major mode, and prog stands for every programming language.

3.8.2 Settings

SettingDefaultWhat it changes
*tab-width*4The columns from one tab stop to the next, a whole number from 1 to 64.
*indent-tabs-mode*nilt puts tab characters in where TAB goes on to a tab stop. nil puts spaces in.
*tab-always-indent*:completeWhat TAB does in code. :complete indents the line and, when that changes nothing, completes the name. t only indents. nil indents when the cursor is in the leading blanks and otherwise goes to the next stop.
*tuatara-normal-tab-modes*(org-mode)The modes where TAB works in NORMAL state, and the modes made from them.
*fill-column*80The column filled lines end by.
*fill-ask-column*tnil fills at once, without asking for the column.
*fill-paragraph-limit*1048576The most bytes a paragraph may span to be filled.
*sentence-end-double-space*nilt for two spaces between sentences: a sentence ends at a full stop followed by two spaces, and filling keeps two.
*extra-sentence-abbreviations*()Abbreviations of your own whose full stop ends no sentence, such as '("Ph.D." "et al.").
*removed-sentence-abbreviations*()Abbreviations of Tuatara's own list that should end a sentence after all, such as '("St.").

3.9 Spelling

M-x spellcheck-mode underlines the words spelt wrong in the buffer you are in. It looks only at the words you can see, so a large file costs no more than a small one. In text and Org every word is checked except code, links, dates and tags. In code only comments and strings are checked. It uses enchant, a spelling library, and needs a dictionary for your language installed. It is off until you turn it on, and it never runs in a file opened safely or shown as bytes.

3.9.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x spellcheck-modespellcheck-modeMarks the words spelt wrong in this buffer, or stops.
noneM-x global-spellcheck-modeglobal-spellcheck-modeThe same for every buffer.
z nC-z z nspellcheck-nextGoes to the next word spelt wrong. A number goes that many on.
z pC-z z pspellcheck-previousGoes to the word spelt wrong before the cursor.
z =C-z z =spellcheck-correctOffers suggestions for the word, lets you type a replacement, or keeps the word as right.
z gC-z z gspellcheck-add-wordAdds the word to your own word list for a language. Other programs that use enchant share that list.
z fC-z z fspellcheck-add-word-to-fileKeeps the word as right in this file only, in a LocalWords: line at the end of it, written as a comment.
noneM-x spellcheck-languagesspellcheck-languagesSets the languages this buffer is checked in, such as en_NZ sv_SE.

z n, z p, z =, z g and z f work in NORMAL state. In the other states they are C-z z n, C-z z p, C-z z =, C-z z g and C-z z f.

3.9.2 Settings

SettingDefaultWhat it changes
*global-spellcheck-mode*nilt checks every buffer.
*spellcheck-modes*nonePer major mode, such as '((org-mode . t) (prog-mode . :comments) (csv-mode . nil)). :strings checks strings only, and :all checks all of a code buffer.
*spellcheck-languages*the locale'sA list such as '("en_NZ" "sv_SE"). A word is right when any of them takes it. nil takes the language of the system's locale, else en_US.
*spellcheck-excluded-faces*code, links, dates, tags, keywordsIn text, the faces whose words are not checked.
*spellcheck-comment-faces*(:comment)In code, the faces of comments that are checked.
*spellcheck-string-faces*(:string)In code, the faces of strings that are checked.

3.9.3 Faces

FaceDefaultWhat it paints
:spellcheckwavy yellow underlineA word spelt wrong. (set-face :spellcheck :underline :dotted) in your init file makes dots, and :underline t a plain line.

3.10 Sorting and tidying lines

These commands work on the lines a selection touches. Without a selection they do nothing and say so. A large selection is handled in the background, so Tuatara never waits on it. With a number, a sort runs in descending order.

Try it, with a shopping list

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/shopping.txt, RET. Press i and type the lines milk, eggs, bread, eggs, butter, each ended with RET except the last. Press C-g.
  2. Press g g (non-modal: M-<), then V and J four times to select all five lines.
  3. Press M-x, type sort-lines and press RET. The list reads bread, butter, eggs, eggs, milk.
  4. Select the five lines again with g g, V and J four times, as the sort ended the selection. Press M-x, type delete-duplicate-lines and press RET. The second eggs goes, and the echo area says one line was deleted.
  5. Press u (non-modal: C-/) twice to get the original list back.
  6. Select the lines again, run flush-lines, type e and press RET. Every line with an e in it goes, so only milk is left. Press u.

3.10.1 Commands

CommandWhat it does
sort-linesSorts the lines by their text. Capital and small letters compare by their codes unless *sort-fold-case* is on.
sort-fieldsSorts the lines by one field. Fields are apart by spaces. A number names the field, and a negative one counts from the end of the line. In a CSV file or a log it asks for a column and moves each record whole, the header staying first.
sort-numeric-fieldsSorts by the number at the start of a field. 0x starts a hexadecimal number. A field with no number counts as 0.
sort-columnsSorts by the text between the columns where the selection starts and ends.
sort-paragraphsSorts paragraphs, which are apart by blank lines.
sort-pagesSorts pages, which end with a form feed at the start of a line.
sort-regexp-fieldsSorts the pieces a pattern finds, by a key you name: \& for the whole piece or \1 to \9 for a group.
sort-lines-reverse, sort-fields-reverse, sort-numeric-fields-reverse, sort-columns-reverse, sort-paragraphs-reverse, sort-pages-reverse, sort-regexp-fields-reverseThe same sorts, largest first.
reverse-regionPuts the lines in the opposite order.
delete-duplicate-linesDeletes all but the first of each set of identical lines. C-u keeps the last. C-u C-u deletes only a line identical to the one before it. C-u C-u C-u keeps all blank lines. Says how many went.
flush-linesAsks for a pattern and deletes the lines that match it. ^$ matches the empty lines.
keep-linesAsks for a pattern and deletes the lines that do not match it.

None of these has a key. Run them with M-x. flush-lines and keep-lines use the same pattern rules as search, which chapter 6 describes. In a CSV file or a log they first ask which column to try the pattern on, and a header line always stays.

3.10.2 Settings

SettingDefaultWhat it changes
*sort-fold-case*nilt ignores the case of ASCII letters, so b sorts before C.

3.11 Recording keys

When you want the same few keys on line after line, record them once and play them back. C-x ( starts recording, C-x ) stops, and C-x e plays the keys as if you had pressed them again. What you type in answer to a question is recorded too, so a search for a word searches for the same word each time. The mouse is not recorded, and a passphrase is never recorded. A play stops where a passphrase was typed and leaves that question to you. While you record, the mode line shows Rec.

A number before C-x e plays that many times, and 0 plays until a play fails. A play fails when a command in it fails, a search finds nothing or a move cannot go on. e pressed straight after a play plays once more, and again, until you press another key. Each play is one step for undo. A long run shows its progress in the mode line as Played 120/300, and C-g stops it between two plays. C-g while recording gives the recording up, and the keys recorded before it are kept. In INSERT state the first C-g only leaves INSERT state.

Try it, with a numbered list of birds

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/birds.txt, RET. Press i, type kea, RET, weka, RET, kiwi, RET, takahe, RET, kaka. Press C-g, then g g.
  2. Press C-x (. Press M-x, type insert-keys-counter, press RET. Then press i, type a full stop and a space, press C-g, then C-n and C-a, and press C-x ).
  3. The first line now begins with 1. =. Press ~C-u 4 C-x e~. The other four lines are numbered. The last play meets the end of the buffer when it moves down, so the echo area says =Stopped after 3 of 4 plays: End of buffer, but the number is already in.
  4. Press u (non-modal: C-/) four times. The four plays are taken back one at a time.

3.11.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x (start-recording-keysStarts recording keys.
noneC-x )stop-recording-keysEnds the recording. The keys are kept for C-x e.
noneC-x eplay-recorded-keysPlays the recorded keys. A number plays them that many times.
noneM-x insert-keys-counterinsert-keys-counterTypes a number and adds 1 to it, so recorded keys number the lines as they go. A number first adds that number.
noneM-x set-keys-counterset-keys-counterSets the number typed next.
noneM-x set-keys-counter-formatset-keys-counter-formatSets how the counter is written: %d for the number, %03d for three digits with zeros, %3d with spaces before, %-3d with spaces after, and Item %d. for Item 7.
noneM-x name-recorded-keysname-recorded-keysGives the recorded keys a name, which then plays them as M-x NAME. The name lasts while Tuatara runs.
noneM-x insert-recorded-keys-definitioninsert-recorded-keys-definitionTypes the init file lines that make the keys a command again and bind it to a key. You put them in the init file yourself.

The lines insert-recorded-keys-definition types look like this, with your own name and keys.

(define-recorded-keys 'kill-after-date "C-s date RET C-k")
(bind-key "C-c d" 'kill-after-date)

Cutting and pasting

How to move text from one place to another, and to other programs.

Cutting takes text out of the buffer and keeps it. Copying keeps text and leaves it where it is. Pasting puts the kept text in at the cursor. Emacs calls cutting "killing" and pasting "yanking", and Tuatara's command names use those words, so you will meet them here. This chapter shows the keys that cut, copy and paste in both states, where the cut text is kept, how it reaches other programs, how to keep several pieces of text at once and how to set lines aside so that one key takes them together.

Chapter 5 teaches selecting, rectangles and many cursors. Here a selection is only a way to say which text a key acts on.

4.1 The kill ring

Everything you cut or copy goes on the kill ring, a list of your latest cuts with the newest first. A paste puts the newest one in. Figure 4.1 shows the ring after three cuts.

The ring keeps *kill-ring-max* cuts. When it is full, the oldest is forgotten. Tuatara has no command that steps back through the older cuts, so a paste always gives you the newest. To keep a piece of text while you go on cutting and copying other things, put it in a register, described below.

Two cuts in a row, with no other command between them, join into one. Press C-k (modal: D) twice and the second cut is added to the first, so that one paste brings both back, in order.

A cut that is too large for the system clipboard (see *clipboard-size-limit* below) stays where it is in the buffer instead of being copied, and the echo area says so when you copy it. It stays good after you kill the buffer it came from. Text from an encrypted file never goes on the clipboard, and it leaves the ring when its buffer is closed.

A cut that would take part of the text a folded heading hides shows the fold instead. Press the same key again to cut.

4.2 Cutting, copying and pasting with the Emacs keys

These keys mean the same in NORMAL and INSERT state. They act on the region, the text between the cursor and the mark. A selection made with v is a region too. If you have not selected anything, C-SPC sets the mark at the cursor, and the region grows as you move away from it.

Try it, with a shopping list

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/shopping.txt and press RET. Press i, then type eggs, RET, bread, RET, milk, RET, butter.
  2. Press M-< (modal: g g) to go to the top. Press C-k (modal: D). The word eggs is cut and the line is empty. Press C-k again. The empty line goes, and bread is now on the first line.
  3. Press C-y. The cuts come back as one, eggs and its line end, in front of bread. Press C-/ (modal: u) to undo that.
  4. Press C-SPC, then C-n (modal: j). The region covers the first line. Press M-w. The echo area says Copied and nothing is removed.
  5. Press M-> (modal: g e) to go to the end, then C-y. The copied line is pasted after butter, and as that line has no line end the two run together. Press C-x C-s to save.

4.2.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-wkill-regionCuts the region. A rectangle is cut as a block that C-y pastes as a block.
noneM-wkill-ring-saveCopies the region and leaves it in place. Lines that a search filter hides are left out of the copy.
noneC-yyankPastes the newest cut at the cursor, or what another program copied to the system clipboard since. The mark is left at the start of the pasted text, so C-x C-x selects it.
DC-kkill-lineCuts from the cursor to the end of the line. At the end of a line it cuts the line end.
noneC-S-<backspace>kill-whole-lineCuts the whole line and its line end. A number cuts that many lines, a negative number that many lines back, and 0 cuts the line without its line end.
noneM-zzap-up-to-charAsks for a character, then cuts up to the next one of that kind and leaves it. A number takes the Nth one, and a negative number goes back.
noneM-x zap-to-charzap-to-charThe same, but the character is cut too.
noneM-x kill-sexpkill-sexpCuts the bracketed group, or the word, after the cursor. A number cuts that many.
noneC-M-DELbackward-kill-sexpCuts the one before the cursor.

C-d and DEL delete a character without keeping it. They are in chapter 3.

4.3 Cutting, copying and pasting in NORMAL state

In NORMAL state the letter keys do the same work on one key each. With a selection they act on it. Without one they act on the character under the cursor, or on as many characters as the number you gave first.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
dnonedelete-selection-or-charCuts the selection and keeps it. With no selection it deletes the character and keeps nothing, because a character under the cursor is a typo being fixed. A line selection is widened to whole lines.
cnonetuatara-changeCuts the selection and starts INSERT state. With no selection it deletes the character, unkept, and starts INSERT state.
ynonecopy-selection-or-charCopies the selection, or the character. A line selection is copied with its line end, so that it pastes as a line of its own.
pnoneyank-over-selectionPastes the newest cut, or what another program copied since. It replaces the selection if there is one. A number pastes that many copies. The replaced text is not kept.
DC-kkill-lineCuts to the end of the line, as C-k does.
PC-x r yyank-rectanglePastes the last rectangle cut or copied from a rectangle. See chapter 5.

If the kill ring is empty, p says so and changes nothing.

Try it, with a letter

  1. 1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/letter.txt and press RET. Press i and type four lines: Dear Hana,, See you at Easter., Thanks for the weekend in Raglan. and Love, Aroha, each followed by RET except the last. Press C-g to go back to NORMAL state. 2. The thanks should come before the other line. Press g g j j to go to the third line, then V (non-modal: C-z V) to select it and d to cut it. The line is gone. 3. Press k (non-modal: C-p) to go up, g h (non-modal: C-a) to go to the start of the line, then p. The thanks line is pasted above See you at Easter. Press u (non-modal: C-/) to undo it. 4. Press V, then y. The echo area says Copied. Press g g p. The copy is pasted above Dear Hana,. Press u to undo it. 5. Press g g D. The text of the first line is cut and the line stays, empty. Press u to bring it back. The text that D (non-modal: C-k) cut is on the kill ring, and p would paste it.

4.4 The system clipboard and the primary selection

The system clipboard is the one every program on your desktop shares. What you cut or copy in Tuatara goes there as well, so you can paste it in another program. When another program has copied something since, C-y and p paste that instead and put it first on the kill ring.

The primary selection is a second place that many Linux programs have. It holds whatever text was selected last, with no copy command. In Tuatara, a selection you make by dragging with the mouse becomes the primary selection when you let go. Clicking the middle mouse button in another program pastes it. In Tuatara, the middle button pastes the primary selection of any program at the place you clicked, with the mark left at its start. If nothing is selected anywhere, the echo area says Nothing is selected anywhere. A selection made with the keys does not become the primary selection.

The same limits apply to both. Text larger than *clipboard-size-limit* is not sent, and neither is any text from an encrypted file, and with *use-system-clipboard* set to nil nothing is sent or taken.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
none<mouse-2>mouse-yank-primaryPastes the primary selection where the middle button was pressed.
noneM-x gpg-copy-to-clipboardgpg-copy-to-clipboardPuts the text copied last on the system clipboard even when it came from an encrypted file. Other programs, a clipboard manager among them, can then read and keep it.
noneC, C-c Cserver-toggle-clipboardIn the list of servers, shares the clipboard with the server on the line, or stops sharing it. See chapter 18.

4.4.1 Settings

SettingDefaultWhat it changes
*use-system-clipboard*tWhether cuts and copies go on the system clipboard, and whether a paste takes in what another program copied. nil keeps them in Tuatara.
*clipboard-size-limit*8388608The most characters a cut may have and still go on the clipboard and the primary selection. That is 8 MB. A larger cut stays in the buffer's own text.
*kill-ring-max*120How many cuts the kill ring keeps. The oldest go first.

4.5 Registers

A register keeps one thing under one character, for as long as Tuatara runs. The character is a letter, a digit or a sign. A capital letter and a small letter name different registers. A register can hold text, a block of columns, a place in a file or a whole number. Keeping something in a register does not touch the kill ring, so a register is where to put what you want to paste later, however much you cut in between.

Every register command asks for its character with one key and no RET. C-g gives up. Keeping again under the same character replaces what was there.

Try it, with a recipe

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/pancakes.txt and press RET. Press i and type 2 eggs, 200 g flour, milk, RET, Mix, rest, fry., RET.
  2. Press M-< (modal: g g), C-SPC, C-e (modal: g l) to select the first line without its line end. Press C-x r s, then e. The echo area says Register e keeps text.
  3. Press C-n C-a C-k to cut the text of the second line. Press C-x r i, then e. The ingredients are written in at the cursor, although the kill ring holds the method.
  4. Press C-u 4 C-x r n, then n. Register n keeps the number 4. Press C-x r +, then n. It now keeps 5. Press C-x r i, then n to write 5 into the text.
  5. Press C-x r l. The list shows each register with what it keeps. Press q to close it.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x r sregister-copyKeeps the selected text under a character, or the block of columns when a rectangle is selected.
noneC-x r pregister-pointKeeps the place of the cursor. It follows the text through edits, and it is found again after the buffer is closed when the buffer had a file.
noneC-x r nregister-numberKeeps a whole number: the number you gave first, or one it asks for.
noneC-x r +register-addAdds to a number register: the number you gave first, or 1. A negative number takes away. For a text register it puts the selected text after what is kept.
noneM-x register-prependregister-prependPuts the selected text before the text a register keeps.
noneC-x r iregister-insertWrites what a register keeps at the cursor. Text goes in as it was, with the mark before it. A block goes in as a block, each row as many times as the number you gave first. A number goes in as digits.
noneC-x r jregister-jumpGoes to the place a register keeps.
noneC-x r lregister-listLists the registers in a buffer, one per line. RET on a place goes there, and q or h closes the list.

A register that keeps something that is not the right kind says what it keeps instead. A place worth keeping beyond this session is a bookmark rather than a register.

4.6 Banked lines

Banking sets whole lines aside, wherever they are in the text, and shows them in a colour of their own. Then y, d or p takes all the banked lines at once, together with the lines of any selection you have made. This is the easy way to gather lines that are far apart. Banking works in NORMAL state.

You can bank a line, move away and bank another. Banked lines follow the text through edits, and they stay banked until you take them out of the bank or until y, d or p uses them. C-g leaves them as they are, and c does not act on them.

Try it, with a shopping list

  1. 1. Open ~/shopping.txt from the first try, or make a new file with six lines: eggs, bread, milk, apples, tea, butter. Press C-g so that you are in NORMAL state. 2. Press g g j to go to bread, then m l (non-modal: C-z m l). The line changes colour and the echo area says Banked this line (1 total), then what to do next. 3. Press j j j to go to tea, then m l again. Now two lines are banked. 4. Press m u on tea. It leaves the bank. Press m l to bank it again. 5. Press d. Both lines are cut together and leave the bank, and the echo area says Deleted 2 lines. 6. Press g g p. bread and tea are pasted above eggs, as one cut. Press C-x C-s to save.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
m lC-z m lbank-linesBanks the line, or the lines the selection touches, and drops the selection. On lines that are all banked already it takes them out again, and on lines partly banked it banks the rest. A number banks that many lines from the cursor. A line whose end a fold hides is banked with all that the fold hides. Lines a search filter hides are not banked.
m uC-z m ubank-release-lineTakes the line at the cursor out of the bank and keeps the others.
m UC-z m Ubank-release-sectionTakes out the whole run of banked lines the cursor is on, the lines beside each other at once. Banked lines elsewhere stay.
m DEL, m <delete>C-z m DEL, C-z m <delete>bank-clearLets go of every banked line in the buffer. The text is not changed.

With lines banked, y copies them as one cut and d cuts them as one cut and one change, so that one u (non-modal: C-/) puts them back. p puts the newest cut in place of them, as one change. Each of the three takes the banked lines out of the bank. A cut too large to paste over banked lines is refused, and the echo area gives its size.

4.6.1 Faces

FaceDefaultWhat it paints
:banked-linethemeThe banked lines, across the full width of the window.

4.7 Pasting into prompts

When Tuatara asks you a question in the minibuffer, you can paste the answer.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-y, C-V, S-<insert>minibuffer-pasteWrites in the system clipboard's text, without the line end after it. With nothing on the clipboard it writes the text cut last. A suggested answer that is highlighted is replaced.

C-V is Control, Shift and v together, the paste key of most terminals. Typing in a prompt does not touch the kill ring: C-k (modal: D) deletes the rest of the answer and C-u clears all of it, and neither keeps what it removed. A password prompt takes only what is on the clipboard, puts it in the answer and nowhere else, and never in the kill ring.

Try it, with a file name

  1. In another program, such as your file manager, copy a file name, for example shopping.txt.
  2. In Tuatara press C-x C-f. The prompt asks for a file.
  3. Press C-y. The name is written after the prompt. Press RET to open it.

In a terminal buffer, terminal-paste pastes into the program that runs there, and a middle click does the same with the primary selection (terminal-paste-primary). Chapter 17 describes both, with the setting *terminal-paste-keys*.

When you paste into the terminal that Tuatara itself runs in, with that terminal's own paste key, insert-pasted-text puts the text in at the cursor as text. None of it is taken for keys or commands. Its line ends become the buffer's, and one u (non-modal: C-/) takes it all back. It has no key.

Selecting, rectangles and many cursors

How to pick out text, a block of columns, or many places at once.

Most commands in an editor act on something: a word to delete, a line to copy, a block to indent. A selection is the text the next command acts on. It shows in the :region face, usually as reversed colours. This chapter teaches how to make a selection by hand, by the shape of the text and by the shape of the code. It then goes on to blocks of columns, called rectangles, and to working in many places at once, with many cursors or with a pattern that holds every match.

Chapter 4 showed what d, y and p do with a selection. Chapter 2 showed how to move without selecting. Here the keys only make the selection, and a few commands that work on it follow.

5.1 Selections and the mark

Tuatara has two ways to select, and both end up as the same thing.

The Emacs way uses the mark. The mark is a second place in the buffer, kept beside the cursor. The region is the text between the mark and the cursor. C-SPC sets the mark where the cursor is and shows the region, and every move after that stretches it. C-g lets go. C-x C-x swaps the cursor and the mark, which is how you reach the other end of a region to change it. Chapter 2 describes the mark and the mark ring, the list of places the mark has been.

The NORMAL state way has keys for it. v starts a selection at the cursor and any move stretches it. Pressing v again while it is live starts it afresh from where the cursor is now. V (non-modal: C-z V) selects whole lines instead. % selects the whole buffer. You can use whichever you like in either state, and a selection made by one is a region for the other.

Figure 5.1 shows a selection made with v and one made with V.

With a selection live, most letter keys act on it: d cuts it, c cuts it and starts INSERT state, y copies it. A line selection is widened to whole lines before it is cut or copied, so a deleted line leaves no empty line behind.

Try it, with a recipe

  1. 1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/pancakes.txt and press RET. Press i and type Pancakes, RET, 2 eggs, 200 g flour, 1 cup milk, RET, Mix and rest., RET, Fry in butter. Press C-g. 2. Press g g j to go to the second line. Press v, then w w. The first words of the line are selected. Press C-g to let go. 3. Press V. The whole line is selected. Press J (non-modal: C-z J). The line below is selected too. Press d. Both lines are cut. Press u (non-modal: C-/) to undo. 4. Press V on the second line, then K: the line above joins the selection. Press C-g. (K alone, with nothing selected, only moves up.) 5. Press %. The whole buffer is selected. Press C-g.

5.1.1 Keys that select

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
vnonestart-selectionStarts a selection at the cursor. Any move stretches it.
VC-z Vselect-linesSelects the cursor's line. Pressed with a line selection live, it lets go.
J, KC-z J, C-z Kselect-next-line and select-previous-lineMove down or up a line, adding it to a line selection. Without one they only move.
%noneselect-whole-bufferSelects everything, the cursor at the start.
noneC-x hmark-whole-bufferThe same with the Emacs keys, the cursor at the start and the mark at the end.

With a line selection, j and k (non-modal: C-n, C-p) move a character-wise cursor, while J and K move by whole lines. Press C-g in NORMAL state to let go of any selection.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
vnonestart-selectionStart a selection at point: any motion extends it.
VC-z Vselect-linesStart a line selection anchored on the current line, or cancel a live one.
JC-z Jselect-next-lineMove down, extending the line selection if one is active.
KC-z Kselect-previous-lineMove up, extending the line selection if one is active.
%noneselect-whole-bufferSelect the whole buffer: point at the start, the mark at the end.
noneC-SPCset-mark-commandSet the mark at point and activate the region (C-SPC).
noneC-x C-xexchange-point-and-markSwap point and mark.
noneC-x hmark-whole-bufferSelect the whole buffer: mark at the end, point at the start; where point was goes on the mark ring, with the mark before.
noneC-gtuatara-quitC-g: in INSERT state return to NORMAL; in NORMAL drop the selection.

5.2 Text objects, the m keys

Typing v w w w works, but it is slow when you want exactly one word, one sentence or the text inside a pair of brackets. Tuatara has keys that take such a piece whole. They all begin with m, which you can remember as "mark". The piece is called a text object.

The small letter takes the piece as a word, a sentence or a paragraph. Pressed again, it takes one more. The capital letter does the same but grows the selection the other way, backward, for the objects that have a direction. For brackets and quotes it takes the pair with its brackets instead of what is inside.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it selects
m wC-z m wselect-wordThe word at the cursor. In a gap between two words, the next one.
m bC-z m bselect-word-backwardThe same, growing backward.
m W, m BC-z m W, C-z m Bselect-symbol, select-symbol-backwardA symbol: a name with its - and _, so shopping-list is one symbol.
m s, m SC-z m s, C-z m Sselect-sentence, select-sentence-backwardThe sentence, as far as its full stop.
m p, m PC-z m p, C-z m Pselect-paragraph, select-paragraph-backwardThe paragraph with one blank line next to it.
m iC-z m iselect-inside-pairWhat is inside a pair of brackets or quotes, without them.
m aC-z m aselect-pairThe pair of brackets or quotes and what is inside.
m I, m AC-z m I, C-z m Aselect-sexp-inside, select-sexpWhat a bracketed expression holds, and the expression with its brackets.

A paragraph selection takes one blank line with it, the one before it. When you delete it, one blank line is left between its neighbours, which is what you want most of the time.

The pairs that m i and m a know are in the setting *pair-delimiters*. Put the cursor on a bracket and press m i. The echo area tells you it selected the content, and m a the content with the brackets. The pair of the bracket under the cursor is taken at once. With the cursor anywhere else, m i and m a ask for a bracket: press the one you mean, such as (.

Try it, with a letter

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/letter.txt and press RET. Press i and type Dear Hana,, RET, The kereru ate (all 12) of the berries., RET, It was a good day. See you at Easter. Press C-g.
  2. Press g g j w to land on kereru. Press m w (non-modal: C-z m w). The word is selected. Press m w again and kereru ate is selected. Press C-g.
  3. Move to the brackets: press g g j, then press w (non-modal: M-f) until the cursor is on the closing bracket after 12. Press m i. The text inside, all 12, is selected without its brackets. Press m a, then (, and the brackets come in. Press c, type (many) and press C-g. Press u to undo.
  4. Press j (non-modal: C-n), then m s. The sentence It was a good day. is selected. Press m s again and the second sentence joins it. Press C-g.
  5. Press m p. The paragraph is selected, with the blank line before it. Press C-g.

5.2.1 Wrapping a selection

With a selection live, a bracket or a quote wraps it. Press m w on a word and then " to put quotes round the word. Press " once more while the word is selected inside its quotes and they come off. This works with the other brackets and quotes of *pair-delimiters*, and on a rectangle it wraps each row.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
m wC-z m wselect-wordSelect the word at point; from the gap between two words, the one ahead (the last one at the end of the text).
m bC-z m bselect-word-backwardSelect the word at point, or grow a word selection backward, as select-word grows it forward: from the gap between two words, the one behind.
m WC-z m Wselect-symbolSelect the symbol at point (a name with its _ and -, Lisp's own characters in Lisp), punctuation at either end left out: from the gap between two, the one ahead, brackets and quotes crossed.
m BC-z m Bselect-symbol-backwardSelect the symbol at point, or grow a symbol selection backward: from the gap between two, the one behind.
m sC-z m sselect-sentenceSelect the sentence at point, as far as its full stop; from the gap between two, the one ahead.
m SC-z m Sselect-sentence-backwardSelect the sentence at point, or grow a sentence selection backward: from the gap between two, the one behind.
m pC-z m pselect-paragraphSelect the paragraph at point with one blank line, the one before it (the one after, for the first paragraph), so that deleting it leaves one blank line between its neighbours: from a blank line between two, the one below.
m PC-z m Pselect-paragraph-backwardSelect the paragraph at point, or grow a paragraph selection backward: from a blank line between two, the one above.
m iC-z m iselect-inside-pairSelect what is inside a pair of delimiters, the delimiters left out: the pair of the delimiter at point, or the one whose half is typed next ((, ), [, ", ', =, * and the rest of pair-delimiters).
m aC-z m aselect-pairSelect a pair of delimiters and what it holds, as select-inside-pair finds it.
m IC-z m Iselect-sexp-insideSelect what is inside the bracketed expression around point, its brackets left out: point at the start, the mark at the end.
m AC-z m Aselect-sexpSelect the bracketed expression around point, its brackets included: point at the start, the mark at the end.
", $, 'C-z ", C-z $, C-z 'wrap-selection-with-keyWrap the selection in the delimiter pressed and its partner, or take them off when they stand just outside it: " on a word quotes it, and " on the word of a quoted word unquotes it.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*pair-delimiters*((#\{ . #\}) (#\[ . #\]) (#\( . #\)) (#\...a list, each (OPEN . CLOSE)The pairs of delimiters.

These keys do much the same with Emacs's names for them. They work in both states.

5.3 The mark run

Sometimes one object is not enough. You want a word, then the next word, then the symbol before it. A mark run lets you keep adding to a selection with single keys. Press M (non-modal: C-z M), the m held down, and you are in a run. The keys of a run are the ones you would have pressed after m, without the m.

ModalNon-modalWhat it does in a run
w, bnoneAdd the next word, or the one before.
W, BnoneAdd a symbol forward or backward.
s, SnoneAdd a sentence forward or backward.
m p, m PnoneAdd a paragraph forward or backward.
h, l, j, knoneMove the cursor end by one character or line, without ending the run.
g h, g lnoneStretch the cursor end to the start or end of its line.
g g, g enoneStretch the cursor end to the start or end of the buffer.
J, KnoneGrow the run down or up by whole lines.
*noneSwap the two ends, so that h j k l then move the other end.
u, UnoneTake the last step back, or put it forward again.
MnoneEnd the run and let go of the selection.

v and V are refused in a run, because a run is already making a selection. To take a selection you made another way into a run, so that these keys grow it from where it is, use mark-run-adopt.

Try it, with a shopping list

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/list.txt and press RET. Press i and type fresh bread and butter from the shop. Press C-g and g g g h.
  2. Press M. The first word, fresh, is selected. Press w (non-modal: M-f) twice. Now fresh bread and is selected.
  3. Press u (non-modal: C-/). One step goes back. Press U (non-modal: C-?) and it is forward again.
  4. Press M to end the run.

The echo area names the keys of the run while it lasts. See also the section on many cursors below, where the run goes on at every cursor.

noneM-x mark-run-step-forwardmark-run-step-forwardPut the mark run forward where u stepped it back from.

noneM-x mark-run-rightmark-run-rightMove point forward a character, or the count's, without ending the mark run.

noneM-x mark-run-buffer-endmark-run-buffer-endStretch the run's end on to the end of the text, or with no run go there.

5.4 Growing a selection by the code

In a file whose language Tuatara reads, it knows the structure: which words make an expression, which expressions make a statement, and so on up to the whole file. The keys below select by that structure. M-o, M-i, M-n and M-p work in every state; the m keys after them, in NORMAL state or under C-z. They need a file that has a syntax tree. In a file with no tree, such as a plain text file, the echo area says there is none.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
M-oM-oexpand-selectionSelects the smallest piece of syntax around the selection, or at the cursor. Again, a larger one.
M-iM-ishrink-selectionGoes back to the selection before the last M-o.
M-nM-nselect-next-siblingSelects the piece beside it, the next argument, statement or item.
M-pM-pselect-previous-siblingThe one before it.

A number before M-o grows that many steps at once.

The m keys have a second set that picks out pieces of code. The small letter takes what is inside, and the capital the whole piece. Pressed again at once, they take the next one out.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it selects
m f, m FC-z m f, C-z m Fselect-function-inside, select-functionA function's body, or all of it.
m t, m TC-z m t, C-z m Tselect-type-inside, select-typeThe fields or items of a type, or all of it.
m r, m RC-z m r, C-z m Rselect-parameter-inside, select-parameterA parameter or argument, or the same with its comma.
m c, m CC-z m c, C-z m Cselect-comment-inside, select-commentA comment, or with the comment lines next to it.
m y, m YC-z m y, C-z m Yselect-test-inside, select-testA test's body, or the whole test.
m e, m EC-z m e, C-z m Eselect-entry-inside, select-entryThe key or value of an entry in JSON, YAML or TOML, or the whole entry.
m x, m XC-z m x, C-z m Xselect-element-inside, select-elementWhat the tags of an HTML or XML element hold, or the element with its tags.

Try it, with a small Python file

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/count.py and press RET. Press i and type def count(birds, colour):, RET, and then, without any spaces of your own, found = [b for b in birds if b.colour = colour]=, RET, return len(found). Press C-g and C-x C-s.
  2. Press g g (non-modal: M-<) and w w to reach count, then l (non-modal: C-f) to land on birds.
  3. Press M-n. The next parameter, colour, is selected. Press M-p to go back to birds.
  4. Press M-o. The parameters are selected, with their brackets. Press M-o again. The whole function is selected, which in this small file is also the whole file. Press M-o once more and the echo area says that nothing larger can be selected.
  5. Press M-i until you are on birds again. Press C-g.
  6. Press j (non-modal: C-n) to go down into the body. Press m f. The body of the function is selected; on the def line itself it says there is no function around point. Press C-g and then m F for the whole function.

5.5 Rectangles

A rectangle is a block of columns over several lines. It is the right tool for a column of numbers, a bullet at the start of each line, or text that lines up. Figure 5.2 shows one.

A rectangle covers the columns between the cursor and the mark on every line from one to the other. A line that ends inside the block gives only the part it has. The character under the cursor is part of the block, so three l (non-modal: C-f) presses from the first column cover four columns.

5.5.1 Rectangles in NORMAL state

m v (non-modal: C-x r SPC) starts a rectangle in NORMAL state, and any move sizes it. y copies the block, d cuts it and c cuts it and starts INSERT state with a cursor on every row, so that what you type goes on every line. P (non-modal: C-x r y) pastes the block back as a block, one row to a line. m v again, or C-g, ends the rectangle without doing anything.

Try it, with a price list

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/prices.txt and press RET. Press i and type four lines, each followed by RET but the last: coffee 4.50, scone 5.50, pie 7.00 and tea 3.80. Each price starts in the ninth column. Press C-g.
  2. Press g g g h, then l (non-modal: C-f) eight times. The cursor is on the 4. Press m v (non-modal: C-x r SPC), then j j j l l l. The four prices are the block. The echo area says any move sizes the block.
  3. Press y. The echo area says it copied a rectangle of four rows. Press g e and P (non-modal: M->, C-x r y). The prices are pasted again at the end of the last line, one row to a line, below it. Press u (non-modal: C-/) to undo.
  4. Press g g g h and l eight times, then m v j j j l l l and d. The prices are cut. Press g g g h and P. The column of prices has moved to the front of the lines. Press u twice to bring it all back.
  5. With the block made again, press c, type n/a and press C-g twice. Every price is now n/a. Press u.

5.5.2 Rectangles with the Emacs keys

The keys under C-x r work on the block between the cursor and the mark. You can start a rectangle with C-x r SPC, which does what m v does. Pressing it again, or C-g, cancels. Outside NORMAL state a new rectangle starts with no width, and C-f and C-n (modal: l, j) size it.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x r kkill-rectangleCuts the block to a store of its own, apart from the kill ring.
noneC-x r M-wcopy-rectangle-as-killCopies the block to that store.
noneC-x r ddelete-rectangleDeletes the block and keeps nothing. The store keeps what it had.
PC-x r yyank-rectanglePastes the store as a block.
noneC-x r tstring-rectangleAsks for a text and puts it on every row in place of the block.
noneC-x r cclear-rectangleTurns the block into spaces.
noneC-x r Nnumber-rectangle-linesNumbers the rows 1, 2, 3 at the block's left column.
noneM-x number-rectangle-lines-replacenumber-rectangle-lines-replacePuts numbers in place of the block, with nothing after them.

Try it, with the same price list

  1. Open ~/prices.txt again. Press g g g h and m v j j j. The block is the first column of the four lines.
  2. Press C-x r N. The lines are numbered 1 to 4 and the text moves over. Press u (non-modal: C-/).
  3. Make the block again and press C-x r t. Type =- = and press RET. Every line now starts with a dash and a space, which take the place of its first letter. Press u.
  4. Press g g g h and l (non-modal: C-f) eight times, then m v j j j l l l and C-x r c. The prices are blanked and the lines are shorter. Press u.
  5. Make the block once more and press C-x r k. Press g e (non-modal: M->), then C-x r y (modal: P). The prices are pasted as a block at the end. Press u u.

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*rectangle-cursors-limit*10000nil, or a whole number, 0 or moreThe most rows M-x tuatara-change on a rectangle (M-x rectangle-mark-mode) puts a cursor on.

When you change a rectangle with c, every row of the block gets a cursor and what you type appears on all of them. On a very tall block that would make every key slow, so *rectangle-cursors-limit* caps the number of rows that hold a cursor. It is 10000 as standard. Past the cap, the rows in sight hold the cursors, and the other rows are emptied and written when you finish typing. You see the same result, only the cursors are fewer. A whole number, 0 or more, sets the cap, and nil means as many as the memory has room for. To keep it small on a slow machine:

(setf *rectangle-cursors-limit* 500)

5.6 Many cursors

t (non-modal: C-z t) puts another cursor on the line below, at the same column. T (non-modal: C-z T) puts one above. From then on, nearly every key you press works at every cursor. Move, select, type, delete: each key runs once at each place. This is the fast way to do the same small edit on many lines.

Figure 5.3 shows four cursors made with three presses of t.

A line shorter than the column gets its cursor at its end. If lines are selected, the first t puts one cursor on every selected line instead. At the start of each line when the selection was made with V, or in the cursor's column otherwise.

Press i and type, and the text appears at every cursor. Press C-g and you are back in NORMAL state with the cursors still there. Press C-g again and the cursors end. One u (non-modal: C-/) takes back what was done at all of them.

Try it, with a list of names

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/names.txt and press RET. Press i and type four lines, each followed by RET but the last: Hana Raglan, Aroha Kerikeri, Tane Napier and Mere Taupo. Press C-g, then g g.
  2. Press t t t. There are four cursors, one on each line. Press i, type =- = and press C-g. Each name has a dash in front. Press C-g to end the cursors. Press u (non-modal: C-/) to take the dashes back.
  3. Press g g t t t then DEL. The last cursor goes and three remain. Press C-g twice.
  4. Press g g t t t, then m w. Each cursor selects the word it is on. Press M-u to put them in capitals. Press u, then C-g twice.
  5. Press g g t t t, then A. Type . and press C-g twice. Each line now ends with a full stop.

5.6.1 What each key does at the cursors

While the cursors stand, a key in NORMAL state does what it always does, at each cursor. The table lists the keys that need a word of explanation.

ModalNon-modalWhat it does at every cursor
t, TnoneAdd one more cursor below or above.
DELnoneTakes back the cursor added last.
moves, m keysnoneMove or select at each cursor on its own line.
v, VnoneStart a selection at each, or select each cursor's line.

I, AnoneType at the start or the end of the line.

A key the cursors do not know ends them and then does its own work.

The copy and paste rule is worth a moment. Say you select four lines, one at each of four cursors, and press y. The four lines are one kill. p at the same four cursors puts each line back at its own cursor. If you paste a kill that has as many lines as there are cursors, each cursor gets one line. In every other case each cursor gets the whole kill.

M at the cursors starts a mark run at each one. Each run begins as the word at its cursor, or as the selection it had. w (non-modal: M-f) then adds a word to every run at once, and u (non-modal: C-/) takes the last step back at all of them.

5.6.2 Limits

Every key but typing runs once at every cursor, so a great many cursors make every key slow. Tuatara holds up to *cursors-limit* cursors. A cursor in sight beyond the limit still works as one. Those out of sight are written to in the background as each thing is done, and they move only together: h, l, g h and g l (non-modal: C-b, C-f, C-a, C-e) move them all alike, and i, a, I, A, c and d edit at them. Any other key says what works and leaves them as they were.

5.6.3 Showing the cursors

The cursors other than the real one are drawn in their own colours, one for NORMAL state and one while you type. The places a split holds, described next, have a face as well.

5.7 Splitting a selection on what matches

A pattern can make the cursors for you. Select some text and press f (non-modal: C-z f). Tuatara asks for a regular expression, a pattern as used in a search (chapter 6). It holds every match inside the selection at once, one place for each, and waits for you to say what to do with them.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does with every match
inonesplit-insertTypes before every match.
anonesplit-appendTypes after every match.
cnonesplit-changeEmpties every match and types there.
dnonesplit-deleteDeletes every match.
a bracket or quotenonesplit-wrap-keyWraps every match in the pair. Press it again to take it off.
C-gnonesplit-quitLets go and ends the split.

Without a selection, f searches the line the cursor is on. If you put % in front of the pattern, as in %kereru, the whole buffer is searched whatever is selected. What you type at one match appears at all of them, and the writing is one change, so u (non-modal: C-/) takes it all back. Case is ignored when the pattern has no capital letter. As you type the pattern, the number of matches shows before the prompt.

If the selection is a rectangle, f searches its block. With a number first it searches each row's whole line.

Try it, with the recipe

  1. Open ~/pancakes.txt. Press g g j V to select the second line, the one with the quantities.
  2. Press f, type [0-9]+ and press RET. The three numbers are held. The echo area says how many places it holds and what you can do.
  3. Press (. Each number is wrapped in brackets. Press u.
  4. Press V, then f, type , and press RET. Press c, type ; and press C-g. The commas are now semicolons. Press u (non-modal: C-/).
  5. Press % and f, type pancake, press RET and then i. Type * and press C-g. The word Pancakes has a star in front of it. Press u.

f may miss a match of more than 4 KB that runs across several lines. For text where that matters, split-selection-thorough finds every match of up to a megabyte. It is slower, so it has no key of its own. A pattern with many matches is limited by *split-limit*, and *split-limit-ask* lets you hold them all even so.

Searching and replacing

Finding text, changing it, and narrowing what you look at to the lines that matter.

A search answers the question "where is this?". A replacement answers "change this everywhere". Both start from a pattern, a short description of the text you want. This chapter begins with the search you will use all day, then covers replacing, narrowing a list to its matches, searching a whole directory of files, and going to a heading. A table at the end of each section lists every command, setting and face that belongs to it.

6.1 Searching a buffer

Press C-s and Tuatara asks Regex search forward: in the minibuffer, the same row where it asks for a file name. Type a few letters. The cursor jumps to the first match while you type, and the matches in sight are lit. C-r does the same going backward, towards the start of the buffer.

You do not need to finish the word. Typing kere finds the first place that has those four letters, and typing kereru moves to the first place with all six. If you make a mistake, DEL takes a letter off the end and the cursor goes back to where the shorter pattern matched.

Three keys end a search.

  • RET ends it at the match. The cursor stays there, and the place where you began is saved as the mark, so C-x C-x takes you back.
  • C-g or ESC gives up. The cursor goes back to where you began.
  • C-s or C-r do not end it. They go to the next match, or the one before. At the last match, C-s goes round to the first.

Straight after RET, the keys C-s and C-r keep working: the echo area says Repeat with C-s, C-r, and each press moves to the next or previous match without asking again. Any other key ends that.

Figure 6.1 shows the screen while a search is open.

The 1/2 before the prompt says the cursor is at the first of two matches. It is exact however large the buffer is. In a very large buffer the count may wait until you pause (see "The count before the prompt" below), and typing never waits for it.

6.1.1 Capital letters

A pattern that has no capital letters ignores case: kiwi finds Kiwi, KIWI and kiwi. As soon as the pattern has a capital, case counts: Kiwi finds only Kiwi. So you can search loosely most of the time, and type one capital when a word is too common.

6.1.2 Regular expressions and plain text

What you type after C-s is a regular expression, called a regex for short. It is a pattern in which a few characters are special. A dot stands for any one character, a star means "any number of the one before", and so on. That lets you search for "a digit in brackets" or "a line that starts with a date". Table 6.1 lists the forms you will use most. The regex handbook teaches the whole language.

When the text you want is full of special characters, you do not want to escape each one. Press M-r in the middle of a search to switch to plain text. The prompt changes to Literal search forward: and every character stands for itself, so (4) finds the four characters ( 4 ). Press M-r again to switch back. C-M-s and C-M-r start a search that is plain text from the first key.

A regex that is not finished, such as kea(, cannot be searched for. The prompt says why in brackets, for example [incomplete], and RET waits until you mend it. Either fix it or press M-r to take it as plain text.

Table 6.1. The regex forms you will use most.
FormFindsExample
.Any one characterk.a finds kea, kia, k-a
\.A real dot (a backslash makes a special character plain)3\.5 finds 3.5
\dOne digit\d\d finds 07, 42
\wOne letter, digit or underscore\w+ finds a whole word
\sOne space or tab\s+$ finds spaces at a line's end
[abc]One of the characters in bracketsgr[ae]y finds gray, grey
[^abc]One character not in the brackets[^0-9] finds a non-digit
*The one before it, any number of times, even noneka* finds k, ka, kaaa
+The one before it, at least once\d+ finds 7, 2026
?The one before it, once or not at allcolou?r finds color, colour
^, $The start, the end of a line^Dear finds lines starting with Dear
\bThe edge of a word\bkea\b does not find kearns
=a\b=Either one=tui\kea=
(...)A group; later it can be called \1, \2(\d+)-(\d+)

A pattern that is only an edge, such as ^$ for an empty line, is a match too. Searching for it goes from one empty line to the next.

6.1.3 Starting from the word under the cursor

Put the cursor on a word and press C-s, then M-.. The word is added to the pattern as a whole word, so that searching for tui never stops in the middle of tuition. In plain text mode (M-r) the word goes in as it is.

6.1.4 Search history

Every pattern you finish a search with is remembered while Tuatara runs. In the prompt, M-p or the up arrow brings back the one before, and M-n or the down arrow a later one. One history serves every question that asks for a pattern: searching, replacing, and the filters below. Press C-s with nothing typed and RET, and the last pattern is used again.

6.1.5 Keeping the matches lit

After a search ends, its matches stay lit as you move on, which is handy when you want to see how many there are and where. C-g, or keyboard-quit, puts them out. C-x T s lights them again, or takes them away if they are lit.

6.1.6 The count before the prompt

Before the question, Tuatara shows a count such as 3/12. In a search it says the match the cursor is at and how many there are. In a question that offers choices, such as the list of files for C-x C-f, it says which choice is selected and how many there are. When nothing matches it says 0/0 and the search says No match. It always stands in the same six columns, so what you type does not move as you go from match to match.

Counting takes time in a large buffer, and Tuatara does it in the background so that typing never lags. A text of up to a megabyte is counted at every key. A larger one is counted at every key when Tuatara can go through it in about a hundredth of a second. Otherwise the count waits until you stop typing for *typing-pause* seconds, half a second as standard. While a new pattern is being counted, the old count stays in view. If you do not want the count, set *show-completion-count* to nil.

6.1.7 Matches that cross many lines

A regex search is fast because it looks only at the part of the text in view, plus what it needs. It will find a match of more than 4 KB that runs across lines only when the text after the match is already in view. For a block such as BEGIN[\s\S]*?END use a thorough command instead. It finds every match of up to a megabyte, at up to twice the time. The prompt says thorough when it is in use. The thorough form of replacing is described in the next section.

Try it, with a list of names

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/birds.txt and press RET. Press i and type these six lines, RET after each: Kereru, Tui at Akaroa, Kea (4), Fantail at Kaikoura, kiwi, Tui (2). Then C-g and g g to go to the top.
  2. Press C-s and type tui. The cursor goes to the first Tui, because a pattern with no capital ignores case. The prompt says 1/2. Press C-s to go to the second one and RET to stay.
  3. Press g g (non-modal: M-<), then C-s and type Kiwi with the capital. Nothing matches Kiwi here, because the list has only kiwi, and the prompt says 0/0. Delete the capital and type k instead: now it matches. Press C-g.
  4. Press C-s and type (2). In a regular expression the brackets only make a group, so the search stops at the digit 2 alone. Press M-r: the prompt now starts Literal search forward: and the match is the three characters (2) on the last line. Press C-g.
  5. Press g e (non-modal: M->) to go to the end. Press C-r and type k. The search goes backward and stops at kiwi. Press C-g, then C-s and M-p: the pattern you used before comes back. Press C-g.
