When a region is active, a search stays inside it, and the text outside is faded (:search-outside-scope) so that you can see the limit. A pattern that begins with % searches the whole buffer instead.

6.2 Replacing

Replacing uses the same prompt as searching. In NORMAL state press r r (non-modal: C-z r r). The prompt reads Regex replace on this line:. Type the pattern, then RET, which types the / for you, then the new text, then RET. You can also type it all on one line as pattern/new text.

What gets changed depends on what is selected. With nothing selected, only the line the cursor is on, and only the first match on it. With a selection, the selected lines. A % in front of the pattern, as in %tui/Tui, means every match in the whole buffer. A replacement is a single change, so one u (non-modal: C-/) takes the whole thing back, however many places it changed.

While you type, Tuatara shows what will happen. Each match that is going away is lit as :replace-going, and the new text stands beside it in :replace-coming, before you press RET. Look before you press it. Afterwards the echo area says how much was done, for instance Replaced 3 occurrences on 3 lines.

Typed at the C-s prompt, a pattern with a / in it also replaces, the way it does in the Vim editor. A word after the last slash gives flags: g replaces every match on a line, c asks at each match, n only counts what would be replaced, and i or I ignores or keeps case.

6.2.1 What goes in the new text

WriteTo get
&, \0The whole text that matched
\1 to \9What the matching bracket group found
\n, \tA line break, a tab
\u, \lThe next letter in capitals, in small letters
\U, \LEverything up to \E in capitals, in small letters
\/A real slash (also in the pattern)

If the pattern has no capital letters, the replacement follows the case of each match: a match in capitals is replaced in capitals, and one that starts with a capital gets a capital. So %tui/kokako turns Tui into Kokako.

6.2.2 Replacing with questions

r q (non-modal: C-z r q) replaces a regular expression and asks about each match, with Query replacing ... with ...: and the keys y n ! . q:

ModalNon-modalDoes
noneyReplace this one and go to the next
nonenLeave this one and go to the next
none!Replace this one and all the rest
none.Replace this one and stop
noneqStop

M-% is the same for plain text, with no special characters to think about. C-z r q is the key for r q in every state.

When you want to be sure of each change, use the question form. When a change is plain and mechanical, use r r and look at the preview.

If the text you replace can run over many lines, use the thorough forms of the commands. They are described under searching, above.

Try it, with a letter

  1. Open ~/letter.txt and type this text: Dear Hana,, a line break, We met the tui at Akaroa. The tui sings at dawn. Tui are rare., a line break, Yours, Aroha. Press C-g and g g.
  2. Press j (non-modal: C-n) to move to the second line, then r r and type tui/kea, then RET. Only the first match on this line changes. Press u (non-modal: C-/) to take it back.
  3. Press r r and type %tui/kea, RET. Every tui of the whole letter changes, and the third one keeps its capital: Kea are rare. The echo area says Replaced 3 occurrences on 1 line. Press u.
  4. Press r q (non-modal: C-z r q), type %tui/kea, RET. Press y at the first, n at the second and ! at the third. Only the first and the last were changed. Press u.
  5. Press r r and type %(\w+) at (\w+)/\2 at \1, RET. Look at what \1 and \2 did: the two words either side of "at" swap places, as in Akaroa at tui. Press u.

6.3 Narrowing a list to its matches

A list is any buffer made of lines you choose among: the buffer list from C-x C-b, the list of jobs, the packages, the keys. Each such list can be cut down to the lines that match a pattern, and each file of records, such as a log or a table of values, can be cut down in the same way. This is called a search filter. The filter hides lines. Nothing is deleted, and the file on disk does not change.

Press C-x / s in a list and type a pattern. The list shrinks as you type, and the count before the prompt says how many lines are left, for example 1/5 Regex filter: dr. RET keeps the filter. C-g drops the one you were typing and keeps the earlier ones. Press C-x / s again and a second filter narrows what the first left. Above the list a line (:list-filters) says by what it is narrowed and how many entries are left.

C-x / l lists your filters in a buffer of their own, each with the number of entries it leaves. There, d takes the filter on the line away, and D (non-modal: C-k) takes them all away. C-x / r takes them all away too, from the narrowed list itself, and the whole list is shown again.

The same filter works on files whose lines are records, such as a log or a CSV. The modes that count are named in *line-record-modes*. In these, the first line of a CSV is a header and is always shown. C-x / f shows only the records whose one column matches a pattern, and C-x / h hides them. These ask which column first. The lists and the data chapters describe columns in full.

Two keys delete instead of hide. C-x / k keeps the records that match and deletes the others. C-x / d deletes the ones that match. Both can be undone with u (non-modal: C-/). C-x / t makes the first line of a file of records its header, or a record like the rest, and C-x / L keeps the header at the top of the window as the rest scrolls.

You can still type in the lines you see. A change that would reach a hidden line is refused with a message, so a filter never changes what you cannot see. Press C-x / r to see everything again.

Try it, with the buffer list

  1. Press C-x C-b to list your buffers. If you did the earlier chapters it holds shopping.txt, pancakes.txt, birds.txt and letter.txt.
  2. Press C-x / s and type txt. Lines that do not hold those letters go away, such as the starred buffers. The count in front of the prompt follows what you type. Press RET.
  3. Press C-x / s again, type pan and press RET. This narrows the list to what the first filter left, so only pancakes.txt remains. Look at the line above the list.
  4. Press C-x / l. The two filters are listed with how many entries each leaves. Move to the first line, press d to take it away, then q.
  5. Press C-x / r. Every buffer is back.

6.4 Searching many files

M-s g finds text in many files at once. It looks in the project that holds your file. A project is the directory above your file that holds a .git or .project entry (see *project-root-markers*). If there is no such directory, it looks in the directory of the file. In a directory listing it searches that directory, and with a prefix argument (C-u first) it asks for a directory.

Type words and Tuatara lists every line that holds all of them, in any order, each as path:line: text. Nothing is listed before the third character (*search-files-min-input*). The files are read in the background while you type, and Tuatara skips hidden files, backups, binary files and whatever the project's .gitignore leaves out. Each word is a regex, as for C-s, and M-r switches to plain text, where the whole line you typed is found as it stands, spaces and all. At most *search-files-lines-limit* lines are listed. If the search stops there, the first line of the list says so.

Move down the list with C-n (modal: j) and RET opens the file at that line. With *preview-file-search* set to true, the file of the selected line is shown meanwhile in your window, so you can read around a match without leaving the search. After the search, M-g n and M-g p go to the next and previous place in the list, the way they go through the errors of a compile.

A search of your files with formatted names, the ones that carry a date and keywords in their name, is C-x n g (search-in-formatted), and works the same way, with *preview-formatted-search* as its preview setting.

6.4.1 Changing the lines a search found

While the question is open, C-c C-l turns the lines found so far into a buffer of their own. C-x C-q there makes the text after path:line: changeable. You can edit the lines as in any text, but you cannot change a path or a line number or split a line. C-c C-c writes the changed lines back into their files. It runs in the background, and a line is written only when the file still has the text that was found. A file that is open in a buffer is changed there, as a step you can undo. Other files are saved and closed again, unless *search-results-save-files* is nil, in which case each stays changed and unsaved for you to look at. C-c C-k throws the changes away and leaves the files as they were.

Files that you opened safely, files you may not write and read-only buffers are never written. The message log says why.

6.4.2 Keeping directories read

A big directory takes a while to read. Name the directories you search often in *indexed-directories* in your init file, for example (setf *indexed-directories* (list "~/notes/")). Tuatara then keeps their file names and text in memory. It reads them in the background when it starts, and again when something changes on disk. After that M-s g in them answers at once, and so does the search of your files with formatted names. While a directory is being read the mode line shows U after the P sign, and while a kept directory is searched it shows S. They stand always in the same place and are faint when idle (*indexing-indicator*, *searching-indicator*).

By default what was read is also kept on disk between sessions (*indexes-kept-on-disk*), so that at the next start only the files that changed are read again. Set it to nil for a directory whose text must not be copied anywhere. *search-files-limit* is the most text Tuatara keeps for one search or one kept directory, 128 MB as standard. Files past it are searched from the disk, more slowly.

Try it, with a directory of notes

  1. Make a directory called notes in your home directory, with your file manager or with mkdir ~/notes in a terminal. Open ~/notes/akaroa.txt with C-x C-f and type Tui and kereru near the harbour. Save it with C-x C-s. Make a second file, ~/notes/kaikoura.txt, with Fantail and tui by the stream and save it.
  2. With kaikoura.txt showing, press M-s g and type tui. Nothing is listed before the third letter. Then both lines are, each as path:line: text.
  3. Press RET. akaroa.txt opens at its line. Press M-g n to go on to the next match, in kaikoura.txt. (C-n before RET would take you to the second line of the list instead.)
  4. Press M-s g and type tui harbour. Only the akaroa.txt line is listed, because it holds both words. Press C-c C-l to put the lines in a buffer, C-x C-q to change them, replace harbour with bay on the line, then C-c C-c to write it back. Look at akaroa.txt: it says bay.
  5. To keep the directory read, add (setf *indexed-directories* (list "~/notes/")) to your init file and restart. The U in the mode line lights up while it is read, and is faint again when it is done.

6.5 The outline of a buffer

M-g o lists the headings of the buffer you are in and goes to the one you choose. In an Org file they are the headings. In Lisp they are the comments that start with three semicolons and the top-level forms. In a language that Tuatara has a grammar for, they are its definitions, such as functions and types, and in Markdown its headings. Each is shown as its line, after the line's number, in the order of the text.

Type a few letters of a name and the list narrows to the headings that hold them. The window behind follows the first one (:outline-preview), and RET goes there. C-g takes you back to where you were. Start with a digit and a space to see only the outer headings: =2 = then the words shows the headings two levels deep or less.

When a language server is running for the file and *lsp-outline* is true, the list uses the names the server knows, including fields and methods inside types. Otherwise it uses the headings Tuatara finds itself.

Try it, with a long Org file

  1. Open any Org file with several headings, for instance one you made in the earlier chapters, or press C-x C-f and make ~/trip.org with * Akaroa, ** Harbour, * Kaikoura, ** Whale watching and ** Crayfish on separate lines.
  2. Press M-g o. Every heading is listed with its line number.
  3. Type whale. Only the matching heading is left, and the window behind shows it. Press RET to go there.
  4. Press M-g o again, type =1 = and a space, and see only the top headings. Press C-g to go back.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*lsp-outline*tt, nilWhether M-x buffer-outline lists a file's names as its language server knows them (functions, types, their fields and methods, nested), where it has one that does.
FaceWhat it paints

Buffers and sessions

Keeping track of what is open, and getting it back after you leave.

Chapter 1 explained that a buffer is a piece of text Tuatara holds in memory, and that a window is a view of one. After an afternoon of work you may have a dozen buffers open: a letter, a shopping list, some notes, a directory listing, the help. This chapter is about managing them. It shows the list of all buffers, how to get rid of the ones you are done with, how to find a file you had open yesterday, and how to leave a place marked so that you can come back to it. It also explains what Tuatara does so that a crash or a closed terminal does not cost you your work: it can remember what was open, and it keeps a copy of changes you have not saved. The last part shows how to look at just one part of a buffer.

Before you start, one reminder about the state keys. i starts INSERT state, and C-g or ESC returns to NORMAL state. Every key in this chapter is pressed in NORMAL state unless it starts with C-x, which works in both.

7.1 The buffer list

C-x C-b shows every buffer in a buffer of its own called *Buffers*. The one you used last is at the top. You use the list when you have lost track of what is open, when you want to close several buffers at once, or when you want to save several files in one go.

Figure 7.1 shows a list for someone who has a directory of letters under version control, a few loose notes, and the log of what the echo area said.

Each buffer has one line, starting under the text of its section's heading, the titles of the columns above in line with it. The line gives the buffer's marks, its name, its size, its major mode (the kind of text it is, such as Text or Org) and the file it visits. The marks come first. A > means you marked the buffer for a command to act on. A D means you marked it for deletion. A * means it has changes that are not saved, and a % means it is read-only. In the figure, council.txt is marked and has unsaved changes, and old-draft.txt is marked for deletion.

The names of buffers that Tuatara made itself, such as *Messages*, are set apart in their own colour, as are read-only buffers, help buffers and marked names. The last line of the list adds up how many buffers there are and how much text they hold.

7.1.1 Sections

The list is divided into sections, one for each project. A project is a directory that holds a .git or a .project file, with every file in it and every directory below it. In the figure, letters is a project because ~/letters/ is under version control. Buffers that belong to no project are in a section called No project. The section of the project you came from is first. Each heading says the project's directory name and how many buffers the section holds.

A heading starts with ▾ when its section is open and ▸ when it is folded. The setting *project-root-markers* holds the file names that make a directory a project. If you keep your own projects in directories marked some other way, add the name of the marker file there.

7.1.2 Folding

A long list is easier to read with the sections you do not need folded away. A folded section shows only its heading. TAB folds the section the cursor is in, or opens it again if it was folded. S-TAB folds every section, or opens them all if every one is folded. On a heading, l and RET open the section, and h folds it. On any other line h does nothing, so a stray press does not close the list; q does that.

7.1.3 Marks

The list works on one buffer at a time, or on several if you mark them. Marking is how you say "these ones". m puts a > on the buffer the cursor is on and moves down a line, so you can mark a run of buffers by pressing m over and over. A number before the key marks that many lines. u takes a mark off the line and moves down, and U takes every mark off. t swaps the two states: what was marked becomes unmarked and the other way round. That is a quick way to say "everything except these".

d puts a D on a buffer instead. It means "kill this one". Nothing is killed until you press x, which kills every buffer marked with D. It is the same two-step as in a directory listing: first mark, then do it. Buffers with unsaved changes are asked about first, so a mark does not lose your work.

There are two commands that act on the buffers marked with >. s saves the marked buffers that have a file. D, with a capital, kills the marked buffers after asking. If you have marked nothing, both act on the buffer the cursor is on. On a section's heading, D kills every buffer of that project.

7.1.4 Opening, and keeping the list current

RET and l show the buffer on the cursor's line in the window you came from. o shows it in another window and leaves the list open beside it. n and p move to the next and the previous buffer, skipping the headings, and j and k (non-modal: C-n, C-p) move a line at a time. r makes the list again. You rarely need that, because the list updates itself while it is on the screen, and your marks stay.

When Tuatara runs in the background, serving several windows of its own (a daemon, described in chapter 18), each of those windows is a client and the list has a section for each client instead. K on a client's section makes that client the one that stays when its last buffer is closed. The setting *client-kept-without-buffers* says which one stays when you do not choose. You can skip this until chapter 18.

Try it, with a letter and a shopping list

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/letter.txt and press RET. Press i and type Dear Aroha,. Press C-g and then C-x C-s to save.
  2. Open ~/shopping.txt the same way and type eggs, RET, bread. Press C-g and save with C-x C-s.
  3. Press C-x C-b. The two files are listed, the shopping list at the top because you used it last. The cursor is on the buffer you came from.
  4. Press j (non-modal: C-n) to move to the letter. Press m. A > shows before its name and the cursor moves down a line. Press k (non-modal: C-p) and u to take the mark off, then k and m to put it back.
  5. Move to the shopping list with k k and press d. A D shows. Press x. shopping.txt is gone from the list.
  6. Press o on the letter. It opens in another window and the list stays. Press C-x o to go back to the list, then q to close it.

7.2 Scratch buffers

Sometimes you want somewhere to type that is not a file: a number to add up, a phone number to keep in front of you for a minute, a few lines you may throw away. Tuatara has two buffers for this. They have no file, so they are never saved, and Tuatara has no file to ask about when you quit.

*lisp-scratch* is a buffer for Lisp, the language Tuatara is written in. You can use it as plain text too. Type a Lisp expression, such as (+ 2 3), and press C-x C-e with the cursor after it, and Tuatara runs it. C-j puts the answer on the lines after the expression. That makes it a calculator that shows its working. *org-scratch* is the same idea for notes in Org, the outline format described in chapter 14.

When Tuatara starts without a file, it shows one of them, chosen by *startup-buffer*. It also makes both scratch buffers for you, a list that *auto-scratch-buffers* holds, and makes them again when you kill your last buffer so that you are never left with an empty screen. If you have killed one and want it back, run lisp-scratch or org-scratch with M-x; they make a new one when none is there. In a client of the daemon of chapter 18 they show the client's own scratch buffer of that kind, and make one when the client has none, numbered when the name is taken (*org-scratch*<2>).

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x lisp-scratchlisp-scratchShow lisp-scratch, the Lisp buffer that is not saved, where C-x C-e evaluates in the running editor and C-j puts what the expression before point printed and its value on the lines after it; when it was killed, a new one.
noneM-x org-scratchorg-scratchShow org-scratch, the Org buffer for notes that are not saved; when it was killed, a new one.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*startup-buffer*"*lisp-scratch*"textThe buffer shown when the editor starts without files.
*auto-scratch-buffers*("*lisp-scratch*" "*org-scratch*")a list, each textThe scratch buffers made without being asked for, at startup and when the last buffer is killed.

A file name typed in a scratch buffer is taken from the directory in *default-directory*, which is your home directory unless you say otherwise. Saving a scratch buffer with C-x C-s asks where to put it, as for any new file.

7.3 Saving and killing buffers

Killing a buffer removes it from memory. If it visited a file, the file stays where it is. The usual way is C-x k, which kills the buffer you are in. If it has changes you have not saved, Tuatara asks first. Chapter 1 mentioned C-x 4 0, which does the same and closes the window too.

When you have finished with a whole piece of work, C-x p k kills every buffer of the project the current buffer is in: its files, its directory listings and the buffers standing in them. It says how many have unsaved changes and asks about each of those. It is the quick way to tidy up after you have finished the letters and want to start on something else. The same thing is done by pressing D on the heading of the project in the buffer list. In a daemon (chapter 18), where each client has buffers of its own, C-x p k kills only your client's buffers of the project. C-u C-x p k kills those of every client, after a question saying how many each has: Kill 5 buffers of letters: 3 of client 2, 2 of client 3? Without a daemon C-u changes nothing.

In a daemon two clients can have the same buffer, when both opened the same file. C-x k in one of them does not kill it then. Your client lets it go and shows one of its own buffers in its place, and the other client keeps it as it is, unsaved changes and all. Nothing is asked. The buffer is killed only by the last client that has it, with the usual question when it has unsaved changes. D in the buffer list and C-x p k work the same way. C-u C-x p k kills it for every client.

C-x s goes the other way. It saves every file buffer with unsaved changes, after asking once. It is handy after a rename that touched many files. Leaving Tuatara with C-x C-c asks first when any buffer visiting a file has changes that are not saved.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x kkill-bufferKill the current buffer, asking first when it has changes not saved.
noneC-x p kkill-project-buffersKill every buffer of the project the current buffer is in (a directory above it holding one of PROJECT-ROOT-MARKERS, .git or .project), its files, its directories listed (C-x d), and the buffers standing in them; after asking, saying how many are modified, each modified one asked about as it goes.
noneC-x ssave-some-buffersSave every buffer visiting a file with changes not saved, after asking once, the files named: the files a rename across a project changed, say.
noneC-x C-csave-buffers-kill-editorExit the editor, asking first if a buffer visiting a file, or one made by C-x n e, has unsaved changes.

7.4 Recent files and places

Most days you work on the same few files. You do not have to type their names each time. Tuatara keeps a list of the files you have opened, the latest first, and C-x C-r asks you to pick from it. Each file is listed with its permissions, its size and when it last changed, which helps when two files have similar names. The list is kept between sessions, so on Monday morning it still holds Friday's files.

The list keeps *recent-files-limit* files. A file that no longer exists is taken out when Tuatara starts. If you want to keep such files in the list, shown as not found, set *recent-files-auto-cleanup* to nil. To keep no list at all, set *remember-recent-files* to nil.

Tuatara also remembers where the cursor was in each file you leave. When you open the file again, the cursor is back at that line, even in a later session. That is the setting *save-place-mode*, and *save-place-limit* sets how many files it remembers. It is useful for a long document you read a little at a time.

Try it, with a letter and some notes

  1. Press C-x C-f and open ~/letter.txt, then use j to go down a few lines. If the file is short, type a few lines first and save.
  2. Open ~/notes.txt the same way. If it is a new file, type a word in it and save it, as a file that was never written is not remembered. Press C-x k to kill the notes buffer, then C-x k again for the letter.
  3. Press C-x C-r. Both files are listed, notes.txt first.
  4. Pick the letter and press RET. It opens with the cursor at the line where you left it.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x C-rfind-recent-fileVisit a file visited lately: the latest first, each with its permissions, size and when it last changed beside it.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*remember-recent-files*tt, nilWhether a list of the files you visit is kept, the latest first, for find-recent-file (M-x find-recent-file, M-x find-recent-file) to offer.
*recent-files-limit*25a whole number, 0 or moreHow many files the list of recent files keeps.
*recent-files-auto-cleanup*tt, nilWhether the files no longer there are taken out of the list of recent files when the editor starts.
*save-place-mode*tt, nilWhether point's place in each file you visit is remembered and put back when you visit the file again, in this session or a later one.
*save-place-limit*400a whole number, 0 or moreHow many files' places are kept, the latest first.

7.5 Bookmarks

A bookmark is a named place that Tuatara keeps for good. It is like a recent file, but you choose it and give it a name. You would use one for the place in a long letter where you stopped, or for the section of your notes that you open every day. A bookmark remembers the file and the place in it, and it finds the place again even when you have added text above it.

C-x m m sets a bookmark where the cursor is. It asks for a name, and offers the file's name. It then asks which categories the bookmark is in. A category is a word of your own, such as letters or house; you may type several, apart by commas, and the ones you used before are offered. C-x m b asks for a name and goes to the place. C-x m d forgets a bookmark.

C-x m l opens the bookmark manager, a list that works like the buffer list. It has a section for each category, with a heading saying how many bookmarks the section holds, and one for the bookmarks in no category. A bookmark in two categories appears in both. Folding, marking and the RET, l and o keys work as described for the buffer list. In the manager, r gives the bookmark under the cursor another name and c changes its categories. A bookmark whose file has gone is shown faint.

A bookmark on a directory listing keeps the directory and the entry the cursor is on, so you can bookmark a directory you visit often.

Try it, with some notes

  1. Open ~/notes.txt and type a few lines, such as Plumber: Wanaka Plumbing, Dentist: 9 May, Car service: Taupo Motors, each ended with RET. Save.
  2. Move to the Dentist line. Press C-x m m, type dentist and RET. At the question about categories, type house and RET. The question comes again, for one more category: press RET on the empty answer to finish.
  3. Press C-x C-r and open some other file, so that the notes are out of sight. Press C-x m b, type dent and RET. You are back on the line.
  4. Press C-x m l. The bookmark is in a section called house. Press q to close the list.

noneC-x m mbookmark-setKeep where point is in the current file (or the directory a directory list shows and the entry the cursor is on) under a name you give, the file's name offered, then in the categories you choose, those used already offered, new ones typed (BOOKMARK-SET-ASKS-CATEGORIES).
noneC-x m bbookmark-jumpGo to a bookmark, chosen by its name (each listed with its file): its file visited, point where it was set, found again when the text above it changed.

*bookmark-set-asks-categories*tt, nilWhether M-x bookmark-set asks, after the name, which categories the bookmark is in.
*bookmarks-kept*1000a whole number, 0 or moreHow many bookmarks you may have before setting another says you have more.

*bookmark-set-asks-categories* is t as standard, so C-x m m asks for categories after the name. If you never sort your bookmarks, turn the question off and a bookmark is set with the name alone:

(setf *bookmark-set-asks-categories* nil)

You can still give a bookmark categories later, with c in the manager. *bookmarks-kept* is the number of bookmarks, 1000 as standard, after which setting another says in the echo area that you have more than that. No bookmark is ever dropped, whatever the number. To be told sooner:

(setf *bookmarks-kept* 200)

7.6 Registers

A register is a place to keep text, a number or a position under a single character, for as long as Tuatara runs. A register that keeps a position is a short-term bookmark. Registers are described in chapter 4, with the kill ring that they sit beside. Bookmarks are the choice when you want the place next week.

7.7 The session kept

When you close Tuatara with C-x C-c, everything that was open is gone from the screen. The session is the name for what was open: the files and the directory listings, and how the windows were split. If you turn on *keep-session*, Tuatara writes the session down as it stops, and opens it again the next time it starts without a file named. You see your windows as they were, each on its file, at the place where the cursor was. It is off until you turn it on.

Put this line in your init file, the file described in chapter 8:

(setf *keep-session* t)

The session is also written now and then while Tuatara runs, as often as *keep-session-interval* seconds when something has changed. If Tuatara crashes, you lose at most that long. The file that holds it is in Tuatara's state directory and only you can read it. A file you opened with care, because you do not trust it, is opened with the same care next time. A file that is no longer there is left out.

If you start Tuatara with a file name, as in tuatara letter.txt, you get that file, and the session's files are opened behind it. The session is not replaced by that start.

Try it, with a letter and a shopping list

  1. Add (setf *keep-session* t) to your init file and restart Tuatara.
  2. Open ~/letter.txt. Press C-x 3 to split the window, then C-x o to go to the new window and open ~/shopping.txt there.
  3. Press C-x C-c. Tuatara leaves.
  4. Start Tuatara again with no file name. Both windows are there, each on its own file. The echo area says the session was opened again.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*keep-session*nilt, nilWhether the editor keeps its session: the files and directories open and how the windows show them.
*keep-session-interval*30a number, 0 or moreSeconds between the writings of the session while the editor runs, when it has changed (KEEP-SESSION).

7.8 Auto-save and getting changes back

Saving is your decision. Tuatara never writes your file until you press C-x C-s. But it does not leave your unsaved typing exposed to a crash or a slip. When a buffer that visits a file has changes you have not saved, Tuatara writes them to a copy of their own, in a directory of its own, a few seconds after you stop typing. If you keep typing without a pause, it still writes one every minute. The file you are editing is never touched. When you save, or kill the buffer with nothing to save, the copy is deleted.

If Tuatara stops without your saving, whether because of a crash, a power cut or a quit without saving, the copy stays. When you open the file again, Tuatara tells you it holds changes that are newer than the file. M-x recover-file takes them into the buffer, after asking. They arrive as one edit. C-/ (modal: u) takes it back if you change your mind, and C-x C-s writes it to the file if you do not.

You can also see every copy that is waiting with M-x list-auto-saves. The list shows when each copy was written, how big it is and which file it belongs to, with the newest first. It marks and acts as the buffer list does: RET recovers the copy on the line, after asking, and x and D delete copies.

Auto-save is on as standard, through *auto-save*. With t the changes of every buffer that visits a file are written now and then to a copy of their own, never to the file. If you want no copies at all, put this in your init file:

(setf *auto-save* nil)

A buffer larger than *auto-save-size-limit* octets is not copied, because each copy is written whole. Files opened with care are never copied. *auto-save-directory* says where the copies go, and you can point it at a directory on another drive. *auto-save-idle* and *auto-save-interval* set the two waits.

Try it, with a letter

  1. Open ~/letter.txt. Press i, type P.S. Thank you for the plums. and press C-g. Do not save. Wait ten seconds.
  2. Press C-x C-c. Tuatara asks about the unsaved file. Leave without saving it.
  3. Start Tuatara again and open the letter. The echo area says it holds changes newer than the file.
  4. Press M-x, type recover-file and press RET. Answer yes. The postscript is back. Press C-x C-s to save it.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x list-auto-saveslist-auto-savesList the auto-saved copies of changes not saved (AUTO-SAVE-DIRECTORY), the newest first: after a crash or a quit without saving, what can be taken back.
noneM-x recover-filerecover-fileTake into the current buffer the changes auto-saved for its file (AUTO-SAVE) after asking, as one edit: C-/ takes it back, a save writes it to the file.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*auto-save*tt, nilWhether buffers visiting files have their changes not saved written now and then to a copy of their own in AUTO-SAVE-DIRECTORY.
*auto-save-directory*nilnil, or a directory's nameThe directory auto-saved copies are kept in.
*auto-save-idle*5a number, 0 or moreSeconds without a change after which a buffer's changes not saved are auto-saved (AUTO-SAVE).

7.9 Narrowing to a part of a buffer

A long file can be a distraction. If you want to rewrite one paragraph of a letter, you do not want a search to wander off into another part of the file, or a replacement to change the other places by mistake. Narrowing shows only a part of the buffer and keeps every command inside it. Moving, searching, replacing, editing and selecting all stop at the edges of the part. The rest of the buffer is out of sight and out of reach until you widen it again.

While a buffer is narrowed, the mode line says Narrow in a warning colour, so you cannot forget it. Nothing is lost. Saving still writes the whole file, and the line numbers stay those of the whole file.

C-x x n narrows to the text you have selected. C-x x s narrows to the section the cursor is in. In an Org file that is the heading it is under, with everything below it. In a program it is the function. C-x x w shows all of the buffer again.

Going to a place outside the part, with a bookmark for example, widens the buffer and says so. A command that would change text outside the part is refused, and the echo area says so.

Try it, with a shopping list

  1. Open ~/shopping.txt and make it eight lines long: eggs, bread, milk, butter, apples, tea, rice and honey, one per line. Save.
  2. Press M-< (modal: g g) to go to the top, then j j to reach the line milk. Press V and J J to select milk, butter and apples.
  3. Press C-x x n. Only those three lines are left on the screen, and Narrow shows in the mode line.
  4. Press C-s, type rice and RET. It is not found, because it is out of reach.
  5. Press C-x x w. All eight lines are back, and Narrow is gone.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x x nnarrow-to-regionShow only the selected text, and keep every command to it: motion, search and replacement, editing and selecting stop at its edges, and the rest of the buffer is out of sight and out of reach until C-x x w.
noneC-x x snarrow-to-sectionShow only the section point is in, and keep every command to it, as C-x x n does for the selection: in Org, the subtree of the headline point is under, the headline with it; in code, the definition point is in (or the one after it), as C-M-a and C-M-e find it.
noneC-x x wwidenShow all of the buffer again after C-x x n or C-x x s, every command reaching all of it, point staying where it is.
FaceWhat it paints
:mode-line-narrowedNarrow, in the mode line of a buffer narrowed to a part of it (C-x x n, C-x x s): lit up in the theme's warning colour, so that it is seen at once that the rest of the buffer is out of sight and out of reach until C-x x w.

Commands, keys and help

Running a command by its name, the keys that start longer keys, and the help that Tuatara keeps for itself.

Everything Tuatara does is a command. Moving down a line is a command, so is saving a file, and so is sorting a list. Most commands have a key, but many do not, and nobody remembers all of them. This chapter is about the ways of finding and running a command without knowing its key. It starts with M-x, which runs any command by name, and with the count that you can give to a command. It then explains the prefix keys, the keys that start a longer key, and the key hints that show you what can follow. The longest part is about help: how to ask what a key does, what a command does, what a setting is and where to look when you do not know the name. The end of the chapter has the page that introduces Tuatara, the check of what your system has, and a short look at running Lisp in the editor.

Before you start, one reminder about the state keys. i starts INSERT state, and C-g or ESC returns to NORMAL state. The keys in this chapter that start with C-x, C-h or M-x work in both states, and the others are pressed in NORMAL state.

8.1 Running a command by name

M-x asks for the name of a command in the minibuffer, the row at the bottom of the screen where Tuatara asks its questions, and runs the command you choose. It is the way to run anything that has no key, and the way to run something you only need once in a while. You use it when you know what you want done but not which key does it.

You do not type the whole name. As you type, Tuatara lists the commands that match, and each one shows its keys and the first line of what it does. The words you type may be in any order, so lines sort finds sort-lines. The first letters of the words also match, so sbke finds save-buffers-kill-editor. C-n and C-p move down and up the list, TAB puts the chosen name into what you typed, and RET runs it. C-g gives up and nothing runs. The commands you ran lately come first, so a command you use often needs only a few letters.

Figure 8.1 shows the minibuffer after typing sort lines with some text selected.

A command that needs something from you asks for it after you press RET, in the same row. sort-lines, for example, works on the lines you have selected, and flush-lines asks for the text to look for. A command made for one kind of buffer says so when you run it in another, and tells you where it works.

Try it, to find a command for sorting lines

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/shopping.txt and press RET. Press i and type milk, RET, eggs, RET, bread, RET, apples. Press C-g.
  2. Press M-< (modal: g g) to go to the top. Press V to select the first line, then J J J to take in the other three.
  3. Press M-x and type sort lines. The list shows sort-lines first, with its first line of help beside it. Press RET.
  4. The four lines are in alphabetical order: apples, bread, eggs, milk. Press C-/ (modal: u) to put them back.
  5. Press M-x and type sbke. The list shows save-buffers-kill-editor. Look at the key beside it, then press C-g. Nothing ran.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-xexecute-extended-commandRun a command chosen by name, with completion over every command: the candidates show each command's keys and the first line of its documentation.

8.1.1 The count before M-x

A count given before M-x goes to the command you choose. C-u 3 M-x upcase-word makes the next three words capital letters. The next section says how a count is typed.

8.2 Counts

A count tells a command how many times to do its work, or gives it a number to work with. You type C-u, then the number, then the key or command. In NORMAL state C-u 5 j moves five lines down. C-u alone means 4 and C-u C-u means 16, and a minus sign makes the count negative, which turns many commands around. Chapter 2 shows counts with moves, and the other chapters name what a count does for their commands, such as how many cursors to add or how many lines to kill. The count is always taken by the command that follows it.

. (non-modal: C-x z) runs the last command again, with the count it had. It is the quickest way to do the same small thing three times. After C-u 4 j, pressing . goes four more lines down. A command started with M-x is repeated as well, with its count. Without the modal layer, each z pressed after C-x z repeats once more, until another key is pressed.

Inside a question, C-u does something else. In the minibuffer it clears what you typed, and leaves the question as it is. That is useful when you started a long name and want to begin again.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-uuniversal-argumentBegin a numeric prefix argument: C-u alone means 4, C-u C-u 16, digits after it give their number, a leading minus negates.
.C-x zrepeatRun the last command again, other than repeat itself, with the prefix argument it had (one given to repeat is used instead) and as the key that ran it (C-x C– shrinks again, it does not grow); repeat again, and it runs that command once more, as often as you like.

8.3 Giving up

C-g is the key to press when you are unsure. It closes a question, closes a list of choices, closes the key hints, drops a selection and leaves INSERT state. Whatever you were in the middle of is abandoned, and nothing is run.

ESC is a key of its own as standard. It does what it is bound to, and where it is bound to nothing it does what C-g does. It closes a question typed in the minibuffer and leaves INSERT state, but it does not end a question that is answered with one key. If you would rather have ESC do everything that C-g does, set *escape-quits* to t in your init file, the file described in chapter 20.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x keyboard-quitkeyboard-quitAbandon the current operation and deactivate the region; what stays shown until then goes, such as the matches of the last search.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*escape-quits*nilt, nilWhether Escape does what C-g does everywhere.

8.4 Prefix keys

Most of the keys you press are one key. Longer keys are made by pressing a prefix first and then another key, as in C-x C-f. A prefix key gathers a family of commands under one key, so that a small number of keys at the top leads to many commands. Tuatara uses four of them in particular ways.

C-x is the family of global commands. Its keys are the same in every buffer and in both states: C-x C-f finds a file, C-x C-s saves it, C-x b goes to another buffer, C-x C-b lists them. Under it are smaller families with a name: C-x w for windows, C-x r for rectangles and registers, C-x m for bookmarks, C-x p for projects, C-x T for things you switch on and off. The chapter for each subject says which keys it uses.

C-c is the family of the buffer you are in. Its keys differ from mode to mode. In a list of buffers, C-c shows what the list can do. In an Org note it shows what Org can do, and in a PDF it shows how to turn a page. It is the one prefix to try when you wonder what a particular buffer offers. In the terminal that Tuatara can run, C-c is not a prefix, because it goes to the program that is running there. The keys C-c x, C-c s and C-c t are never given to a mode, and are left for your own commands.

SPC in NORMAL state is the leader, a prefix that belongs to you. As Tuatara comes, nothing is under it. You put there the keys that you use most, in the places that suit you, and nothing the editor updates will move them. C-x SPC opens the same keys in every buffer and in both states, so that the leader works in INSERT state too. If another key suits you better than SPC, set *leader-key* to it, for example ",". How to bind keys is the subject of chapter 20.

C-h is the family of help, described below.

Two more prefixes you meet in NORMAL state are g, which starts moves such as g g (non-modal: M-<) for the top of the buffer, and m, which starts the selecting keys of chapter 5. They work the same way, and the key hints show them.

Tuatara has a setting that turns the modal states off. With *modal-editing* set to nil every key writes text as it does in a plain editor, and the Control and Meta keys do the commands. The prefixes in this section work in the same way. C-z is a prefix of its own for this: under it are the commands of NORMAL state's selecting, cursor, spelling and replacing keys, on the same letters (C-z m f for m f), and the key hints list them.

8.5 Key hints

Press a prefix key and wait a moment. Under the text, a panel opens that lists every key that can come next with the name of its command. You do not need to remember the keys of a family; you need only remember the first key. Figure 8.2 shows the panel after C-x in a buffer that visits a letter.

The names that start with a plus sign are further prefixes, and pressing their key opens another panel one level down. A key whose command cannot run in the buffer you are in is dimmed, and pressing it tells you why. C-g closes the panel. If the keys do not all fit, the last row ends in … and says that C-h lists them all.

C-h pressed right after any prefix key lists every key under it in a buffer of its own, the prefixes unfolded, so that you can read them at leisure: C-x C-h for the global keys, C-c C-h for those of the buffer you are in. q closes that buffer.

A panel of hints takes as many rows as the frame has room for. If you want it shorter, set *key-hint-rows* to the most rows it may take. The panel's colours are the faces below.

Try it, with the keys of a buffer you do not know

  1. Press C-x C-b to open the list of buffers. The cursor is in it.
  2. Press C-c and wait a moment. The panel lists what the list can do: mark a buffer, mark it for deletion, open one and so on, each with its key.
  3. Press C-g. The panel closes and nothing was run.
  4. Press C-c C-h. The same keys are listed in a buffer of its own, in a window beside the list, and the cursor stays in the list. Press C-x o to move to it and q to close it, then q again to close the list of buffers.
  5. Press C-x and wait. Press w to see what is under C-x w, then C-g.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*key-hint-rows*nilnil, or a whole number, 1 or moreThe most rows the key hints take after a prefix key (C-x, SPC).
FaceWhat it paints
:key-hint-keyKeys in the panel that lists the bindings under a prefix key.
:key-hint-commandCommands in the key-hint panel shown after a prefix key.
:key-hint-prefixPrefix keys (further keymaps) in the key-hint panel.
:key-hint-unavailableA key in the key hints or a menu whose command cannot run here, such as one that would change a git repository looked at only: dimmed, and pressing it says why.

8.6 Menus

Some commands have more to say than one key can. Git's commit command has switches, options and several ways to finish. For these Tuatara opens a menu: a panel of the same kind as the key hints, but with a title, and with keys that are not all commands. There are three kinds of entry. An action runs a command and closes the menu. A switch turns something on or off, as in "sign this commit", and keeps the menu open. An option asks you for a value, such as a number of commits, and keeps the menu open too. A switch or option that is on is drawn in its own colour, and the rest in a fainter one, so that you can see at a glance what the action will be given.

C-h in a menu lists every entry in a buffer of its own, with the command or argument behind each, including the entries that are left out of the panel for now. C-g leaves a menu. A menu that holds changes you made asks first, so that you do not lose them. The git chapter shows menus in use, and the commands in them can be run from M-x without the menu.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x menu-toggle-switchmenu-toggle-switchTurn the switch of the open menu whose key was typed on, or off, or say it is left out of the menu now; the menu stays open.
noneM-x menu-set-optionmenu-set-optionGive the option of the open menu whose key was typed a value, asked for, or take its value away when it has one, or ask it again with that value when the option says so (MENU-ENTRY-REPLACE), or say it is left out of the menu now; the menu stays open.
noneM-x menu-leavemenu-leaveLeave the open menu, asked first when anything in it was changed; it stays open unless the answer is yes.
noneM-x menu-describemenu-describeList in Help every entry of the open menu: its keys, what it says and the command or argument behind it, those not shown now too.
FaceWhat it paints
:menu-argument-onAn argument a menu has on (a switch, an option given a value): what its actions are given.
:menu-argument-offAn argument a menu has off: shown, not given.

8.7 Asking what a key does

You press a key by accident and something happens, or you see a key in a book and want to know what it is. C-h k answers. It waits for a key or a longer key and then shows, in a window of its own, the command the key runs, what the command does and where the command is defined. You do not need to leave the key you were using; the question is answered the moment the key is complete.

C-h k takes a prefix as well. Press C-h k, then C-x, and it waits for the rest, then shows C-x C-f when you press C-f. A key with no command says it is undefined.

? in NORMAL state, or C-h b anywhere, lists every key that is in effect in the buffer you are in. The list goes keymap by keymap, the one for this buffer first and then those it falls through to. A key that a mode has taken away is shown as (none here). It is a long list, but a search with C-s finds a key or a command in it.

Try it, when you forgot what a key does

  1. Press C-h k. The echo area asks Describe key:.
  2. Press g e (non-modal: M->). A second window opens, and the cursor stays in the one you were in. The new window says that g e runs the command end-of-buffer, lists the keys that run it, and says what it does.
  3. Press C-x 1 (modal: F) to leave only one window. Press C-h k again, and this time press C-x and then C-s. It names save-buffer.
  4. Press ? (non-modal: C-h b) to see every key in force. Press C-x o to move into the list, then C-s, type save and RET to find the keys for saving. Close the list with q.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-h kdescribe-keyRead a key sequence and show the command it runs and that command's documentation, the question taken away once the keys are read.
?C-h bdescribe-bindingsList every key binding in effect, keymap by keymap, each followed by the keymaps it falls through to.

8.8 Asking what a command does

C-h x asks for a command by name, with the same list as M-x, and shows the command: what it does, which keys run it and in which file it is defined. You use it when M-x offered a command whose first line was not enough, or when you want to see the keys that a command has so that you can learn them. Every command is offered, including those that belong to other kinds of buffers. The file in the last line is a link. Press RET on it and the source opens beside the help, with the cursor on the definition. A release carries its Lisp sources, so this works in the AppImage and the distribution packages too.

C-h f is the same for any function of Lisp, not just for the commands. It shows the parameters as well. It is for people who write their own commands. In a Lisp buffer it offers the name at the cursor first.

C-h v does the same for a variable. A setting is a variable, so this is how you ask what a setting is for and what it is now. Press C-h v, type *fill-column* and RET, and the help gives the value, 80 as Tuatara comes, and what it is for. A very long value, such as a list of hundreds of items, is cut after a few thousand characters, and says so. For a setting, a line of its own says which values it takes: t, nil for one that is on or off, the words it understands, or a kind of value such as a whole number or text. The description below it says what each value does.

The help is shown in a window of its own, and you stay where you were, in the text. If you would rather be taken to the help, so that you can scroll it, set *help-window-select* to t. q then closes the window and returns you to where you were. Either way q closes a help window when you are in it, and TAB goes from one link to the next, RET following a link.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-h xdescribe-commandShow what a command does, which keys run it and where it is defined, the file a link that shows the definition.
noneC-h fdescribe-functionShow what a function, macro or command does: its parameters, its documentation, the keys that run it when it is a command, and where it is defined, the file a link that shows the definition.
noneC-h vdescribe-variableShow a variable's value and documentation, and where it is defined, the file a link that shows the definition.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*help-window-select*nilt, nilWhether you move to the window a help buffer is shown in (M-x describe-function, M-x describe-key and the rest).
FaceWhat it paints
:help-key-bindingKeys named in help, documentation and messages: those that run a command now.
:buttonA button: text that does something when RET is pressed on it or it is clicked: the source file a command's help names, say.

8.9 Finding a command when you do not know its name

You know what you want, such as turning a line of text into capital letters, but not what it is called. Here are three ways to look.

The first is M-x itself. Type a word that is likely to be in the name and read the list. Words may come in any order, so upper and case together find the commands with both. The list shows the first line of what each one does, which is often enough.

The second is C-h a, apropos. It asks for words and searches both the names and the documentation of every command and setting, which finds things that M-x cannot, because the word you chose is in the help and not in the name. The matches appear in a buffer called *Apropos*, the commands first and then the settings, with the first sentence of each one's help. Each name is a link: RET on it shows its full help, and TAB goes to the next name.

The third is the keys. ? (non-modal: C-h b) lists everything that has a key, and C-c or C-x with a wait shows what a family offers. A command that has a key has usually been put there because it is common.

Try it, to find how to make words capital

  1. Press C-h a, type capital and press RET. The *Apropos* buffer lists the commands and settings that mention capital letters.
  2. Press TAB until a name you like is selected, and RET on it. Its help opens.
  3. Close the help with q, and the list with q again.
  4. Press M-x and type upcase. The list shows the commands that change to upper case, and the keys of those that have one.
  5. Press C-g.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-h aapropos-commandList the commands and variables whose names or documentation match the words typed, in Apropos.

8.10 What a face looks like

A face is a name for a way of drawing text: its colour, whether it is bold, and so on. Chapter 1 explained them. M-x describe-face asks for a face by name and shows all that is known of it: a sample drawn in it, what it colours, what the theme and your init file set for it, the face it inherits from, and each attribute as it is drawn now. M-x list-faces shows every face, grouped by the first word of its name, each with a sample and the first sentence of what it colours. RET on a face in the list shows its full description.

M-x describe-char does the same for a character. It shows its number in Unicode, its name, the bytes it takes in the file, the face it is drawn in and, in a language Tuatara can parse, the part of the code it is in. It is how you find out which of two letters that look alike you have.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x describe-facedescribe-faceShow all that is known of a face: a sample drawn in it, what it colours, its definition, what the theme in force and your init file set for it, the face it inherits from and each of its attributes as it is drawn now.
noneM-x list-faceslist-facesList every face a theme can colour in Faces, in sections by the first word of their names: each face's name, a sample drawn in it as the theme in force draws it, and the first sentence of what it colours.
noneM-x describe-chardescribe-charShow in Help all that is known of the character at point: where it is, its code in decimal, octal and hexadecimal, its Unicode name and kind, its octets and the columns it takes, the face it shows in and the major mode.

8.11 Messages, notifications and the log of what Tuatara says

Tuatara says short things in the echo area, one at a time, and they are gone after a moment. C-h e shows them all in *Messages*, the latest at the end, with repeats counted. It is the first place to look when something went by too fast to read. The buffer keeps the last *message-log-max* lines.

C-h N shows *Notifications*: what was told to you during this session by the agenda, when an entry marked for a reminder came due, and by packages. Each one is a line with the date and time. Each notification is also sent to the desktop by the program that *notify-program* names, notify-send as Tuatara comes. Set it to nil to keep them in the buffer only.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-h eview-echo-area-messagesShow the Messages buffer: the messages shown in the echo area so far, repeats counted, the latest at the end.
noneC-h Nview-notificationsShow Notifications, what was told so far this session, the agenda's entries tagged :notify: as their time came and what packages told, a line each with the date and time it was told and who told it, the latest at the end.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*message-log-max*1000nil, or a whole number, 0 or moreThe lines the Messages buffer keeps of the messages shown.
*notify-program*"notify-send"nil, or textThe program that shows a notification on the desktop.

8.12 The tutor and manual pages

M-x tuatara-tutor opens the tutor, a buffer that teaches the modal keys by making you use them. It is an ordinary buffer with its own instructions. Each lesson tells you what to type and gives a line to practise on, marked with an arrow, and the keys it names are the keys you really have, even if you moved them. You edit the tutor as it says, and nothing you do in it is saved. Half an hour with it is the quickest way to get used to the two states. The page *About Tuatara* below has a button that opens it.

The system's own manual pages, the ones that explain programs such as ls or grep in a terminal, can be read in Tuatara. M-x man asks for a name, as in ls, ls(1) or 1 ls, and lists the names of the pages the system has as you type. The page opens read-only in a window of its own, laid out for the width of the window, with its headings, bold text and underlined text drawn in faces. Every mention of another page, such as chmod(1), is a link. RET or l follows it, TAB goes to the next link, and h comes back to the page you came from. n and p go to the next and the previous section, r lays the page out again if you changed the size of the window, and q closes it.

If you open the source of a page, a file such as tool.1, M-x man offers that file first, so that you can see what you wrote as it will look.

The page is made by the system's man and groff, run with no network and none of your files, and it is in English. If they are not installed, M-x check-health says so.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x tuatara-tutortuatara-tutorOpen the tutor: an ordinary buffer holding its own lessons, to learn the modal keys by editing it as it says, with every key the one you have.
noneM-x manmanShow a manual page in a buffer of its own, read-only: ask for it by name (ls), with its section (ls(1)) or by section and name (1 ls), completing on the names of the pages the system has.
nonen, C-c nman-next-sectionGo to the start of the next section heading of the manual page.
nonep, C-c pman-previous-sectionGo to the start of the section heading before the line point is on.
noneh, C-c hman-backShow the page a link was followed from; close the window when this page was not reached by a link.

8.13 About Tuatara and what is there

C-h C-a opens =*About Tuatara*, the page that introduces the editor. It says which version you have, who wrote it and under which licence, where its ideas came from, where the sources are and where to report a fault, and it has buttons for the ways in: the tutor, the help keys of this chapter, your init file and the health check. TAB and S-TAB go from one button to the next, RET presses one, and a click does too. Opening a web address from it asks first and uses your desktop's browser.

C-h C-c shows the licence, the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later, and C-h C-w the part of it that says there is no warranty. M-x credits shows the projects that Tuatara owes its ideas to and what it took from each. M-x tuatara-version says which Tuatara this is: the version, the commit and date it was built from, the Steel Bank Common Lisp (SBCL) it runs on and whether it shows in a window or a terminal. With C-u it writes the line at the cursor instead of saying it, which is useful in a report of a fault.

noneC-h C-aabout-tuataraShow About Tuatara, the page that introduces Tuatara.
noneC-h C-cdescribe-copyingShow the license Tuatara comes under.
noneC-h C-wdescribe-no-warrantyShow the part of the license that says Tuatara comes with no warranty.
noneM-x creditscreditsShow where Tuatara's ideas come from: the projects it owes, and what it took from each.

8.14 Checking what your system has

Tuatara uses a few programs outside itself: for example, the sandbox that protects it when it opens a file you do not trust, the programs that read PDFs and Office files, and GnuPG for encryption. It also loads a grammar for each programming language it colours and indents. M-x check-health reports what is there and what is not. It runs in the background, because some of it takes a moment, and shows *Health* when it is ready. The top of the report says where your init file is and what the sandbox and the programs need. A cross beside a program the editor needs is a problem, and the message says how to get it. A fainter cross beside a program that only adds a feature says what the feature needs, and is nothing to worry about. Further down, a table has a row for each language, with a tick when its colours, indentation and selections work, and then the major modes and the files they take. In a window, the report also measures how quickly each way of drawing is on your machine and which is faster.

In the report r checks again and q closes it. Run it first when something does not work, and send it with a report of a fault.

If a command fails and you want to see why, M-x debug-mode keeps a record of what the editor does: commands with their keys, background jobs, files parsed and errors. C-h E shows it in *Debug*. The same lines go to a file that survives a crash, so that it can be read afterwards. Debug in the mode line says it is on, and M-x debug-mode again turns it off. *debug-mode* set to t turns it on when Tuatara starts, and *debug-log-limit* is how many lines *Debug* keeps.

noneM-x check-healthcheck-healthShow what each language and major mode has here.
noneM-x debug-modedebug-modeSwitch debug mode on or off.
noneC-h Eview-debug-bufferShow Debug, the reports of debug mode (M-x debug-mode), where Messages is shown, its end in sight.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*debug-mode*nilt, nilWhether the editor starts with debug mode on, as M-x debug-mode switches it.
*debug-log-limit*10000nil, or a whole number, 1 or moreThe lines Debug keeps, the oldest going first.

8.15 Lisp in the running editor

Tuatara is written in Common Lisp, and the Lisp you type runs inside the editor. This is how an init file works. It is also a calculator, a way to look at a value and a way to try something small. You do not need Lisp for any other chapter, so you may skip this part.

M-: asks for one Lisp expression in the minibuffer and shows its value, in any buffer. M-: (+ 2 3) RET shows 5. In a Lisp buffer, such as *lisp-scratch* (chapter 7) or a file that ends in .lisp, C-x C-e runs the expression before the cursor, C-j puts what it printed on the lines after it, and C-M-x runs the whole top-level form the cursor is in. M-x eval-region runs the selection, and M-x eval-buffer runs the whole buffer. They run only in Lisp buffers, and run nothing in a file opened with care because you do not trust it.

M-x ielm opens *ielm*, a buffer with a prompt where you type Lisp and read the answer below. RET runs the input when it is whole expressions and starts a new line when it is not. M-p and M-n bring back earlier inputs, and C-c C-u clears what you typed. The modal keys are off in it, so you type at once without i.

If Lisp meets an error, the echo area says what it was. M-x toggle-debug-on-error makes it show the calls under way too, in *Backtrace*. That is for people who write Lisp, and is easy to leave off.

Try it, with a sum

  1. Press M-:, type (* 12 7) and press RET. The echo area shows (* 12 7) => 84, then the same number in other bases.
  2. Press M-x, type ielm and press RET. After the prompt type (reverse "kiwi") and press RET. The answer is "iwik".
  3. Press M-p. The input comes back. Press C-c C-u to take it away.
  4. Press C-x k and RET to close *ielm*. It has changed, so it asks; type y and press RET.

8.16 Binding keys yourself

The prefixes, the leader and the labels that the key hints show are yours to set. You can bind a key to any command, and give it a label that the hints show in place of the command's name, in your init file. That is described in chapter 20, together with the settings that move the leader.

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*leader-key*"SPC"textThe key that opens the leader's keys (bind-key's :map :leader) in NORMAL and support states, in lists and in the calendar.
*modal-editing*tt, nilWhether Tuatara's modal editing is on: NORMAL and INSERT states in editing buffers, NORMAL's reading keys in support buffers, the leader on SPC.

Files

Opening, saving and keeping track of the files on your disk and on other machines, and keeping private ones encrypted.

Chapter 1 explained that Tuatara shows a file in a buffer: a copy of the text that you change freely, kept apart from the file until you save. This chapter is about the file end of that. It shows how to open a file, how to make a new one, and what happens when you save. It explains what to do when the file has changed on disk behind your back, and how to give a file a new name. It also covers the way Tuatara handles line endings and letters from other languages, the file names that say what a file holds, files that live on another machine, and files you keep encrypted so that nobody else can read them. It ends with the ways of opening a file from outside Tuatara: with another program, and from the command line.

The directories that hold files are the subject of chapter 10, and very large files of chapter 11. Files from a source you do not trust are in chapter 12. The list of recent files, bookmarks and auto-save are in chapter 7.

Every key in this chapter is pressed in NORMAL state unless it starts with C-x, which works in both states. i starts INSERT state, and C-g or ESC brings you back.

9.1 Opening a file

C-x C-f asks for a file name at the bottom of the screen. The question has a directory filled in, and a list of what is in it. Type to narrow the list, and press RET to open what you have chosen. If the name is a directory, you go into it and the list shows what it holds. The question starts in the directory of the last file or directory you chose, so when you work on one project you seldom type more than the end of a name. S-TAB puts your home directory, ~/, in place of what is typed, and lists it. Typing ~/ after a directory does the same, starting the path again from home.

Beside each file the list shows its permissions, its size and when it last changed. Where a file is one you opened safely before, the list marks it, and a buffer with changes you have not saved is marked as well.

Opening a file you already have open does not make a second buffer. It takes you to the first. This holds for a file reached by two names, such as a link and the file it leads to.

If the name you typed is not there, you get a new, empty file with that name. Nothing is written yet. The next section says more.

Opening is quick even when the file is large, because Tuatara reads files in the background. A very large file is opened in a special way, described in chapter 11.

9.1.1 Other places to open a file

C-x 4 f opens the file in another window and goes there, so you can read two files side by side. C-x 5 f opens it in another frame, a window of its own, which chapter 1 described. C-x C-p opens the file whose name is written in the text, such as ~/letters/council.txt in a note. A directory written there opens as a list of its files.

When Tuatara runs in a window of its own, you can also drag files from your file manager and drop them on it. Each one opens in the window it was dropped on. If you want these opened safely, which is the careful way described in chapter 12, set *open-dropped-files-safely*. With C-u before C-x C-f a file opens safely too. M-x find-file-safely does the same.

*last-used-first* is t. The questions that ask for a file or a directory then start in the directory you chose from last time, whichever of them it was, and list first what you chose there. If you opened ~/letters/council.txt, the next C-x C-f starts in ~/letters/, with council.txt at the top. Directories come before files either way. A file opened safely is never remembered. To start in the directory of the buffer you are in, as many editors do:

(setf *last-used-first* nil)

M-x show-file-name says in the echo area which file the buffer you are in shows, with its directory. You use it when two files have the same name and you want to be sure which one this is.

C-x C-f and the other ways above take the file name as you type it. A name starting with /ssh: is a file on another machine, described later in this chapter.

9.1.2 The file's own settings

A file can say how it should be shown. The first line of a program, for instance, may hold -*- mode: org -*- to say that it is an Org file, or a block of lines near its end may set the width of a tab. Tuatara reads those settings when it opens the file, unless you turn off *file-local-variables*. You will meet this in files written for Emacs. It is of no use to you until you see it.
