9.1.3 Seeing a file before you choose it

With *preview-files* set to t, the question for a file shows the file under the cursor in the window beside it while you move through the list. The file is opened safely, so nothing in it is acted on, and the preview goes away when you answer. It helps when you have several files with names like letter-2.txt and letter-3.txt. It is off until you turn it on.

Try it, with a letter

  1. Press C-x C-f. The question shows a directory. Type ~/letters/ and the list shows what is in the directory, or nothing if it is not there yet.
  2. Type council.txt and press RET. The buffer is empty and the echo area says it is a new file. If ~/letters/ does not exist yet, it says that its directory is not there and that saving asks to make it.
  3. Press i, type Dear Mr Taupo, and press C-g. The mode line shows [*], which means changes not saved.
  4. Leave the buffer as it is. You will save it in the next section.

9.2 Creating a file

You do not make a file by a separate command. You open one with a name that is not there. The buffer is empty and nothing exists on disk until you save. That suits a letter or a note: open the name, type, save, or throw the buffer away.

If the directory you named does not exist either, the echo area says so when you open the file, and saving asks The directory ... is not there; make it? with a single key. y makes the directory and saves. n stops and writes nothing. You can name a file three directories deep in one go this way. If Tuatara cannot make the directory, because you may not write where it would go, the buffer is read-only and the message says why.

A name that says a file is encrypted but is not encrypted by GnuPG, for instance one ending .age, is refused when you save it, because the text would be there to read. Names that end .gpg are encrypted every time they are saved. The file gets the permissions your account normally gives a new file. A directory listing, chapter 10, can show a file's permissions.

9.3 Saving

C-x C-s saves the buffer to its file. The echo area says Wrote and the file's name, and the mode line goes from [*] to [-]. If there is nothing to save, it says (No changes need to be saved) and writes nothing. A buffer with no file asks where to put it, in the same way as C-x C-f asks.

Chapter 7 described C-x s, which saves every file with changes after one question, and C-x C-c, which asks before it leaves.

9.3.1 What a save does with your file

Tuatara never edits the file in place. A save writes the whole text to a new file beside the old one. It gives the new file the owner and the permissions of the old one, and makes sure the text is on the disk, then renames the new file over the old one. The file on disk is always either the old one or the new one, even after a power cut, and a save that fails halfway leaves nothing behind.

There is no backup copy, so you will find no letter.txt~ next to letter.txt. The safety net for a crash is the auto-saved copy of chapter 7, and the safety net for a mistake is undo. A rewritten file is easier to see than a backup would be, since Tuatara asks before it writes over a file that changed behind its back.

A few files cannot be replaced by a new file without losing something. These are files with more than one name (hard links), files whose owner or group your account cannot give to a new file, and a few special files that the system makes up. Tuatara writes these in place, after copying the old text to a spare copy of its own. If the write fails, the spare copy is kept and its name is said.

9.3.2 When a save asks first

A save asks a question before it does something you may not want. It asks if:

  • the file was changed on disk after you opened it, as council.txt changed on disk since it was read; overwrite it with this buffer?. Say n and read the other version first, as described later in this chapter;
  • the file is write-protected: File ... is write-protected; try to save anyway?;
  • you save as a name that is already a file: ... exists; overwrite it?;
  • you save as a name that another buffer has open. Tuatara offers to write over it and kill that buffer.

A question that cannot be undone, such as writing over a file that exists, is answered by typing yes or no and pressing RET. This is the same as for leaving with changes unsaved, described in chapter 1.

A large buffer takes time to write. If the save takes longer than half a second, Tuatara carries on in the background and the mode line shows Saving and a percentage. You can keep typing. Leaving Tuatara waits for saves still running. *save-in-place* is for very large files, which chapter 11 explains.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x C-ssave-bufferSave the current buffer to its file, asking for one if it has none, as C-x C-f asks.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*save-in-place*nilt, nilWhether a large file is saved by writing only what changed into the file itself, where that is quicker than writing it whole.

9.4 Save as, and a new name

C-x C-w writes the buffer to another file. The question works like the one for C-x C-f, and starts in the directory of the file you are in, with the name to change. After the save, the buffer is the new file. The old file stays as it was, which makes C-x C-w the way to copy a file: open it, press C-x C-w, and give the copy a name.

M-x rename-visited-file gives the file itself a new name, and the buffer follows it. The question offers the old name to edit. A name alone keeps the file in its directory. A path, such as ~/letters/sent/council.txt, moves it there, provided that is on the same drive. Use this when you named a file in a hurry. The file on another machine is the exception: this command leaves that file where it is.

Try it, with a letter

  1. In the letter from the previous try, press C-x C-s. If ~/letters/ is not there yet, the echo area asks whether to make it: press y. It then says Wrote ~/letters/council.txt, and the mode line shows [-].
  2. Press C-x C-s again. It says (No changes need to be saved).
  3. Press C-x C-w. The prompt offers the directory. Type ~/letters/thanks.txt, which takes its place, and press RET. The buffer is thanks.txt now, and council.txt is as you saved it.
  4. Run M-x rename-visited-file. The old name is offered. Change it to thanks-to-aroha.txt and press RET. The echo area says it was renamed, and thanks.txt is gone from the directory.
  5. Press C-x C-b. The buffer list shows the new name and its path.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x C-wwrite-fileWrite the current buffer to another file, asked for as C-x C-f asks (C-x C-w), from the directory of the path chosen last in a question for a path, else the buffer's own directory.
noneM-x rename-visited-filerename-visited-fileGive the file the current buffer visits a new name, asked for, its own offered to change: a name alone keeps it in its directory, a path (~/notes/a.org, ../a.org) moves it there on the same drive.

9.5 Read-only files and buffers

A buffer is read-only when you cannot change its text. Tuatara makes a file's buffer read-only when your account may not write the file, and the mode line shows [%]. You can still look at it, search it and copy from it. A key that would change the text is refused.

C-x C-q turns read-only on and off for the buffer you are in. Use it to guard a file that you are only reading, so that a stray key does no harm, or to make a read-only buffer editable when you know the file will let you save. A number before the key sets it: a positive number makes the buffer read-only and zero or a negative number makes it editable.

If you turn read-only off in a file you may not write, the save still asks File ... is write-protected; try to save anyway? and the system may refuse.

A file opened safely is read-only too, and so are files in evidence directories. Those are the subject of chapter 12.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x C-qread-only-modeMake the current buffer read-only, or editable again if it is; with a count, read-only when it is positive, editable when it is zero or less.
noneM-x end-safe-visitend-safe-visitOpen the file of this buffer, opened safely, as usual from now on, where it is.

9.6 The file changed on disk

Another program may change a file you have open. A build may rewrite it, a program may add to a log, or a copy may arrive from another machine. Tuatara watches the files that you have open and tells you. The echo area and the mode line say Changed on disk, Deleted on disk or Stale, read-only. The last word means that the file was rewritten while it was shown from the disk, so the text on the screen is no longer what the file holds, and the buffer is read-only until you read the file again.

In every case Tuatara asks before it does anything to your text. A file that was changed on disk and a buffer with changes of your own are two versions of the same file, and you choose which to keep.

9.6.1 Reading it again

M-x revert-buffer reads the file again and replaces the text in the buffer. It asks first when the buffer has changes you have not saved. The reading is one step in the undo history, so C-/ (modal: u) takes it back if you made a mistake. Point and the window stay on the same text, so you do not lose your place. If the file only grew, only the new part is added.

Opening the file again, with C-x C-f or with RET in a list such as the git status, also reads it again when its buffer has no changes of your own. With changes of your own the buffer is left as it is, and the echo area says so. A buffer that M-x follow-file stopped following is not read again, and a file deleted on disk is said.

In a buffer that Tuatara made for you, such as a list of buffers, r reads it again from what it shows. g r does the same. This is how a list is brought up to date. The buffer list does it by itself.

If you want to see how the two versions differ before you choose, use M-x diff-files, which compares the file with another one you name, or a copy you saved under another name with C-x C-w.

9.6.2 Keeping up by itself

Some files are meant to change under you: a log that a program is writing, or a build's output. For those you want the buffer to follow the file. M-x follow-file turns that on for the buffer you are in. What a program adds to the end of the file is added to your buffer as it arrives, and if point is at the end, it stays at the end, as tail -f does in a terminal. A file that is rewritten is read again, if you have no changes of your own. The mode line says Following while it is on. Run the command again to stop.

*reload-changed-files* does the same for every buffer. It is off as standard, because most of the time you do not want the text to move under you. With it on, a file that changed on disk while you have unsaved changes of your own is not read again, since that would lose them. Tuatara says so, and you decide with M-x revert-buffer, which takes the file's version, or C-x C-s, which writes yours over it.

Try it, with a recipe

  1. Open ~/recipe.txt, type Pikelets: 1 cup flour, 1 egg, milk and RET, so that the line has its end, and save with C-x C-s.
  2. In a terminal, run echo "Add a pinch of salt" >> ~/recipe.txt.
  3. Go back to Tuatara. The echo area, and the mode line, say that recipe.txt changed on disk, and that M-x revert-buffer reads it again.
  4. Run M-x revert-buffer. The new line is there. Press C-/ (modal: u) and it is gone again, since a revert is one step of undo. Press M-_ (modal: U) to bring it back.
  5. Run M-x follow-file. The mode line says Following. Run echo "Serve warm" >> ~/recipe.txt in the terminal again. The line appears in Tuatara at once, with no command from you.
  6. Run M-x follow-file again to stop.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noner, g r, C-c rrevert-bufferRead the current buffer's file again, replacing its text: one step that undo takes back, unless the text could no longer be trusted (then the history goes too).
noneM-x follow-filefollow-fileKeep the current buffer up with its file on disk, or stop.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*reload-changed-files*nilt, nilWhether every buffer keeps up with its file on disk by itself.

9.7 Line endings and letters from other languages

9.7.1 Line endings

A line in a text file ends with a code. Unix and Linux write one character, a newline. Windows writes two, a carriage return and a newline. Very old Macintosh files used a carriage return alone. You rarely see the difference until you open a file from another system.

Tuatara looks at the first line end in a file and keeps to it. A file of Windows lines shows CRLF in the mode line, and one of carriage return lines shows CR. A file of plain newlines shows nothing, since that is the normal case. When you press RET, or paste text, the new line ends the same way as the rest of the file. A save writes every line end as it was read, so opening and saving a Windows file does not turn it into a Unix file, and does not change the lines you did not touch.

In a file whose lines end with a newline, a stray carriage return before the newline shows as ^M. That is how a file of mixed endings shows where it is mixed. A carriage return that stands alone ends a line and shows no mark.

Line numbers, searching, sorting and every other command count lines the same way, whatever the endings. A search for ^ or $ matches at every line end.

9.7.2 Letters from other languages

Tuatara works in UTF-8, the way of writing letters that nearly all modern files use. It holds accented letters, letters of other alphabets and emoji, and it saves them back as they were.

There is no setting for the encoding of a file, and no command to change it. If a file is not UTF-8, Tuatara does not stop. Every part that is not valid UTF-8 is kept as a character of its own, shown as \xE9 for the octet E9, and is written back to the file exactly as it was. A letter with an accent in an old file in the Latin-1 encoding is such a case. You see \xE9 where you would expect an e with an accent, and you can edit around it, but the file is not changed by opening and saving it. If you need to turn such a file into UTF-8, use a tool such as iconv outside Tuatara.

A file that begins with a UTF-8 byte order mark opens normally. The mark is kept when you save.

A setting described in chapter 12 shows characters that draw nothing as their codes, in files opened safely. It helps you find what a file hides.

9.8 Files with formatted names

A file name that says what the file holds is easy to find a year later. A formatted name has three parts: the moment it was made, a title, and some keywords. The scheme follows Denote, a package for Emacs, so such names read the same in both editors.

The identifier is the year, month and day, a T, then the hour, minute and second, so a directory of such names sorts by age by itself. Two dashes follow, then the title in small letters with hyphens between the words. Two underscores begin the keywords, which are joined by single underscores. The file's extension ends the name: .org, .txt or .md.

You keep all such files under one directory, set by *formatted-file-directory*. It is your home directory until you set it. A good place is a directory of notes:

(setf *formatted-file-directory* "~/notes/")

9.8.1 Making and finding

C-x n n makes a new file. It asks for a title, a subdirectory, some keywords and the kind of file, in that order. The keywords you used before are offered. Press RET with nothing typed to skip a question. The new buffer is named from what you answered, and begins with a header for its kind, holding the title, the date, the keywords and the identifier. Nothing is written until you save with C-x C-s. The date and identifier are those of the moment you asked, not of the moment you saved.

C-x n o opens one of your files by any part of its name. The list is grouped by kind, newest first, and shows each name as its date, its title and its keywords, with the size and when it changed on the right. You type a few letters of the title or a keyword, and RET opens the best match. The preview of *preview-formatted-files* works here as it does for C-x C-f.

C-x n f is C-x C-f for such files. It opens a file by its path, and if the name you type is not there, it makes a new file with a formatted name in the directory you typed. It asks for the title and the keywords, and for the end of the name, which you can have filled in by *formatted-file-extension*.

9.8.2 Renaming

You can give an old file a formatted name. C-x n r asks for a title and keywords, offering the ones the file already has, and renames the file. The identifier is kept if the file has one, or made from the time the file last changed. The extension is kept. A buffer that shows the file follows the new name, and the list of recent files is updated.

C-x n k changes only the keywords. It keeps the titles and asks once for new keywords, which it gives to the file, or to every marked file when you use it in a directory listing. Use it to put a whole month of letters under done.

Try it, with some notes

  1. Add (setf *formatted-file-directory* "~/notes/") to your init file and run it, or restart Tuatara. Make the directory in a terminal with mkdir ~/notes.
  2. Press C-x n n. Answer the title with Pikelets for Sunday, the directory with RET, the keywords with recipe, house and RET twice, and the kind with RET for Org.
  3. The buffer is named like 20261109T091500--pikelets-for-sunday__house_recipe.org. The keywords are in alphabetical order. Press C-x C-s.
  4. Press C-x n o, type pike and RET. You are back in the file.
  5. Press C-x n k, type recipe, sunday and press RET twice. The name now ends __recipe_sunday.org, the header is changed to match, and the buffer follows.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x n ffind-file-formattedVisit a file, or make a new one with a formatted name.
noneC-x n oopen-file-formattedOpen one of your files with formatted names, those in FORMATTED-FILE-DIRECTORY and its subdirectories, choosing among them by any part of the name: listed under their subdirectory or their kind, the ones changed last first, each as its date, its title and its keywords, with its size and when it changed at the right.
noneC-x n nnew-file-formattedMake a new file with a formatted name in FORMATTED-FILE-DIRECTORY: asks what FORMATTED-FILE-PROMPTS says (as standard the title, the subdirectory, the keywords, the kind of file and the template), and names it as find-file-formatted does, with the header for its kind.
noneC-x n rrename-formattedGive a file a formatted name: its identifier kept, or made from when it was last changed; a title and keywords asked for, the file's own offered; its extension kept.
noneC-x n krename-formatted-keywordsGive files formatted names with other keywords, their titles kept, asked for once for them all: the current buffer's file, or in a list of a directory the marked files or the one on the line.

The other commands that work on these files, such as searching their text and writing links between them, are described with Org in chapter 14.

9.8.3 Settings for new files

*formatted-file-keywords* lists keywords to offer when you make a file, in addition to those already in the names of your files. It is empty as standard. A list of your own saves typing the same words again:

(setf *formatted-file-keywords* '("project" "garden" "house"))

*formatted-file-sort-keywords* is t as standard, which is why house, recipe came out as __house_recipe above whatever the order you typed. With nil the keywords stay as you gave them, so recipe, house gives __recipe_house:

(setf *formatted-file-sort-keywords* nil)

*formatted-file-prompts* is the list of questions C-x n n asks, in the order of the list. The five it knows are :title, :subdirectory, :keywords, :file-type and :template. The last asks for one of your note templates, or a blank file, and only when you have templates. A question left out is not asked. To ask for the title and the keywords only:

(setf *formatted-file-prompts* '(:title :keywords))

*formatted-file-type* is the kind of file made when the list does not ask for :file-type, and the one offered first when it does. It is :org as standard. The other kinds that come with Tuatara are :text (a .txt file), :markdown (a .md file) and the same three ending in -encrypted (.gpg, encrypted when saved). To make Markdown notes without being asked:

(setf *formatted-file-prompts* '(:title :keywords))
(setf *formatted-file-type* :markdown)

*formatted-file-types* is the list of kinds. Each entry has four parts: the kind's name, the end of the file's name, the style in which its header writes the date and keywords (:org, :text or :markdown), and the header a new file begins with. In the header, {title}, {date}, {keywords} and {identifier} stand for the file's own. To add a kind for plain notes ending in .note, with a short header:

(setf *formatted-file-types*
      (append *formatted-file-types*
              (list (list :note ".note" :text
                          (format nil "{title}~%{date}~2%")))))

A name ending in .age is refused. To change the header of a kind that exists, use set-formatted-file-header in the init file.

9.9 Files on another machine

A file on a server can be opened as if it were here. Write the machine's name in front of the path, between /ssh: and a colon. The name is the one you give to ssh: a plain name, me@pinetree, or a name from your ~/.ssh/config.

C-x C-f /ssh:pinetree:/etc/hosts RET

Nothing has to be installed on the server. Tuatara uses the file protocol that every ssh server offers, through the ssh program already on your computer, with your own keys. It sends nothing else to the machine: it runs no commands there. Everything is done in the background, so Tuatara never waits for a slow connection.

This is not the daemon of chapter 18, which runs the whole editor on the other machine. Here Tuatara runs on your computer, and only the files are elsewhere.

Typing /ssh:pinetree:/etc/ offers the names in that directory, as for a directory on your own computer. /ssh:pinetree: alone is your home directory there. A file from a server opens as a local file does: a picture is drawn, and a PDF shows its pages. Any other file that is not text opens as octets, in the hex view.

9.9.1 Saving

C-x C-s saves as usual. The text goes to a new file beside the one on the server, which takes the old file's owner, group and permissions, and takes its place only when the file there is still as you read it. If somebody changed it meanwhile, the echo area says the file was not written, since it was changed on the server since it was read. The buffer stays as it is, so nothing is lost. M-x revert-buffer reads the server's version, and then you can copy your changes over it. A new name is a new file on the server when you save.

A file with more than one name, or one whose owner a new file cannot be given, is written in place, and the echo area says so. If such a write fails halfway, the file there is partly written. The buffer keeps your text, and the next save asks whether to write it over, whatever the file now holds. Answer yes to write it whole.

Tuatara keeps the file you work on as a copy under ~/.cache/tuatara/remote/, which only you can read. The copy is deleted when you kill the buffer. A file on another machine has no git marks, no language server, no auto-saved copy and no build, since those would read what is around the file, and what is around it is not here. A file's own settings are taken only from a machine you trust, listed by M-x server-list, chapter 18. Each request has *remote-seconds* to be answered, 30 as standard. Past that, the work in hand fails and says so.

9.9.2 The first time you meet a machine

When ssh meets a machine for the first time it asks if you trust it. Tuatara asks the same question. While the question is open, a buffer below the windows shows ssh's own words in full, with the fingerprint of the machine's key. At the bottom is a short prompt for your answer. Completing a file name as you type never asks anything. The question comes when you press RET. If a connection takes more than a second, the echo area says Connecting to pinetree... until it is made or has failed.

Compare the fingerprint with one you got from whoever runs the server. Then type yes and press RET. You can type the fingerprint instead. Anything else refuses, a plain y as well. A key that has changed since ssh last saw it is never offered. ssh refuses the connection, and the echo area says the key differs from the one ssh knows. That is the sign of a machine that has been replaced, or of one pretending to be it. Ask the person who runs the server.

9.9.3 Passwords

If your key is in your ssh agent, nothing is asked. A key with a passphrase is asked for once, at a prompt saying it stays here, on your computer. If you log in with a password, the prompt says the server asks, and that what you type goes to the server. A jump host, if you use one, is named. What you type shows as stars, and is passed to ssh and kept nowhere else: not in a history, not in a recorded macro, and not in a log.

To paste a password from a password manager, copy it there and press C-y in the prompt. In a terminal, the paste of the terminal works too. The password is not put in the kill ring. C-g gives the question up, and the connection fails with a message that the question was not answered. Nothing is left running.

9.9.4 Directories and previews on a server

C-x C-f /ssh:pinetree:/srv/notes/ RET, or C-x d with that name, lists the directory as one is listed on your computer. Chapter 10 describes the list. What would read many files, or keep watching them, is left out on a server: there is no git column and no directory size, and the list is read again after each change you make, not as files change.

A preview shows each file beside the list as you move. On a server each file must come to your computer first, so the preview starts off. P in the list turns it on, and moving to another file stops the transfer under way. A file larger than *remote-preview-size-limit* is not fetched, and the preview says it is too large. The standard is 20 million octets. RET still opens it. Files in evidence directories are not read for a preview, and a list opened safely has no preview.

A server keeps no trash. A file deleted there is deleted for good, and the list says so in its question.

Evidence directories may be on a server as well. An entry of *evidence-directories* may name a directory there, and files in it open safely and are never saved. Chapter 12 describes it.

Try it, with notes on a server called pinetree

These steps need a machine you can reach with ssh. Use your own name for pinetree.

  1. In a terminal, run ssh pinetree once, so you know the login works. Leave it again with exit.
  2. In Tuatara, press C-x C-f and type /ssh:pinetree:. Your home directory there is offered. Add notes.txt and press RET. The buffer is empty.
  3. Press i, type Sheep: 41 counted on Friday and press C-g. Press C-x C-s. The echo area says Wrote /ssh:pinetree:notes.txt.
  4. In another terminal, run ssh pinetree 'echo "Gate fixed" >> notes.txt'. Back in Tuatara, press i, type x and press C-g, then C-x C-s. The echo area says the file changed on the server since it was read and was not written. Your buffer is unchanged.
  5. Run M-x revert-buffer. The line Gate fixed is there.
  6. Press C-x d and type /ssh:pinetree:, then RET. Your home directory opens as a list. Move to notes.txt and press P to see it beside the list.
  7. If you wish, press C-x k on the buffer. The private copy on your computer is deleted, and the file on pinetree is as you saved it.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneP, C-c Plist-toggle-previewTurn the preview beside this list on or off: the entry on the current line shown in a window beside the list, on its right when there is room, else below it, following the cursor from line to line.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*remote-seconds*30a number, 0 or moreSeconds a server reached for its files (/ssh:HOST:/path) has to answer each request, and ssh to connect.
*remote-preview-size-limit*20000000a whole number, 0 or moreThe most octets a file on another machine may hold to be shown in the preview of its list (M-x list-toggle-preview).

9.10 Encrypted files

Some of your own files should be read by nobody else. Tuatara uses GnuPG (the program gpg) to encrypt and sign them. Encrypting turns text into something that only a key or a passphrase can turn back. Signing adds a mark that shows who wrote a file and that it has not been changed since.

9.10.1 A file that ends in .gpg

A file whose name ends in .gpg opens decrypted. The text on disk stays encrypted. The decrypted text lives in memory only. It is never auto-saved, and it is not placed on the system clipboard unless you ask for that. Each save encrypts it again. If the file is encrypted to a passphrase and not to a key, gpg-agent's prompt asks at once. When the minibuffer is what asks (next section), the buffer waits until you press RET first. M-x gpg-decrypt-with-passphrase is the same.

Whom a file is encrypted to is a choice for each save. M-x gpg-choose-encryption-keys chooses again, between keys and a passphrase, and the next save uses the new choice. M-x gpg-lock makes gpg-agent forget every passphrase it keeps, so the next file you open asks again. It does not close buffers you already have open: kill those too, if you want their text gone from memory.

When gpg will not encrypt to a key, the save fails and the echo area says why: the key has expired, is revoked, or is not among your keys. A key you trust that gpg does not yet count as valid is common on a second machine, after the key was brought over: the message names gpg --check-trustdb, which counts the trust again, and gpg --edit-key KEY trust, which sets it.

9.10.2 The passphrase prompt

Who asks for the passphrase is the setting *gpg-passphrase-from*. As it comes (:auto), gpg-agent's own window asks on a desktop, its prompt in the terminal asks if Tuatara runs in one, and the minibuffer asks last. Either of the first two keeps the passphrase out of Tuatara altogether. The minibuffer is the fallback. It shows stars as you type, and the passphrase then passes through the editor. Each character is wiped from memory as it is typed or deleted, and at once if you give up with C-g. Still, the editor's memory is not locked, a look-alike program could ask in its place, and the garbage collector may have copied text before it was wiped. So when the minibuffer asks, a window above it says what that risks. *gpg-loopback-warning* is true as it comes. Turn it off only when you know the risks by heart.

Which gpg runs is not left to chance. Tuatara runs the program found in the system's own directories (/usr/local/bin, /usr/bin, /bin), never one that a directory on your PATH might hold. *gpg-program* names a different one, by a full path from the root. Before each run Tuatara also checks that the directory gpg takes its keys and options from (~/.gnupg, or the directory GNUPGHOME names) is yours, is not a link, and cannot be written by others. If the check fails, gpg is not run, and the message says which directory is wrong and why.

9.10.3 Encrypting and decrypting

M-x gpg-encrypt-file encrypts the file shown, or the one on the line of a directory list, into FILE.gpg. It asks whom to encrypt to in the minibuffer: your keys, or a passphrase, with commas between several. It then offers to wipe the original. Say no if you are not sure, since a wiped file cannot be recovered and a solid state disk may keep old copies anyway. M-x wipe-file does that wipe by itself. M-x gpg-decrypt-file writes a decrypted copy to a file you name, after warning you that its text is then on disk. To read an encrypted file, open the .gpg file instead.

You can also encrypt part of a buffer. Select some text and use M-x gpg-encrypt-region. The text becomes a block that starts with -----BEGIN PGP MESSAGE-----. This is useful for one paragraph of a note that you still want to share as plain text. M-x gpg-decrypt-region turns the block under the cursor, or the nearest one, back into text in place. The buffer is then kept from the disk as an encrypted file is: no auto-save, no clipboard. A save asks before writing the decrypted text unencrypted, so a habit of pressing C-x C-s does not leave it on the disk.

M-x gpg-copy-to-clipboard is the one way out. It puts the text you copied last on the system clipboard, even if it came from an encrypted file. Other programs, and clipboard managers, can read it and keep it.

9.10.4 Signing and checking

M-x gpg-sign-file signs a file with your key. It asks which kind: a detached signature, FILE.sig, which leaves the file as it is; clear-signed text, FILE.asc; or a signed file, FILE.gpg. M-x gpg-sign-region clear-signs the selected text in place. M-x gpg-verify-file and M-x gpg-verify-region check a signature. They say who signed, when, and how far that key is trusted.

Read the answer for what it says. A good signature tells you the text has not changed since that key signed it. It does not tell you the text is safe, and it tells you who signed only as far as you trust the key.

9.10.5 Keys

M-x gpg-list-keys opens a list of your keys and those you have of others. The list fills in as gpg answers. M-x gpg-keys-details shows one key's fingerprint, names and expiry. M-x gpg-import-keys and M-x gpg-import-keys-region add keys from a file or from selected text. M-x gpg-keys-export writes the public part of marked keys to a file, and M-x gpg-keys-insert puts it at the cursor in the buffer the list was opened from. The directory list (chapter 10) has keys for the same jobs on files.

Try it, with an encrypted note

  1. In a terminal, make a note: printf 'The alarm code is 4411.\n' > ~/code.txt.
  2. Open it with C-x C-f. Press M-x gpg-encrypt-file and RET. Choose a passphrase, press RET for no more, and give a passphrase twice. When it asks about wiping the original, answer n.
  3. Open ~/code.txt.gpg with C-x C-f. Give the passphrase if asked; gpg-agent may still hold it. The text appears. No auto-save copy of it is made.
  4. Press i, add a line, press C-g and C-x C-s. Give the passphrase twice. The file on disk is encrypted again. In a terminal, cat ~/code.txt.gpg shows nothing readable.
  5. Press M-x gpg-lock, kill the buffer with C-x k and open the file again. You are asked for the passphrase once more.
  6. Open ~/code.txt and select its line. Press M-x gpg-encrypt-region, choose a passphrase and give it twice. The line becomes a block. Put the cursor in it and press M-x gpg-decrypt-region. Press C-x C-s: Tuatara asks whether to save the text decrypted. Answer n and press RET.

9.11 Opening a file with another program

Tuatara shows text, and also pictures, PDFs and some office documents. There is work it does not do, such as printing, filling in a PDF form, or playing a video. For that you can hand the file to the program your desktop uses for that kind of file. O does it in a directory listing, in a picture and in a PDF's view, and M-x open-externally does it for the file of the buffer you are in. Tuatara runs xdg-open, the command desktops provide for this, so the file opens in what you would get by double-clicking it.

The other program is not shut in as Tuatara's own readers are. It can read everything you can. So Tuatara asks first, unless you turn off *open-externally-ask*. It also looks at what the file is, not what its name says. A program named holiday.jpg is refused. Only the kinds of file in *open-externally-kinds* are handed over: pictures, PDFs, sound and video, and office documents.

To use another program for a kind, set *open-externally-programs* to a list of a type and a program:

(setf *open-externally-programs*
      '(("application/pdf" . "zathura")
        ("video/*" "mpv" "--fs")))

The program given there is run as it is, with the file's name after it. *open-externally-program* names the command used for every other kind, which is xdg-open as standard.

9.12 Starting Tuatara with files

tuatara letter.txt opens the file in the terminal you typed it in. Several names open several buffers, the first one shown. tuatara --gui letter.txt opens a window of its own instead. Other files you had open, if you keep a session as chapter 7 described, are opened behind the ones you named.

A number with a plus before a file name says which line to start on. tuatara +2 letter.txt opens the letter with the cursor on its second line. +2:5 adds a column. The numbers count from 1. A file with fewer lines opens at its last line, and says so. You can name a line for each file: tuatara +120 main.lisp +3 notes.org.

tuatara --safe letter.txt, or -R for short, opens the files safely, as described in chapter 12: read-only, with nothing in them acted on. It holds for every file in that command. --hex opens them in the hex view instead of as text. A single - reads what another program sends: ls | tuatara - shows the output in a buffer called *stdin*. After --, every word is a file, so tuatara -- -odd.txt opens a file named -odd.txt.

In bash, pressing TAB after tuatara - completes the options, and after an option that takes a file, or after a plain word, the file names. The distribution packages install this completion, and the AppImage does with --install-desktop. Both need the bash-completion package of the system.

The table at the end of this section lists every option, as tuatara --help does. The ones that start the daemon, make a client, compare files or merge them are explained in chapters 15 and 18.

Try it, with a letter

  1. In a terminal, make a letter of five lines: printf 'one\ntwo\nthree\nfour\nfive\n' > letter.txt.
  2. Run tuatara +4 letter.txt. The cursor is on four, and the mode line says L4.
  3. Press C-x C-c to leave. Run tuatara --safe letter.txt. The mode line says Safe. Press i. The buffer is read-only, so nothing can be typed.
  4. Press M-x end-safe-visit and RET. The file opens as usual.
  5. Leave with C-x C-c.

9.12.1 Options

OptionWhat it does
--guiOpen a window of its own instead (as when started with no terminal). Use it when the terminal is the limit: the window draws pictures and PDFs itself, shows 24-bit colour whatever TERM says, and takes the desktop's clipboard through GTK. It needs a graphical session (WAYLAND_DISPLAY or DISPLAY), which a console or an ssh login has not. How the window is drawn is the setting gui-renderer.
--frames NOpen N frames, from 1 to 16: with –gui each a window of its own, in the terminal screens shown one at a time (C-x 5 o goes to the next); the files named are shown one in each frame in turn, those left over open behind the first; –frames=N does as well. Use it to start with several views of the same buffers. With –gui they are windows you can put on different screens. In a terminal only one frame shows at a time, so more than one is for C-x 5 o; to see two views at once, split the window (C-x 2, C-x 3). The cost is small: measured once here, 16 frames on a small file added about 30 ms to the first screen and no memory worth naming.
-c INIT-FILE, --config INIT-FILERead INIT-FILE as the init file instead of ~/.config/tuatara/init.lisp; –config=INIT-FILE does as well. Use it to keep several setups (one for writing, one for a work machine), to try a changed init file without touching the one you rely on, or to start from a file kept elsewhere. The file is read as the usual one is, so the packages it names are loaded. A file that is not there ends the start with status 2; the usual init file is not used in its place.
+LINE[:COLUMN]Before a file: open it with the cursor on that line (from 1; the last line when the file has fewer) and column (from 1; the C in the mode line counts from 0), as in tuatara +120:8 main.lisp +3 notes.org.
--diff OLD NEWOpen the differences between the two files, or two directories, as M-x diff-files shows them, and exit when you quit; for git, as git config difftool.tuatara.cmd 'tuatara –diff "$LOCAL" "$REMOTE"'.
--merge LOCAL BASE REMOTE MERGEDMerge the three files into MERGED, the conflicts marked there to resolve, then save it; exits 0 when MERGED is saved with no conflict left, else 1; for git, as git config mergetool.tuatara.cmd 'tuatara –merge "$LOCAL" "$BASE" "$REMOTE" "$MERGED"' and mergetool.tuatara.trustExitCode true.
--safe, -ROpen the files safely, whatever directory they are in: read only, no mode or hook acting on them, nothing written. Use it to look at a file you do not trust or must not alter: a download, the contents of a disk image, evidence. Nothing in the directory acts on the file and nothing is written, so opening it leaves it as it was. What you give up is what the directory's own settings and tools would add, and saving changes.
--hexOpen the files in the hex view, never first as text. Use it for a file that is not text (a program, an image, a database), or for text whose bytes you must read as stored, where the text view could hide a stray byte or a different line ending. A byte takes more room on the screen than a character. Measured once here, a 1 GB file showed its first screen in the same time as hex or as text (about 0.35 s).
-As a file: read standard input into a buffer, stdin, opened safely (tuatara - < data, or … | tuatara -); the terminal stays the keyboard. Use it to look at what another program writes, in a pipe, before it goes on. The buffer is opened safely, as –safe does, so it is for reading and for taking parts of out.
--tutorStart in the tutor.
--daemon[=NAME]Run one editor in the background, with no screen, for tuatara –client to show in terminals, and return once it is ready; it reads the init file and loads the packages as Tuatara does, and runs until M-x daemon-quit or tuatara –stop, or until it is sent SIGTERM, as at logout, which keeps the changes not saved as auto-saved copies and asks nothing; NAME, default when none is given, tells several apart; its log is ~/.cache/tuatara/daemon-NAME.log, its session ~/.local/state/tuatara/session-daemon-NAME. Use it for an editor that is already there when you want one: a client (tuatara –client) shows a frame in about 0.23 s, against about 0.32 s to start an editor of its own (measured once here, on a small file), and the buffers stay open when a terminal closes. Several names keep several separate sessions. The cost is a process that stays in memory until it is stopped, with whatever it has open: a large file stays held. It needs XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, where its socket is.
--client[=NAME]Show the daemon NAME in this terminal, or with –gui in a window of its own (C-x 5 2 opens another), a frame of its own, the files named opened in it, with +LINE, –safe, –hex, - and –frames as for Tuatara itself; –diff and –merge as well, with their exit codes; C-x C-c closes this client alone, its buffers kept in the daemon, and the daemon goes on; as git's editor (GIT_EDITOR='tuatara –client') the commit is made when the message is finished; exits 1 when no daemon of that name runs, or when it ends. Use it for the quicker start a daemon gives (about 0.23 s against about 0.32 s here) and one set of buffers in every terminal. In return, a change to the init file or a package reaches the daemon only when it is stopped and started again, and every client works in the one editor. As git's editor, add –start so that it works when no daemon runs.
--client=HOST[:NAME]Show the daemon NAME running on the machine HOST, reached with the system's ssh, as –client shows one here: HOST as ssh takes it (build.example, me@build.example), a name from ~/.ssh/config written with a colon after it (build: or build:work); its host key must be known already; the files named are that machine's, a relative name from your home directory there; - is not taken, and pictures stay on each side, the clipboard, dropped files and your agents too unless HOST is trusted with them (M-x server-list); with –start, the daemon there is started first when none runs; –stop=HOST[:NAME] stops it. Use it to work on the machine that has the files, a build server or a remote box, with your own screen and keys. Tuatara must be installed there, and the system's ssh is all it needs here. The editor runs there, so files are read at the speed of its disks, and each key crosses the network: a slow link shows as lag. The clipboard, dropped files and pictures stay on each side unless HOST is trusted with them, so a copy made there does not reach this machine's clipboard by itself.
--daemon-socket[=NAME]Say where the daemon NAME listens, which Tuatara this is and whether it runs, in lines a client on another machine reads over ssh, with where gpg here looks for its agent, and exit; with –start, start it first when none runs.
--receive-file PATHWrite standard input, a file dropped on the window of a client on another machine, at PATH, from your home directory unless it begins with /, for you alone and under a name nothing has yet; say where, and exit.
--startWith –client: start the daemon first when none runs. Use it in a script or as git's editor, where there may be no daemon yet: the first call starts one and later calls find it. Without it, a client with no daemon exits 1.
--fallbackWith –client: when no daemon runs, start Tuatara as it starts without –client instead, the files opened in an editor of its own; the desktop's Tuatara (client) starts it so. Use it where an editor must always open, as in a desktop entry. When no daemon runs it costs the ordinary start (about 0.32 s here) and gives an editor of its own, not shared with later clients.
--stop[=NAME]Stop the daemon NAME, asking in this terminal about the changes not saved in it, as M-x daemon-quit does; with no terminal, nothing is asked, and the changes are kept as auto-saved copies that M-x recover-file offers. Use it to free the memory of a daemon you no longer need, or to start it again after you change the init file or a package. With no terminal nothing is asked, so a script can stop it without waiting; what was not saved is kept as auto-saved copies.
-Q, --no-initStart without the init file and so without packages, with what Tuatara keeps between sessions (files visited lately, the session, bookmarks) kept apart in a directory that goes with the session, the real one neither read nor changed. Use it when something in the init file or a package gets in the way: a setting that slows the editor or a package that fails to load. You get the editor as it ships, so you can tell whether the fault is yours. What you do meanwhile is not remembered. It is no faster to start: with the starter init file the first screen took the same time with and without it (about 0.3 s, measured once).
--generate-configWrite the init file Tuatara writes when there is none, every setting in it commented out, as ~/.config/tuatara/generated-init.lisp, and exit; a file there already is left as it is. Use it for a fresh list of every setting after an update, to compare with your own init file. It never replaces a file that is there, and the list is all comments, so you copy out the few settings you want to change.
--generate-autostartWrite the entry that has the desktop start the daemon as you log in, ~/.config/autostart/tuatara-daemon.desktop, running tuatara –daemon, and exit; with –daemon=NAME, the daemon NAME's, tuatara-daemon-NAME.desktop; a file there already is left as it is. Use it for a daemon that is ready from login, so that the first terminal or window you open starts quickly. It costs the daemon's memory from the start of every session, whether or not you edit that day. Delete the file to undo it.
--help, -hShow this and exit.
--version, -VShow the version and exit.
--The arguments after it are all files, even when one starts with a dash or a plus.
--install-desktop(the AppImage) copy it to ~/.local/bin/tuatara and put Tuatara and Tuatara (client) in the desktop's applications, the icon too. Use it to start the AppImage from the application menu. The copy at ~/.local/bin/tuatara does not update itself: run this again from a new AppImage.
--remove-desktop(the AppImage) take them away again.
--dark, --light(the AppImage) show the window's title bar in the dark or the light style; with –install-desktop, for the desktop's applications. Use it when the window's title bar clashes with the desktop. It changes only the title bar's style; the text and colours come from the theme.
--dynamic-space-size SIZEThe most memory Tuatara's own data may take, such as 6GB; by default half the machine's memory, from 2GB to 16GB, or $TUATARA_HEAP_MB megabytes. Use it to set the heap for one run; $TUATARA_HEAP_MB does for every run. That variable says what raising or lowering it does.

Directories

Looking at a directory, and copying, moving, renaming and deleting what is in it.

A directory holds files, and sometimes other directories. When you want to find a photo, tidy a pile of letters or clear out last year's downloads, you need to see what is there and then do something to it. Tuatara's file manager is called rimu. It shows a directory as a list, a line for each thing in it, and it lets you pick some of those lines and act on them. The picking works as it does in the buffer list of chapter 7, so most of what you learned there applies here.

This chapter starts with opening a directory and moving about in it. Then it shows how to change what the list shows, how to look at a file without opening it, and how to choose entries. The rest is what you can do with the choice: make, copy, move, rename, delete, pack into an archive and compare. Chapter 9 explained how to open a single file. This chapter is about many files at a time.

As in the other chapters, every key here is pressed in NORMAL state unless it starts with C-x. i starts INSERT state, and C-g or ESC returns to NORMAL. In a list you rarely need INSERT, because the keys are commands.

10.1 Opening a directory

C-x d asks which directory you want and lists it. The question already holds the directory of the buffer you are in, so you often only press RET. To go elsewhere, type the rest of a path, or start again from your home directory with ~/. TAB completes a name as you type it.

If you are looking at a file and want to see what else is in its directory, C-x C-j lists that directory with the cursor on the file. C-x 5 d does what C-x d does in a new window of its own.

From a terminal you can start Tuatara on a directory, for example with tuatara ~/Photos/holiday/, and the list is the first thing you see.

Figure 10.1 shows a list for a directory of holiday photos.

The first line is the directory's whole name. Below it come the entries, one to a line, with directories first and then files. Names are in the order that ls uses, so capital letters come before small ones. The two spaces before each name are where marks go. In the figure, two photos have a >.

Names that start with a dot are hidden. Those are files that programs keep for themselves, such as .bashrc, and you seldom want to see them. Directory names have a colour of their own. Names of files that are only a by-product, such as compiled files, are set back in a fainter colour.

The mode line at the bottom says Rimu and how the list is sorted. q leaves the list and returns to the buffer you were in before.

Rimu keeps a list up to date. If another program adds, renames or removes a file in the directory, the line appears or goes within a moment. r reads the directory again at once, and your marks stay.

10.1.1 Commands for opening a directory

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x drimuList a directory with rimu, asked for with completion from the directory of the path chosen last in a question for a path, else the current buffer's: its name, then its entries a line each, directories first.
noneC-x 5 drimu-other-frameList a directory with rimu in another frame and work in it, the directory asked for as C-x d asks.
noneC-x C-jrimu-jumpList the directory of the current buffer's file with rimu, point on the file; a buffer with no file lists the directory it stands in.

10.2 Moving about

Moving into a directory shows it in the same list. You do not collect a buffer for every directory you pass through. The keys are the ones you know from chapter 2, with a few more for the places a list has.

ModalNon-modalWhat it does
j, kC-n, C-pDown and up a line
nonel, RETOpen the entry: a directory in this list, a file
nonehUp to the directory that holds this one
g g, g eM-<, M->To the top of the list, to the end
none>, <To the next directory in the list, to the previous
noneg fTo an entry, by name, with completion
noneg hTo your home directory
noneg lBack to the directory listed before
noneqLeave the list

When you go up with h, the cursor lands on the directory you came from. So you can walk down into a directory and back out again without losing your place. g l swaps between the last two directories, so pressing it twice returns to where you started. This helps when you are working in two places.

g f is the quickest way to a name in a long list. Type a few letters of the name, and RET puts the cursor on it.

h j k l only move in a list. The keys that move by word or select text do nothing here, and the echo area says so. Each line is one whole entry, so there is nothing to select inside it.

RET on a file opens it as C-x C-f does (chapter 9). A file that looks like a program's data rather than text opens in a safe view. C-u RET opens any file that way. Chapter 12 explains what a safe view is.

Try it, with a directory of photos

  1. Press C-x d. The question holds the directory you are in. Type ~/Pictures/ after clearing it with C-a C-k, and press RET. Use any directory you like if you have no Pictures.
  2. Press j (non-modal: C-n) a few times, then l on a directory to go into it.
  3. Press h. You are back, with the cursor on the directory you left.
  4. Press g l to go into it again, and g l once more to come back.
  5. Press g f, type the first letters of a name and press RET.
  6. Press g h to see your home directory, and q to leave the list.

10.2.1 Commands for moving

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
nonel, RET, C-c lrimu-openOpen the entry on the current line: a directory is listed in its place in this list; a file is visited as C-x C-f visits it, safely where that would be, and with a prefix argument (C-u) safely always.
noneC-orimu-displayShow the entry on the current line in another window, staying in the list: a directory in a list of its own, a file as l opens it.
noneh, C-c hrimu-upList the directory holding this one, in this list, point on the one left; in a list of files found, list the directory they were found in.
none>, C-c >rimu-next-directoryGo to the next directory of this list.
none<, C-c <rimu-previous-directoryGo to the previous directory of this list.
noneg frimu-goto-fileGo to an entry of this list, its name asked for with completion; among those the search filters leave, while they narrow the list.
noneg hrimu-homeList your home directory in this list's place.
noneg lrimu-last-directoryList again the directory this list listed before, point on the entry it was on; again, back to this one, as cd - goes back and forth.

10.3 What a list shows

At first a list shows only names. You can ask for more, one part at a time. Each key switches its part on and off for the list you are in, and none of them changes a file.

I shows details before each name: the same ones that ls -l gives, which are permissions, the number of links, the owner, the group, the size and the time of the last change. The inode number, which says where the file sits on the disk, comes first. The line under the directory's name then gives how much free space the drive has. Here is a directory with details on.

The permissions say who may read, write and run a file. The first letter is d for a directory and - for a file. The next nine are three groups of three, for the owner, for the owner's group and for everyone else. In each group, r means may read, w may write and x may run or, for a directory, may go into it. So -rw-r--r-- is a file its owner may read and change and everyone else may only read. Rimu shows these but does not change them. If you would rather read them as numbers, as the chmod command does, set *rimu-permissions* to :octal.

H shows the names that start with a dot. s swaps the order between by name and by time, with the most recently changed first. The mode line says which one is in force. S shows a size before each name. For a directory it is the size of everything inside, and it is worked out in the background, so the column fills in after a moment while you carry on. G shows, after each name, when the file was last committed to git and the first line of what the commit said. Chapter 15 describes git.

The standard for each of these is off, with directories first and the order by name. The settings below change the standard for every list.

Try it, with a directory of letters

  1. Open a directory of letters with C-x d. If you have none, make one in a terminal first, or use any directory with several files.
  2. Press I. Details appear. Press I again to hide them.
  3. Press s. The list is now ordered by time, the newest first. Press s again to go back to names.
  4. Press S and wait a moment for the sizes. Find the largest one.
  5. Press H to see the hidden names, and H again to hide them.

10.3.1 Commands for what a list shows

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneI, C-c Irimu-toggle-detailsShow or hide the details before each name in this list: its inode number, as ls -i shows it, then its permissions, links, owner, group, size and when it last changed, as ls -l shows them, and where a symbolic link leads.
noneH, C-c Hrimu-toggle-dotfilesShow or hide the entries of this list whose names start with a dot, .
nonesrimu-toggle-sortOrder this list by name or by time, those changed last first; the mode line says which.
noneS, C-c Srimu-toggle-sizesShow or hide, before each name in this list, how much it takes: a file its size, a directory the size of everything in it and under it, hidden files too, directories of another drive mounted in it left out, worked out in the background while the list shows it.
noneG, C-c Grimu-toggle-gitShow or hide, after each name in this list, the entry's last commit in git's history: when it was made and the first line of its message.

10.3.2 Settings for what a list shows

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*rimu-details*nilt, nilWhether rimu shows the details of each entry before its name.
*rimu-permissions*:symbolic:symbolic, :octalHow rimu's details write each entry's permissions.
*rimu-dotfiles*nilt, nilWhether rimu shows the entries whose names start with a dot, .
*rimu-sort*:name:name, :timeThe order rimu lists entries in.
*rimu-directories-first*tt, nilWhether rimu lists directories, and the symbolic links that lead to directories, before everything else, as ls –group-directories-first does.
*rimu-directory-sizes*nilt, nilWhether rimu's lists show each entry's size before its name, a directory's with everything under it.
*rimu-git-info*nilt, nilWhether rimu's lists show, after each name, the entry's last commit in git's history.
*rimu-hidden-columns*nila list, each :inode, :permissions, :links, :owner, :group, :size, :time, :sizes, :gitThe columns rimu's lists never show, however they are asked for.
*rimu-ignored-extensions*(".o" ".so" ".a" ".fasl" ".elc" ".pyc" "...a list, each textEndings of names rimu shows set back, in the :list-dim face.
*rimu-follow-changes*tt, nilWhether rimu's lists are read again by themselves when their directory changes on disk.
*rimu-reuse-lists*tt, nilWhether a directory a bookmark goes to (M-x bookmark-jump), or a list goes to across a project's edge, is listed in a rimu list that already belongs to its project.

Each key above has a setting that sets what a list starts with. They are all written in the init file (chapter 8).

*rimu-details* is nil as standard. With t every list opens with the details of I shown:

(setf *rimu-details* t)

*rimu-hidden-columns* leaves parts out, however a list is asked for them. It is a list of the names :inode, :permissions, :links, :owner, :group, :size and :time, which are the details, and :sizes and :git, which are the columns of S and G. It is empty as standard. This leaves out the inode numbers and the groups, so a line of Figure 10.2 starts at the permissions and has no group:

(setf *rimu-hidden-columns* '(:inode :group))

*rimu-dotfiles* is nil, so names that start with a dot stay hidden. Set it to t to start with them shown, as H does.

*rimu-sort* is :name or :time. :name puts capital letters before small ones, as ls does in its plain mode. :time puts the newest change first. For a directory you open to find what changed last:

(setf *rimu-sort* :time)

*rimu-directories-first* is t, so directories, and links that lead to directories, come before the files. With nil everything is in the one order, directories among the files.

*rimu-directory-sizes* and *rimu-git-info* are nil, so the size column and the git column wait until you press S or G. Set either to t and it is there when the list opens. The size of a directory is still worked out in the background.

*rimu-ignored-extensions* is a list of endings. A file whose name ends in one of them is shown faint, in the :list-dim face, so the files you work on stand out from those a program made. Nothing more is done to it: it is still listed, and you can still open, mark, copy and delete it as any other. As standard the endings are .o, .so, .a, .fasl, .elc, .pyc, .pyo, .class, ~ and #: compiled files, backups and the files some editors keep while you type.

An ending is any text the name ends with, not only what follows a dot: ~ sets back notes.org~, and -old would set back report-old. Capital letters count, so .log sets back build.log but not BUILD.LOG; give both to have both. The name must be longer than the ending, so a file called just .o is not set back. Directories and links are never set back, whatever their names end with.

To add your own endings to the standard ones, add them to the list:

(setf *rimu-ignored-extensions*
      (append *rimu-ignored-extensions* '(".log" ".tmp" ".LOG")))

Setting the list itself replaces the standard endings. This sets back only backups and Python's compiled files:

(setf *rimu-ignored-extensions* '("~" ".pyc"))

With nil no name is set back, and every file is shown alike.

*rimu-follow-changes* is t, so a list reads its directory again by itself when a file in it is made, deleted, renamed or finished being written by another program. You see the list change as you watch it. Many changes at once are read as one. Set it to nil and the list stays as it was until you press g r (non-modal: M-x revert-buffer). On a directory that changes without stopping, for example one a program writes to all day, that quiets the list:

(setf *rimu-follow-changes* nil)

*rimu-reuse-lists* is t. When a bookmark takes you to a directory, or you go to a directory across the edge of a project, Tuatara lists it in the list that already belongs to that project, the one used last, and does not open another. If a list shows that directory already, you are taken to it either way. With nil such a directory gets a list of its own each time.

10.4 The preview beside the list

When you rest the cursor on an entry, Tuatara shows it in a window beside the list: the start of a file, or for a directory the list of what is inside. It follows the cursor as you move, so you can look through a directory of notes or photos without opening any of them. On a wide screen the preview stands to the right of the list, and on a narrow one below it. It closes when you leave the list.

A text file shows its text. A picture shows the picture itself in the window (tuatara --gui) and in terminals that can draw pictures, such as kitty. In other terminals you see a line that describes it, such as its kind and size. A PDF shows its first page. T switches between a file's picture and its text. For a PDF the text is the words on all of its pages, which is a quick way to read one. Binary files show in the hex view, as bytes. The preview shows only the first megabyte of a file, so a very large file does not slow the list down.

P turns the preview off and on in the list you are in. If it gets in your way, P is the quickest answer. To turn it off for every list, set *rimu-preview* to nil in your init file (chapter 20).

C-o shows the entry in another window and leaves the cursor in the list. With the preview off it opens a window of its own for the purpose.

10.4.1 Quick edit

Sometimes you only want to fix a word in a file. o turns the preview into the file itself and puts the cursor in it. You can type there as in any buffer. When you are done, press q in NORMAL state, or C-c C-c in any state, and Tuatara asks whether to save what you changed. Then the preview shows the file again and you are back in the list.

Try it, with a directory of letters

  1. In your directory of letters, move to a text file. A window opens beside the list and shows the start of it. If not, press P.
  2. Press P to close the preview, and P again to open it.
  3. Press o. The cursor is now in the file.
  4. Press g e (non-modal: M->) to go to the end, i to type, and add a line such as Thank you. Press C-g.
  5. Press q. Tuatara asks Save letter.txt? (y or n). Press y.
  6. Press k and j (non-modal: C-p, C-n) to move over other entries and watch the preview change.

Two more keys help when you are deciding what a file is. g i shows what the system knows of it: its kind, size, owner, times and checksum. It leaves the file's access time as it was. O hands a copy of a picture, a PDF, a sound or a video to your desktop's own program, after asking, so you can play a video that Tuatara cannot.

10.4.2 Commands for the preview

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneP, C-c Plist-toggle-previewTurn the preview beside this list on or off: the entry on the current line shown in a window beside the list, on its right when there is room, else below it, following the cursor from line to line.
noneT, C-c Trimu-toggle-pictureSwitch the preview between the picture of a file and its text: the first page of a PDF or its text, an image or its octets in the hex view.
noneo, C-c orimu-quick-editEdit the file on the current line where the preview shows it, the quick edit: the preview becomes the file itself, opened as C-x C-f opens it (safely where that would be, and with C-u safely always), and the cursor goes there.
noneM-x rimu-quick-edit-finishrimu-quick-edit-finishGo back from the quick edit of this file to the preview beside the rimu list (as the cursor going back to the list does), asking first whether to save the changes made: y saves them; n lets them go (a buffer open before the quick edit keeps them); M-x keyboard-quit goes on with the quick edit.
noneg ishow-file-metadataShow what the file shown is and what it says of itself, in a buffer of its own, which q closes: the file the buffer visits, the entry on the line in a list of a directory, the PDF or picture in its view; with C-u, or where there is none, asked for.
noneO, C-c Oopen-externallyOpen the file shown, in the desktop's own program for its kind (xdg-open), or the one OPEN-EXTERNALLY-PROGRAMS gives its Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) type, for what Tuatara does not do: printing, forms, playing.

10.4.3 Settings for the preview

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*rimu-preview*tt, nilWhether rimu lists show the entry on the current line in a window beside the list, once point has rested on it RIMU-PREVIEW-DELAY seconds.
*rimu-preview-delay*0.1a number, 0 or moreSeconds point rests on an entry of a rimu list before the preview shows it.
*rimu-preview-size*1048576a whole number, 0 or moreThe most of a file rimu's preview shows, in octets from its start.
*remote-preview-size-limit*20000000a whole number, 0 or moreThe most octets a file on another machine may hold to be shown in the preview of its list (M-x list-toggle-preview).

*rimu-preview-delay* is how long the cursor rests on an entry before the preview reads it, 0.1 seconds as standard. Moving quickly down the list reads none of the files passed over. A longer wait reads fewer files as you move, which helps on a slow disk or a directory on another machine. A shorter one shows the preview at once and reads more.

(setf *rimu-preview-delay* 0.4)

*rimu-preview-size* is how much of a file the preview shows, counted in octets (bytes) from its start. It is a megabyte as standard, as said above. A larger file shows its start, and its name says that. To see less of a big file, so the preview is quicker, or more, to read further in:

(setf *rimu-preview-size* (* 256 1024))

10.5 Marks

Marking works as it does in the buffer list. m puts a > on the entry and moves down a line, so pressing it again and again marks a run. A number before it marks that many. u takes the mark off, U takes every mark off, and t turns the marks about, which is the quick way to say "everything but these". d puts a D on an entry instead, which means "delete this one". It does nothing until you press x.

With nothing marked, a command acts on the entry the cursor is on. With entries marked, it acts on them.

A mark stays with its file when you go to another directory. You can mark two photos in one directory, go to another and mark a third, and then copy all three at once. This is useful and also something to watch. Under the directory's name the list says how many entries are marked in other directories, so you are never surprised, and the question that a command asks counts all of them. U takes away every mark in every directory.

K takes the lines of the marked entries out of the list. The files stay as they are, and only the list shows fewer lines. It is a way to cross off what you have dealt with and look at what is left. r brings the lines back.

10.5.1 Filtering a list

A long list is easier to use when it shows only what you want. C-x / s asks for a pattern and keeps the lines that contain it. If you type jpg, only the lines with jpg in them remain, and a line at the top says how many of the entries are shown. A second C-x / s narrows it further. C-x / r takes every filter away. C-x / l lists the filters in force. Marks stay on entries that a filter hides, and a question that counts the entries says how many are hidden, so nothing goes without your knowing.

With the details shown, C-x / f and C-x / h ask for a column first, such as the owner or the size, and then keep or hide the entries whose value in that column matches. Chapter 6 describes the pattern language.

Try it, with holiday photos

  1. Open your directory of holiday photos with C-x d.
  2. Press m on three photos you like. Each gets a >.
  3. Press t. Now every other entry is marked, and the three are not. Press t again to turn them back.
  4. Press U to clear every mark.
  5. Press C-x / s, type jpg and press RET. Only the pictures stay.
  6. Press C-x / r to see the whole directory again.

10.5.2 Commands for marks and filters

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
nonem, C-c mlist-mark-entryMark the entry on the current line of the list (>), for the list's commands that act on those marked, and move down; with a count, as many entries, up the list for a negative one.
noneu, C-c ulist-unmark-entryTake the mark off the entry on the current line of the list, of any kind, and move down; with a count, off as many entries, up the list for a negative one.
noneU, C-c Ulist-unmark-allTake every mark off the entries of the list, of any kind; in rimu, those of the files marked in other directories too.
nonetlist-toggle-marksMark the entries the list shows that are not marked and take the mark off those marked; those marked for deletion (D), or given a mark of another kind, stay so, as do the entries a filter or a folded section hides.
