noneK, C-c Krimu-take-out-linesTake the lines of the entries marked in this directory out of this list, or with none marked here the line point is on, their marks taken away: the files stay as they are, only the list shows fewer, to look at what is left.
noneC-c f mrimu-mark-masterMark the file on the line of this rimu list as a master (M), a file that the files marked (m) are compared with by the commands that compare files, a photo of the person looked for among photos, and go to the next line; u takes the mark away.
noneC-x / ssearch-filter-regexNarrow the list here to the entries a regular expression matches, as it is typed: those whose line matches, or what more the list holds of them (a mailbox the headers and contents of its messages).
noneC-x / lsearch-filter-listList the search filters narrowing the list here (C-x / s) in a buffer of their own, each with how many entries it leaves; there d takes away the filter on the line and D all of them.
noneD, C-c D, C-x / rsearch-filter-remove-allTake away every search filter narrowing the list here, or the list the list of filters here is for: the whole list is shown again.
noneC-x / fsearch-filter-show-recordsShow only the records whose line a regular expression matches, hiding the others, as C-x / s does, deleting nothing.
noneC-x / hsearch-filter-hide-recordsHide the records whose line a regular expression matches, showing the others, deleting nothing: asked for as C-x / f asks, kept with the other filters.

10.6 Making things

+ makes a new directory in the directory the list shows. Type the name after the directory that is offered. If you type Napier/Hawke/2026, Tuatara makes every directory along the way that is not there yet.

a touches a name. The word comes from the touch command. A name that does not exist becomes a new empty file, with the cursor on it so that l opens it. A name that exists has its times set to now and nothing else changes. If you press RET at the question without typing, the marked entries are touched, or the one under the cursor.

A makes a file with a formatted name, such as one that starts with the date and time and has your keywords at its end. It asks for a title and keywords, and writes the header of the file for you.

10.6.1 Commands for making things

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
none+, C-c +rimu-make-directoryMake a directory, asked for, in this list's directory unless given elsewhere, with those above it that are not there; the list shows it.
nonea, C-c arimu-touchTouch a name asked for in this list's directory, as touch does: a name not there is made a new, empty file, the list on it for l to open it; a file or directory there has its times set to now (a link's own, not those of where it leads).
noneA, C-c Arimu-make-formatted-fileMake a new file with a formatted name in this list's directory, asking what new-file-formatted asks but the subdirectory (the title, the keywords, the kind and the template), with the header of its kind, saved at once; the list shows it, point on it.

10.7 Copying, moving and linking

C copies the marked entries, or the one under the cursor. M moves them. The question asks where to, as C-x C-f asks for a file: you type a path, and TAB completes it. If another rimu list is open in the next window, its directory is offered first. That makes it easy to copy from one directory to another that you can see.

A directory goes with everything in it, however many directories are inside. The setting *directory-tree-depth-limit* stops this at a very deep nesting, so that a loop made by mistake cannot run for ever.

M moves only into a directory. To move a file and also give it a new name, use R and a path, or copy it. When you copy a single entry you may type the whole new path, name included.

A large copy runs in the background and the editor stays free. P lights at the front of the mode line while it works. C-x j lists the jobs with how far each has got, and C-x J stops one, taking away a file only half copied.

Nothing is replaced without asking. If a file of that name is already there, Tuatara asks whether to replace it, and the old one goes to the trash first, so you can still get it back. Tuatara also never puts a file on top of itself. Asking to copy a link onto the file it leads to is refused.

Y makes a symbolic link, which is a small file that says where another file is. L makes a hard link, which is a second name for the very same file. A change made through one name shows under the other, and the file stays until both names are gone. A hard link can only be made on the same drive, and never to a directory.

= compares two marked entries and shows what differs, line by line, as git does. With two directories marked, it compares the files that have the same name.

Try it, with holiday photos

  1. In your directory of photos, press m on three photos.
  2. Press M. At the question type the name of a directory, such as Napier/, and press RET. If the directory is not there, Tuatara says so and moves nothing: make it with + and try again.
  3. The three photos leave the list, and Tuatara says Moved 3 files.
  4. Press g f, go to Napier, and press l. They are there.
  5. Put the cursor on one photo and press C. Copy it to your home directory by typing ~/ after clearing the question with C-a C-k.
  6. Press C-x j to see the job list. A small copy has finished already, so the list says there are no jobs.

10.7.1 Commands for copying, moving and linking

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC, C-c Crimu-copyCopy the marked entries, or the one on the line, to a place asked for: the directory of the other list beside this one offered first, or this one; one entry may be given a new name.
noneM, C-c Mrimu-moveMove the marked entries, or the one on the line, into a directory asked for, navigating to it as C-x C-f does, only directories offered: the directory of the other list beside this one offered first.
noneY, C-c Yrimu-symlinkMake symbolic links to the marked entries, or the one on the line, in a place asked for, as C asks: the directory of the other list beside this one offered first; one entry's link may be given a new name.
noneL, C-c Lrimu-hardlinkGive the marked files, or the one on the line, a second name in a place asked for, as C asks: one file, two names, on the same drive only, and no directory.
none=, C-c =rimu-diffCompare the two entries marked, from every directory they are marked in, the one shown first taken as the old, and show the differences in a buffer of their own, which q closes, as M-x diff-files does: unified, the old's lines taken out after -, the other's put in after +; two directories with all in them.

10.7.2 Settings for copying and moving

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*directory-tree-depth-limit*200a whole number, 1 or moreThe most directories, one inside another, that copying, moving or deleting a directory goes down through.

10.8 Renaming

R renames the entry under the cursor in its place. The question offers the old name, so you can edit it rather than type it all again. A name only: a slash is refused, because moving is M's job. A buffer that visits the file follows it to its new name, and so do the recent files and other lists of the same directory.

To rename many names at once, press C-x C-q. The names of the directory's entries appear as text in a buffer of their own, one to a line. You can now change them with every key that edits text. You can add a word to the start of each line with a many-cursor edit (chapter 5), or run a replacement over all of them (chapter 6). When you press C-c C-c, every line that changed is renamed. C-c C-k leaves the names as they were.

Each line stands for one file. If you delete a line, add one or join two, nothing is renamed, and Tuatara tells you why. Before it renames anything it checks all the names together, so a name used twice, or one that another file already has, is reported and no file is renamed. You can swap two names.

Try it, with a directory of photos

  1. Open a directory that holds a few photos, such as IMG_0412.jpg.
  2. Press C-x C-q. The names appear as text, with the cursor on the first.
  3. Press I to start INSERT at the beginning of the line. Type Napier- and press C-g.
  4. Press j (non-modal: C-n) and repeat on the next line.
  5. Press C-c C-c. Tuatara says how many were renamed and the list shows the new names.

10.8.1 Commands for renaming

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneR, C-c Rrimu-renameRename the entry on the line, or the one marked, in its place, the new name asked for, the old offered: a name only, no directory; a name there already is refused.
noneC-x C-qrimu-edit-namesEdit the names of this list's entries as text, a line each, in its window, with every key that edits text: C-c C-c renames those whose line changed, C-c C-k leaves them.
noneC-c C-crimu-names-finishRename the entries whose line changed, and go back to the list: all or, when a line does not do, none, and why is said.
noneC-c C-krimu-names-cancelLeave the names as they are, and go back to the list.

10.9 Deleting, the trash and wiping

D puts the marked entries, or the one under the cursor, in the trash. This is the same trash your desktop's file manager uses, so a file you delete here can be put back from there too. x does the same for the entries marked with D. Deleting is a two-step in that case: first mark with d, then press x when you are sure.

C-u D deletes for good, and asks twice. Nothing deleted this way can come back. The setting *rimu-delete-to-trash* decides what D does. If you set it to nil, every deletion is for good, after asking twice.

g t lists the trash, as the buffer list lists buffers: a section for your own trash and a section for each drive that has one. The thing that was put in last is at the top, and each line says when it was deleted and where it was. In the list, R puts the marked things back where they were, D deletes them for good and x deletes those marked with D. X empties the whole trash and asks twice. RET opens a thing safely so that you can look at it before you decide. h or q returns to your directory.

A file that you trash on a USB stick goes to the stick's own trash and comes back to where it was. That is why the trash list has a section for each drive. When you pull the stick out, its trash goes with it.

The trash only moves a file. The bytes stay on the drive until the space is used again. If you really want a file's contents gone, g w wipes the marked files: it writes over them and then deletes them. This is slow, and it asks once.

Try it, with some letters

  1. Make two new files in a directory with a: type old-1.txt and RET, then old-2.txt and RET.
  2. Put the cursor on old-1.txt. Press d, which marks it and moves down, then d on the next, so both show D.
  3. Press x and answer y. Both are in the trash.
  4. Press g t. The two are at the top of the trash list.
  5. Put the cursor on old-1.txt and press R. Answer y. It is back.
  6. Press q to return. old-1.txt is in the list again.

Do not press X while you practise. It empties the whole trash, not only what you put there.

10.9.1 Commands for deleting and the trash

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
nonexlist-executeDelete the entries of the list marked for deletion (D), after asking, as the list deletes: the buffer list kills its buffers, rimu puts files in the trash, the list of jobs drops those waiting and stops those running.
noneD, C-c Dlist-delete-markedDelete the marked entries of the list (>), or with none marked the one on the current line, after asking, as the list deletes, as M-x list-execute does those marked for deletion; in rimu, with C-u, for good rather than to the trash.
noneg trimu-trashList what is in the trash, as the buffer list (C-x C-b) lists buffers: a section for your own trash and one for each drive's, the last to go there first, each thing's name, when it went and where it was.
noneR, C-c Rrimu-trash-restorePut the marked things (>), or with none marked the one on the current line, back where they were, after asking, where they go said; another name asked for when one's is taken, the directories above it made again when they are gone.
noneX, C-c Xrimu-trash-emptyEmpty the trash: everything the list of the trash shows deleted for good, after asking twice, in the background.
noneg wrimu-wipe-filesWipe the files marked (or the one on the line) as M-x wipe-file does, asked once: overwritten, then deleted.

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*rimu-delete-to-trash*tt, nilWhether rimu's deletions (M-x list-delete-marked, M-x list-execute) move files and directories to the trash.

10.10 Archives

An archive is one file that holds many files, often squeezed to take less room. A zip of recipes that a friend sent you is an archive. Rimu works with the common kinds: tar archives (plain, or ending .gz, .bz2, .xz or .zst), zip, 7z and rar, ISO disc images and cpio. It reads all of them and makes tar, zip and 7z ones. c packs the marked entries into an archive, Z extracts archives and C-c e shows what one holds.

10.10.1 Looking inside

C-c e shows what an archive holds, in a buffer of its own, without unpacking it. q closes it. It is a way to look inside a zip before you decide whether to unpack it. Each line gives the kind and permissions, the owner, the size, the time and the name, and where a link leads.

Tuatara tells the kind from the first bytes of the file, never from its name, so an archive with a wrong name still works. Word, EPUB and Java files are zip archives and open as such.

10.10.2 Extracting

Z extracts the archives marked, or the one under the cursor. It asks for a directory, and offers one named after the archive, which it makes if it is not there. Several marked archives go into the one directory you give.

Unpacking is careful because an archive can hold anything. It happens in the background and shut in a sandbox. Nothing is written outside the directory you chose, whatever names are inside, and a file already there is left as it is. Everything is first unpacked into a new directory of its own and moved into place after, so a half-finished unpack never damages what you had. The files are yours, with the permissions your umask gives; none is setuid, and no named pipe or device is made. Unpacking stops before the drive has less than *archive-free-reserve* free, which is a gigabyte unless you change it, so that a small archive that holds a great deal cannot fill the drive. Archives inside an archive stay packed.

10.10.3 Locked archives

If an archive is locked with a password, Tuatara finds that out in the background and then asks for the password, showing only stars. The password reaches the unpacking program on its standard input, never on its command line, and a wrong one unpacks nothing. 7-Zip opens locked zip, 7z and rar archives; bsdtar opens only locked zip ones. The old zip encryption checks a password by a single byte, so one wrong password in 256 gets past the check and fails only while unpacking; Tuatara then says the password is not right or the archive is damaged.

10.10.4 Making an archive

c goes the other way. It packs the marked entries, or the one under the cursor, into one archive. The question asks for a name, and its ending says what kind of archive it is and how it is squeezed:

EndingKindSqueezed with
.tartarnothing
.tar.gz, .tgztargzip
.tar.bz2, .tbz2, .tbztarbzip2
.tar.xz, .txztarxz
.tar.zst, .tzsttarzstd
.zipzipDeflate
.7z7zLZMA

Another ending is refused. If you give a directory and no name, the archive is named after what it holds and ends .tar.gz. Entries marked in several directories go into one archive and keep their paths below the directory that holds them all. Directories go in with everything in them. A symbolic link goes in as a link, never as the file it leads to.

The archive is made in the background, shut in the sandbox. The program sees what it packs only to read, and writes only in the directory the archive goes to. It writes under a passing name, and the archive gets its own name only once it is whole, so a failed or stopped one leaves nothing behind. If a file of that name is there already, Tuatara asks whether to replace it, and the old one goes to the trash.

10.10.5 Locking an archive with a password

Press C-u c in place of c to lock a zip or 7z archive with a password. The question for the name says with a password, and if you give a directory the name ends .zip. After the name, Tuatara asks for the password twice, showing only stars. If the two differ, nothing is made.

  • A zip archive is locked with AES-256, never with the old zip encryption, which is easy to break. Anyone can still read the names of the files in it, and with bsdtar where its links lead; only their contents are locked.
  • A 7z archive is locked with AES-256 and its names are locked too. Without the password nobody can even list it. Only 7-Zip makes one.
  • A tar archive takes no password.

A password may hold letters, digits, spaces and the signs of plain ASCII. A letter such as ā is refused, because 7-Zip and bsdtar would each read it differently and the archive might never open again. Keep the password somewhere safe: nothing can open the archive without it.

The password goes to 7-Zip or bsdtar on its standard input, never on its command line, where other programs on the machine could read it. It is not written to the debug log, and Tuatara wipes it from memory once the archive is made.

10.10.6 Which program does what

Tuatara uses programs installed on your system for archives:

ProgramReadsMakes
GNU tartar, plain or squeezedtar, plain or squeezed
7-Zipzip, 7z and rar, locked or notzip and 7z, locked or not
bsdtarzip, 7z, rar, ISO 9660 and cpio;zip, locked or not; 7z, not
locked only ziplocked

For zip and 7z archives Tuatara takes 7-Zip when it is installed, and bsdtar when it is not. bsdtar opens no locked 7z archive and makes none; 7-Zip opens and makes both. The programs that squeeze tar archives (gzip, bzip2, xz and zstd) must be installed for their endings. 7-Zip may be called 7zz, 7z or 7za; an old p7zip of the same name is not taken.

What to install for what:

  • tar archives: GNU tar, with gzip, bzip2, xz or zstd for the ending.
  • zip and plain 7z archives: 7-Zip, or bsdtar (libarchive-tools on Debian and Ubuntu, bsdtar on Fedora, libarchive on Arch).
  • locked 7z archives, and rar ones: 7-Zip (7zip on Fedora, Debian, Ubuntu and Arch).

M-x check-health says which of them it found.

10.10.7 When Tuatara refuses

Each refusal says why, and nothing is written. When making an archive:

  • Name the archive .tar, .tar.gz, ... or .7z: nothing archived: the name has none of the endings in the table above.
  • a tar archive takes no password: name it .zip or .7z: C-u c was given a tar name.
  • The two passphrases differ: nothing done: the password was typed differently the second time.
  • no password was given: the password was left empty.
  • a password takes only letters, digits, spaces and signs of plain ASCII: the password holds another letter or sign.
  • bsdtar locks no 7z archive with a password, 7-Zip does: install 7-Zip: a locked 7z archive was asked for and only bsdtar is installed. The message names the package for your system.
  • neither 7-Zip nor bsdtar is installed to make zip archives: there is no program for zip or 7z archives. The message names what to install.
  • gzip is not installed: install it for archives compressed so: the program for the ending is missing. The same goes for bzip2, xz and zstd.
  • ... names are too many to give 7-Zip at once: so many entries are marked that 7-Zip cannot be given all their names. Mark the directories that hold them instead.
  • ... would be inside what it holds: the archive would be put inside a directory it packs.
  • Nothing archived: ... is there already: you said no to replacing a file.

When extracting or looking inside:

  • it is no archive: the file is none of the kinds above, whatever its name.
  • it is locked with a password: Tuatara then asks for the password.
  • the password is not right: nothing is unpacked.
  • the password is not right, or the archive is damaged: the old zip encryption let a wrong password past its check.
  • bsdtar opens no 7z archive so locked; 7-Zip does: install 7-Zip.
  • bsdtar is not installed: there is no program for zip, 7z, rar, ISO 9660 or cpio archives.
  • it was read as ..., not as the ... archive its first octets say it is: the file pretends to be one kind and is another.
  • unpacking stopped: the drive came near *archive-free-reserve*.

Try it, with a zip of recipes

  1. Put a zip file called recipes.zip in a directory, or pack one: mark a few text files and press c, type recipes.zip after the directory offered and press C-j.
  2. Press U to clear the marks, as Z would work on the marked files. Put the cursor on the archive and press C-c e. A list of what it holds opens.
  3. Press q to close it.
  4. Press Z. The question offers a directory named recipes. Press C-j to take it.
  5. Tuatara says Extracted 1 archive. Press l on recipes and see the files.

Try it, with a locked 7z archive

  1. Mark a few files and press C-u c. Type private.7z after the directory offered and press C-j.
  2. Type a password, press RET, type it again and press RET. Tuatara says Archived when it is done.
  3. Put the cursor on private.7z and press C-c e. Tuatara says it is locked: not even the names can be read.
  4. Press Z and C-j. Tuatara asks for the password. Type a wrong one: Tuatara says it is not right and unpacks nothing.
  5. Press Z again and give the right one. The files are back in private.

10.10.8 Commands for archives

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
nonec, C-c crimu-archive-createPack the marked entries, from every directory they are marked in, or the one on the line, into one archive asked for, navigating to it as C-x C-f does: the directory of the other list beside this one offered first.
noneZ, C-c Zrimu-archive-extractExtract the archives marked, from every directory they are marked in, or the one on the line, into a directory asked for, navigating to it as C-x C-f does, made when it is not there: for one archive, a directory of its name beside it offered first.
noneC-c erimu-archive-listShow what the archive shown holds, in a buffer of its own, which q closes: the entry on the line in a list of a directory (C-c e there); with C-u, or where there is none, asked for.

10.10.9 Settings for archives

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*archive-free-reserve*1073741824a whole number, 0 or moreThe octets left free on the drive an archive is unpacked onto.
*archive-listing-limit*67108864a whole number, 0 or moreThe most octets of an archive's list of contents shown.
*archive-seconds*86400a number, 0 or moreThe seconds tar, 7-Zip or bsdtar may take to make, list or unpack one archive before it is ended.

*archive-listing-limit* is the most of an archive's list of contents that C-c e shows, counted in octets of that list. It is 64 megabytes as standard. A longer list is not shown, and the echo area says so. Raise it to see what a very large archive holds, which costs the memory of the whole list. Lower it to refuse a huge list sooner:

(setf *archive-listing-limit* (* 256 1024 1024))

*archive-seconds* is how long the program that lists, packs or unpacks one archive may run before Tuatara ends it. It is a day as standard, for the largest archives. Lower it to end a program that hangs sooner; C-x J (stop-job) ends one at once. The number is in seconds:

(setf *archive-seconds* (* 60 60))

10.11 Drives and the directory tree

A drive is a disk, a USB stick or a network share that has been attached to the computer, which is called mounting it. Rimu does not mount drives. Your desktop does that when you plug one in, and then you list the drive's directory like any other.

Rimu knows about drives in a few places. A size worked out with S counts what is inside a directory on the same drive only, so a drive attached inside it is not added in. A hard link works only on one drive. The trash of a drive is kept on that drive, as the last section explained.

A directory tree is a directory with its directories and theirs, as deep as they go. S adds up a whole tree. Copying, moving or deleting a directory goes through the entire tree. In a network or a mounted drive that is slow, but the editor stays usable, because the work is done in the background.

10.12 Finding, checking and encrypting

A list can also be made from a search. The commands below make a list of results, and you work on that list as on any other: mark, copy, move, delete.

M-x rimu-find lists the files whose names match a pattern, where * stands for any characters and ? for one. *.pdf finds every PDF below the directory you give. M-x rimu-find-text lists the files whose text holds the words you type. M-x rimu-duplicates lists files that are the same as another, in groups, so you can mark one of each pair for deletion.

The keys that start with : encrypt, decrypt and sign. : e and : d encrypt a marked file into FILE.gpg and decrypt it back. : s signs a file and : v checks a signature.

10.12.1 Commands for finding, checking and encrypting

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x rimu-findrimu-findList in a rimu list the files and directories under a directory asked for whose names match a pattern: * stands for any characters, ? for one (.pdf, report-202?.); upper and lower case alike unless the pattern has an upper-case letter.
noneM-x rimu-find-textrimu-find-textList in a rimu list the files under a directory asked for whose text matches what you type, as M-s g matches a line: each word a regular expression or its own characters, all on one line.
noneM-x rimu-duplicatesrimu-duplicatesList in a rimu list the files that are the same as another, in groups: in the directories marked in this rimu list, or else under a directory asked for.
none: erimu-encrypt-filesEncrypt the files marked (or the one on the line), each into FILE.gpg, to the keys or with a passphrase chosen in the minibuffer, asked once; and, when you say so, asked once too, wipe each file once it is encrypted (M-x wipe-file): with a passphrase, only after it, asked again, opens what was made.
none: drimu-decrypt-filesDecrypt the files marked (or the one on the line), each into its name without .gpg, for you alone, after asking once: their text is then on disk.
none: srimu-sign-filesSign the files marked (or the one on the line) with your key, the kind of signature asked once.
none: vrimu-verify-filesCheck the signatures of the files marked (or the one on the line), each said in turn and kept in Messages.

10.13 Colours of a list

A list uses faces to tell its parts apart: marked entries, entries marked for deletion, directories, sizes, dates and the rest. Links that lead nowhere have a face of their own, so a broken one stands out. Chapter 20 shows how to change a face.

FaceWhat it paints
:list-markedAn entry marked (>) in any list whose entries are marked, rimu's too, for the commands that act on those marked: the mark and the name, in the colour of warnings.
:list-marked-otherAn entry given a mark of another kind in a rimu list (a master's M, RIMU-MARK-MASTER): the mark and the name.
:list-deletionAn entry marked for deletion (D) in any list whose entries are marked, rimu's too: the mark and the name, in the colour of errors.
:list-directoryThe names of directories in a list: in rimu (C-x d) and where a link to a directory leads, in the trash (M-x rimu-trash) and among bookmarks (C-x m l).
:list-sizeSizes in a list or beside completion candidates: of files and buffers, and a rimu list's sizes column (S).
:list-dateDates and times in a list or beside completion candidates: when a file last changed, the date in a formatted name, a rimu list's last commits (G), when a message was sent.
:list-noteWhat is said of an entry beside it in a list: the first line of a rimu list's last commit messages, the first sentence of a face's description in M-x list-faces, the details under a finding in a report.
:list-filtersThe line above a list narrowed by search filters (C-x / s), saying by what and how many entries are left.
:list-dimWhat is of less interest in a list, set back: help buffers and the headings of clients that ended in the buffer list (C-x C-b), packages not loaded, bookmarks whose file is gone, files ignored in rimu and in a git status, a value missing in the health report (M-x check-health), a line saying more are not shown.
:rimu-symlinkThe names of symbolic links in a rimu list.
:rimu-broken-symlinkSymbolic links in a rimu list that lead nowhere, and what they hold.
:rimu-specialThe names of named pipes, sockets and devices in a rimu list.
:rimu-perm-writeThe permission to write (w) of the group and of others, among the details of an entry in a rimu list.
:rimu-set-idThe set-user, set-group and sticky letters (s, S, t, T) among the permissions of an entry in a rimu list.

Large files and work in the background

Opening a file of many gigabytes, and working on while Tuatara is busy.

Most files are small. A letter is a few thousand characters, and even a long book is a few megabytes. Now and then you meet a file of another kind: a year of a shop's sales with a line for every till receipt, or the log a web server has written for months. Such a file can hold a hundred million lines and take more room than your computer has memory. Many editors refuse it, or make you wait a minute before the first line shows.

Tuatara opens a file of any size at once and lets you work in it straight away. This chapter explains how it does that and what you see on the screen meanwhile. It then describes jobs, which is the name for work that takes a while and is done in the background, such as replacing a word in six million lines. You will learn how to see which jobs are running, how to stop one, and what the letter P at the front of the mode line means. The last parts are about saving a large file, about memory, and about a large file that lives on another machine.

One rule holds through all of it. Tuatara never makes you wait. Whatever it is doing, the next key you press is answered at once.

Every key in this chapter is pressed in NORMAL state unless it starts with C-x or M-, which work in both states. i starts INSERT state, and C-g or ESC returns to NORMAL state.

11.1 Opening a very large file

You open a large file as you open any other, with C-x C-f and its name. The first lines are on the screen at once, whether the file is 100 megabytes or 100 gigabytes.

The reason is that Tuatara does not read the file before showing it. A file of up to 64 megabytes is read whole into memory, which takes no time you would notice. A larger file stays on the disk, and Tuatara reads only the part your window shows, with a little before and after it so that paging down does not wait for the disk. The start and the end of the file are kept ready too, so g g and g e (non-modal: M-<, M->) are instant. Figure 11.1 shows the idea.

You can type, move, search and save from the first moment. Nothing waits until the whole file has been looked at.

11.1.1 The line number while the lines are counted

To say which line the cursor is on, Tuatara has to know how many line ends come before it. In a small file that is known as the file opens. In a large file it would mean reading everything first, so Tuatara counts the lines in the background while you work.

The mode line tells you about it. Where the line number normally stands, after the buffer's name, you may see L… with three dots instead of a number. To the right, after the mode's name, it says Counting lines and a percentage:

 TUATARA[N] P [-] sales.csv  L… C0  CSV  Counting lines 40%

L… means "the count has not reached this line yet". It shows only for lines the count has not passed. Near the start of the file you see the real number straight away. If you jump to the end with g e (non-modal: M->) just after opening, you see L… until the count gets there, and then the number takes its place, such as L100,000,001. When the count is done, Counting lines goes away.

The column can show C… in the same way. That happens on a single line so long that measuring it would take time, such as a file of a gigabyte with no line ends in it at all.

The count keeps up with you. If you type or delete lines while it runs, the number it ends with is right for the text as you left it.

11.1.2 Going to a line

: and M-g g ask for a line number and take you there, as chapter 2 explained. While the lines of a large file are still counted, a line the count has passed is found at once. For a line further in, the echo area shows how far the count has got until it reaches your line, and then you are there. C-g gives up the wait and leaves the count running.

11.1.3 Line numbers in the gutter

If you show line numbers beside the text (chapter 1), they follow the same rule. The gutter shows a number for each line the count has reached.

Try it, with a shop's sales

A shop in Motueka keeps every sale as a line of a CSV file: the receipt's number, what was sold and how many. This makes a pretend file of six million sales, about 100 MB.

  1. In a terminal, type this on one line and press RET: seq 1 6000000 | awk '{ print $1 ",kereru," $1 % 50 }' > ~/sales.csv
  2. In Tuatara press C-x C-f, type ~/sales.csv and press RET. The first lines are there at once. The mode line says Counting lines and a percentage. A fast computer may finish the count before you can look.
  3. Press g e (non-modal: M->) straight away. The last line, 6000000,kereru,0, shows at once. If the count is still running, the mode line says L….
  4. Without waiting, press g g (non-modal: M-<), then i, type note, and press C-g. The word is typed at the start of the first line at once. Press u to take it away.
  5. Watch the mode line for a few seconds. Counting lines goes. Press g e again and the mode line shows the line number in full.

11.2 Jobs: work in the background

Some commands have a lot to do. Replacing a word in every line of sales.csv means changing six million lines. Sorting them means comparing each with many others. If Tuatara did such work while you watched, the screen would freeze until it was done.

Instead, work of that size becomes a job. A job runs in the background. You give the command, and at once you can move, read, search and type again. When the job is done, its result is taken into the buffer and the echo area tells you, for example Replaced 6,000,000 occurrences on 6,000,000 lines.

You do not choose whether a command runs as a job. Tuatara decides by how much there is to do. In a short letter a replacement is done before you lift your finger. In a large file the same keys start a job, and the echo area says so:

Replacing in the buffer in the background; carry on (C-x J stops it)

11.2.1 What runs as a job

These are the kinds of work that go to the background when they would take time:

  • counting the lines of a large file, described above
  • a replacement over a large text, and counting the matches of a search
  • sorting lines, and keeping or deleting the lines that match a pattern
  • a change at every row of a tall rectangle or at a great many cursors
  • a save that takes more than a moment
  • a count of words (M-=) and a checksum of a file (M-x sha256-sum)
  • copying, moving and deleting files from a directory listing (chapter 10)
  • reading a file from another machine

Other chapters describe these commands. What they share is told here: each shows the sign P, each is listed with C-x j, and each can be stopped.

11.2.2 The sign P

The mode line starts with a few signs that keep their place, described in chapter 1. The first one is P, for processing. It belongs to the buffer shown in that window. While a job runs in the buffer, or waits its turn there, P is bright. The rest of the time it is faint, so faint that you hardly see it. A glance at the front of the mode line tells you whether this buffer is still being worked on.

P is lit too when another program is working for the buffer, such as a language server reading a project (chapter 13).

The setting *processing-indicator* holds what is shown. You can put another character there, or nil to have no sign at all:

(setf *processing-indicator* "*")

11.2.3 What a job will change is painted

While a job works through the buffer, the text it has still to change is shown in a colour of its own, the face :job-queued. As the job moves on, the painted part shrinks. If a second job waits behind the first, the text it will change is painted in another colour, :job-waiting. You can see at a glance which part of the file is finished and which is not.

For a replacement, the lines in your window are changed first, the moment you press RET. The rest of the file follows in the background. What you look at is never out of date.

11.2.4 Jobs take turns

A buffer runs one job at a time. If you give a second command while the first is still at work, the second waits, and the echo area says where it stands:

Queued, first in line: Sorting the buffer (C-x j lists the jobs)

It starts by itself when the one before it ends. A job that works line by line also waits while the lines of a newly opened large file are counted. You do not have to do anything, and you can keep typing while jobs wait.

Jobs in different buffers do not wait for each other. A sort in one file and a save of another run side by side.

11.2.5 Typing while a job runs

You may edit the buffer while a job works on it. What you type stays as you typed it. A replacement that reaches a line you changed meanwhile leaves your change alone and says so when it ends.

A sort and a filter are different, because they move whole lines about and an edit in the middle would spoil the result. If you try to change text they are working on, Tuatara asks whether to stop the job. Answer y to stop it and make your change, or n to let it finish.

11.2.6 Undo and jobs

Each job is one step to undo, however much it changed. One u takes back a replacement of six million lines.

The step stands at the place in the history where you gave the command, even if the job finished much later. Suppose you start a replacement, then start a second one that has to wait, then type a word. The first u takes back the word, the next the second replacement, the next the first. U brings them back in the same order. When a job's change comes back, the cursor stays where it is. You are not thrown to the last line the job touched.

11.3 The list of jobs

C-x j shows every job in a buffer called *Jobs*. Use it when P is lit and you wonder what is going on, when a job takes longer than you expected, or when you gave a command by mistake and want to drop it before its turn comes.

Each line is a job. The first column names the buffer it works in. The second says what it is doing and how far it has got, or that it waits and where it stands in the line. The third says in words what the job is. Jobs are listed buffer by buffer, the running one first and those waiting below it in the order they will run. The list keeps itself up to date while it is on the screen.

The list works like the buffer list of chapter 7. d marks the job on the cursor's line with a D, and x carries it out after asking: a job that waits is dropped, and one that runs is stopped. m marks a job and u takes the mark off. D drops or stops the marked jobs, or the one on the line if none is marked. q closes the list.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x jlist-jobsList the jobs in the background in Jobs: in each buffer those running, with how far they have got, and those waiting their turn, in the order they will run, their text painted in the buffer meanwhile.
noned, C-c dlist-mark-for-deletionMark the entry on the current line of the list for deletion (D), for the list's command that deletes them, and move down; with a count, as many entries, up the list for a negative one.
nonexlist-executeDelete the entries of the list marked for deletion (D), after asking, as the list deletes: the buffer list kills its buffers, rimu puts files in the trash, the list of jobs drops those waiting and stops those running.
nonem, C-c mlist-mark-entryMark the entry on the current line of the list (>), for the list's commands that act on those marked, and move down; with a count, as many entries, up the list for a negative one.
noneu, C-c ulist-unmark-entryTake the mark off the entry on the current line of the list, of any kind, and move down; with a count, off as many entries, up the list for a negative one.
noneD, C-c Dlist-delete-markedDelete the marked entries of the list (>), or with none marked the one on the current line, after asking, as the list deletes, as M-x list-execute does those marked for deletion; in rimu, with C-u, for good rather than to the trash.

11.3.1 Stopping a job

C-x J, with a capital J, stops the job running in the buffer you are in. It asks first, so a slip of the finger costs nothing. The buffer is left as it is, and a file that was being saved is left as it was before the save. If other jobs wait behind the one you stopped, they start one after another. To get rid of those as well, drop them in the list.

If nothing is running, C-x J says Nothing is running in this buffer.

One kind of save is always finished before it stops: a file being written in place, described below. Stopping it half-way would leave the file spoiled.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x Jstop-jobStop the work running in the background in the current buffer, after asking.

Try it, with the shop's sales again

The shop finds that what it sold as kereru soft toys were kea all along.

  1. Open ~/sales.csv from the first Try it and wait until Counting lines has gone.
  2. Press r r, type %kereru/kea and press RET. The lines on the screen say kea at once. The echo area says the rest goes on in the background, and P lights up at the front of the mode line. A fast computer may end the job within a second. Then make the file ten times longer, with 60000000 in place of 6000000 in the command, and start again.
  3. Press C-x j straight away. The list shows the replacement and how far it has got. Press q.
  4. Press g e (non-modal: M->), then g g (non-modal: M-<). You move freely while the job works.
  5. When the echo area says how many it replaced, press u. All six million lines say kereru again.
  6. Press r r, type %kereru/kea and RET once more, and this time press C-x J and answer y. The job stops.
  7. Press C-x k and answer that the changes may go. Nothing was saved, so the file on disk is as you made it.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*processing-indicator*"P"nil, or textWhat the mode line shows first, before [-] and the signs of directories kept read (INDEXING-INDICATOR).
FaceWhat it paints
:mode-line-signThe mode line's signs before [-] while their work goes on: P while a job of the buffer runs or waits its turn (processing-indicator), U while a directory of indexed-directories is being read (indexing-indicator), S while one is searched (searching-indicator), D while the editor runs as a daemon (daemon-indicator); in the theme's warning colour, to stand out.
:mode-line-sign-idleThe mode line's signs before [-] (P, U and S) while their work is not going on: faint, barely seen.
:job-queuedText a job in the background (a replacement, a sort, a rectangle's change) has still to work through (for a replacement only its matches), all of what it changes again while the lines of its new text are counted, until it is taken in; and a job's state in the list of jobs (C-x j).
:job-waitingText a job waiting its turn behind another in the background will change.

11.4 Searching a large file

C-s searches a large file the way it searches a small one (chapter 6). You type, and the first match after the cursor is shown as you type. Matches in the window are found at once, because that text is already read.

Two things differ, and both keep your typing quick.

The first is the count of matches beside the prompt. Counting every match in a file of gigabytes takes a while, and doing it again for each letter you type would be wasted work. So in a large text the count starts only when you stop typing for a moment, half a second as standard, and it runs in the background. The setting *typing-pause* holds how long that moment is. Until the count is done you can already press RET or go on to the next match.

The second is a match that lies far away, in a part of the file that has not been read. The search then reads the file through, a piece at a time, in the background. You can keep typing the pattern or give the search up with C-g while it looks.

Commands that work on the lines a pattern finds run as jobs in a large file. M-x keep-lines keeps only the lines that match and M-x flush-lines deletes them, both within the selection, so select the whole buffer first with C-x h.

Try it, with a huge log file

A web server in Timaru writes a line to its log for each page it serves. Most lines are fine. You want only the ones that say error.

  1. In a terminal, make a pretend log of six million lines. Type this on one line and press RET: seq 1 6000000 | awk '{print $1, ($1 % 50000 ? "ok" : "error")}' > ~/access.log
  2. Open ~/access.log with C-x C-f. Press C-s and type error. The first match is far down the file. The search looks for it in the background and shows it when found. Stop typing, and the count of matches appears beside the prompt a moment later. Press RET.
  3. Press C-x h to select everything, then M-x, type keep-lines and RET. A log has columns, so the prompt asks Filter by the column:. Press RET to take the whole record, type error and RET. P lights up while the job works.
  4. When it is done, the buffer holds 120 lines, each ending in error.
  5. Press u. All six million lines are back.
  6. Press C-x k and let the changes go.

11.5 Saving a large file

C-x C-s saves a large file as it saves any other. Tuatara waits half a second for the save, so a quick one says Wrote at once. A save that takes longer goes on in the background. The mode line shows Saving and a percentage, P is lit, and you carry on working. A key you press during that first half second is answered at once too, and the save carries on behind it. If you leave Tuatara while a save is running, it waits for the save to end.

How long a save takes depends on the kind of drive, because of how Tuatara keeps your file safe. A save does not write over the old file. It writes a new file beside it and, when that is complete, puts it in the old one's place. If the power fails in the middle, you have either the old file or the new one, whole. You never have a mix of both.

On some file systems, btrfs and XFS among them, the new file can share with the old one every part that did not change. A save then takes only as long as your change, even in a file of 10 GB. Tuatara does not go by the kind of file system alone: the first time it writes on such a drive, it tries sharing with two new empty files, which leaves nothing behind, and keeps the answer until you quit. An older XFS made without reflink shares nothing, so there it saves as on ext4.

On the others, ext4 among them, a new file means writing every part of it again. Changing one line of a 10 GB file then costs about a minute of writing. It happens in the background and you can go on working, but the disk is busy all that time.

11.5.1 Saving in place

If you often save very large files on such a drive, the setting *save-in-place* shortens the wait. Put this in your init file:

(setf *save-in-place* t)

Tuatara then writes only what changed, into the file itself, when that comes to less than about two thirds of the file. That is the case for a change that keeps the text the same length, and for any change in roughly the last third of the file. One changed line near the end of a 10 GB file is saved in a fraction of a second. A change near the start that makes the file longer or shorter moves everything after it, so it is still saved as a new file, which is the quicker way for it.

There is a price, and it is the reason the setting is off as standard. Before it writes into the file, Tuatara notes the old contents of the parts it will overwrite in a small file beside yours, named .NAME.tuatara-journal, and removes it when the save is complete. If the computer loses power in the middle of the writing, your file is half saved until Tuatara opens it again. The next time you open, save or revert it, Tuatara puts the old contents back from the journal and tells you that a save was cut short. Another program that reads the file before then, a backup for one, may see it half saved.

Leave the setting off if other programs read your large files, or if you do not mind the minute.

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*save-in-place*nilt, nilWhether a large file is saved by writing only what changed into the file itself, where that is quicker than writing it whole.

11.6 Memory, and pauses you might notice

You do not have to manage memory in Tuatara. This part tells you what to expect, so that nothing surprises you.

11.6.1 A file larger than your memory

A file of 11 GB opens on a laptop with 16 GB of memory, and so does one of 100 GB. Because a large file is used where it lies on the disk, opening it takes almost no memory.

Work that reads the whole file, such as counting its lines, a search, a replacement or a checksum, takes the file into memory a piece at a time and lets each piece go once it is well past it. Your other programs are not pushed aside while it runs. With a large file open and nothing to do, Tuatara uses no processor time at all.

11.6.2 Auto-save and large buffers

Tuatara keeps a copy of your unsaved changes so that a crash does not cost you your work (chapter 7). Each such copy is the whole buffer, so copying a huge one every few seconds would keep the disk busy for nothing. A buffer larger than *auto-save-size-limit*, 256 MB as standard, is not copied. In a file that size, save with C-x C-s when you have made changes you want to keep.

11.6.3 Undo

The undo history remembers every change so that u can take it back. A change to all of a large file is remembered in a compact way, but a long day of such changes adds up. As standard there is no limit. If memory runs short, *undo-limit* sets the most memory, in octets, that one buffer's history may hold.

11.6.4 Collecting garbage

As it works, Tuatara makes short-lived data: the text of a message, the result of a search. When that data is no longer needed it is garbage, and from time to time Tuatara stops for a moment to clear it away. The moment is short, usually too short to see.

Tuatara chooses that moment with care. When you have pressed no key for a short while, 0.3 seconds as standard, it clears the garbage then, if enough has gathered. The pause falls while you are thinking and does not come between two keys. The setting *idle-collection-seconds* holds how long you must be still. There is rarely a reason to change it.

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*auto-save-size-limit*268435456a whole number, 0 or moreThe largest buffer auto-saved, in octets.
*undo-limit*nilnil, or a whole number, 1 or moreThe most memory, in octets, the undo history of one buffer may hold.
*idle-collection-seconds*0.3nil, or a number, 0 or moreHow long you leave the editor alone before the garbage made since the last collection is collected, so the pause comes while you think, not between two keys.
*typing-pause*1/2a number, 0 or moreThe seconds without a key typed before work over a text too large to go through at each key starts.

11.7 A large file on another machine

Chapter 9 showed how to open a file on a server by writing /ssh: and the machine's name before its path. A small file comes across whole and then opens. A large one would keep you waiting for minutes on a slow line, so Tuatara treats it differently.

A file on another machine that is larger than 64 MB opens as soon as its first part has come. The rest goes on arriving in the background, and you can read what is here while it does.

C-x C-f /ssh:akaroa:/var/log/access.log RET

11.7.1 What you see while it arrives

A part of the file that has not come yet is shown as a single row in square brackets, saying how much is on its way. When the part arrives, the row is replaced by the text.

The transfer brings what your window looks at first. After that it brings the start and the end of the file, and then works forward from the start. If you jump to a place far ahead, that place comes next. You steer the transfer just by looking.

While any of the file is missing:

  • P is lit, and C-x j lists the transfer with how far it has got.
  • The buffer is read-only. Trying to change it says that the file has not all arrived.
  • The lines are not counted yet, so the mode line shows L….
  • A search, a copy or a checksum that reaches a missing part stops and says that part of the file has not arrived. Tuatara never puts made-up text in the place of what is missing.

When the last part has come, the echo area says All of access.log has arrived. From then on the file behaves like any other large file: its lines are counted, you can change it, and C-x C-s writes it back to the server.

11.7.2 Stopping the transfer, or losing the connection

C-x J stops the transfer, after asking. What came stays on the screen and can be read. The mode line then says incomplete, and the missing parts are shown as not arrived. The same happens if the connection is lost. An incomplete buffer is never written back to the server, so a half file cannot replace a whole one. M-x revert-buffer fetches the file again from the start.

Killing the buffer ends the transfer and deletes the copy on your computer.

Each request to the server has *remote-seconds* to be answered, 30 as standard. A server that stays silent longer than that ends the transfer, and the echo area says why.

Try it, with a log on a server

You need a machine you can reach with ssh that holds a file larger than 64 MB. Here it is called akaroa and the file is /var/log/access.log. Use your own names.

  1. Press C-x C-f, type /ssh:akaroa:/var/log/access.log and press RET. The first lines show as soon as they have come. P is lit.
  2. Press g e (non-modal: M->). The end of the file is there, since it was fetched early.
  3. Press C-x j. The list shows the transfer and its percentage. Press q.
  4. Press i and type a letter. Tuatara refuses, because the file has not all arrived. Press C-g.
  5. Wait for the message that all of it has arrived, or press C-x J and answer y to stop. After stopping, the mode line says incomplete.
  6. Press C-x k. The copy on your computer is deleted with the buffer.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*remote-seconds*30a number, 0 or moreSeconds a server reached for its files (/ssh:HOST:/path) has to answer each request, and ssh to connect.

11.8 In short

You want toDo this
Open a file of any sizeC-x C-f, as for any file
Know whether the buffer is busyLook for a bright P
See what is running, and how farC-x j
Stop the job in this bufferC-x J
Drop a job that waitsC-x j, then d and x
Take back a whole jobu (non-modal: C-/)
Save one line of a huge file quickly*save-in-place*, on ext4

Files you do not trust

Looking at a file without letting anything in it happen.

Most files you open come from you. Some do not: an attachment from an email you were not expecting, a directory a client sent, a download, a disk someone handed you. You want to read these, and you do not want to find out what they do. This chapter is about reading a file without running or changing anything. It starts with the safe way to open one file. It goes on to directories whose files are always opened that way, to the programs that decode pictures and PDFs behind a wall, and to git repositories you only look at. The opposite problem, a file you trust that nobody else should read, is in chapter 9: you keep it encrypted.

Be modest about what this gives you. The safeguards stop Tuatara itself from acting on a file and from changing it. They do not make a file harmless to the rest of your computer. If you copy a program out of a directory and run it in a terminal, no safeguard of an editor helps you. Each section below says what it covers and what it leaves out.

12.1 Opening one file safely

An ordinary open does some work for you. Tuatara guesses the kind of text (letter, code, notes) and chooses a major mode, which colours the text and changes some keys. It reads any settings the file gives for itself. It looks for a git repository around the file. It keeps a copy of your unsaved changes. All of that is help when the file is yours. For a file from a stranger it is also a lot of ways for the file to take part.

Opening a file safely turns that work off. The file is shown as plain text and it is read-only. No major mode and no hook runs on it. Version control is not looked up. No auto-save copy is made (chapter 7), and the directory is left as it was. The access time of a file of your own is left as it was too. The system lets only a file's owner read it without setting its access time, so reading another person's file still sets it. Mount such a drive read-only if that matters. The mode line says Safe just before the buffer's name.

Characters that draw nothing, such as a zero-width space, a soft hyphen or a mark that turns text right to left, are shown by their codes. Control characters and terminal escape sequences are shown as text, such as ^[, and do nothing. That does not close every way of hiding text. Variation selectors, the blank Hangul and Braille characters and spaces such as the no-break space are drawn as they are, and a letter of another alphabet that looks like a Latin one is not marked.

There are four ways to open a file safely.

  • C-u C-x C-f, a count before the ordinary command, asks for a file and opens it safely. M-x find-file-safely does the same.
  • tuatara --safe FILE from a terminal, or -R for short, opens every file named on the line that way. A file piped in with ls | tuatara - is a safe buffer too.
  • The setting *safe-directories* lists directories whose files always open safely, however you open them. An example is "~/Downloads/".
  • A file that looks like a program's data and not text opens safely by itself. The test is a null byte in its first 64 KB. Compiled programs, most archives and disk images have one, and so does text in UTF-16. A file with no null byte there, such as a script, or one whose first null byte comes later, opens the usual way. The setting *open-binary-files-safely* turns this off. Files you drop on the window open the usual way unless *open-dropped-files-safely* is true.

Files you opened safely are remembered. In the list of recent files (chapter 7) they carry a mark, and C-x C-r opens them safely again.

Safe does not mean fixed. C-x C-q makes a safe buffer editable, for the case where you really do want to write in it. It is still never auto-saved. M-x end-safe-visit opens the file as usual: it gets its mode, its colours and version control, and it is editable if you may write the file. Your cursor position, your unsaved changes and your undo history stay as they are. A file that is evidence (next section), or was when you opened it, refuses this, and says that it stays safe. So does a buffer whose file name now leads to another file than the one it read, as when a link was changed in the meantime.

Two more settings decide what a safe buffer shows. *invisible-characters-when-safe* is true as it comes, and shows the characters that draw nothing. And *text-direction-when-safe* is false, so that text written right to left (Arabic, Hebrew) is shown in the order it is stored and not the order it is read. The stored order is the one that tells you what is in the file.

12.1.1 What is never run

A safe buffer is for looking. A Lisp file opened safely has no Lisp mode, so C-x C-e and C-M-x are not defined there, and M-x does not offer eval-region or eval-buffer. If you turn on M-x lisp-mode yourself, those keys refuse, even after C-x C-q, and the echo area says that the buffer is opened safely and that nothing was evaluated. A list of a directory in rimu (chapter 10) opened safely refuses to pack, unpack, wipe, rename, move or delete the file on the line.

12.1.2 Why a file's own settings are not taken

Some files carry instructions for the editor in the file itself. A first line such as -*- mode: org; fill-column: 72 -*-, or a block near the end that begins Local Variables:, can choose the mode, the tab width, whether tabs or spaces are used, the fill column and the spaces between sentences. These are convenient in your own files. Tuatara takes only those few settings. It never runs anything a file says: a line that asks for an evaluation is left alone, and Tuatara says so. A package can ask to take more settings, and it is given the plain text of each, never anything to run.

A file opened safely is not read for these settings at all. For a file you do not trust, the less it can say to the editor the better. The setting *file-local-variables* is true as it comes. Set it to false and no file is read for them, safe or not.

Try it, with an attachment you were not expecting

  1. In a terminal, make a note with a character in it that draws nothing: printf 'From the council.\nMeet at the gate\342\200\213 at noon.\n' > ~/attachment.txt.
  2. Start Tuatara and press C-x C-f. Type ~/attachment.txt and press RET. Look between gate and at. There is nothing to see. Press C-x k to close the buffer.
  3. Press C-u C-x C-f, type ~/attachment.txt and press RET. The line now reads Meet at the gate<200B> at noon. and the mode line says Safe.
  4. Press i and type a letter. The echo area says the buffer is read-only. Press C-g.
  5. Press M-x end-safe-visit and RET. The file opens as usual and can be edited. Close it again with C-x k.
  6. Press C-x C-r. The list marks attachment.txt as one you opened safely. Press C-g to leave it.

noneM-x find-file-safelyfind-file-safelyOpen a file safely, for looking at a file from a source you do not trust: read-only, with no major mode, no hooks and no version control, so that nothing in the file is acted on; its file system left exactly as it was (no copy beside it), and its access time too where the system allows.
noneM-x end-safe-visitend-safe-visitOpen the file of this buffer, opened safely, as usual from now on, where it is.

noneM-x open-dropped-filesopen-dropped-filesVisit the files dropped on the window, in the window they were dropped on, as C-x C-f does, the last one shown; safely, as C-u C-x C-f does, when OPEN-DROPPED-FILES-SAFELY is true.

12.2 Evidence directories

Sometimes one safe look is not enough. If you work with files that may be evidence, such as a case directory from a client, nothing of yours must ever be written among them. A stray backup file, an auto-save copy or a changed access time can be a problem later. An evidence directory is a directory that you tell Tuatara about, and from then on it does two things. Every file in it opens safely, however it is opened. And nothing is written in it or below it by anything Tuatara does.

The setting is *evidence-directories* and it is empty as it comes, so no directory is evidence until you say so. Put it in your init file (chapter 20). A good plan is one directory for each case, with the evidence in one and your own work in another beside it:

Never put your work directory inside the evidence directory. Everything below an evidence directory is evidence, so a note kept there could not be saved.

12.2.1 Naming the directories

The setting is a list. Each entry is written in one of three ways, and the list may mix them.

EntryWhat it names
"~/cases/*/evidence/"A path. * stands for the name of any one directory, ** for any directories at all, none too.
(:name "evidence" :within "~/cases/")Every directory called evidence inside ~/cases/. Without :within, anywhere.
(:regex "^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{4}$" :within "~/cases/" :then "evidence")In every directory of ~/cases/ whose whole name matches, the directory named by :then. Without :then, the matching directory itself.

For the layout in Figure 12.1, the first entry is enough:

(setf *evidence-directories* '("~/cases/*/evidence/"))

Capital letters do not count in the comparison. A file is evidence by where it really is, with every link followed. A link in your work directory that leads into evidence does not make a loophole: the file behind the link is evidence. An entry that cannot be read is left out and reported in *Messages* and by M-x check-health. The other entries still count. Give :name and :regex entries a :within. Without it, Tuatara cannot tell from the setting alone which repositories hold evidence and has to search for it.

12.2.2 What happens to a file of evidence

A file in an evidence directory is opened safely whatever way you open it, whether by C-x C-f, from a directory list, from a link, or on the command line. The mode line adds the word Evidence before Safe, lit in the colour of errors, so that you see at once where you are. M-x end-safe-visit refuses.

Nothing is written there. This covers saving, C-x C-w, an export to PDF or Word, and Tuatara's own backup, auto-save and lock files. It also covers making, renaming, moving or deleting anything in the directory or below it. A refusal says what could not be done, and ends with the directory and the entry of *evidence-directories* that made it evidence. A question that asks where to write, such as C-x C-w or where to export to, does not start in an evidence directory. It starts in the last directory you chose that is not one, or in your home directory.

A terminal that you open from a file of evidence starts in your home directory. Then the shell's prompt and helpers do not read what the directory holds, such as a .git directory or an .envrc file.

12.2.3 Asking, and copying out

M-x describe-evidence tells you whether the file or directory here is evidence. It looks at the entry on the line of a directory list, at a path written at the cursor, or at the file of the buffer. It names the entry of the setting that made it so. A link is evidence when what it leads to is. For a file with another name that may be in an evidence directory, it says maybe. With the setting empty, it says that no directory is named.

To work on a file, copy it out. M-x copy-from-evidence asks for a directory, which must exist and may not be evidence, and copies the files marked in a directory list, or the one on the line, or the file at the cursor, or the file of the buffer. It works in the background. Whether a file is evidence is decided again by the file it opens to copy, so a link changed in the meantime to lead out of evidence copies nothing. Each copy is checked against its original by its SHA-256 sum (a number worked out from the contents, so that a single changed byte shows). A copy that differs is taken away. Nothing is written over a file that is already there. Next to the copies is a log, copied-from-evidence-DATE-TIME.log, readable by you alone. It says for each file what it was, where it came from, its size, both sums and the time. A directory is not copied: mark the files in it.

Saving a file of evidence under a new name in your work directory with C-x C-w is also a copy. The buffer then visits the copy. It is still opened safely, because the text is the evidence's, but the word Evidence is gone and you can edit it. Use M-x end-safe-visit when you decide it is safe to open as usual.

12.2.4 What the guard does not cover

The guard is Tuatara's own. Be clear about its edges.

  • A file with several names (a hard link) may have another name in an evidence directory. While evidence directories are named, Tuatara does not write such a file in place. It saves a new file and says so, and the other names keep what they held. Their link count and change time do change. If saving a new file is not possible, the save is refused. Such a file opens safely, M-x end-safe-visit refuses, and M-x describe-evidence says maybe, but the mode line does not show Evidence.
  • The access time of a file that is not yours cannot be kept (see Opening one file safely). Git itself sets the access time of directories it reads, so C-x g in a repository of evidence can change those. Mount evidence read-only if access times must stay. To tell whether a path is evidence, Tuatara follows its links one at a time and stops at the first evidence directory, so it never reads a link inside one, which would change that link's access time. A directory list of evidence does read the links it shows.
  • A directory list shows a preview of the file on the line. For a picture or a PDF in an evidence directory, that decodes a copy in the sandbox (next section).
  • Tuatara looks at where a directory really is just before it writes. A link or a drive changed in that moment is not seen until the next look.
  • Programs you run yourself write wherever they like. M-x compile and a shell in a terminal are not guarded.
  • A file opened in a background daemon (chapter 18) stays open there for as long as the daemon holds the buffer, even after the window that opened it is gone, and the drive it lives on cannot be unmounted. Do case work in plain tuatara.

A second guard is the system's own. Make the evidence read-only for everyone with chmod -R a-w evidence/. Tuatara's guard does not replace it.

Try it, with a directory of case files

  1. In a terminal, make a case: mkdir -p ~/cases/2026-0001/evidence ~/cases/2026-0001/work/more and printf 'The report, as it was given.\n' > ~/cases/2026-0001/evidence/report.txt.
  2. Open your init file with C-x C-f ~/.config/tuatara/init.lisp RET and add (setf *evidence-directories* '("~/cases/*/evidence/")). Save, and start Tuatara again.
  3. Open ~/cases/2026-0001/evidence/report.txt with C-x C-f, not the safe way. The mode line shows Evidence and Safe.
  4. Press M-x describe-evidence and RET. It says yes, and names the entry.
  5. Press C-x C-q, i, type a letter, C-g, then C-x C-s. Tuatara asks whether to save a write-protected file. Press y and RET. The save is refused and the message ends with and nothing is written in it.
  6. Press C-x C-w and type ~/cases/2026-0001/work/report.txt and RET. The copy is written. The buffer is now the copy: Evidence is gone.
  7. Open the original again, and press M-x copy-from-evidence. Give ~/cases/2026-0001/work/more/ as the directory. Look in it with C-x d for the copy and the log.

noneM-x copy-from-evidencecopy-from-evidenceCopy files out of an evidence directory (EVIDENCE-DIRECTORIES) to a directory asked for, which may not be in one: in a rimu list the marked files, or the one on the line; elsewhere the file at point or the buffer's file, each of them in an evidence directory.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*evidence-directories*nila list, each a directory's path, (:name …) or (:regex …)The directories whose files are evidence.

12.3 The sandbox around decoders

Pictures, PDFs and office files are not text. Showing one means decoding it, and decoders have bugs: a crafted file has been known to take over the program that reads it. Tuatara does not decode these files itself. It starts a separate program of the system for each job, inside a sandbox, and takes back only the result. A sandbox is a closed room: what happens inside does not reach the rest of the machine. Tuatara uses a program called bubblewrap, whose name on the command line is bwrap.

The decoder reads the file from a copy held in memory. It is given no name for the file, so it cannot reach the other files beside it and cannot write to the original. Beyond /usr it sees only a few files of /etc: the linker's cache, the alternatives and the font settings. Its time, its memory and the size of what it may write are limited. On top of that the kernel refuses it system calls that no decoder needs, such as making new rooms, loading kernel modules or opening network sockets other than local ones. When the decoder finishes, when you press C-g in its buffer, when you kill the buffer or when you leave Tuatara, it is ended with everything it started. While a picture is drawn or the text of a PDF is taken out, the work is a job: C-x j lists it and the mode line lights P.

Where this helps: a PDF or picture that carries an attack against the decoder finds a room with nothing in it to steal and no way out to send it. Where it does not: it does not stop you from being misled by what the file says, and it does not protect a program you start yourself. Some commands leave the sandbox on purpose, such as M-x open-externally, which hands the file to the desktop's own program. That command asks first, as long as *open-externally-ask* is true.

Several programs use the same room. Code formatters (chapter 13) run inside it with the project directory visible read-only, and no network. LaTeX that makes a PDF sees the document's directory, the TeX installation and your own fonts, all read-only, and writes only in its own working directory; so do biber, bibtex and makeindex when they make the document's bibliography and index. Language grammars run in it too, where a sandbox exists. Without a sandbox, the setting *syntax-helper-unconfined* decides whether the grammars of projects you trust run on their own without one.

Press M-x check-health to see whether bwrap was found and which version. Tuatara looks for it on the PATH, so a bwrap installed somewhere of your own is found when its directory is on the PATH. If it was not found, or if you set *sandbox* to nil, Tuatara does not decode: pictures and PDFs are shown as bytes and text. Your files are not at risk for that reason. Exports to PDF still work, and say that LaTeX ran without a wall.

(setf *sandbox* nil)

The limits are settings. A decoder gets 10 seconds (*sandbox-seconds*) and 1 GB of memory (*sandbox-memory*). All the decoders working on one file may use 2 GB together (*sandbox-total-memory*), where your system can hold them to it. A file larger than 1 GB is not decoded (*sandbox-input-limit*). It opens as bytes, and the echo area says why. A PDF that grew past the limit after it was opened says so in its view when it is read again. *sandbox-seccomp* is the kernel's refusal of unneeded calls, on x86-64 and AArch64. Keep it true unless a decoder of yours fails because of it.

Try it, with a PDF from a stranger

  1. Open any PDF with C-x C-f. It is decoded in the sandbox and shown as pages (chapter 16).
  2. While it loads, press C-g. In a shell, run ps -eo pid,args | grep [b]wrap | grep -v syntax-helper. Nothing of Tuatara's is listed: C-g ended the decoder. The buffer says it was stopped, and M-x revert-buffer reads it again. The syntax helpers you filtered out stay running, each in a sandbox of its own.
  3. Press M-x check-health and look for the line called Sandbox. It names bwrap and its version, and says whether the decoders are held to a total amount of memory.
  4. Press M-: *sandbox-seconds* RET. The echo area shows the number of seconds.

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes

12.4 Repositories you only look at

A git repository can run programs. Its hooks run when you commit. Its filters and helpers run when you check out or compare files. A language server for its code runs the project's build scripts. A repository you downloaded may have set these up for you. So Tuatara does not run any of it for a project you have not said you trust.

The first time you open C-x g (the git status, chapter 15), start a language server with C-c L, or compile in a project, Tuatara asks. The question says everything a yes would allow. There are three answers.

ModalNon-modalWhat it does
noneyTrust the project. Its programs may run. You are then asked once more, y and RET, because trusting cannot be taken back after programs ran.
nonelLook only. Git reads the project and nothing it names is run. The answer is remembered.
nonenNot now. Nothing runs, and you are asked again next time.

In a look-only repository the git status works and shows branches, commits and changes. Git reads the working files and a private copy of the repository's settings and index. The repository's own settings, hooks and filters never reach git, and nothing in the repository is written, not even its index. Git does set the access time of the directories it reads. The mode line of every git buffer says Look only in the colour of warnings, and the first line of the status says why. Commands that would change the repository are refused.

M-x trust-project asks again, whatever you answered before. Use it to move a project from look-only to trusted once you have read what is in it, or the other way. A project can also be trusted in your init file. The setting *lsp-trusted-projects* lists directories whose projects run their own programs without asking. A link from a trusted directory to another does not give the other any trust: a project is known by where it really is.

A repository that is, is inside, or holds an evidence directory is never trusted, and it is never asked about. It is look-only for as long as the evidence is there, even if it is in *lsp-trusted-projects*.

What this does not cover: it is a decision about Tuatara's own work. If you open a terminal inside the repository and run its build script, you have trusted it.

Try it, with a repository you were sent

  1. In a terminal, make a small repository to stand for a stranger's: mkdir ~/sent && cd ~/sent && git init && printf 'hello\n' > note.txt && git add note.txt && git commit -m first.
  2. In Tuatara, open ~/sent/note.txt and press C-x g. The question about trusting the project appears. Press l.
  3. The status opens. The mode line says Look only, and the first line of the status says why and that git only reads.
  4. Press M-x trust-project and RET. The same question appears. Press n to take the answer back. The status is look-only until you decide.

12.4.1 Command, setting and faces

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x trust-projecttrust-projectAsk again whether you trust the project of the current buffer (the git repository its file or directory is in, else its project, or the repository a git buffer shows), whatever was answered before.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*lsp-trusted-projects*nila list, each a directory's nameDirectories whose projects you trust to run their own programs.
FaceWhat it paints
