Writing code

Colours, indentation, comments, brackets, finding your way and running the program.

You can write code in Tuatara with nothing set up. A Python or shell script opens coloured, a new line starts at the right depth, and a few keys move you over whole functions. If you install a language server for your language, you get more: errors marked as you type, a jump to where a name is defined, a rename that changes only the real uses. This chapter goes through all of it in the order you meet it when you start a small program: what Tuatara knows about the language, how lines are laid out, how to comment code in and out, how to move over brackets and definitions, how to find where something is defined, how to run the program and read its errors, and how to settle a merge conflict in a file of code.

The last part is about Lisp. Tuatara is written in Common Lisp, and the Lisp you type can run inside the editor. If you do not write Lisp you can skip it, though it is the quickest way to try a small idea.

Two reminders from earlier chapters. i starts INSERT state, and C-g or ESC returns to NORMAL state. Every key in this chapter is pressed in NORMAL state unless it starts with C-x, C-c, C-M- or M-, which work in both. The C-c keys for code work in the buffers of programming languages. In a text file or an Org file they are free for other things.

13.1 What Tuatara knows about code

When you open a source file, Tuatara picks the language from the file's name, or from its first line when the name says nothing (a line such as #!/bin/sh). The language gives the buffer its major mode, such as python-mode or bash-mode, and the mode decides how the buffer behaves.

Two helpers then look at the code. Figure 13.1 shows which does what.

The first helper is built in. A grammar is a description of how a language is put together. Tuatara has one for about three hundred languages and reads your text with it as you type, building a syntax tree: the function holds a statement, the statement holds a call, the call holds its arguments. The tree is what tells a keyword from a name and a string from a comment, so it gives the colours. It also gives the indentation, the pieces that can be selected, and where each definition starts and ends. All of this works with no setup and with no other program installed.

The second helper is a language server, a separate program for each language, such as rust-analyzer for Rust or pylsp for Python. It knows the whole project and not only the file you are in, so it can answer questions the grammar cannot. It is optional. The sections on language servers and on finding definitions say how to start one.

A grammar is code someone else wrote, and a file you were sent can be made to confuse it. So Tuatara never runs a grammar inside the editor. A small program of its own does it, shut in a sandbox with its memory held and no network. If a grammar fails on a file, only that buffer loses its colours, and the echo area says so. The grammars of the common languages are on from the start. For one you use less, Tuatara asks the first time whether to turn it on. The setting *grammars-on* lists the languages that are on without asking.

Files you do not trust, such as evidence, are opened a different way, and chapter 12 describes it. A file opened that way is not coloured by a grammar and is never given to a language server.

13.1.1 How much colour

Colour comes in three styles. Rich colours everything the language's rules name, and it is the standard. Sparse colours only some kinds of thing, which suits a reader who finds a full palette tiring. None shows plain text. M-x rotate-colouring moves the buffer's language to the next style, in the order rich, sparse, none, and rich again. Every buffer in that language changes with it.

To start a language in another style, put a line in your init file (chapter 20 describes it): (set-colouring 'python :sparse). Sparse has four levels. Level 1 colours comments and strings. Level 2 adds keywords and functions. Level 3, the standard, adds types and constants. Level 4 colours everything. Give the level with :level, as in (set-colouring 'python :sparse :level 2). The language can be named as python, as a mode such as python-mode, as prog-mode for every programming language, or as t for every buffer.

13.1.2 Seeing what a language has

M-x check-health shows a table with a line for each language: whether its grammar, colours, indentation, selections and definitions work, which formatter and language server it knows, and a tick after each one that is installed on your machine. Use it when something does not work, to see whether the language is missing a piece or you are missing a program.

:preprocessorPreprocessor directives.

13.2 Indentation and tabs

Indenting a line means putting blanks before it, so that the shape of the code shows its structure. Tuatara indents a line by the language's own rules, read from the syntax tree. A Python line after def f(): goes in one level, a closing } in C lines up with the line that opened it, and the lines of a long Lisp call line up under its first argument.

You do not have to type the blanks yourself. A new line you make with RET, or in NORMAL state with o and O, begins at the indentation the language wants. If you leave such a line empty, the blanks are taken away again when you press C-g.

TAB indents the line the cursor is on. The cursor can be anywhere in the line. When the line is already right, TAB does something else: it completes the name before the cursor, as the section on language servers describes. The setting *tab-always-indent* says what TAB does. Its default, :complete, indents and then completes. With t it only indents. With nil it indents only while the cursor is in the blanks at the start of the line, and anywhere else it moves on to the next tab stop.

To lay out more than one line, select them and press C-M-\ (indent-region). In NORMAL state > (non-modal: C-z >, indent-selection-or-line) does the same for the selected lines, or for the current line when nothing is selected. M-m (back-to-indentation) moves the cursor to the first character of the line that is not a blank.

Lines inside a comment or a string that began on an earlier line are left as they are, because their blanks are part of the text.

13.2.1 Tabs and spaces

A tab stop is a column that a tab character moves to. Tuatara puts them 4 columns apart. *tab-width* changes that. Indentation is made of spaces unless you say otherwise, which keeps a file looking the same in every program. Some projects, a Makefile or a C project with its own style, use tab characters. For those, M-x indent-tabs-mode switches the buffer between tabs and spaces, and *indent-tabs-mode* sets the starting choice. M-x insert-tab puts in one tab character whatever the settings say, and C-z TAB (tab-to-tab-stop) moves on to the next tab stop with spaces or a tab as the buffer wants.

The init file has forms for one language at a time:

(set-indentation 'c 2)            ; two columns a level in C
(set-tab-width 'c-mode 8)         ; tab stops 8 apart in C files
(set-indent-tabs-mode 'bash t)    ; tabs in shell scripts

set-indentation takes 1 to 16 columns for a language whose rules indent by levels. set-tab-width takes 1 to 64, and prog-mode in place of a language means every programming language. A file can also say its own settings in its first line or in a block of Local Variables: at its end, and Tuatara reads them while *file-local-variables* is t.

Whole files are laid out by a formatter, a program that sets the code out as the language's community expects, such as rustfmt for Rust, ruff for Python and shfmt for shell scripts. The section on language servers covers it.

Try it, with a shell script

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/code-practice/count.sh and press RET. Tuatara asks to make the directory when you save, if it is not there. Press i and type these seven lines, pressing RET at the end of each. Do not type any blanks in front. If Tuatara has already put some in, leave them.

       sum_up() {
   for n in "$@"; do
   total=$((total + n))
   done
   echo "$total"
   }
   sum_up 3 4 5

    Press C-g.

  2. Press % to select the whole buffer, then C-M-\. The lines inside the function move in, the line inside the loop moves in again, done lines up with for, and the last line is at the left edge.
  3. Press C-g and C-x C-s to save. Press M-x, type compile and press RET. Press C-a and C-k to clear the command offered, type sh count.sh and press RET. If Tuatara asks whether you trust the directory, it is your own, so type y, and at the second question type y and press RET (the section on running a build explains why it asks).
  4. A window opens under the script with the name *compile*. The output is 12, and the last line says the command finished with exit code 0.
  5. Press g g and j (non-modal: M-<, C-n) to reach the for line. Press I, type four blanks and press C-g. The line sits too far in. Press >. It moves back to where the language wants it. Press u (non-modal: C-/) to undo that.
  6. Try the tab setting. Press M-x, type indent-tabs-mode and press RET. Press g g, j j to reach the total line, I, type four blanks and press C-g. Press >, then M-m. The mode line says C1: the indentation is one tab character. With spaces it says C4. Run the command again to switch back. Lines already in the right column are left as they are, which is why you spoil one first.

13.3 Comments

You comment out a line to stop the program running it without losing it, and you write a comment to say something to the next reader, which may be you in six months. Both are a single key.

C-z C (toggle-comment-lines) comments the current line. In NORMAL state the single key C does the same. If you have selected lines, it comments every line the selection touches. If the lines are all commented already, it takes the comment marks away instead, so the same key switches the comment on and off. The marker is the language's own: # in Python and shell scripts, // in Rust and C, ;; in Lisp. It goes at the indentation of the least indented line, so the block stays tidy, and the cursor stays where it was.

If you like the cursor to move down to the next line afterwards, so that you can press the key again and again to comment a run of lines, use toggle-comment-lines-ret. It has no key. Give it one in your init file:

(bind-key "C-z C" 'toggle-comment-lines-ret)
(bind-key "C" 'toggle-comment-lines-ret :map :normal)

M-; (comment-dwim, "do what I mean") does the sensible thing for where you are. With lines selected it comments them as C-z C (modal: C) does. On a line with no comment it starts one at the end of the code, with the marker and a space, and leaves you in INSERT state ready to type the words. On a line that has a comment already it moves you into it. In Python it writes # adds the numbers after the code, in Rust // adds the numbers.

The comment is also something you can select: m c selects the comment around the cursor, and m C the comment with the comment lines right before and after it.

13.3.1 Commands

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
CC-z Ctoggle-comment-linesComment the lines the selection touches, or the current line, or uncomment them when they are all commented: with the language's marker (;; in Lisp, / in Rust, # in shell scripts and Org) at their smallest indentation, or each line between the two a comment has where it has an end (<!– –> in HTML, /* * in CSS).
noneM-x toggle-comment-lines-rettoggle-comment-lines-retComment the lines the region touches, or the line point is on, then going to the next line, or uncomment them when they are all commented; it has no key of its own.

13.4 Brackets and pairs

Code is full of brackets, and a missing one is a common reason a program does not run. Tuatara helps in three ways.

Showing the partner. When the cursor is on a bracket, or just after a closing one, the bracket that pairs with it is lit in the :paren-match colour. A bracket with no partner, or the wrong kind, is lit in :paren-mismatch. It is on as standard, and M-x show-paren-mode turns it off and on in every buffer. To start every session with it off, put (setf *show-paren-mode* nil) in your init file. When you type a closing bracket whose partner is out of sight, the echo area tells you what it matches (*blink-matching-paren* controls that).

Closing them as you type. M-x electric-pair-mode makes an opening bracket write its closing half too, with the cursor between. Typing the closing half when it is already there steps over it, and DEL between an empty pair takes both away. It is off as standard. To turn it on for every session, put (setf *electric-pair-mode* t) in your init file. It does not pair everything, because some characters are usually plain text: the apostrophe in "don't", for example. *electric-pair-typing* says which are paired. Its default, :safe, pairs the delimiters of *pair-delimiters* except those in *electric-pair-safe-exclusions*. :all pairs every one.

Putting a pair round something. Select some text and press M-( (insert-pair) to put brackets round it. With nothing selected it writes an empty pair with the cursor inside. On text that has the pair already, it takes it off. M-x delete-pair takes away the pair round the expression after the cursor and keeps what was inside.

Selecting is just as direct. In NORMAL state m a selects a pair with what is in it, and m i selects only what is inside. For bracketed expressions of code, m A selects the whole expression and m I only its inside. These are the same selection keys as in chapter 5, with the pair as the thing selected.

Try it, with a Python script

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/code-practice/sum.py and press RET.

  2. Press i and type this one line, then C-g:

       print(add_up([3, 4, 5]))

Press g g (non-modal: M-<) then O to open a line above it. Type def add_up(numbers):, press RET and type return sum(numbers). Press C-g. The second line is indented one level.

  1. Put the cursor on the first ( after print, with g g, j j and l if you need to move. The matching ) at the end of the line is lit.
  2. Press m i. The text inside the brackets is selected, and M-o makes the selection one piece larger. C-g lets go.
  3. Press M-x, type electric-pair-mode and press RET. On a new line type [. You get [] with the cursor between. Type 1 and then ]. The closing bracket is stepped over and you have [1]. Press u (non-modal: C-/) until the line is gone, and run the command again to switch pairing off.
  4. Press C-x C-s to save.

13.5 Moving by definitions and lists

Moving a character or a word at a time is slow in code. Code has a shape, and Tuatara can move by the shape. A balanced expression is a word, a string or a bracketed group taken whole. A definition is a function or a type: in Lisp a bracket at the start of a line, and in Rust, C, Python and shell scripts whatever the language's grammar calls one. The keys use Control and Alt together, written C-M-, and they come from Emacs. Figure 13.2 shows what some of them do on a Lisp function, because Lisp, being nothing but brackets, shows it most plainly.

C-M-f and C-M-b (forward-sexp, backward-sexp) move over the next or the last balanced expression. C-M-n and C-M-p (forward-list, backward-list) do the same for bracketed groups only. C-M-d goes into the next group, just after its opening bracket, and C-M-u goes back out of the group the cursor is in, to its opening bracket. M-x up-list goes out past the closing bracket instead. In NORMAL state W and B do the work of C-M-f and C-M-b.

For whole definitions, C-M-a goes to the start of the one the cursor is in (beginning-of-defun) and C-M-e to its end (end-of-defun). A count first goes that many. M-x mark-defun selects the whole definition with the comments above it. Press it again to add the next one. In a LaTeX file the definitions are the sections (from \part down to \subparagraph) and the environments, so C-M-a and C-M-e step over those and not over each \textbf.

Some commands change the code by its pieces. C-M-SPC or C-M-@ (mark-sexp) selects the next expression. M-x kill-sexp cuts the expression after the cursor and C-M-DEL cuts the one before it, and C-M-t (transpose-sexps) swaps the two either side of the cursor, which is a quick way to put two arguments in the other order.

13.5.1 Selecting by the code

In every state the syntax tree grows and shrinks a selection for you. M-o (expand-selection) selects the smallest piece around the cursor, and each press after that selects the next larger one: the word, the call, the statement, the function, the file. M-i (shrink-selection) goes back a step. M-n and M-p move the selection to the piece beside it, the next argument or the next statement. A count before M-o grows several steps at once.

The m keys (non-modal: C-z m and the same letter) name a piece directly. m f selects the body of the function around the cursor and m F the whole function. m t and m T do the same for a type, m r and m R for a parameter, and m y and m Y for a test. Which pieces a language has depends on its grammar. Where the language has none of the piece, the echo area says so.

13.5.2 An outline of the file

M-g o (buffer-outline) lists the definitions of the file, each with its line number, in the order of the text. Type a few letters to narrow the list and press RET to go there. In Lisp the list holds the top-level forms. Where a language server runs, the list is its list of names, with functions, types and fields nested.

Try it, with the shell script again

  1. Open ~/code-practice/count.sh from the earlier box, and press g g.
  2. Press C-M-e. The cursor goes to the end of the function, past the }. Press C-M-a. It returns to the start of sum_up.
  3. Press j (non-modal: C-n) to go into the body, then m f. The body of the function is selected. Press C-g.
  4. Put the cursor on the word total in the loop, with j and l. Press M-o a few times and watch the selection grow: first a small piece, then the loop, then the whole function. Press M-i to shrink it step by step.
  5. Press M-g o. The list shows the definition. Press C-g to close it.

13.6 Finding definitions

Reading code is mostly going from a name to where it is defined, and from a definition to every place that uses it. Tuatara has a few ways, from the cheap to the thorough.

M-. and C-c d (xref-find-definitions) go to where the name under the cursor is defined. With a count, or where there is no name under the cursor, it asks for one. When a name has several definitions they are listed in a buffer called *xref*, and RET on one goes there. M-, or C-c D (xref-go-back) takes you back to where you were, and pressing it again goes further back. C-M-, (xref-go-forward) goes forward again.

In Lisp files this works with no setup, because the running Lisp knows its own definitions. For other languages it needs a language server, as the next section describes.

With a server, you can also ask more of the project:

  • C-c r (lsp-find-references) lists every place the name is used, in *xref*.
  • C-c g (lsp-find-symbol) asks for a name and goes to a function or type of the project by it, with the name at the cursor offered.
  • C-c T goes to the definition of the type of the thing at the cursor, and C-c I to the implementations of a trait or an interface.
  • C-c c lists the places that call the function at the cursor and C-c C the functions it calls.

In an *xref* list, n and p show the next and the previous place in the window you came from and leave the list where it is. RET or l goes to the place. o shows it in the other window, and h or q closes the list.

For what no server knows, such as a word in a comment or a message in a string, M-s g (search-in-files) searches the text of every file in the project as you type. The lines it finds can be gone through with M-g n and M-g p, the same keys as for a build's errors, described below.

13.7 Language servers

A language server takes some time to start, and it runs in the background, so you can go on typing while it starts. While it reads the project, a P shows at the front of the mode line.

13.7.1 Starting one, and trust

Tuatara knows the usual server for most languages and uses the ones it finds on your PATH. Install one with your system's packages or the language's own tool, such as rust-analyzer for Rust or python3-lsp-server for Python, and open a file of that language again. M-x check-health says which are installed.

A server runs the project's own code: build scripts, macros, plugins. For that reason nothing starts until you say you trust the project. C-c L (lsp) starts the servers for the buffer's language and asks, the first time, whether you trust the project. There are three answers.

  • y trusts it. Its servers start by themselves whenever one of its files is opened, in later sessions too. Its build commands (M-x compile) run, and so do the programs git runs for it.
  • l looks only. Nothing of the project runs: no server, no build, and git only reads the repository. The answer is kept.
  • n leaves the question for now, and you are asked again next time.

M-x trust-project asks again for the project of the current buffer, whatever was said before. M-x lsp-forget-project takes the trust back and ends its servers. To trust a whole directory of your own projects without being asked, put it in *lsp-trusted-projects* in the init file, but never the directory where files others send you are kept.

A project is the directory that holds the language's own mark, such as Cargo.toml for Rust, or else the nearest directory above holding .git or .project. An empty .project file makes a directory a project.

If a language has no server installed, the commands that need one say so. For example, C-c d says there is no way to find definitions in buffers of that language, and nothing is broken. M-x lsp-restart ends a stuck server and starts it again, M-x lsp-shutdown ends it, and M-x lsp-events lists the last messages sent to and from it, which is the place to look when a server does not do what you expect.

13.7.2 What the server tells you as you type

When the cursor rests in code, after *lsp-idle-delay* seconds, the echo area shows the parameters of the call you are in, or else what the name under the cursor is. A name and its other uses in the file are lit, and the mode line counts the problems found after the mode's name. A line with a problem has an E (an error) or a W (a warning) beside it, and the faulty text is underlined. A box under the cursor says what is wrong where it rests.

Some of these can be turned off. *lsp-signature-help* is the parameters, *lsp-hover-echo* is what the name is, and *lsp-highlight-symbol* is the lighting of a name's other uses. *lsp-diagnostics-display* says how a problem is said: :box under the cursor, :echo in the echo area, or nil not at all. *lsp-diagnostics-style* is the underline: :wave, :dotted, :line or :background.

The keys that go through the problems are C-c n and C-c p, which go to the next and the previous one and say what it is, and C-c l, which lists all of them in a window across the bottom. In that list RET opens the file at the place.

C-c h (lsp-describe-thing-at-point) shows what the server knows of the thing under the cursor, its type and its documentation, in the help window.

13.7.3 Completion

C-M-i or M-TAB (completion-at-point) opens a list beside the cursor of the names that fit what you have typed, each with what it is, and the chosen one's documentation beside the list. Typing narrows the list. C-n and C-p choose, TAB or RET puts the chosen name in, and C-g closes the list. In Lisp it offers the names of Lisp, and elsewhere what the server offers. Because *tab-always-indent* is :complete, TAB also completes when the line is already indented right.

Without a server you can still complete from the words you already have. M-/ (expand-word) replaces the start of a word with the nearest word that begins the same, from this buffer and then from others. Press it again for the next nearest. C-M-/ (complete-word) shows those words as a list. Terminals send that key as something else, and C-M-i lists the same words in a language with no completion of its own.

13.7.4 Rename, fixes and tidying

Renaming a function by searching for its name and replacing it is a classic way to break a program. The same letters may be in a string or a comment, and you miss the files you did not open. C-c R (lsp-rename) asks the server instead. It asks for the new name, then changes only the real uses, in every file of the project. Each file's changes are one step for u (non-modal: C-/) to take back, and nothing is saved until you save (C-x s saves them all).

C-c a (lsp-code-actions) offers the server's own fixes and changes for the selection or the cursor, with those for what is wrong there first: fill in a type, add an import, apply the suggestion for an error. C-c o (lsp-organise-imports) puts the file's imports in order and, where the server does it, takes out the unused ones.

C-c z (lsp-fold) hides the body of the block the cursor is in under its first line, and shows it again when pressed on that line. C-c Z (lsp-fold-all) hides every outermost block of the file, or shows them all again when some are hidden.

Three more things can be shown within the code, each switched on and off by its key. C-c i shows inlay hints: the types of variables and the names of the parameters a call fills in, written faint. C-c S colours each name by what the server says it is, a parameter, a field, a macro, over the usual colours. C-c K shows code lenses, short notes such as 3 references or Run test at the end of a line, and C-c k runs the one on the current line. Their settings are *lsp-inlay-hints*, *lsp-semantic-tokens* and *lsp-code-lenses*, which say whether each is on as a file opens.

The colours of C-c S come from *lsp-semantic-faces*, a list that pairs the name of a kind, as the server says it, with a face. ("function" . :function) colours every name the server calls a function in the :function face. A kind the list lacks keeps the colour the mode gave it. Most kinds are there as standard: types, parameters, variables, properties, functions, methods, macros, keywords, strings, numbers and so on. To set macros apart in the colour of comments, say, add an entry in front of the others:

(setf *lsp-semantic-faces*
      (cons '("macro" . :comment) *lsp-semantic-faces*))

The faces are those of the theme, so the colours stay with it. Switch the colouring on for every file with (setf *lsp-semantic-tokens* t).

13.7.5 Formatting

A formatter is a program that sets code out as the language's community has agreed, so that every file of a project looks alike and a change shows only what changed. C-c f (format-buffer) runs the language's formatter in the background. It is shut in the sandbox, which lets it read the project and change nothing else. It runs from the project's directory, so a settings file of the formatter's own is found. If no formatter is installed the language server lays the code out, and if neither is there Tuatara indents each line by its own rules. The whole change is one step: u (non-modal: C-/) takes all of it back. C-c F (format-region) does the same for the selected lines.

To choose another formatter for a language, set *language-formatters* in the init file. *format-on-save* names the languages formatted before each save, or t for every language with a formatter installed. A formatter that takes longer than *format-seconds* is stopped and nothing changes. *format-in-sandbox* turns off the sandbox for a formatter that cannot work shut in.

13.7.6 Settings of your own

*lsp-languages* lists the languages whose servers are used. *language-servers* names a server of your own choice for a language in place of the usual one. *lsp-wait* is the seconds a command waits for an answer it needs at once, and a key press stops the wait sooner. *lsp-watch-files* tells servers about files other programs changed, and *lsp-watch-skipped* names the directories it never watches, such as target and node_modules. *lsp-outline* makes M-g o list the server's names.

Try it, with the Python script

This needs a language server for Python, such as pylsp, ty or ruff. Without one, the steps still show what Tuatara says.

  1. Open ~/code-practice/sum.py. Put the cursor on add_up in the print line.
  2. Press M-x, type lsp and press RET. If Tuatara asks whether you trust the directory, it is your own, so type y and press RET. The echo area says the server is starting and then that it is ready.
  3. Press C-c d. The cursor jumps to the def line. Press C-c D to go back.
  4. Press C-c h. The window shows what the server knows of the function. Press C-x 1 (modal: F) when you have read it.
  5. Press C-c R, type total_of and press RET. The name changes in both places. Press u (non-modal: C-/) to undo both at once.
  6. In the return line, press A and type x, then C-g, to make a mistake. After a moment an E shows beside the line and the mode line counts 1. Press C-c l to list it, RET to go there, and u to take the mistake away.
  7. Press C-c f. With a formatter installed, the file is laid out by it. The echo area names the formatter, or says why none could be used. Press M-x, type lsp-shutdown and press RET when you are done.

13.8 Snippets

A snippet is a piece of text with places to fill in, which you put in by typing a short key and pressing TAB. It saves typing the same few lines every time, such as the top of a script. Nothing in a snippet is ever run.

Your snippets are files in ~/.config/tuatara/snippets/, in a directory named after the major mode: python-mode/, prog-mode/ for every programming language, or fundamental-mode/ for every buffer. A snippet file starts with lines that name it and give its key, then a line of two dashes, then the text:

# name: Script header
# key: hdr
# --
# ${1:What this file does}
# Written on $CURRENT_YEAR-$CURRENT_MONTH-$CURRENT_DATE
$0

In the text, $1, $2 and so on are the places to fill in, in order. ${1:words} is a place that starts with some words, which your typing replaces. ${1|a,b|} offers a choice. $0 is where the cursor ends up. A name with a dollar stands for a value: $CURRENT_YEAR, $CURRENT_MONTH and $CURRENT_DATE for today, $TM_FILENAME for the file, $AUTHOR for the name in *user-full-name*.

Type the key and press TAB, and the text goes in with the cursor in the first place. TAB moves on to the next place and S-TAB back to the one before. After the last place the cursor goes to $0. C-c y (insert-snippet) chooses a snippet from a list by name, each with its key, and with text selected the selection goes where the snippet has $TM_SELECTED_TEXT. M-x copy-snippet copies one of Tuatara's own into your directory so that you can change it, and yours takes the place of Tuatara's.

Try it, with a Python script header

  1. In a terminal, make the snippet. Type this as one command.

       mkdir -p ~/.config/tuatara/snippets/python-mode && printf '# name: Script header\n# key: hdr\n# --\n# ${1:What this file does}\n# Written on $CURRENT_YEAR-$CURRENT_MONTH-$CURRENT_DATE\n$0\n' > ~/.config/tuatara/snippets/python-mode/header
  2. Open ~/code-practice/sum.py. Press g g and O to open a line above the first. Type hdr and press TAB.
  3. Two comment lines appear. The first has What this file does ready to be typed over. Type Adds up some numbers, and press TAB. The cursor is on the line after, which is where $0 was.
  4. Press C-g and u (non-modal: C-/) until the lines are gone. Delete the snippet file if you do not want to keep it.

13.8.1 Commands and settings

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-c yinsert-snippetPut in a snippet chosen by its name among those of the current buffer's mode (each listed with its key), at point; with the selection active, in its place, the selected text where it has $TM_SELECTED_TEXT.
noneM-x copy-snippetcopy-snippetCopy one of Tuatara's own snippets, chosen by its name, into your snippets directory (the first of snippet-directories, in the directory of its mode) and visit it: your copy, changed as you like, takes the place of Tuatara's.
noneM-x snippet-next-fieldsnippet-next-fieldGo to the next field of the snippet being filled in; past the last, end it where it puts the cursor.
noneM-x snippet-previous-fieldsnippet-previous-fieldGo back to the field of the snippet before the one the cursor is in.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*snippet-directories*nila list, each a directory's nameThe directories your snippets are in, each with a directory for each major mode (org-mode/, prog-mode/, fundamental-mode/), a snippet a file in it.
*snippet-tab*tt, nilWhether TAB puts in the snippet whose key is before the cursor.
*user-full-name*nilnil, or textYour full name, as "Ann Taranaki": the author of an exported document with no #+author:, %author% in a note template and $AUTHOR in a snippet.

*snippet-directories* is the list of directories your snippets are in. Each directory holds a directory for each major mode, as described above. It is nil as standard, which means snippets/ in your configuration directory, the directory named at the start of this section. To keep them with your notes, or to use a directory you share with someone, name it:

(setf *snippet-directories* '("~/notes/snippets/"))

*snippet-tab* is t, so TAB puts in the snippet whose key stands before the cursor, as in the try-it above. With nil TAB never does that, and you choose a snippet with C-c y instead. Use it if a key you typed, hdr perhaps, is also a word you really write before pressing TAB to indent:

(setf *snippet-tab* nil)

13.9 Running a build or the tests

Writing code is a loop. You change something, run it, read what went wrong, go to each place, fix it, and run it again. M-x compile runs the build or the tests from inside the editor and turns every error in the output into a place you can jump to, so the loop never leaves the keyboard.

M-x compile asks for a command. Type anything you would type in a shell: make -k, cargo build, python3 -m unittest or sh count.sh. Tuatara runs it with your shell from the root of the project the current file is in, or from the file's own directory when the file is in no project. The first time it offers make -k (the setting *compile-command*), and after that the command you used last. M-p goes back through earlier ones. The command runs with no terminal, so a program that asks for a password, such as sudo or ssh, cannot reach your screen. Chapter 17 is for those.

A build runs the project's own code, so in a project you have not trusted Tuatara asks first, the same question the language servers ask. Answer n or l and nothing runs.

The output appears in a buffer called *compile* as it comes, and you go on working meanwhile. Read the first error and start fixing it while the rest is still being built. When the command ends, a last line says how it ended and how long it took. Only one compile runs at a time. If you start a second, Tuatara asks and starts it when the first has finished. C-c C-k in *compile* stops a command that is still running, r there runs it again, and q closes the window. The output kept is capped at *compile-output-limit* octets.

Lines in the output that name a file and a line are places. Tuatara knows the form of the errors of GCC and Clang, of rustc and cargo, of Python, and the file:line: of grep -n and make. Errors are in the :compile-error colour, warnings in :compile-warning and notes in :compile-note. M-g n (next-place) goes to the next place and M-g p (previous-place) to the one before, from any buffer. At the end of the list the echo area says there are no more. Tuatara counts columns from 0, while compilers usually count from 1, so a compiler's column 5 shows as column 4 in the mode line.

The same two keys go through any list of places made last: the lines found by a search of files (M-s g), the problems a language server found in a buffer, or the errors in *LaTeX errors* when a PDF could not be made cleanly (chapter 14). In *compile*, RET on a line opens that place.

Try it, with a mistake in the Python script

  1. Open ~/code-practice/sum.py. Press g g, then j j to reach the print line, then A, type x and press C-g. The line now reads print(add_up([3, 4, 5]))x, which is not valid Python.
  2. Press C-x C-s. Press M-x, type compile and press RET. Press C-a and C-k, type python3 sum.py and press RET. If asked to trust the directory, type y, then y and RET.
  3. *compile* opens under the file. It shows Python's own words, a line beginning File with the file's name and line 3, then the line itself and SyntaxError. The last line says the command failed with a non-zero exit code.
  4. Press M-g n. The cursor goes to line 3 of sum.py, and the echo area shows the line from the output.
  5. Press u (non-modal: C-/) to take the x away, C-x C-s, then M-x, compile and RET, and RET again to run the command offered. The output is 12.

13.9.1 Commands and settings

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x compilecompileRun a command asked for, a build or the tests (make -k, cargo build, pytest), with your shell from the root of the project the current buffer's file is in (see PROJECT-ROOT-MARKERS), or from its directory when it is in none, and show what it prints in compile as it comes, the editor free meanwhile.

:compile-warningThe lines of a compile's output (M-x compile) that say a warning: as warnings are marked in text.
:compile-noteThe lines of a compile's output (M-x compile) that say a note or give help: as information is marked in text.

13.10 Merge conflicts

When two people change the same lines, or you change them on two branches, Git cannot choose which to keep. It writes both versions into the file between marker lines and stops, and you decide. The file then holds this:

<<<<<<< HEAD
name = "Aroha"
=======
name = "Hemi"
>>>>>>> other-branch

The first version, after <<<<<<<, is yours in a merge. In a rebase it is the branch the commits are being made again onto. The second version, after =====, is the other one. When Git is set to show it, a third part after ||||||| has the lines as they were before either change, which is called the base.

Putting this right by hand means deleting marker lines with care, and a marker left behind breaks the build. Tuatara looks through each file you open for conflicts. It colours the first side, the second side, the base and the marker lines, and the mode line says how many there are. The keys under C-c ^ settle each one in a single step, and each step goes on to the next conflict.

ModalNon-modalWhat it does
noneC-c ^ nGo to the next conflict.
noneC-c ^ pGo to the one before.
noneC-c ^ uKeep the first side, the upper one.
noneC-c ^ lKeep the second side, the lower one.
noneC-c ^ aKeep both sides, first then second.
noneC-c ^ bKeep the base, the lines from before either change.
noneC-c ^ =Show how the two sides differ, in a buffer of its own.

Every choice is one step for u (non-modal: C-/), so a wrong choice is easy to take back.

How the merge began, which branch is which, and how to finish it afterwards, is in chapter 15. This chapter only covers the file.

Try it, with a small conflict

  1. In a terminal, make a file with a conflict in it. Type this as one command.

       printf 'greeting = "hello"\n<<<<<<< HEAD\nname = "Aroha"\n=======\nname = "Hemi"\n>>>>>>> other-branch\nprint(greeting, name)\n' > ~/code-practice/greet.py
  2. Open ~/code-practice/greet.py. The two sides and the marker lines are coloured, and the mode line says there is a conflict.
  3. Press g g (non-modal: M-<) and then C-c ^ n. The cursor goes to the line with the <<<<<<< marker, and the echo area says which conflict it is and how many there are.
  4. Press C-c ^ =. A buffer shows the lines only one side has. Press q to close it.
  5. Press C-c ^ l. The marker lines and the first side are gone, and name = "Hemi" stays. Press u (non-modal: C-/) and the conflict is back. Press C-c ^ a to keep both lines instead, and u again.

13.10.1 Commands and faces

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x conflict-markers-modeconflict-markers-modeShow the conflicts a merge left in the current buffer, and give it the keys that put them right, or stop.
noneM-x conflict-nextconflict-nextGo to the start of the next conflict, its <<<<<<< line, and say which of how many it is.
noneM-x conflict-previousconflict-previousGo to the start of the conflict before point, its <<<<<<< line, and say which of how many it is.
noneM-x conflict-keep-first-sideconflict-keep-first-sidePut the conflict point is in right by keeping its first side, the lines after its <<<<<<< line, and taking away the rest and its marker lines; then go to the next conflict.
noneM-x conflict-keep-second-sideconflict-keep-second-sidePut the conflict point is in right by keeping its second side, the lines after its ===== line, and taking away the rest and its marker lines; then go to the next conflict.
noneM-x conflict-keep-both-sidesconflict-keep-both-sidesPut the conflict point is in right by keeping both its sides, the first then the second, the base and the marker lines taken away; then go to the next conflict.
noneM-x conflict-keep-baseconflict-keep-basePut the conflict point is in right by keeping its base, the lines after its ||||||| line, as they were before either side changed them, the sides and the marker lines taken away; then go to the next conflict.
noneM-x conflict-show-sides-diffconflict-show-sides-diffShow how the two sides of the conflict point is in differ, in a buffer of their own in another window, which q closes: the lines only the first side has after -, those only the second has after +, three lines around each change, the sides named by their marker lines.
FaceWhat it paints
:conflict-firstThe first side of a conflict a merge left in a file, the lines after its <<<<<<< line: as the lines a difference takes away unless set.
:conflict-secondThe second side of a conflict a merge left in a file, the lines after its ===== line: as the lines a difference adds unless set.
:conflict-baseThe base of a conflict a merge left in a file, the lines after its ||||||| line, as they were before either side changed them.
:conflict-markerThe marker lines of a conflict a merge left in a file (M-x conflict-markers-mode): <<<<<<<, ||||||| and >>>>>>> with the names after them, and =====, out to the window's edge.

13.11 Lisp development

The Lisp you type runs in the editor itself. That is how the init file works, and it is a quick way to try a small function or to look at a value. A file ending in .lisp opens in Lisp mode, which has keys for running what you have written. No language server is needed: the running Lisp knows its own definitions, so M-. goes to them.

The keys that run text work only in Lisp buffers: a .lisp file, the scratch buffer *lisp-scratch* (M-x lisp-scratch) and your init file.

  • C-x C-e (eval-last-expression) runs the expression just before the cursor and shows its value in the echo area. A whole number is also shown in octal and hexadecimal.
  • C-M-x (eval-top-level-form) runs the whole top-level form the cursor is in, that is, the one whose bracket is at the start of a line. A defvar in it takes its new value even when the variable already had one.
  • M-x eval-region runs every form in the selection, and M-x eval-buffer every form of the buffer, one after another, as a file's forms are run when it is loaded.
  • C-j (eval-print-last-expression) in *lisp-scratch* runs the expression and writes its value into the buffer.
  • M-: (eval-expression) works anywhere. It asks for an expression, shows its value, and runs only what you typed.
  • C-c C-m (pp-macroexpand-last-expression) shows a macro call expanded once, laid out in a window of its own.

A file opened safely (chapter 12) runs nothing: the keys say so and do nothing.

M-x ielm opens *ielm*, a prompt where you type Lisp and read the answer at once. The modal keys are off there, so you type without pressing i. RET runs the input when it is a whole expression, and otherwise starts a new line of it. C-j runs it as it is. M-p and M-n go back and forward through what you typed before, C-c C-u clears the input, and TAB completes a name. C-c C-b chooses the buffer that the Lisp you type sees as current, so that (insert "x") puts text there.

When something fails, M-x toggle-debug-on-error makes the next error show the calls that were running when it happened, innermost first, in *Backtrace*. The setting *debug-on-error* makes that the standard.

Try it, with a Lisp function that adds numbers

  1. Open ~/code-practice/sum.lisp, press i and type these lines. RET indents each line for you.

       (defun add-up (numbers)
     (reduce #'+ numbers))

   (add-up '(3 4 5))

    Press C-g.

  2. Put the cursor inside the defun (g g) and press C-M-x. The echo area shows the form and then ADD-UP. The function now exists in the editor.
  3. Go to the last line with g e (non-modal: M->), move to its end and press C-x C-e. The echo area shows the value, 12, and then the number in octal and hexadecimal.
  4. Put the cursor on add-up in the last line, with C-a (modal: g h) and l l, and press M-.. It goes to the defun. Press M-, to come back.
  5. Press M-x, type ielm and press RET. After the prompt type (add-up '(10 20)) and press RET. The answer is 30. Press M-p and the same input comes back.
  6. Press M-x, type lisp-scratch and press RET for a buffer of your own to try things in. Press g e and i, type (+ 1 2) and press C-j. The value is written on the next line.

13.12 LaTeX

In a LaTeX file C-c C-e (latex-insert-environment) asks for the name of an environment and writes its \begin and \end on lines of their own, with the cursor on an empty line between them. The names the file already uses come first, then the usual ones (itemize, enumerate, figure, table, equation, align and so on), the last one you gave at the top; any other name can be typed. With text selected, the lines it touches are put between \begin and \end instead. The lines are indented as the mode indents them.

C-c ] (latex-close-environment) writes the \end for the nearest \begin that has none yet, on a line of its own and indented like its \begin. A \begin or \end after a % is a comment and does not count. When every environment before the cursor is closed, it says so. Both keys work in NORMAL and INSERT state.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-c C-elatex-insert-environmentAsk for the name of an environment and write its \begin{NAME} and \end{NAME} on lines of their own, indented as the mode indents them, with point on an empty line between.
noneC-c ]latex-close-environmentWrite \end{NAME} for the nearest \begin{NAME} before point that no \end{NAME} closes yet, on a line of its own when the line has text, indented as that \begin is.

C-x T p shows a LaTeX file's formulas as pictures, as it does in an Org note (see "Formulas as pictures" in the Org chapter): $...$ and \(...\) in the line, \[...\], $$...$$ and the environments of equations (equation, align, gather, multline and the like) centred on rows of their own when they stand alone on their lines. Only the body is read, after \begin{document}, never a comment or a verbatim environment. The formulas are drawn after the file's own preamble, so its macros work in them; when the sandbox cannot set that preamble (it takes in a package of your own beside the file), they are drawn after *formula-preamble* instead.

Org

Notes, lists, tasks, dates, tables and documents, all in plain text.

Org is a way of writing plain text so that a program can help you with it. A line that begins with a star is a heading. A line that begins with a hyphen is an item of a list. A heading with the word TODO in front is a task. From a handful of marks like these, Tuatara can fold a long note down to its headings, tick off a shopping list, show you what is due this week, add up a column of numbers and turn the whole note into a PDF or a Word document.

The file stays plain text throughout. You can read it in any program, send it to anyone and keep it for decades. Org began in the editor Emacs, and files written there open in Tuatara as they are. Tuatara's Org is its own, written for Tuatara, so nothing in this chapter needs Emacs.

This is a long chapter because Org does a lot. You do not need all of it. The first three sections are enough to keep notes and lists. Read about tasks, dates and the agenda when you want Tuatara to remind you what to do. Read about tables when you have numbers, and about exporting when a note must become a document for someone else.

One reminder about the state keys. i starts INSERT state, and C-g or ESC returns to NORMAL state. Keys that start with C-c, C-x or M- work in both. Where this chapter says "type", do it in INSERT state.

14.1 An Org file

A file whose name ends in .org opens in Org mode, and the mode line says Org. Any other buffer becomes an Org buffer with M-x org-mode. The scratch buffer *org-scratch* of chapter 7 is one already, and is a good place to try things.

Here is a small note as you type it:

#+title: My garden

* Vegetables
The beds by the fence get the most sun.
** Tomatoes
Water *every* morning, /not/ at noon.
** Beans
* Fruit

The first line gives the note a title. Lines that begin with #+ tell Org something about the note and are not part of its text. One star makes a heading of the first level and two stars make a heading under it. There must be a space after the stars. The text below a heading belongs to it, down to the next heading.

Within the text a few marks change how words look, and how they come out in an exported document.

You typeIt means
*bold*Bold
/italic/Italic
_underlined_Underlined
~code~Code, such as a command's name
=verbatim=Text shown exactly as written
[fn:1]A footnote, its text on a line beginning with the same mark

14.1.1 How a note is shown

Tuatara shows an Org file a little tidier than it is written. A heading shows a round sign in place of its last star and the stars before it are hidden. Each line is set in by the level of the heading it is under. None of this changes the file, which still holds the stars at the left edge. This is the indented view. M-x org-indent-mode turns it off for the buffer, so that you see the file as it is, and on again.

If you would rather see the stars always, set *org-startup-indented* to nil in your init file. It is t as standard, which opens every Org file in the indented view; at nil a file opens as it is written, and M-x org-indent-mode still turns the indented view on for a buffer. A single note can say so for itself with the line #+STARTUP: noindent, and #+STARTUP: indent asks for the indented view. The line wins over the setting.

 t (standard)        nil

 ◉ Garden            * Garden
   ○ Beds            ** Beds
     ○ Tomatoes      *** Tomatoes

*org-bullets* holds the signs that stand for the stars, one for each level. As standard it is ("◉" "○" "✸" "✿"): a first-level heading shows ◉, a second-level one ○, a third-level one ✸, a fourth-level one ✿, and the fifth starts the round again with ◉. Any list of signs works, of any length, and nil shows the stars themselves. To have a plain dot for the first three levels:

(setf *org-bullets* '("•" "◦" "▪"))

Lines like #+STARTUP: are read when the file is opened. After you change one, kill the buffer with C-x k and open the file again.

With the indented view or *org-bullets*, the stars before the last one of a heading are hidden, and that is *org-hide-leading-stars*, t as standard. Set it to nil and they are shown, faint, in front of the sign:

 t (standard)        nil

 ◉ Garden            ◉ Garden
 ○ Beds              * ○ Beds
 ○ Tomatoes          ** ○ Tomatoes

The init-file line is (setf *org-hide-leading-stars* nil). It helps when you count levels by the stars. A note that is shown with the stars as they are written (#+STARTUP: noindent with *org-bullets* nil) shows all of them either way.

Org text can nest: a list in a list in a quote block, emphasis inside a link label. The parser follows that down only as far as *org-depth-limit*, 200 as standard. Text nested deeper is read as plain words, so that a file made of nothing but nesting cannot bring the editor to a stop. No real note comes near it. A lower number such as (setf *org-depth-limit* 50) is for someone who opens files from strangers and wants the parser held tighter.

noneM-x org-indent-modeorg-indent-modeShow the current Org buffer indented, or as it is again: each line indented by the level of the headline it is under, a headline's stars but the last hidden.

14.2 Headings and folding

Headings are what make a long note manageable. You can hide everything under a heading, move a heading with all that belongs to it, and jump to one by name. A heading together with everything under it, its text and its own headings, is called a subtree.

14.2.1 Folding

Folding hides text without changing it. Press TAB on a heading and everything under it is hidden. Three dots after the heading say there is more. Press TAB again and you see the headings directly under it, each still folded. A third press shows all of it, and a fourth folds it again. The echo area names each step. Figure 14.1 shows the three.

S-TAB does the same for the whole note at once, wherever the cursor is. The first press shows only the headings of the first level, which the echo area calls Overview. The second shows every heading and no text, called Contents. The third shows everything.

A folded part counts as one line. The cursor steps over it and never stands inside it.

A note can say how it wants to open. #+STARTUP: overview near the top opens it folded to its first-level headings, and #+STARTUP: content opens it with every heading and no text. This is worth doing for a long file you open often.

Under a task Org keeps some records of its own, in blocks called drawers that begin with a line such as :LOGBOOK: and end with :END:. They are folded to one line when a file opens, because you seldom want to read them. TAB on a drawer's first line opens it.

14.2.2 New headings

M-RET makes a new heading of the same level, after the subtree the cursor is in. You can press it anywhere under a heading. It leaves you in NORMAL state with the cursor after the new stars, so press i and type the heading. M-S-RET does the same and writes TODO for you, which starts a task.

14.2.3 Moving and changing level

The keys that move the cursor, held with Alt, move headings.

ModalNon-modalWhat it does to the heading the cursor is in
noneM-j / M-kMoves its subtree down or up, past the next heading of its level
noneM-h / M-lTakes away or adds a star, on this heading alone
noneM-H / M-LTakes away or adds a star on it and on every heading under it

Taking a star away is called promoting, and adding one is called demoting. The arrow keys with Alt do the same as the letters. Each move is one step for undo.

To jump to a heading by name, press M-g o, which chapter 13 describes. It lists every heading of the note, and typing a few letters narrows the list. To work on one heading without seeing the others, C-x x s narrows the buffer to its subtree, as chapter 7 explains.

Try it, with notes about a garden

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/garden.org and press RET. Press i and type the note shown at the start of this chapter, eight lines from #+title: to * Fruit. Press C-g and save with C-x C-s.
  2. Move to the line Vegetables and press TAB. Its text and its two headings are hidden. Press TAB twice more to see the other two steps.
  3. Press S-TAB three times and watch the echo area say Overview, Contents and Show all.
  4. With the cursor on Vegetables, press M-j. The heading moves below Fruit and takes Tomatoes and Beans with it. Press M-k to move it back.
  5. Move to Beans and press M-l. It gets a third star and is now under Tomatoes. Press M-h to put it back.
  6. Press M-RET, then i, and type Carrots. Press C-g.

The records Org keeps are the drawers and the notes it writes under a task (- State "DONE" ..., - Note taken on ... and CLOCK: lines), under headings and list items alike. Three settings say how they are folded.

*org-fold-metadata* is t as standard: a file opens with each of these folded to one line, so a task shows its title, its SCHEDULED: and DEADLINE: lines (those are always shown) and a single line with dots for the rest. TAB on that line opens it. With nil every file opens with them all shown, which is what you want when you are reading the log of a project rather than its tasks. A note can decide for itself: #+STARTUP: showdrawers opens them whatever the setting says, and #+STARTUP: hidedrawers folds them.

 t (standard)                    nil

 ◉ TODO Paint the fence          ◉ TODO Paint the fence
   SCHEDULED: <2026-11-14 Sat>     SCHEDULED: <2026-11-14 Sat>
   :LOGBOOK:...                    :LOGBOOK:
                                   - Note taken on [2026-11-10 Tue 09:12]
                                     Bought the paint.
                                   :END:

*org-cycle-hide-drawers* is about TAB on a heading or an item. At t, the standard, the second and third press show the headings and text but leave the drawers and notes folded, so cycling does not unfold the log of every task under it. (setf *org-cycle-hide-drawers* nil) makes TAB show them with the rest.

*org-cycle-include-plain-lists* is t as standard, and TAB on a list item that has sub-items or more lines folds it, as on a heading: folded, then its sub-items, then all. At nil TAB on an item indents it, as in a plain text file, and an item is folded only as part of its heading.

14.3 Lists and checkboxes

A list is for things that do not each need a heading: what to buy, the steps of a recipe, points to raise at a meeting.

A line that begins with a hyphen and a space is an item. A line that begins with 1. and a space is an item of a numbered list. An item set in further than the one above it is a sub-item of that one. A line written as - term :: what it means is an item of a description list, useful for a short glossary.

- Weed the beds
- Mulch the feijoas
  - Bark, if there is any left
1. Soak the seeds overnight
2. Plant them a finger deep

M-RET on an item makes the next item of the same kind after it. In a numbered list the items after it are numbered again. C-c - changes the bullet of every item in the list to the next kind. The kinds are a hyphen, a plus, a star, 1. and 1), and a list at the left edge skips the star. That is the quick way to turn a plain list into a numbered one. TAB on an item that has sub-items or more lines under it folds it, as on a heading.

14.3.1 Checkboxes

An item that starts with [ ] has a checkbox, something to tick off. You do not have to type all of it. Type the hyphen, a space and [, and Tuatara completes the box and leaves the cursor after it.

*org-complete-checkboxes* is the setting behind that. At t, the standard, typing [ right after the bullet and its space (- [) makes the whole box, - [ ], and leaves the cursor after it, ready for the words. At nil the bracket is typed like any other character and you write the box yourself.

C-c C-c on the item's line ticks the box, which then reads [X], or clears it again. In NORMAL state RET on the line goes round three states: empty, [-] for half done, and ticked.

*org-return-cycles-checkboxes* is the setting for RET. At t, the standard, RET in NORMAL state on an item with a box goes round the three states and brings the counts above it up to date. A link under the cursor is followed first. Set it to nil with (setf *org-return-cycles-checkboxes* nil) and RET does not touch the box, and C-c C-c is the one way to tick it. That suits you if you press RET in lists mainly to follow links or to move down.

Put [/] at the end of the heading above the list, or at the end of an item that has sub-items, and Org counts for you. It shows how many boxes are ticked out of how many there are, such as [2/5], and keeps the count current as you tick. [%] shows a percentage instead.

When you tick a box, Tuatara notes the time in a small drawer under the item. That lets the agenda show later what you finished on which day. If you do not want these notes, set *org-log-checkboxes* to nil. It is t as standard. At t the note is the same kind of line a task's change of state leaves, the old and the new state with the time; at nil the box changes and nothing is written. With (setf *org-log-checkboxes* nil), ticking bread leaves:

 t (standard)                      nil

 - [X] bread                       - [X] bread
   :LOGBOOK:
   - State "DONE" from "TODO"
     [2026-10-13 Tue 10:00]
   :END:

Try it, with a shopping list

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/shopping.org and press RET. Press i and type * Shopping [/], then RET.
  2. Type a hyphen, a space and [. The box completes itself. Type eggs and press RET. Do the same for bread and for milk.
  3. Press C-g. Move to the line bread and press C-c C-c. The box reads [X] and the heading says [1/3]. A drawer under the item holds the time. It is shown open now and is folded when you open the file again.
  4. Move to eggs and press RET twice. The box goes to [-] and then to [X], and the heading says [2/3].
  5. Still on eggs, press M-RET, then i, and type butter. The new item has a box of its own. The count in the heading stays [2/3] until you next tick or clear a box. Press C-g.
  6. Press C-c - a few times and watch the bullets change. Stop when they are hyphens again. Save with C-x C-s.

The signs can be prettier than the plain text. *org-list-bullets* and *org-checkbox-signs* name a character to show for each bullet and each state of a box. The file itself keeps the plain marks.

*org-list-bullets* is nil as standard, and the bullets are shown as written. Give it a list of pairs, a bullet and the sign to show for it. Numbered items keep their numbers. *org-checkbox-signs* is the same for the three boxes, [ ], [-] and [X], and it is nil as standard too. A sign is shown with a space after it, so that one drawn wider than a column is not cut. C-c C-c ticks the box as before, and C-c - still changes the bullet. With

(setf *org-list-bullets* '(("-" . "•") ("+" . "◦"))
      *org-checkbox-signs* '(("[ ]" . "☐") ("[-]" . "◐") ("[X]" . "☑")))

the list of the shopping note reads:

 as written            shown

 - [X] bread           • ☑ bread
 - [ ] eggs            • ☐ eggs
 + [-] milk            ◦ ◐ milk

14.4 Tasks

A checkbox is enough for a shopping list. A task is for work that takes longer, that may have to wait for someone, or that has a date. A task is a heading with a keyword after its stars:

* TODO Paint the fence
* WAIT Quote from the plumber
* DONE Ring the council

Four keywords come as standard. TODO is for something still to do. WAIT is for something that is waiting on a person or an event. DONE is for something finished, and CANCELLED for something you gave up. The first two count as open and the last two as closed.

C-c C-t gives the heading the next keyword: none, TODO, WAIT, DONE and none again. S-<right> and S-<left> go forward and back through the same round. In NORMAL state RET on a task's line also moves it to the next keyword, and never leaves it without one. CANCELLED is left out of the round so that you do not cancel something by pressing a key once too often. C-c C-x C cancels the task the cursor is in.

When a task becomes DONE, Tuatara writes a line under it that says when:

* DONE Paint the fence
  CLOSED: [2026-10-13 Tue 10:00]

The agenda can list what you closed on each day from these lines. Taking DONE away again removes the line. Set *org-log-done* to nil if you want nothing written. It is :time as standard, the line with the time, and nil is the only other value; (setf *org-log-done* nil) leaves a closed task without it, so the agenda's log mode does not list it.

14.4.1 Tasks with parts

A task can have smaller tasks under it, or a list of checkboxes. Put [/] at the end of its heading and it counts them. When the last one is done, the task becomes DONE by itself, and it becomes TODO again if you reopen one. While a part is still open, RET passes over the closed keywords, so a task is not marked done by accident with work left under it. C-c C-t still lets you close it if you mean to.

The task follows its parts by *org-todo-follows-checkboxes*, t as standard. It applies to a TODO heading with a count, [2/3] or [66%], and the count is its sub-tasks, or, when it has none, the checkboxes right under it. When everything counted is done, the heading becomes DONE and gets its CLOSED: line. When you reopen one part it goes back to TODO. A task above it that has a count follows in turn. A task whose keyword is one of those left out of the round (CANCELLED) is not changed.

* TODO Pack for the trip [2/3]        ,* DONE Pack for the trip [3/3]
  CLOSED: ...                            CLOSED: [2026-11-11 Wed 18:20]
- [X] Tent                             - [X] Tent
- [X] Stove                            - [X] Stove
- [ ] Torch                            - [X] Torch

The counts keep up to date either way. If you want to close a task yourself whatever its parts say, set (setf *org-todo-follows-checkboxes* nil).

14.4.2 Notes on a task

C-c C-z asks for a note and files it under the task with the date and time. Use it for what you would otherwise forget: "rang twice, no answer", "the paint is in the shed". Notes go into the task's :LOGBOOK: drawer, the newest first, with the other records Tuatara keeps of the task. Open the drawer with TAB on its first line.

14.4.3 Keywords of your own

A note can name its own keywords on a line near the top. Those before the bar are open and those after it are closed:

#+TODO: TODO NEXT WAIT | DONE CANCELLED

Two settings shape the round that C-c C-t, S-<right> and RET make. *org-todo-keywords-not-cycled* lists the keywords the round passes over. Its standard is ("CANCELLED" "CANCELED"), which is why the round is none, TODO, WAIT, DONE and none again, and why C-c C-x C is the way to cancel. It applies to the keywords of a file's own #+TODO: line too, and to the agenda's key for a task. With (setf *org-todo-keywords-not-cycled* '("CANCELLED" "SOMEDAY")), a note with #+TODO: TODO NEXT | DONE SOMEDAY CANCELLED goes TODO, NEXT, DONE and round, and SOMEDAY is only set by hand. With nil every keyword takes its turn.

*org-return-cycles-todo* is t as standard: RET in NORMAL state on a task's headline gives it the next keyword in that round, never none. Where the date of a task repeats, making it done leaves it open with its next date. While a checkbox right under the task is not ticked or a task under it is not done, the done keywords are passed over, so that RET does not close work that is still open; with nothing else to go to, the echo area says what is open, and C-c C-t still closes it. With nil, RET leaves the keyword alone and C-c C-t is the way to change it.

To change the keywords for every file that has no such line, set *org-standard-todo-keywords* in your init file. It is a pair, the keywords of tasks still open and then those of tasks closed. The standard is (("TODO" "WAIT") "DONE" "CANCELLED"): TODO and WAIT are open, DONE and CANCELLED are closed. A file's own #+TODO: line takes its place for that file. For keywords like those of the example above everywhere:

(setf *org-standard-todo-keywords* '(("TODO" "NEXT" "WAIT") "DONE" "CANCELLED"))

*org-todo-keyword-faces* gives a keyword a face of its own, in the headlines and in the agenda. It is a list of pairs, a keyword and a face. As standard WAIT has :org-wait and CANCELLED has :org-cancelled, and the standard spelling CANCELED too. A keyword not in the list is shown in :org-todo while its task is open and in :org-done once it is closed. To give NEXT the look of WAIT:

(push '("NEXT" . :org-wait) *org-todo-keyword-faces*)

The colours of the faces come from your theme, chapter 2.

14.4.4 Priorities

A task can carry a priority, written by hand after its keyword as [#A], [#B] or [#C]. It is shown in its own colour, here and in the agenda, so that the important tasks stand out.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-c C-torg-todoChange the TODO keyword of the headline point is in to the next of the document's (#+TODO:, else TODO, WAIT and DONE), none after the last, those of org-todo-keywords-not-cycled passed over (CANCELLED, which M-x org-cancel-task sets); a task done is noted with CLOSED: and when.
noneS-<right>org-shiftrightOn a headline, its next TODO keyword, as M-x org-todo does.
noneS-<left>org-shiftleftOn a headline, its TODO keyword before, none before the first.
noneC-c C-x Corg-cancel-taskCancel the task of the headline point is in: its keyword made CANCELLED, a done keyword that M-x org-todo and the other keys that go round the keywords pass over, noted with CLOSED: and when as a task done is.
noneC-c C-zorg-add-noteAdd a note to the entry point is under (C-c C-z): the note is asked for, and logged where Org logs notes, at the top of its :LOGBOOK: drawer with ORG-LOG-INTO-DRAWER, else after its planning line and properties, in the form - Note taken on [2026-10-01 Thu 18:00] \\ and the note under it.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes

*org-return-cycles-todo*tt, nilWhether RET on a task's headline in NORMAL state changes its TODO keyword.
*org-log-done*:time:time, nilWhat is noted when a task is done.
*org-log-into-drawer*tt, nilWhere the notes logged of a task go.
*org-log-repeat*:time:time, nilWhat Org notes when a task that repeats is done.
*org-log-reschedule*nil:time, nilWhat Org notes when a task's scheduled date is changed or taken away.
*org-log-redeadline*nil:time, nilWhat Org notes when a task's deadline is changed or taken away.
FaceWhat it paints
:org-todoOrg's keywords of tasks not done (TODO).
:org-waitOrg's keyword of tasks open but waiting on something (WAIT), apart from TODO.
:org-doneOrg's keywords of tasks done (DONE).
:org-cancelledOrg's keyword of tasks cancelled (CANCELLED), closed but apart from DONE.
