:org-priorityAn Org headline's priority, [#A].
:org-log-noteThe notes a task's log keeps of its changes of state, wholly, the time included: - State "DONE" from "TODO" [2026-10-01 Thu 18:00].
:org-special-keywordOrg's CLOSED: and CLOCK:.

14.5 Tags

A tag is a word at the end of a heading, between colons, that says what the heading is about:

* TODO Mow the lawn :outside:weekend:

Tags cut across the outline. A note about the house and a note about work can both hold headings tagged phone, and the agenda can list every one of them when you sit down to make calls. A heading also has the tags of the headings above it, so tagging a whole project once is enough.

C-c C-q sets the tags of the heading the cursor is under. It offers the tags the heading has. Type the words with spaces between them, or nothing to remove them all. You can also type tags by hand.

As standard the tags sit one space after the heading's text. If you like them lined up at the right, set *org-tags-column* to a negative number, such as -77 for tags that end at column 77. M-x org-align-tags then puts the tags of one heading in place, and M-x org-align-all-tags those of every heading in the buffer.

Two tags have a meaning to Tuatara. A heading tagged notify is announced on your desktop when its time comes, as the next section explains. A heading tagged TOC holds a table of contents, described under code blocks.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-c C-qorg-set-tags-commandSet the tags of the headline point is under (C-c C-q): asked for with its tags offered, work urgent or :work:urgent:, nothing for none; they go at the end of its line, where ORG-TAGS-COLUMN says, by default one space after its text.
noneM-x org-align-tagsorg-align-tagsPut the tags of the headline point is under where ORG-TAGS-COLUMN says: by default one space after its text.
noneM-x org-align-all-tagsorg-align-all-tagsPut the tags of every headline of the buffer where ORG-TAGS-COLUMN says: by default one space after each one's text, in one step to undo.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*org-tags-column*0a whole numberWhere M-x org-set-tags-command and M-x org-align-tags put a headline's tags.
FaceWhat it paints
:org-tagAn Org headline's tags, :work:urgent:.

14.6 Dates and scheduling

A date in an Org file is written in angle brackets, as <2026-12-24 Thu>, or with a time, as <2026-12-24 Thu 14:00>. You never have to type one out. The commands of this section ask for a date and write it for you, weekday and all.

There are three ways to put a date on something, and they mean different things.

What you want to sayHowModalNon-modal
I plan to work on this that daySchedule the tasknoneC-c C-s
This must be finished by that dayGive it a deadlinenoneC-c C-d
This happens then, whatever I doA date in the textnoneC-c .

Scheduling and deadlines are for tasks. They are written on a line of their own right under the heading, beginning SCHEDULED: or DEADLINE:. A scheduled task that you do not finish is carried forward in the agenda day after day until you do. A deadline shows up in the agenda some days ahead, 14 unless you change *org-deadline-warning-days*, so that it does not take you by surprise.

A date in the text is for an event such as a flight, a birthday or a meeting. C-c . puts one where the cursor is. The agenda shows it on its day and nowhere else.

C-c ! writes a date in square brackets, as [2026-12-24 Thu]. Such a date is only a record. The agenda leaves it out. Use it to note when something happened.

14.6.1 Answering the date question

Every command that needs a date asks in the same way. A calendar of three months opens below, with the cursor on today, and you can answer in either of two ways.

You can point. Before you have typed anything, l and h move a day forward and back and j and k move a week. RET writes the day at the prompt, and a second RET accepts it. Between the two you can add a time, such as 14:00.

Two settings change this. *org-read-date-in-calendar* is t as it comes: the question begins in the calendar, so that h, l, j and k move at once. Set it to nil and the question begins at the prompt, as if you had already typed; every letter you type is then part of the date. *org-read-date-popup-calendar* is also t. It keeps the calendar below while you type, with the day you have written marked, and S-<left> and S-<right> move that day by one while the prompt stays yours. Set it to nil to be asked with no calendar at all.

(setf *org-read-date-in-calendar* nil)
(setf *org-read-date-popup-calendar* nil)

With both set to nil, C-c C-d shows only the prompt, and you answer with words such as +3d.

Or you can type, and Tuatara reads what you mean. The day it has understood is shown as you type, so you can see that it is right before you press RET.

You typeIt is read as
nothing, only RETToday
friThe next Friday
+3d, +2w, +1mThree days, two weeks or a month from today
24The 24th of this month, or of the next once it is past
dec 24, 2026-12-24That date
fri 9am, +2d 14:00A day with a time
10:00-11:30Today, from then until then
every week 10:00Each week at that time, starting today
every second dayEvery other day
first monday every monthThat day of each month

14.6.2 Things that come round again

The last rows of the table make a date that repeats. A repeating date is written with a mark after it, as in <2026-10-13 Tue +1w> for every week. When you mark a repeating task DONE, it is not closed. Its date moves on to the next time, it becomes TODO again, and a note of when you last did it is kept under it. This is the way to keep track of the rubbish day, the rent and watering the lemon tree.

Tuatara can also keep a record of each time a task is moved on. These settings take :time or nil. *org-log-repeat* is :time as it comes: a repeating task marked DONE gets a note of the change and a LAST_REPEAT property with the time. Set it to nil and the date moves on with no record. *org-log-reschedule* and *org-log-redeadline* are nil, so changing a scheduled date or a deadline leaves nothing behind. With :time the old date is written down, with the time you changed it:

(setf *org-log-reschedule* :time)
(setf *org-log-redeadline* :time)

** TODO Clean the gutters
   SCHEDULED: <2026-10-16 Fri>
   :LOGBOOK:
   - Rescheduled from "[2026-10-14 Wed]" on [2026-10-13 Tue 10:00]
   :END:

A deadline puts New deadline from in the same place, and taking a date away puts Not scheduled, was or Removed deadline, was. Where all these notes go, and the notes of a change of state and of C-c C-z, is said by *org-log-into-drawer*. As it comes, t, they go into the :LOGBOOK: drawer and fold away with it. With nil they are written right under the heading's planning line and properties, in plain sight.

If you cannot remember how to say a repeat in words, press C-r at the date prompt. A menu opens where you choose the start, the time, how often and when it ends, and it shows in plain words what your choices come to. RET writes it.

14.6.3 Being told on the desktop

Give a heading the tag notify and Tuatara shows a notification on your desktop as its time comes, for as long as Tuatara is running. It tells you ten minutes before and again at the time. An entry with a date and no time is announced at eight in the morning. *org-notify-before* and *org-notify-day-time* change both. *org-notify-before* is the number of minutes, 10 as standard; 0 or nil tells only when the time comes, and a NOTIFY_BEFORE property on one entry says otherwise for it. *org-notify-day-time* is the time of day as text, "08:00" as standard, as in (setf *org-notify-day-time* "07:30"); nil means an entry with a date and no time is never announced. The tag itself is *org-notify-tag*: with (setf *org-notify-tag* "remind") it is the tag remind that Tuatara watches for, and nil turns the notifications off. The notification is shown by the program notify-send, which chapter 8 mentions with the other notifications.

Try it, with a holiday plan

  1. Open ~/holiday.org with C-x C-f. Press i and type these four lines, then press C-g:

       * Holiday in Nelson
   ** TODO Book the ferry
   ** TODO Book the bach at Kaiteriteri
   ** Walk the Abel Tasman track
  2. Move to Book the ferry and press C-c C-d. Type +3d and watch the calendar move three days on. Press RET. A line beginning DEADLINE: appears under the heading.
  3. Move to Book the bach and press C-c C-s. Press l twice and j once, which is nine days from today. Press RET twice. The line under the heading begins SCHEDULED:.
  4. Move to Walk the Abel Tasman track and press o to open a line under it. Press C-c ., type dec 28 9am and press RET. A date with a time is written into the text. Press C-g.
  5. Move back to Book the ferry and press C-c C-t until it says DONE. A CLOSED: line joins the deadline. Save with C-x C-s.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-c C-sorg-scheduleSchedule the task point is under (C-c C-s): the date is asked for (fri, +3d, 10-15, sep 30, 2026-12-24 14:00), what it reads shown as it is typed, and SCHEDULED: goes on its planning line, a repeater and warning it had kept.
noneC-c C-dorg-deadlineGive the task point is under a deadline (C-c C-d): the date asked for as M-x org-schedule asks it, DEADLINE: on its planning line, a repeater and warning it had kept.
noneC-c .org-time-stampPut in a timestamp at point (C-c .), the date asked for as M-x org-schedule asks it: <2026-10-13 Tue>, or with a time <2026-10-13 Tue 14:00>.
noneC-c !org-time-stamp-inactivePut in an inactive timestamp at point (C-c !): as M-x org-time-stamp, written [2026-10-13 Tue], which the agenda leaves out.

These commands work only while a date is being asked for. You will seldom call them by name, but they are what the keys above run.

14.7 The agenda

Dates scattered over a dozen files are of little use unless something gathers them. The agenda does that. It reads your agenda files, finds every task and every date in them, and shows them in one list in the order of the calendar. You look at it in the morning to see what the day holds.

14.7.1 Telling Tuatara which files to read

The agenda reads the files named in *org-agenda-files*. As it comes, that is the one file ~/org/agenda.org. Set it in your init file to the files or directories where you keep tasks. A directory stands for every .org file in it.

(setf *org-agenda-files* '("~/org/" "~/holiday.org"))

14.7.2 Opening it

C-x a a asks which view you want and waits for one more key.

ModalNon-modalView
noneaThe week, day by day
nonetEvery task that is still open, dated or not, with unticked checkboxes
nonemThe headings that match tags you type, such as phone or work+urgent
noneuThe open tasks that have no tag
nonecThe entries whose dates look wrong, each with the reason

C-x a w, C-x a m and C-x a y open the week, the month or the year without asking. Figure 14.2 shows a week.

Each line starts with the name of the file the entry is in, then its time or all day, then what kind of line it is. Scheduled: is a task planned for that day. Deadline: is a task due that day, and In 3 d.: on today is the early warning of a deadline three days off. Event: is a date in the text. The tags are at the right. In the figure, cleaning the gutters appears twice: on Friday when it is due and on today as a warning.

On today the agenda also draws a time grid when something has a time, with a line for the hour it is now, so that you see what is still ahead.

14.7.3 What the agenda shows

Several settings decide how much the agenda shows and how it looks. *org-agenda-span* is :week as it comes. It takes :day, :week, :month, :year or a number of days, so (setf *org-agenda-span* 3) opens on today and the two days after it. A week starts on the day *org-agenda-start-on-weekday* says: 1 for Monday as it comes, up to 6 for Saturday, 7 or 0 for Sunday, and nil for today, so that the week shown is the next seven days and not the calendar week.

*org-agenda-log-mode* is what L turns on and off, and nil as it comes. With (setf *org-agenda-log-mode* t) every agenda opens with the tasks you closed and the time you clocked already listed.

*org-agenda-refresh-minutes* is 10, the ten minutes of the paragraph above. (setf *org-agenda-refresh-minutes* 1) keeps the clock line of the time grid close to true; nil draws the agenda again only after midnight and when a file changes.

*org-agenda-time-grid* holds the lines drawn at the hours of the day. It is a list of four things: when to draw them, the times, the text that follows each time, and the line itself. As it comes, the grid is drawn for today and on a day's agenda, and only when that day has an entry with a time. The times are 800 to 2000 every two hours. Put :weekly in the first list to draw it on every day of a week, and take :require-timed out to draw it on days with nothing timed. nil draws no grid:

(setf *org-agenda-time-grid* nil)

*org-agenda-current-time-string* is the line that marks the time now in the grid, ← now ───... as it comes, after the time it is. Give it other text, or nil for no such line. With this line in your init file, (setf *org-agenda-current-time-string* "now"), at half past two it reads:

  holiday:    14:00 ┄┄┄┄┄ Event:      Dentist in Motueka
              14:30 ┄┄┄┄┄ now

The columns of a line can be changed too. *org-agenda-category-width* is the width of the first column, twelve as it comes; a longer file name is cut with …. *org-agenda-untimed-text* is what the time column says when an entry has no time, all day as it comes. *org-agenda-event-kind-text* is what the column of kinds says for a date in the text of a heading with no keyword, Event:, and *org-agenda-task-kind-text* the same for a date in the text of a task, Task:. For these three, a text is shown, "" leaves the column empty but keeps the lines level, and nil leaves the column out altogether, so the heading moves left. If you want a compact agenda:

(setf *org-agenda-category-width* 8
      *org-agenda-untimed-text* nil
      *org-agenda-event-kind-text* nil)

*org-agenda-date-in-title* is nil: a date written in a heading, such as Dentist <2026-10-15 Thu 14:00>, is taken out of the title on the agenda, because the day and the time column already say it. t leaves it in.

14.7.4 Moving about

j and k move from line to line. l shows the next week and h the one before. g h comes back to today. D, w, m and Y change the span to a day, a week, a month or a year, and g l returns to the view you had before. RET opens the entry on the line in its file, and TAB shows it in another window while you stay in the agenda. c opens the calendar on the line's day, and a in the calendar shows the agenda of the week of the day the cursor is on. q closes the agenda.

The agenda keeps itself current. It is drawn again when one of its files changes, every ten minutes and just after midnight. r draws it again at once.

14.7.5 Changing tasks from the agenda

You do not have to open a file to deal with a task. The keys below act on the entry of the line the cursor is on, and change it in its file.

ModalNon-modalWhat it does to the entry
noneTGives it the next keyword, as C-c C-t does in the file
noneC-c C-sSchedules it for another day
nonedGives it a deadline
nonetSets its tags
nonenAdds a note to it
noneI / OStarts and stops the clock on it
noneuUndoes the last change made from this agenda
nonesSaves every agenda file that has changes

The usual keys from the file, such as C-c C-t and C-c C-q, work in the agenda too. Changes made from the agenda are in the files' buffers and are not on disk until you press s. If you want them saved as they are made, name the files in *org-agenda-autosave-files*. It is nil as standard, no file. t saves every agenda file at once, and a list names some, as *org-agenda-files* does, files, directories or patterns. A change is a keyword, a date, tags, a note or the clock. For one file:

(setf *org-agenda-autosave-files* '("~/notes/agenda.org"))

L turns on log mode. The agenda then also lists, on each day, the tasks you closed and the time you clocked. It is a pleasant way to see on a Friday what the week went on.

i takes down something new for the day the cursor is on, with capture, which is described below.

Try it, with the holiday plan

  1. Tell the agenda about the holiday file for this session. Press M-:, type (push "~/holiday.org" *org-agenda-files*) and press RET.
  2. Press C-x a a and then a. The week is shown with the cursor on today. If booking the bach falls in the coming week, press l to see it there.
  3. Press g h to come back. Press C-x a a and then t. Every open task is listed, Book the bach at Kaiteriteri among them.
  4. Move to that line and press T. It becomes WAIT. Press u to take the change back.
  5. Press TAB. The task is shown in its file in another window.
  6. Press s to save, and q to close the agenda.

14.7.6 Views of your own

*org-agenda-custom-commands* adds views under keys of your own to the question C-x a a asks. Each has a key, a description and a match, such as every open task tagged phone. The view under u is made this way, and its entry in the setting is a pattern to copy.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
nonea, C-c a, C-x a aorg-agendaShow the agenda, asking which view: a the agenda of the week (or ORG-AGENDA-SPAN), t the TODO list, m the headlines a match selects (work+urgent-home, TODO="NEXT"), or a view of your own (ORG-AGENDA-CUSTOM-COMMANDS, u the tasks with no tag), or c the entries whose dates look wrong (M-x org-agenda-check-dates), read from ORG-AGENDA-FILES.
noneM-x org-agenda-listorg-agenda-listShow the agenda of this week (or ORG-AGENDA-SPAN): each day with its scheduled tasks, deadlines and timestamps.

14.8 Capture

A thought arrives while you are in the middle of something else: ring the plumber, an idea for the letter, a book someone recommended. Capture takes it down without making you leave what you are doing. You press a key, type the thought in a small window, press another key, and you are back where you were. The thought has been filed in the right place.

C-x a c starts it and shows the templates to choose from. A template says what kind of entry to make and where to file it. Four come with Tuatara.

ModalNon-modalMakesFiles it
nonetA task, after asking for its tagsUnder Tasks in your agenda file
nonenA quick noteUnder Inbox in your agenda file
nonemNotes of a meeting, with the clock runningUnder Meetings in your agenda file
nonejAn entry in your journalIn today's journal entry

"Your agenda file" is the first file named in *org-agenda-files*. After you choose a template, a window called *Capture* opens below, in INSERT state, with the template filled in. Its top line tells you the keys. Write what you have to say and finish with one of them.

ModalNon-modalWhat it does
noneC-c C-cFiles the entry where the template says
noneC-c C-wFiles it under a heading you choose instead
noneC-c C-kThrows it away

A captured task or note carries the time you wrote it and a link back to where you were, so that "check this paragraph" still makes sense a week later.

In the calendar and in the agenda, i captures for the day the cursor is on and not for today. The entry gets that day's date, so the agenda lists it there. That is how you write down a dentist's appointment three weeks away: go to the day and press i.

Try it, with something to remember

  1. From any buffer, press C-x a c and then t.
  2. The echo area asks for tags. Type phone and press RET.
  3. In the window that opens, type Ring Wanaka Plumbing about the tap.
  4. Press C-c C-c. The echo area says where it was filed and you are back where you started. If the directory ~/org/ does not exist yet, Tuatara asks whether to make it.
  5. Press C-x a a and then t. The new task is in the list.

14.8.1 Templates of your own

A template is a small file. The part above the line # -- says what it is called, which key chooses it and where its entries go. The part below is the entry, with marks that are filled in when you capture.

# name: Book to read
# key: b
# file: ~/org/reading.org
# heading: To read
# --
* %?
Recommended by %^{Who recommended it}
%U
MarkIs filled with
%?Nothing. The cursor is left here for you to write
%U, %uNow, or today, as a record the agenda leaves out
%T, %tNow, or today, as a date the agenda shows
%^T, %^tA date that you are asked for
%^{Words}What you type when asked the words
%^gTags that you are asked for
%aA link to where you were
%iThe text that was selected

Your templates live in the directory capture-templates in your configuration directory, one file each. The easy way to start is M-x org-capture-template-copy, which copies one of Tuatara's there for you to change. A template of yours with the same key as one of Tuatara's replaces it.

*capture-template-directories* says where those directories are. It is nil as it comes, which means capture-templates in your configuration directory. Give it a list to read the templates from other directories, such as one you share with others:

(setf *capture-template-directories* '("~/org/templates/"))

The templates are then read from there, and Tuatara's four are still offered.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x a corg-captureTake a note, a task or a journal entry down from wherever you are: press the key of one of the capture templates (Tuatara's and yours, in CAPTURE-TEMPLATE-DIRECTORIES), answer what it asks, write in the Capture buffer and file it with C-c C-c (or throw it away with C-c C-k); you are back where you were.
noneC-c C-corg-capture-finalizeFile the text of this Capture buffer where its template says, and go back to where you were; with its template's clock, clock it.
noneC-c C-worg-capture-refileFile the text of this Capture buffer under a heading chosen as C-c C-w chooses one, instead of where its template says.
noneC-c C-korg-capture-killThrow away what this Capture buffer holds, and go back to where you were.
noneM-x org-capture-template-copyorg-capture-template-copyCopy one of Tuatara's own capture templates, chosen by its name, into your capture templates directory (the first of CAPTURE-TEMPLATE-DIRECTORIES) and visit it: your copy, changed as you like (where it files, its text), takes the place of Tuatara's on the same key.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*capture-template-directories*nila list, each a directory's nameThe directories your capture templates are in, a template a file.

14.9 Moving an entry to another place

An inbox fills up. Refiling moves a heading, with everything under it, to its proper home. C-c C-w on a heading asks where it should go and lists the headings of your agenda files and of the file you are in, each written as a path such as house.org/Garden/Fruit. Type a few letters to narrow the list and press RET. The heading is put at the end of what is under the one you chose, one level below it.

With C-u first, the command goes to the heading you choose and moves nothing. That makes it a quick way to get anywhere in your agenda files. The same key works on a line in the agenda. *org-refile-targets* says which files are offered and how deep their headings go. It is a list of pairs, where to look and how many levels. Where is :agenda-files, the files of *org-agenda-files*, :this-file, the file of the entry, or the name of a file. The standard is ((:agenda-files . 3) (:this-file . 3)), headings down to *** in both. To offer another file, and only the top two levels of the agenda files:

(setf *org-refile-targets* '((:agenda-files . 2) ("~/notes/archive.org" . 3)))
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-c C-worg-refileMove the heading point is under, with all under it, to another heading: chosen by its path (agenda.org/Commitments and Jobs) among the headings ORG-REFILE-TARGETS offers, put at the end of what is under it, a level below; a clock running in it goes on there.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*org-refile-targets*((:agenda-files . 3) (:this-file . 3))a list, each (WHERE . LEVELS)Where M-x org-refile offers to move an entry, a list of (WHERE .

14.10 Clocking

The clock records how long you spend on a task. It is for anyone who bills by the hour, and for anyone curious where a day went.

C-c C-x C-i starts the clock on the task the cursor is under. A line beginning CLOCK: is written in the task's :LOGBOOK: drawer with the time you started. While the clock runs, the mode line of every window shows the time so far and the task's name, so you cannot forget it. Starting the clock on another task stops the first.

C-x a o stops the clock from any buffer. The line is finished with the time you stopped and how long that was:

CLOCK: [2026-10-13 Tue 10:00]--[2026-10-13 Tue 10:45] =>  0:45

*org-clock-into-drawer* is t, so the lines are kept in the :LOGBOOK: drawer and fold away with it. With (setf *org-clock-into-drawer* nil) the CLOCK: lines are written right under the heading instead.

C-x a j takes you to the task that is being clocked, from wherever you are. C-c C-x C-q stops the clock and removes its line, for when you started it by mistake. In the agenda, I and O start and stop the clock on the line's entry.

If you leave Tuatara while the clock runs, it asks whether to stop it. If you say no, the clock is found again at the next start and goes on counting.

To add the time up, run M-x org-clock-report. It writes a table of the time spent on each heading, with a total, for the subtree the cursor is in or for the whole file when the cursor is above the first heading. Run it again later, or press C-c C-c on the table's first line, to bring it up to date.

#+BEGIN: clocktable :scope file :maxlevel 2
| Headline          |   Time |
|-------------------+--------|
| *Total time*      | *1:05* |
|-------------------+--------|
| Clean the gutters |   0:20 |
| Water the lemon   |   0:45 |
#+END:
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-c C-x C-iorg-clock-inClock in on the task point is under (C-c C-x C-i): CLOCK: and the time go into its :LOGBOOK: drawer, made when it has none, after its planning line and properties; a clock running is clocked out first.
noneC-x a o, C-c C-x C-oorg-clock-outClock out (C-c C-x C-o, from any buffer C-x a o): the clock's line finished with the time it ended and how long it ran; with none running, of the one left open in the agenda files (ORG-CLOCK-RUNNING).
noneC-x a j, C-c C-x C-jorg-clock-gotoGo to the task the clock runs on (C-c C-x C-j, from any buffer C-x a j): its file opened again when its buffer was killed; with none running, one left open in the agenda files, as after a restart, runs again (ORG-CLOCK-RUNNING).
noneC-c C-x C-qorg-clock-cancelStop the clock running and take its line away (C-c C-x C-q): its :LOGBOOK: drawer too, when nothing else is in it; saved when that is its buffer's only change, as C-x a o does.
noneM-x org-clock-reportorg-clock-reportMake the clock table point is in again, or put a new one in: its scope the subtree point is in, or the file before the first headline, its depth two levels.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*org-clock-into-drawer*tt, nilWhere clock lines go.
FaceWhat it paints
:org-mode-line-clockThe clock running on an Org task, in the mode line: [0:22] (Task).

14.11 Tables and formulas

A table in Org is made of lines that begin with a bar, with a bar between each field. You type it roughly and Tuatara lines it up.

| Item  | Cost |
|-------+------|
| Rent  |  450 |
| Food  |  180 |
| Power |   95 |

14.11.1 Making a table

Type a bar, the first field, a bar, the next field, and so on. Then press TAB. The table is aligned, each column as wide as its widest field, and the cursor goes to the next field. At the end of a row TAB starts a new row. So filling in a table is typing a field, TAB, a field, TAB. Numbers are set to the right of their column and words to the left.

ModalNon-modalWhat it does in a table
noneTAB / S-TABAligns, and goes to the next or the previous field
noneRET while typingGoes to the same field of the row below
noneC-c C-cAligns
noneC-c -Puts a rule below this row
noneM-j / M-kMoves the row down or up
noneM-h / M-lMoves the column left or right
noneM-L / M-HPuts in an empty column, or deletes this one
noneM-S-<down> / M-S-<up>Puts in an empty row above, or deletes this one

These are the keys that move headings, doing the matching thing to rows and columns when the cursor is in a table. The rows above the first rule are the table's header.

14.11.2 Formulas

A table can do sums. Its formulas are written on a line right under it that begins #+TBLFM:. A formula names a place in the table, an equals sign, and how to work the value out.

| Crop     | Kg | Price | Value |
|----------+----+-------+-------|
| Tomatoes | 12 |  4.50 |   54. |
| Beans    |  3 |     6 |    18 |
| Total    |    |       |   72. |
#+TBLFM: $4=$2*$3::@>$4=vsum(@2..@-1)

There are two formulas here, with :: between them. The first says that column four is column two times column three, in every row below the rule. The second says that the last row of column four is the sum of the rows above it.

In a formulaMeans
$2The second column
@3The third row, with rules not counted
@>, $>The last row, the last column
@-1The row above
@2..@-1A range, here from the second row to the row above
vsum, vmeanThe sum and the mean of a range
vmax, vmin, vcountThe largest, the smallest, and how many
;%.2f after the formulaWrite the answer with two decimals

The numbers do not change by themselves when you change a field. Press C-c * anywhere in the table to work the formulas out again, or C-c C-c on the #+TBLFM: line.

You do not have to write that line by hand. C-c = asks for the formula of the column the cursor is in and adds it to the line for you. With C-u first, it asks for a formula for the one field.

A field that cannot be worked out shows #ERROR. Usually a field the formula reads holds a word where a number should be, or the formula names a column the table does not have.

Try it, with a small budget

  1. Open ~/budget.org with C-x C-f. Press i and type |Item|Cost, then press TAB. The line becomes a tidy row and a second row starts.
  2. Type Rent, TAB, 450, TAB, Food, TAB, 180, TAB, Power, TAB, 95, TAB, Total. Press C-g.
  3. Move to the row Item and press C-c -. A rule is drawn under it.
  4. Move to the row Total and press o to open a line under the table. Type #+TBLFM: @>$2=vsum(@2..@-1) and press C-g.
  5. Press C-c C-c on that line. The field beside Total shows 725.
  6. Move to the 180 of the Food row and change it to 200. Press C-c *. The total becomes 745. Save with C-x C-s.

A formula can contain brackets inside brackets, signs and powers. *org-formula-depth-limit* is how deep they may nest, 200 as standard. A formula nested deeper is refused and its field shows #ERROR, rather than the editor following it down without end. You will not meet it in a budget; lowering it, (setf *org-formula-depth-limit* 20), only matters for tables from people you do not trust.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x org-table-alignorg-table-alignAlign the Org table point is in: each column as wide as its widest field, numbers to the right, rules as wide as the table.
noneM-x org-table-insert-hlineorg-table-insert-hlinePut a rule below the row point is in, in an Org table (C-c -).
noneM-S-<down>org-shiftmetadownIn an Org table, put an empty row above this one (M-S-<down>).
noneM-S-<up>org-shiftmetaupIn an Org table, delete the row point is in (M-S-<up>).
noneC-c *org-table-recalculateWork out the formulas of the Org table point is in, its #+TBLFM: line (C-c *): column formulas ($3=$1+$2) below the first rule (in every row when it has none), field formulas (@4$2=vsum(@2..@3)) and range formulas (@2$2..@3$3=$1*10), worked out with the table arithmetic.
noneC-c =org-table-eval-formulaAsk for the formula of the column point is in, the one it has offered, and work it out (C-c =); with C-u, the formula of the field point is in.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*org-formula-depth-limit*200a whole number, 1 or moreThe most a formula's parts may be nested.
FaceWhat it paints
:org-tableOrg's tables.
:org-formulaOrg's table formulas (#+TBLFM:).

14.12 Links

A link leads from one place to another: to a heading further down, to another file, to a web page. It is written in double square brackets, with the place it leads to first and the words to show second:

[[file:holiday.org][the holiday plan]]

Tuatara shows only the words, in the colour of a link. C-c C-x L shows every link of the buffer as it is written, and the same key hides them again.

WrittenLeads to
[[*Vegetables]]The heading with that title, in this file
[[shed key]]The place marked <<shed key>> in this file
[[#beds]]The heading whose CUSTOM_ID property is beds
[[file:chores.org]]Another file
[[file:chores.org::*Mow the lawn]]A heading in another file
[[https://orgmode.org][Org]]A web page

14.12.1 Making and following links

You seldom write a link by hand. The usual way has two steps. Go to the place you want to link to and press C-x a l, which remembers a link to it. Then go to where the link should be and press C-c C-l. It offers the links you have remembered, the latest first, and then asks for the words to show. If you have text selected, that text becomes the words. With C-u first, C-c C-l asks for a file to link to. On a link that is already there, it lets you change it.

C-x a l works in any file. Under an Org heading it remembers the heading. In a file that is not Org it remembers the line.

*org-link-descriptive* is the setting for what is shown. At t, the standard, [[target][words]] shows as the words and [[target]] as its target. Entities show as their characters, \dollar{} as $. At nil every link is shown as written. C-c C-x L switches it for the buffer you are in. To have links as written whenever a file opens, put (setf *org-link-descriptive* nil) in your init file; a note can also say #+STARTUP: literallinks.

 t (standard)            nil

 the holiday plan        [[file:holiday.org][the holiday plan]]

To follow a link, press RET on it in NORMAL state, or C-c C-o in either state. A link to a web page or a mail address opens in your desktop's program, and Tuatara asks before it does that. If you would rather RET did not follow links, set *org-return-follows-link* to nil. It is t as standard. At nil, RET on a link does what it does anywhere else, breaking the line, or going to the next row in a table, and C-c C-o is the way to follow it. (setf *org-return-follows-link* nil) in your init file does it.

Two more commands write a link that stands for a set of notes, the files with formatted names of chapter 9 whose names match a pattern. Following such a link lists the matching notes so that you can open one. M-x match-formatted-files-link writes Tuatara's own kind, and M-x match-denote-files-link writes the kind that the Emacs package Denote understands as well.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x a lorg-store-linkKeep a link to where point is, for org-insert-link (M-x org-insert-link) to offer: under an Org headline, to it (by its CUSTOM_ID, else its title); in one of your notes, to the note (denote:ID); in another file, to the line point is on.
noneC-c C-lorg-insert-linkInsert an Org link (C-c C-l): it asks for the link, offering those org-store-link (C-x a l) kept and the kinds of link (file asks for a file, denote for one of your notes), then for its label, one offered selected (the stored link's, the note's title) to take or type over; the text selected becomes the label instead.
noneC-c C-oorg-open-at-pointFollow the link point is on (C-c C-o): to a headline, a custom ID or a target here, a file, an ID, a note by its identifier, or a web or mail address in the desktop's program, after asking.
noneC-c C-x Lorg-toggle-link-displayShow this Org buffer's links as written, label, and its entities as written, \dollar{}, or the links as their labels and the entities as their characters again (C-c C-x L).
noneC-x n lmatch-formatted-files-linkInsert a link to your files with formatted names whose names match a regular expression, asked for, the files it matches listed as it is typed: LABEL.
noneM-x match-denote-files-linkmatch-denote-files-linkInsert a link to your files with formatted names whose names match what is asked for, the files it matches listed as it is typed, as a denote: link, which other programs reading those links follow too, written LABEL; in Markdown [LABEL](denote:query-filenames:TEXT) and in text files <denote:query-filenames:TEXT>.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*org-link-descriptive*tt, nilWhether Org links are shown as their labels.
*org-return-follows-link*tt, nilWhether RET on an Org link follows it.
FaceWhat it paints
:org-linkLinks in Org.

14.12.2 Pictures among the lines

A link to a picture that stands alone on its line, with no words of its own, can be shown as the picture itself:

The garden as it was in March:

#+ATTR_ORG: :width 400 :align center
[[file:garden.jpg]]

C-x T p switches this on and off for the buffer you are in. It is off as standard. It does what C-c C-x C-v does in Emacs's Org, and sits with the other display switches under C-x T. The picture takes rows of its own, as many as its height needs, and the lines after it move down to make room. The text itself does not change: saving, searching, copying and undo all see the link. Move the cursor onto the picture's line and the link shows again, so that you can change it; move off and the picture comes back.

Pictures are drawn in the background, only those you can see, by the same program that draws a picture you open, shut in the sandbox. The size is read from the file first, so the rows are held at once and the text does not jump when the picture arrives. A file opened safely never shows its pictures.

The #+ATTR_ORG: line above the link says how large the picture is and where it stands, as Org reads it:

WrittenMeans
:width 400400 pixels wide; 400px is the same
:width 50%half the width of the text; 0.5 is the same
:width tits own width
:align centerin the middle of the text; right at its right edge
:center tin the middle, as :align center

The width of the text is the window's, or the fill column (C-x f) where that is narrower, so a picture stays inside the column your lines are filled to. The height follows the width, the picture's proportions kept, and a picture is never wider than the text. A width given as a share follows the window as it is split or resized. Where the #+ATTR_ORG: line gives no width, the width on another #+ATTR_...: line is used, such as #+ATTR_HTML: :width 300, and where none does, *inline-picture-width* says: t, the standard, for the picture's own width, or a number of pixels. Alignment counts only for a picture that is alone in its paragraph.

A picture can also stand to one side with the text going round it, as a picture in a printed page does:

#+ATTR_ORG: :float left :width 200
[[file:garden.jpg]]
The beds along the south wall were dug in February, and the ...
WrittenMeans
:float leftat the left, the text going round its right
:float rightat the right, the text ending short of it
:float wrap (on any line)at the left, as LaTeX's export places it
:placement {r} with wrapat the right

The picture's own line takes no row while the cursor is elsewhere: the picture's top is beside the line after it, and the rows from there are narrower for as far down as the picture reaches; after that the text has the whole width again, also in the middle of a paragraph. A picture on rows of its own that comes while a floated one still reaches down begins below it. A long line wraps in the narrower rows when lines wrap (C-x T l), and is cut short there when they do not, the window scrolling sideways to keep the cursor in sight beside the picture. The cursor, moving by rows, scrolling and clicking all follow the narrower rows, and a window that begins beside the picture shows the part of it that is left. A floated picture is never wider than two thirds of the text, so that some room is left for the words. Where pictures cannot be drawn, its line names it as any other picture's does, and nothing is narrower. #+ATTR_LATEX: :float wrap is read as well, so a note written for LaTeX's export looks the same here.

To change the width as you look, put the cursor on the picture's line or on its #+ATTR_ORG: line and press C-c C-x w. The picture shows, and the echo row says its width. Then + or = makes it a fifth wider, - narrower, and 0 takes the width away, back to the size it has when none is written. These keys go on working by themselves until you press another, as the keys that size a window do. Each change is written as :width on the #+ATTR_ORG: line, which is made when there is none and taken away when nothing is left on it. A width written as a share of the window stays a share.

In a terminal that can draw pictures (kitty, Ghostty), the pictures are drawn there too, each taking whole rows and columns. Inside tmux, or in a terminal that cannot, each picture's line shows its name and size instead:

[picture: garden.jpg, 1600×1200]

To have pictures shown whenever an Org file opens, set (setf *inline-pictures-modes* '((org-mode . t))) in your init file, or *global-inline-pictures-mode* to t for every buffer. A note can say it for itself: #+STARTUP: inlineimages shows its pictures, and #+STARTUP: noinlineimages does not, whatever the settings say.

Try it, with a picture beside a note

  1. Copy a photo into the directory of an Org note, and call it garden.jpg.
  2. In the note, write [[file:garden.jpg]] on a line of its own and move the cursor to another line.
  3. Press C-x T p. The photo is drawn where the link was.
  4. Move the cursor onto the photo's line. The link shows again. Press C-c C-x w and then - three times. The photo grows narrower, and a line #+ATTR_ORG: :width ... appears above it.
  5. Press 0. The width is gone and so is the line.
  6. Write a line #+ATTR_ORG: :float left above the link, and a few long lines of words below it. Move off the photo's line. The words now go round the photo on its right, and widen again below it.
  7. Press C-x T p again to show the link as written.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x T pinline-pictures-modeShow the pictures the current buffer links to among its lines, and its formulas as LaTeX sets them, or the text as written.
noneC-c C-x worg-resize-pictureMake the picture on this line, or after the #+ATTR_ORG: line point is on, wider or narrower by the last key that ran it: + or = a step wider (ORG-PICTURE-STEP), - a step narrower, 0 back to the width it has when none is written; any other key shows it and says its width.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*global-inline-pictures-mode*nilt, nilWhether to show the pictures a buffer links to and its formulas among its lines, in every buffer (nil unless set); a buffer's own M-x inline-pictures-mode, and the list for its major mode in INLINE-PICTURES-MODES, say otherwise for it.
*inline-pictures-modes*nila list, each (MODE . VALUE)Major modes whose buffers show the pictures a buffer links to and its formulas among its lines, or not: a list of (MODE .
*inline-picture-width*tt, or a whole number, 1 or moreHow wide a picture shown among the lines of text (M-x inline-pictures-mode) is drawn when nothing gives its width (in Org, :width on its #+ATTR_ORG: line).

14.12.3 Formulas as pictures

The same switch, C-x T p, shows the note's formulas as LaTeX sets them:

WrittenShown
$x^2$ or \(x^2\) in a linein the line, in the columns it stands in
\[ ... \] or $$ ... $$ alonecentred on rows of its own
\begin{align} ... \end{align}centred, all its lines in one picture

A formula in a line is never taller than a row: a tall one, a fraction, is drawn smaller to fit. Put it on a line of its own to see it at full size. Move the cursor into a formula and it shows as written, to be changed.

The formulas are drawn by the first LaTeX program of *latex-engines* found, in the background, those asked for together in one run, in the colour of your text. The program is shut in the sandbox: it sees TeX's own files and your fonts and nothing else, and it never runs without the sandbox. Until a formula is drawn, and where pictures cannot be shown (in tmux, or a terminal without them), it shows as written; so does one LaTeX cannot set.

Each formula is drawn after *formula-preamble* (amsmath and amssymb as standard) and the note's #+LATEX_HEADER: lines above its first heading, so a macro the note defines there can be used in its formulas. When nothing can be drawn after those lines, the formulas are drawn after *formula-preamble* alone. #+STARTUP: latexpreview shows a note's formulas as it opens, as inlineimages does, and nolatexpreview does not.

Try it

  1. In an Org note write a line The area is $\pi r^2$. and below it a line \[ \int_0^1 x^2\,dx = \frac{1}{3} \].
  2. Move the cursor to another line and press C-x T p. After a moment both formulas are drawn, the second centred on rows of its own.
  3. Move the cursor into the first. It shows as written; change r^2 to r^3 and move off. It is drawn again.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*formula-preamble*"\\usepackage{amsmath} \\usepackage{amss...textThe LaTeX put before \begin{document} for every formula shown as a picture ([inline-pictures-mode]), before what the file adds (an Org note's #+LATEX_HEADER: lines).

14.13 Blocks and code

A block is a stretch of text set apart between a line that begins #+begin_ and one that begins #+end_. The word after the underscore says what kind of block it is.

BlockIs for
srcCode, coloured as its language is
exampleText shown exactly as typed, such as what a program printed
quoteWords quoted from someone
versePoetry, where the line breaks matter
centerLines set in the middle

You do not type the two lines yourself. Type <s and press TAB, and a source block is written around the cursor with a list of languages to pick from. <e, <q, <v and <c do the same for the other four. These are snippets, which chapter 13 describes.

#+begin_src shell
echo "Water the beds at dawn"
#+end_src

The code in a source block is coloured as it would be in a file of that language. Org's name for a language is sometimes different from Tuatara's. *org-src-languages* maps one to the other, and you can add your own. It is a list of pairs, the name written after #+begin_src and the language it means. As standard it holds emacs-lisp for elisp, C++ for cpp, sqlite for sql, ksh and the other shells for bash, conf and desktop for ini, and a few more. Three are paired with nil, text, fundamental and calc: those blocks are not coloured. A name that is not in the list is looked up as a language of that name, and failing that as the language of a file ending in that name, so that #+begin_src toml needs no entry. If you write kitty for the configuration of a terminal that is really ini, add it to your init file:

(push '("kitty" . "ini") *org-src-languages*)

A block begun #+begin_src kitty is then coloured as ini.

14.13.1 Writing the code out to files

A note can hold the code of a program or of your configuration, with the explanation around it, and write the code out to the files that need it. Give a source block the words :tangle and a file name on its first line:

#+begin_src shell :tangle water.sh
echo "Water the beds at dawn"
#+end_src

C-c C-v t then writes every such block to its file. Blocks that name the same file go into it in order. Before anything is written, Tuatara lists the files and says which are new and which would change, and asks. This suits settings files well: the note says why each setting is there, and the file the program reads is made from it.

A file name with directories in it, such as :tangle ~/.config/foot/foot.ini, needs the directories to exist. A block with :mkdirp yes makes them as it is written, and one with :mkdirp no never does. For a block that says nothing, *code-files-make-directories* decides: nil, the standard, makes none, so a note writes the same on every machine and a mistyped directory is an error and not a new directory; t makes them for every block. A tangled note that always writes into directories you want made takes (setf *code-files-make-directories* t).

14.13.2 A table of contents

Tag a heading TOC and Tuatara keeps a table of contents under it, a list of links to the note's headings. It is made again each time you save. The tag can say more: TOC_3 lists headings three levels deep. M-x toc-org-insert-toc makes it at any other time.

14.13.3 Blocks that write themselves

A dynamic block is a block whose contents Tuatara writes. The clock table of the section on clocking is one. C-c C-x x puts in a new one and asks which kind. Apart from the clock table, the kinds list or include your files with formatted names: links to those that match a pattern, links to the notes that link to this one, or the text of the matching files themselves. C-c C-c on a block's first line, or C-c C-x C-u anywhere in it, writes it again from how things stand now. M-x org-update-all-dblocks does that for every such block in the buffer.

The tag has three parts, each of which can be left out. TOC_3 says how deep, and without a number it is *org-toc-max-depth*, 2 as standard. The part after the number says how the links are written, and without it that is *org-toc-style*, "gh" as standard. TOC_2_org is a table two levels deep in the org style. *org-toc-on-save* is t as standard, so the table is made again as the note is saved. At nil it is made only by M-x toc-org-insert-toc.

The two styles write the same list with different links. Take this note:

* Contents :TOC:
* Garden plan
** Vegetables
** Fruit & nuts
* Tools

With the gh style (:TOC:, or :TOC_2_gh:) the table under Contents is

- [[#garden-plan][Garden plan]]
  - [[#vegetables][Vegetables]]
  - [[#fruit--nuts][Fruit & nuts]]
- [[#tools][Tools]]

and with the org style (:TOC_2_org:)

- [[Garden plan][Garden plan]]
  - [[Vegetables][Vegetables]]
  - [[Fruit & nuts][Fruit & nuts]]
- [[Tools][Tools]]

Choose gh for a file that is also read on GitHub, a README above all. GitHub makes the anchor of a heading by a fixed rule (lower case, spaces as dashes, other signs dropped, -1 for a second heading of the same name), and the gh links follow that rule, so they work on the web page as well as in Tuatara. Choose org for a note that stays in Org: the link is the heading's title, as you would write one yourself, it reads the same in the file, and it needs no anchor rule to be right. Two headings with one title lead to the first with org, where gh keeps them apart. To use org everywhere, (setf *org-toc-style* "org"); for one table, name it in its tag. Both follow RET on the link. Headings tagged noexport, those under a COMMENT heading, and keywords, priorities and tags in the titles are left out of either.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-c C-v t, C-c C-v C-ttangle-code-filesWrite the code files of this Org file's source blocks (C-c C-v t), each block with :tangle FILE (on its #+begin_src line, in a subtree's property :header-args: or :header-args:LANGUAGE:, or in #+PROPERTY: header-args for the file) goes to FILE.

14.14 Exporting

A note is for you. A letter, a report or a set of minutes is for someone else, who wants a PDF or a Word document. Exporting makes one from the note. The headings become numbered sections, the lists become lists, the tables become tables, and the marks for bold and italic become bold and italic.

Tuatara makes a PDF by way of LaTeX, a typesetting system that produces handsome pages. You do not need to know LaTeX, but it must be installed: the program xelatex or lualatex, from the collection called TeX Live. M-x check-health tells you whether Tuatara found one. A Word document needs nothing else installed.

The export commands have no keys. Run them with M-x. The command you ran last is offered first there, so exporting again after a change is M-x RET.

14.14.1 What goes at the top of the note

A few lines at the top say what the document is.

#+title: The fence between our sections
#+author: Aroha Ngata
#+date: 14 October 2026
#+options: toc:nil num:nil

The title, author and date are printed at the head of the document. Without an #+author: line, the name in *user-full-name* is used. It is nil as standard, and the document then has no author. Give it your name as you want it printed, (setf *user-full-name* "Aroha Ngata"). The same name fills %author% in a note template and $AUTHOR in a snippet. The #+options: line here leaves out the table of contents and the numbers before headings, which suits a letter. Leave the line out and a report gets both. A heading tagged noexport is left out of the document with everything under it, which is handy for notes to yourself.

14.14.2 Making a PDF

M-x org-export-latex-pdf-enhanced-buffer makes the PDF and shows it beside your note. The work is done in the background, so you can go on writing. The mode line shows that a job is running and the echo area says when the file is written and how long it took. The PDF is put beside the note with the same name, letter.pdf for letter.org. If you change the note and export again, the PDF on the screen is read again at the page you were on.

Two more commands do the same and differ only in what happens afterwards. M-x org-export-latex-pdf-enhanced makes the PDF and shows nothing. M-x org-export-latex-pdf-enhanced-xdg opens it in your desktop's PDF reader.

The export takes the note as the buffer has it, saved or not. To export only part of a note, select the lines first.

If LaTeX fails, the echo area names the line of your note where it went wrong, and a buffer called *LaTeX errors* lists each error. RET on one shows that line of the note. The list is also a list of places (chapter 2): M-g n and M-g p go from error to error from any buffer, showing each line of the note in turn. An export is a background job like any other, so chapter 11 applies to it. C-x j lists what is running and C-x J stops it.

14.14.3 Bibliographies and indexes

A note cites its sources the way Org does. Name a bibliography file and the LaTeX package that sets it, then cite by key and say where the list goes:

#+cite_export: biblatex authoryear
#+bibliography: sources.bib
* Findings
The fence line was moved in 1998 [cite:@surveyor1998].

#+print_bibliography:

#+cite_export: takes biblatex with a style (two styles, for the bibliography and the citations, as authoryear/numeric), natbib, or bibtex with a style (plain unless you name one). A citation [cite:@key] becomes \autocite{key} for biblatex, [cite/t:@key] names the author in the sentence, and [cite/t/c:@key] does so with a capital letter. Text before and after a key, [cite:see @key p. 4], is printed around that reference, and text before the first key and after the last, set off by ;, around them all. The #+bibliography: file is taken from the note's directory, so the PDF finds it wherever #+export_file_name puts the LaTeX. A LaTeX file of your own that uses biblatex, \bibliography or \makeindex is handled the same way.

When LaTeX leaves a bibliography or an index to make, the export runs biber (for biblatex), bibtex (for \bibliography) or makeindex (for an index), then LaTeX again, and the status of the job says which is running. Each runs only when what it reads has changed: the citations, the .bib files and a bibtex style, found where TeX finds them. When one of those cannot be looked for, it runs every time to be safe. Making the PDF again after a small change otherwise takes one run of LaTeX, and a bibliography made after the last run LaTeX is allowed gets one run more to take it in. biber unpacks itself once into a directory kept beside the export's working directory, not on every run. If one of them finds a fault, the PDF is made all the same and *LaTeX errors* lists what it said under its name, each error with the line of the .bib file where there is one; M-g n takes you there. A program that is not installed is mentioned once in the echo area when the PDF is written, and the bibliography or index is left out.

They run as LaTeX does, shut in the sandbox (chapter 12): they read the document's directory, the TeX installation and the directories in *export-trusted-directories*, and write only in the export's own working directory. Keep the .bib file beside the note, or in one of those directories, so that they can read it.

14.14.4 Making a Word document

M-x org-export-docx writes the note as a Word document beside it, and M-x org-export-docx-xdg also opens it in your desktop's word processor. The document is laid out as the enhanced PDF is, with the same numbering and the same tables, so you can send whichever the other person prefers.

Try it, with a letter

  1. Open ~/letter.org with C-x C-f. Press i and type the four lines shown under "What goes at the top of the note", with your own name.

  2. Leave an empty line and type the letter:

       Dear Mr Tane,

   Thank you for offering to share the cost of the new fence. The quote
   from Motueka Fencing is *$1,840* for the whole length.

   - Posts and rails: $1,100
   - Labour: $740

   Yours sincerely,

   Aroha Ngata
  3. Press C-g and save with C-x C-s.
  4. Press M-x, type org-export-latex-pdf-enhanced-buffer and press RET. After a few seconds the letter is shown as a PDF at the right, with the title at the top, the sum in bold and the two costs as a list. On a narrow screen the PDF takes the whole window instead. Press C-x k to close it and return to the note before the next step.
  5. Press M-x, type org-export-docx and press RET. The echo area says that ~/letter.docx was written.

14.14.5 Two kinds of export

The commands above all have "enhanced" in their name or, for Word, behave that way. There is a second, plainer family without the word.

FamilyCommands beginWhat you get
Plainorg-export-latex-pdfThe PDF that Emacs's Org would make from the same note
Enhancedorg-export-latex-pdf-enhancedTuatara's own layout, with the additions below

Use the plain export for a note that must come out exactly as it did in Emacs. Use the enhanced export for everything else. It adds four things: tables that are fitted to the page, layout settings written in plain words, templates that give a document your own look, and a way to black out names.

Each family also has a command that stops at the LaTeX file and makes no PDF, M-x org-export-latex and M-x org-export-latex-enhanced, for people who want to work on the LaTeX themselves. If you have a LaTeX file of your own, M-x export-latex-compile-pdf and its two companions make a PDF from it in the same three ways.

14.14.6 From a line to the PDF and back

A PDF made by M-x export-latex-compile-pdf-buffer or one of its companions comes with a note of where each line of the LaTeX went on the pages. In the LaTeX file, C-c C-v shows the line the cursor is on in the PDF: the PDF opens beside the file if it is not shown, turns to the page the line is on, scrolls it into sight and marks it for a moment. In the PDF, C-c C-v goes the other way. It opens the LaTeX file in the other window at the line that made the part of the page you see, the place last marked or the middle of the window. In the window of the desktop version, a double click on a page goes to the line of that point.

When there is no PDF yet, or the file has changed since it was made, C-c C-v saves the file and makes the PDF again first, in the background, and shows the line once the new PDF is there. So after an edit, C-c C-v shows the text as it is now.

From an Org file, M-x show-line-in-pdf does the same for a PDF exported in this session, exporting it again the same way when the note has changed, and C-c C-v in the PDF then opens the Org file, not the LaTeX written from it. There is no key for it in Org files.

When the PDF was made some other way, without the note of where the lines went, Tuatara says so and names the command that makes the PDF again. In a terminal, where pages are shown as their text, the text is turned to the page and the place is not marked.

Going back from the PDF opens only files in the directory of the LaTeX file, or the Org file it was written from. A line that comes from any other file (a class or package of TeX's own, or a file a document read from elsewhere) is named in the echo area instead.

14.14.7 Layout in plain words

In the enhanced export a wide table is made to fit. Columns of sentences wrap, numbers go to the right, and the header row is repeated when the table runs on to another page. Most tables need nothing from you.

When you do want to change how something is set, you say so in a drawer called :EXPORT:, in words. Put it right under a heading to affect the heading and all under it, or just above a table, list, block or picture to affect that.

* Costs
:EXPORT:
new page: before
spacing: 1.5
:END:

This starts the section on a new page and sets its lines one and a half apart. The drawer itself is never printed. You do not need to remember the settings. M-x org-insert-export-drawer writes a drawer for whatever the cursor is on, holding every setting that fits it, each set to auto for you to change. M-x describe-export-settings explains them all, with examples. A word in a drawer that is not a setting is shown in the colour of an error as you type it.

14.14.8 Your own look

A template gives a document its look: the fonts, the margins, a header with a logo. A note chooses one with a line at the top, #+template: and the template's name. Templates are kept in your configuration directory.

The simplest start is M-x export-latex-template-copy. It copies one of the built-in templates to your directory and opens it for you to change. If someone gives you a Word or LaTeX document and asks for reports that look like it, M-x export-template-from-docx and M-x export-template-from-latex make a template from that document.

A note template is the other half: the lines a new note of some kind starts with, such as the #+template: line and the headings every report has. C-x i reads one into the buffer.

The programs that make the PDF are in *latex-engines*, which is ("xelatex" "lualatex") as standard. They are tried in that order, and when one fails the next is tried. A name is looked for on the PATH and then in TeX Live's own directories; a full path, ~/texlive/bin/xelatex for one installed elsewhere, works too. A note or a LaTeX file that names its program in its first line (#+latex_compiler: lualatex in Org, or %!TEX program = lualatex in LaTeX) has that one tried first when it is in the list. (setf *latex-engines* '("lualatex")) tries only that one.

The fonts of the enhanced export are *latex-main-font* for the text, *latex-sans-font* and *latex-mono-font*. Each is the name of a font family installed on your machine, as the system's font list gives it, or nil, the standard. At nil Tuatara picks the first of a list that is installed. For the text that is Libertinus Serif, Noto Serif, Source Serif 4, Liberation Serif, DejaVu Serif. For the sans-serif it is Libertinus Sans, Noto Sans, Source Sans 3, Liberation Sans, DejaVu Sans. For code it is the font of your window, *gui-font*, when it is installed, else JetBrains Mono, Cascadia Code, Noto Sans Mono, Source Code Pro, Liberation Mono, DejaVu Sans Mono. The styles that ask for chosen fonts, the standard one among them, use these three. To set a document in Noto Serif with code in Cascadia Code:

(setf *latex-main-font* "Noto Serif"
      *latex-mono-font* "Cascadia Code")

The text of the PDF is then in Noto Serif, its headings (in the sans-serif face) are as before, and a source block is in Cascadia Code.

A template that shows a logo gets it from the directory *logos-directory* names. At nil, the standard, that is logos/ in your configuration directory, ~/.config/tuatara/logos/. A note's #+logo: firm.pdf line is looked for there. If your pictures are kept elsewhere, (setf *logos-directory* "~/Pictures/logos").

14.14.9 Hiding names

Sometimes a document must go out with a name blacked out. Select the name, or put the cursor on it, press C-c m and choose R. The name is wrapped in a mark and shown in its own colour. In the PDF and in the Word document a black box stands where the name was, and the name is nowhere in the file. C-c M takes the mark away again.

The mark is R for a name. In your own LaTeX files the commands that hide their argument are those in *latex-redaction-commands*, "R", "D" and "redact" as standard, written without the backslash, so that \R{John Otago} is hidden text. export-check-redactions and the PDF export look for them in a LaTeX file just as they do for the marks of a note. If your templates call it \hide{...}, add it: (setf *latex-redaction-commands* '("R" "D" "redact" "hide")).

A box is of little use if the same name stands in plain text two pages later. M-x export-check-redactions looks for every hidden text that also appears unhidden and lists the places. The export runs the same check and asks before it goes on. Only the enhanced export hides text. The plain export refuses a note that asks for it.

14.14.10 Notes from other people

An exported note can pull in other files: pictures it shows and setup files it names. A note that someone sent you could name files of yours that way. So the export takes files only from the note's own directory and the directories in it, and says what it left out. *export-trusted-directories* names further directories you allow. Chapter 12 has more on files you do not trust.

The directory of your note templates is always allowed. *export-trusted-directories* is nil as standard, no other. Give it a list of directories, with ~ standing for your home directory, when setup files are shared by notes that are kept in directories of their own:

(setf *export-trusted-directories* '("~/notes/latex/"))

A note in ~/notes/work/ that says #+SETUPFILE: ~/notes/latex/house.org is then exported with that file. Without the line the export leaves the file out and, when it is done, says house.org was left out. Allow only directories you wrote yourself, since whoever sends you a note can name any file in them.

14.15 Where to go from here

Org rewards starting small. Keep one file of notes and fold it. Add a list with checkboxes when you next go shopping. When the tasks pile up, give them dates and open the agenda each morning. The rest of this chapter will still be here when you need a table or a PDF.

Many people keep their Org files under version control, so that every change to their notes is kept and can be taken back. That is the subject of the next chapter.

Git

Keeping the history of a directory, and working on it with other people.

Git is a program that remembers every version of the files in a directory. You tell it when a piece of work is done, and it keeps that state for good, with a sentence from you saying what changed. Later you can look at any earlier state, see who changed a line and why, try an idea without risk to the work that is finished, and share the directory with someone else without mailing files back and forth. It is used most for programs, but it works as well for a directory of recipes, a set of letters or a small website.

Tuatara does not replace git. It runs the git on your computer for you and shows what git says in buffers you can read and act on. Everything starts from one buffer, the status, which C-x g opens. This chapter explains the status first, then the daily round of staging and committing, then looking at history, branches, sharing with a remote, and the tools for finding out when and why something changed.

The examples use a directory of recipes, ~/recipes, with a text file for each recipe. You need git installed, and git needs to know your name once. If you have never used it, type these two lines in a terminal, with your own name and address:

git config --global user.name "Aroha Example"
git config --global user.email "aroha@example.org"

15.1 What git keeps

A few words come up on every page of this chapter. They are git's own, and the same in every book about it.

A repository is a directory whose history git keeps. Git stores the history in a hidden directory called .git inside it. Your files stay ordinary files that any program can open.

A commit is one saved state of the whole directory, with a message, your name and the time. Commits form a chain, each one pointing back to the one before. Every commit has a name of its own made of letters and digits, called its hash, such as 3f9c2ab. You rarely type one; you pick the commit from a list.

Staging is how you choose what goes into the next commit. Suppose you fixed the oven temperature in one recipe and began a new recipe in the same hour. Those are two pieces of work. You stage the fix and commit it, then stage the new recipe and commit that. Each commit then says one thing, which makes the history easy to read a year later. What is staged is kept in a list that git calls the index.

A branch is a line of commits with a name. A new repository has one, usually called main. You make another when you want to try something, such as rewriting every recipe in metric measures, and keep main as it is until the new work is ready.

A remote is another copy of the repository, most often on a server. You push your commits to it and fetch the commits other people pushed.

Figure 15.1 shows the way a change travels.

The keys on the arrows are the ones you press in the status: s stages, u unstages, c c commits, P p pushes and F u pulls. The rest of the chapter takes them one at a time.

15.2 The status

C-x g shows the state of the repository that the current file or directory is in. It is the place you work with git from. It shows the branch you are on, the files that have changed, what is staged, and the latest commits.

The first time you open the status of a project, Tuatara asks whether you trust it, because git can run programs that a repository names. Chapter 12 explains the question and its three answers. For a directory you made yourself, answer y and then type yes.

Figure 15.2 shows the status of the recipes after an afternoon's work.

The first line names the branch and the subject of its last commit. The second appears when the branch follows a branch on a remote, its upstream, and says how many commits you have that the remote lacks (ahead) and how many it has that you lack (behind). When git is in the middle of something, such as a merge that stopped, a third line beginning Doing: says what and which keys go on with it or stop it.

Below are the sections. Each has a heading with a count, and is left out when it would be empty.

SectionWhat it holds
Unmerged filesFiles with a conflict, while a merge or a rebase has stopped.
Untracked filesNew files that git does not keep yet. A new directory is one line.
Unstaged changesChanges to files git keeps, which you have not chosen yet.
Staged changesWhat the next commit will hold.
StashesWork you put aside (see The stash below).
Unpushed to …Commits the remote does not have yet.
Recent commitsThe latest commits of the branch.
Ignored filesFiles git was told to leave alone. Folded until you open it.

The status is a list in sections, like the buffer list of chapter 7, and the same keys fold it. These are the keys in the order you are likely to need them.

ModalNon-modalWhat it does
j, kC-n, C-pDown and up a line.
nonen, pTo the next and the previous file, hunk or heading.
noneTABShows a file's changes under it, or hides them. On a heading, folds or opens the section.
noneS-TABFolds every section, or opens them all.
noneRET, lOpens the file at the change, or shows the commit or stash on the line.
nonesStages the file, the hunk or the selected lines.
noneuUnstages them.
nonexReverses a change, after asking. It cannot be undone.
nonecOpens the commit menu.
noneL, dOpen the log menu and the diff menu.
noneb, t, zOpen the branch, tag and stash menus.
nonem, ROpen the merge and rebase menus.
nonef, F, POpen the fetch, pull and push menus.
nonerReads the repository again.
noneq, hCloses the status.

You seldom need r. The status reads itself again when you save a file of the repository, and when git changes the repository from anywhere, a terminal included. It waits at least *git-watch-seconds* between two readings. A file made or changed by another program, without git, shows after r.

Staged files have a colour of their own so that you can tell them from the ones not staged, a staged deletion has another, and the commits and stashes a third. A long section shows its first *git-section-lines* files and then a line saying how many more there are; TAB on that line shows more. *git-recent-commits* sets how many commits the last section lists.

15.2.1 Menus

Most keys in the status open a menu, a small panel that lists what you can do next, each action with a key. c opens the commit menu, and c again there starts a commit, so the whole thing is written c c. C-g closes a menu without doing anything, and C-h in a menu lists every action with its description.

Many menus also have switches. A switch changes how the next action runs, and its key begins with -. In the push menu, - n turns on "Only try", and the push that follows only reports what it would send. An option is a switch that takes a value, and its key begins with =. In the log menu, = n asks how many commits to list.

To keep the menus short, they show the actions used most. ~ in the status switches that status between the short menus and the full ones. When this chapter names an action you cannot see in a menu, press ~ first. To have the full menus always, put this in your init file:

(setf *git-menus* :full)

*git-slim-actions* is the list of actions the short menus show, if you would sooner add one or two than see them all.

Try it, with a directory of recipes

  1. In a terminal, make the directory and a first recipe: mkdir ~/recipes && cd ~/recipes && git init && printf 'Scones\n\n2 cups flour\n1 cup milk\n' > scones.txt.
  2. In Tuatara, open ~/recipes/scones.txt and press C-x g. Answer the question about trust with y, then type yes and RET.
  3. The status opens. The first line says the branch and (no commit yet). scones.txt is under Untracked files.
  4. Press n twice to go to the file's line, then l. The file opens. Press C-x g to come back.
  5. Press TAB on the heading Untracked files. The section folds to one line. Press TAB again to open it.
  6. Press q. The status closes. C-x g opens it again whenever you want it.

15.3 Staging

Staging is choosing. s on a file's line moves the file to Staged changes, and u there moves it back. Neither changes the file itself. On a section's heading, s stages every file of the section at once, which is the quick way when all of your changes belong together.

15.3.1 Hunks and single lines

Often a file holds two changes that deserve a commit each. Press TAB on the file and its changes appear under it. Lines that were added begin with +, and lines that were taken away begin with -. The changes come in groups called hunks, each a run of changed lines with a few unchanged lines around it, under a line that begins with @@.

With the cursor on a hunk, s stages that hunk alone. For something finer still, select lines inside a hunk with V and then press s: only the selected lines are staged. u works the same way under Staged changes.

A file with a great many changes shows the first *git-diff-lines* lines of them, then a line saying how many more there are. TAB on that line shows more. Staging the file still takes all of it.

15.3.2 Reversing a change

x throws a change away. On a file under Unstaged changes it puts the file back to how the last commit has it. On a hunk it removes that hunk's change, and with lines selected, those lines. Tuatara asks first and says that it cannot be undone, because git never had a copy of the text you are discarding.

A file that is not tracked is treated more gently. x moves it to the trash, and you can put it back from there (chapter 10).

15.3.3 From the file itself

You do not have to open the status to stage. In a saved file, with the cursor on a changed line, M-x git-stage-hunk stages the change at the cursor and M-x git-unstage-hunk takes it back. M-x git-stage-file and M-x git-unstage-file do the whole file. The same actions are in the file menu, described under Blame and the file menu below.

A file in a repository also shows its changes in the gutter, the narrow strip at the left of the window. There is a mark beside each line added since the last commit, another beside each changed line, and one where lines were deleted. The marks are worked out in the background when the file is first shown and after each save. M-x vc-gutter-mode turns them off everywhere, or on again. M-x vc-gutter-refresh works them out anew, which you may want after a commit made in a terminal.

noneM-x git-unstage-hunkgit-unstage-hunkUnstage the hunk at point: in the status (C-x g) the one on point's line, as u does; in a file's own buffer, saved, the change staged at point's line.
noneM-x git-stage-filegit-stage-fileStage the file you are in (as saved), or the one on point's line of a status.

noneM-x vc-gutter-modevc-gutter-modeSwitch the version-control gutter on or off for all buffers; with a count, on when it is positive, off when it is zero or less.
noneM-x vc-gutter-refreshvc-gutter-refreshRecompute the version-control marks of the current buffer from git.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*git-diff-lines*1000a whole number, 1 or moreHow many lines of a file's changes M-x git-toggle-diff shows under it at first, and how many more each M-x git-toggle-diff on the line after them shows.
FaceWhat it paints
