:vc-changedGutter mark for lines changed since the last commit.
:vc-deletedGutter mark after lines deleted since the last commit.

15.4 Committing

When what is staged is one finished piece of work, commit it. c c opens a buffer for the message, with a list of what is staged under it on lines that begin with #. Those lines are for you to read and are left out of the commit. The buffer starts in INSERT state, so you can type at once.

A good message has a short first line that says what changed, such as Lower the oven temperature for scones. If there is more to say, leave an empty line and write a paragraph on why. The lines are filled at *git-commit-fill-column* as you type.

C-c C-c makes the commit and closes the buffer. C-c C-k gives the message up, and nothing is committed.

Try it, with the recipes

  1. Open the status of ~/recipes with C-x g. Move to scones.txt and press s. The file moves to Staged changes.
  2. Press c, then c. The message buffer opens.
  3. Type Start the recipe directory. Press C-g and then C-c C-c.
  4. The status now has a section Recent commits with your commit in it, and the first line shows its subject.
  5. Open scones.txt, add the line 1 pinch salt at the end and, a few lines up, change 2 cups flour to 3 cups flour. Save with C-x C-s and press C-x g.
  6. Press TAB on scones.txt. Move to the line +1 pinch salt, press V and then s. Only that line is staged.
  7. Press c c, type Add salt to the scones, press C-g and C-c C-c. The change to the flour is still waiting under Unstaged changes.

15.4.1 Changing the last commit

Everyone commits and then sees a spelling mistake. The commit menu has three ways to change the last commit, as long as you have not pushed it yet.

ModalNon-modalWhat it does
nonec aAmend. What is staged goes into the last commit, and you edit its message.
nonec wReword. Only the message is edited.
nonec eExtend. What is staged goes into the last commit, with the message as it is.

Use extend when you forgot a file, reword when the message is wrong, and amend when both need fixing.

The full menu has two more, for a mistake further back. c f (fix up) and c s (squash) make a small commit that is marked as belonging to an earlier one you pick. A later rebase with the switch - q folds it into that commit. Rebasing is described below.

The switches of the commit menu go to git with the commit. - a commits every change to tracked files without staging first. - s adds a Signed-off-by line with your name, which some projects ask for.

15.4.2 Signing commits

A signed commit carries proof that it was made with your key, so that others can check it came from you. Tuatara commits the way git does with your own settings, signing included. There is nothing to switch on in Tuatara. You tell git once, in a terminal, which key to use and that every commit is to be signed:

git config --global user.signingkey YOUR-KEY
git config --global commit.gpgsign true

From then on C-c C-c in a message buffer makes a signed commit. Git's own manual describes the kinds of key it accepts. A tag can be signed as well: in the tag menu, turn on - s before you make the tag.

Signing and signing off are different things. The switch - s in the commit menu only adds a line of text to the message.

To see which commits are signed, press ! in the status and type log --format"%h %G? %s". A =G before a subject means a good signature and an N means none.

15.4.3 Commands and settings for committing

15.5 The log and diffs

15.5.1 The log

The log is the list of commits, the latest first. L L in the status lists the commits of the branch you are on, a line each: the hash, the date, the author, any branch or tag that sits at the commit, and the subject. RET or l on a line shows the commit, with its message and every change it made. q closes.

The log menu lists other things too.

ModalNon-modalWhat it lists
noneL LThe branch you are on.
noneL oAnother branch, or any revision you name.
noneL fThe commits that changed one file: the one on the line, or the current file.
noneL bEvery branch, the remotes' included. (Full menu.)
noneL aEvery reference: branches, tags and stashes. (Full menu.)
noneL rThe reflog: where the branch has been, step by step. (Full menu.)

A revision is any way of naming a commit: a branch name, a tag, a hash, or HEAD, which is git's word for the commit you are on now.

The switches and options shape the list. - g draws the graph of branches beside the commits, which helps after a merge. = a keeps one author's commits, = s those whose message contains a word, and = d and = u those since or until a date; git understands dates such as 2 weeks ago. The log shows *git-log-length* commits unless = n says otherwise.

The reflog is worth knowing about on a bad day. Git records every move of the branch, including the ones that seemed to throw commits away. A commit you lost by a mistaken reset is still listed there for some weeks, and you can check it out or make a branch at it.

15.5.2 Diffs

A diff shows how two states differ, line by line, in the same form as the changes under a file in the status. d d shows everything you have changed since the last commit, in a buffer of its own. It is a good thing to read through before you commit.

ModalNon-modalWhat it shows

noned sWhat is staged: the changes the next commit will make.
noned uWhat is not staged. (Full menu.)
noned rHow your files differ from a revision you name. (Full menu.)
noned RWhat changed between two revisions. (Full menu.)
noned cOne commit.

M-x git-diff-file shows the uncommitted changes of the file you are in.

Among the switches, - w ignores changes in spaces, which helps when a file was only re-indented. - s shows the names of the files and how many lines changed in each, without the lines. = U sets how many unchanged lines are shown around each change.

Added and removed lines have their own colours. A diff larger than *differences-limit* octets is not shown, and Tuatara says so. Comparing two files that are not in git is M-x diff-files, described in chapter 9.

15.6 Branches and tags

15.6.1 Branches

A branch lets you work on something without disturbing what is finished. Suppose you want to convert all the recipes to metric measures. It will take a week, and in the meantime you still want to fix small things in the recipes as they are. Make a branch called metric, do the conversion there one commit at a time, and go back to main whenever you need to.

Going to a branch is called checking it out. Git then changes the files in the directory to that branch's state. If a buffer still shows a file's old text afterwards, M-x revert-buffer reads the file again (chapter 9).

ModalNon-modalWhat it does
noneb cMakes a new branch and checks it out. It asks for the name, then where to start; RET starts from where you are.
noneb bChecks out a branch or a revision you name.
noneb mRenames a branch.
noneb dDeletes a branch, though never the one you are on.

Git refuses to check out another branch when that would overwrite changes you have not committed, and Tuatara shows what it said. Commit them first, or put them aside with the stash.

Deleting a branch whose commits are on no other branch would lose them. Tuatara asks a second time in that case.

If you name a commit or a tag at b b where a branch was expected, git checks out that state with no branch. The status then says (detached) on its first line. You can look around, but commits made there belong to no branch. Check out a branch to return.

The full menu has four more actions. b n makes a branch without checking it out. b x moves a branch to another commit. b u sets a branch's upstream. b s is for the day you find you have been committing on main when you meant to use a branch: it makes a new branch with the commits you have not pushed, checks it out, and puts main back to where its upstream is.

y in the status lists every branch, every branch of the remotes and every tag, each with the commit it is at. RET on a line shows its log.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneb, C-c bgit-branch-menuOpen the branch menu: check out a branch or a revision, make one (checked out or not, or spun off with the work not pushed), rename, move, delete one, or set its upstream.

noneM-x git-branch-renamegit-branch-renameRename a branch, asked for (the one checked out when nothing is typed), to a name asked for.

nonel, RET, C-c lgit-refs-logList the log of the branch or tag on the line of the list of references; on a section's heading, fold or unfold the section.

15.6.2 Merging

When the work on a branch is done, you merge it into main. Check out main, then press m m and name the branch. Git joins the two lines of work and makes a commit that records the join. Figure 15.3 shows the shape.

If main did not change while you worked on the branch, there is nothing to join. Git moves main forward to the branch's last commit, which is called a fast-forward, and makes no extra commit.

The full menu has two more ways to merge. m n merges but stops before the commit so that you can look first. m s brings in all of a branch's changes as one staged change, for you to commit as a single commit. When both branches changed the same lines, the merge stops half way. That is a conflict, and it has a section of its own below.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
nonem, C-c mgit-merge-menuOpen the merge menu: merge a branch, committed or not, squash its changes into one, or stop a merge stopped half way.
noneM-x git-mergegit-mergeMerge a branch, asked for, into the one checked out, committing it with git's own message; files changed on both sides stop it half way, said so in the status (c c commits once they are put right, m a stops it).
noneM-x git-merge-no-commitgit-merge-no-commitMerge a branch, asked for, without committing: the merge is left staged, to look at and commit (c c) or stop (m a).
noneM-x git-merge-squashgit-merge-squashBring the changes of a branch, asked for, into the files and stage them as one change, not a merge: c c commits them.
noneM-x git-merge-continuegit-merge-continueGo on with the merge stopped half way, once the files git could not join are put right and staged.
noneM-x git-merge-abortgit-merge-abortStop the merge, after asking: the branch and the files go back to where they were before it began.

15.6.3 Tags

A tag is a name for one commit that never moves. You would tag the state of the recipes that you printed for the school fair as fair-2026, so that you can always get exactly that state back. t t asks for the revision, offering the commit on the cursor's line, and for the name. t d deletes a tag.

With the switch - a the tag carries a message of its own, and with - s it is signed. Tags are not sent by an ordinary push. The full push menu sends them: P t every tag, P T one.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
nonetgit-tag-menuOpen the tag menu: tag a revision, or delete a tag; P t and P T in the push menu send tags.
noneM-x git-tag-creategit-tag-createTag a revision asked for (the commit on point's line first, else HEAD) with a name asked for; the tag menu's -a makes it annotated with a message asked for, -s signed (with a message too), -f moves a tag of that name.
noneM-x git-tag-deletegit-tag-deleteDelete a tag, asked for, here (not on any remote), after asking.

Try it, with the recipes

  1. In the status of ~/recipes, press b c. Type metric and RET, then RET again to start from where you are. The first line now says metric.
  2. Open scones.txt, change 1 cup milk to 250 ml milk and save. Press C-x g, then s on the file, c c, type Milk in millilitres, C-g and C-c C-c.
  3. Press b b, type main and RET. The first line says main, and the commit you just made is not among the recent commits. On this branch the milk is still in cups.
  4. Press m m, type metric and RET. The commit is now on main too, and the file says 250 ml.
  5. Press L, then - g and L. The log shows the commits with the graph beside them. Press q.
  6. Press b d, type metric and RET, then answer y and RET to the question. The branch is merged, so it can go.

15.7 The stash

Sometimes you are half way through a change and need the files clean for a moment, for instance to check out main and fix a typing mistake someone pointed out. The work is not ready for a commit. The stash is a shelf for it. z z asks for a short message, puts every change aside and returns the files to the last commit. The stash appears in the status under Stashes.

When you come back, z p (pop) puts the changes into the files again and takes the stash off the shelf. z a (apply) does the same and keeps the stash, for when you want the changes on two branches. z d drops a stash without applying it, and that cannot be undone.

If the files changed in the meantime in the same places, popping can end in a conflict. Tuatara then keeps the stash and says so, and nothing is lost.

New files that git does not track yet are left where they are unless you turn on the switch - u first.

The full menu adds z i, which stashes only what is staged, z x, which stashes everything and leaves the staged part in place, z v, which shows what a stash holds, and z b, which makes a new branch out of a stash.

Try it, with the recipes

  1. Open ~/recipes/scones.txt and add a line Serve with jam at the end. Save, and press C-x g. The file is under Unstaged changes.
  2. Press z z, type serving note and RET. The change is gone from the file, and the status has a section Stashes.
  3. Press RET on the stash to see what it holds, then q.
  4. Press z p and pick the stash. The line is back in the file and the section Stashes is gone.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
nonez, C-c zgit-stash-menuOpen the stash menu: put changes aside (all, only what is staged, or keeping it), apply, pop, drop or show a stash, or make a branch of one.
noneM-x git-stashgit-stashPut every change aside as a stash, staged or not, with a message asked for; the files go back to the last commit.
noneM-x git-stash-popgit-stash-popBring the changes of a stash, asked for, back into the files and drop it; one whose changes meet others is kept, said so.
noneM-x git-stash-applygit-stash-applyBring the changes of a stash, asked for, back into the files, the stash kept; git says when they meet changes of their own.
noneM-x git-stash-dropgit-stash-dropDrop a stash, asked for, after asking: its changes are gone.
noneM-x git-stash-indexgit-stash-indexPut only what is staged aside as a stash, with a message asked for; the changes not staged stay.
noneM-x git-stash-keep-indexgit-stash-keep-indexPut every change aside as a stash, with a message asked for, keeping what is staged in place in the files and staged.
noneM-x git-stash-showgit-stash-showShow a stash, asked for: the files it changes and its changes.

15.8 Merge conflicts

A conflict happens when two lines of work changed the same lines of a file. Git cannot know which is right, so it stops and asks you. It can happen in a merge, a rebase, a cherry-pick, or when a stash comes back.

Nothing is broken when this happens. The status says what git is doing on its Doing: line, with the keys that go on or stop, and it lists the files in question first, in a section called Unmerged files. Each line says how the two sides differ, for example both changed.

Git writes both versions into the file, between marker lines:

<<<<<<< HEAD
2 cups flour
=======
300 g flour
>>>>>>> metric

The lines after <<<<<<< are the first side. In a merge that is the branch you are on. The lines after the row of equals signs are the second side, the branch being merged in.

To settle a conflict, follow these steps.

  1. Press RET on the file in the status. It opens with the cursor on its first conflict, with the two sides coloured.
  2. For each conflict, decide. C-c ^ u keeps the first side, C-c ^ l the second and C-c ^ a both. C-c ^ n goes to the next conflict. You can also edit the lines by hand and delete the markers. Chapter 13 describes these keys in full.
  3. Save the file with C-x C-s.
  4. Press C-x g and then s on the file. Staging it tells git the file is settled, and it moves to Staged changes.
  5. When no file is left under Unmerged files, finish: m c commits a merge, R c goes on with a rebase, and A c with a cherry-pick.

If you would sooner not deal with it now, m a stops a merge and puts the branch and the files back as they were before it began. R a and A a do the same for a rebase and a cherry-pick. Each asks first.

Try it, with a conflict made on purpose

  1. In the status of ~/recipes, press b c, type grams and RET RET. In scones.txt change the flour line to 300 g flour. Save, press C-x g, stage with s and commit with c c and the message Flour in grams.
  2. Press b b, type main and RET. In scones.txt, run M-x revert-buffer if the line still says grams, then change it to 2 cups plain flour. Save, stage and commit as Say which flour.
  3. Press m m, type grams and RET. The merge stops. The status shows a Doing: line and scones.txt under Unmerged files.
  4. Press RET on the file. If the line says 2 cups plain flour and has no markers, the buffer is the old one: run M-x revert-buffer. Both versions are there between the markers. Press C-c ^ l to keep 300 g flour, then C-x C-s.
  5. Press C-x g, then s on the file, then m c. If a message buffer opens, press C-c C-c. The merge is done.

15.9 Rebase, cherry-pick, revert and reset

These four change or reuse commits that already exist. You can work for a long time without them. They are here for the day you need one.

15.9.1 Rebase

Rebasing makes your commits again on top of another commit, as if you had started your work later than you did. The usual reason is that main moved on while you worked on a branch. A merge would join the two with an extra commit. A rebase gives a single straight line instead, which many people find easier to read. R e asks what to rebase on, and R u rebases on the branch's upstream.

If one of your commits clashes with the new base, the rebase stops with a conflict. Settle it as described above and press R c to go on. The full menu's R s leaves that commit out, and R a stops the whole rebase and puts everything back.

R i rebases as a list says, and is the tool for tidying your own commits before you share them. It asks which commit to start after, then shows the commits after it in a buffer, one per line, the oldest first:

pick 81d04e7 Add the pavlova
pick 5c2e9a1 Fix a typo in the pavlova
pick 9b7f310 Add the bread

Change the list to say what you want. Move a line to change the order. Change the word pick to reword to give the commit a new subject, to squash or fixup to fold it into the commit on the line above, or to drop to leave it out. In the example, changing the second line to fixup makes the typo fix part of the commit that added the pavlova. C-c C-c rebases as the list says, asking for each new subject first. C-c C-k gives the list up and nothing changes.

One rule keeps you out of trouble: rebase only commits you have not pushed. A rebase makes new commits in place of the old ones, and anyone who already has the old ones would be left with a history that no longer matches yours.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneR, C-c Rgit-rebase-menuOpen the rebase menu: rebase the branch on its upstream or a revision, or go on with, skip a commit of, or stop a rebase stopped half way.
noneM-x git-rebase-ontogit-rebase-ontoRebase the branch checked out on a revision asked for: its commits since they parted made again after it.
noneM-x git-rebase-upstreamgit-rebase-upstreamRebase the branch checked out on its upstream: its own commits made again after the upstream's.
noneM-x git-rebase-interactivegit-rebase-interactiveRebase the commits after a revision asked for (the commit on point's line first) as a list says.

15.9.2 Cherry-pick

A cherry-pick copies one commit from another branch onto the branch you are on. You would use it when a branch holds one fix you want now and the rest of the branch is not ready. Press A A in the status and name the commit. A branch's name stands for its newest commit, and a commit on the cursor's line is offered first. The full menu's A n brings the commit's changes into your files without committing them.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does

noneM-x git-cherry-pick-abortgit-cherry-pick-abortStop the cherry-pick, after asking: the branch and the files go back to where they were before it began.

15.9.3 Revert

A revert makes a new commit that undoes an earlier one. The earlier commit stays in the history, and the new one says that it was taken back. This is the safe way to undo something you have already pushed, because nothing that others have is rewritten. _ _ asks which commit, offering the one on the cursor's line.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
none_, C-c _git-revert-menuOpen the revert menu: make a commit undoing another, or undo it in the files uncommitted; go on with, skip or stop one stopped half way.
noneM-x git-revertgit-revertMake a commit undoing a commit asked for (the one on point's line of a status or a log first), with git's message saying so.
noneM-x git-revert-no-commitgit-revert-no-commitUndo the changes of a commit, asked for, in the files and stage that, not committed.
noneM-x git-revert-continuegit-revert-continueGo on with the revert stopped half way, once the files git could not join are put right and staged.
noneM-x git-revert-skipgit-revert-skipSkip the commit the revert stopped at and go on with the next.
noneM-x git-revert-abortgit-revert-abortStop the revert, after asking: the branch and the files go back to where they were before it began.

15.9.4 Reset

A reset moves the branch itself to another commit. The commits after it are no longer on the branch. It is the way to take back commits you have not pushed. The actions differ in what happens to your files.

ModalNon-modalWhat it keeps
noneX mYour files as they are. The undone commits' changes show as not staged.
noneX sYour files and what is staged. The changes show as staged. (Full menu.)
noneX KChanges you have not committed; the files otherwise follow. (Full menu.)
noneX HNothing. Files and index go to the commit, and uncommitted changes are lost. It asks first.
noneX fPuts one file back to how a revision has it, after asking.

X m is the one to reach for when you committed too early: the commit is gone and its changes are in your files to stage again as you like. X H is for when you want to throw work away, and it does. The reflog can still find the commits afterwards, but changes that were never committed are gone.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneX, C-c Xgit-reset-menuOpen the reset menu: move the branch to a revision, keeping what is staged, the files, or changes not committed, or nothing; or put a file back to a revision.
noneM-x git-reset-mixedgit-reset-mixedMove the branch checked out to a revision asked for, what is staged put back to it too, the files as they are (their changes shown as not staged).
noneM-x git-reset-softgit-reset-softMove the branch checked out to a revision asked for, what is staged and the files as they are (the commits' changes shown as staged).
noneM-x git-reset-keepgit-reset-keepMove the branch checked out to a revision asked for, the files with it, keeping changes not committed; git refuses when they would be lost.
noneM-x git-reset-hardgit-reset-hardMove the branch checked out to a revision asked for, what is staged and the files with it, after asking: changes not committed are lost.
noneM-x git-reset-filegit-reset-filePut a file, the one on point's line of a status or the current one, back to how a revision asked for has it, staged, after asking: its changes not committed are lost.

15.10 Pulling and pushing

A remote is a second copy of the repository that you exchange commits with. It may be on a hosting service, on a server at work, or in a directory on a shared drive. A repository you copied from somewhere with git clone already has one, called origin. To give a repository of your own a remote, press M a in the status. It asks for a name, and origin is the custom for the first, then for the address.

Three verbs cover the exchange.

Fetch downloads the commits the remote has and you lack, and changes nothing in your files or your branch. It is always safe. f u fetches from the upstream's remote and f a from every remote. Afterwards the second line of the status says how far behind you are.

Pull fetches and then brings the new commits into your branch. F u pulls from the upstream. With no switch it only moves your branch forward when that is all there is to do. If you and the remote both have new commits, it stops and tells you, and you choose: - r before u rebases your commits on theirs, and - m merges theirs into yours. Tuatara never makes a merge you did not ask for.

Push sends your commits to the remote. P p pushes the branch to its upstream. The first time, the branch has no upstream yet: press P, turn on - u, then press e and name the remote. From then on P p is enough. If the remote has commits you lack, the push is refused. Pull first, then push again.

Fetching, pulling and pushing run in the background, so you can go on working. The sign P at the front of the mode line is lit while they run (chapter 11).

A forced push, - f or - F, replaces what the remote has with what you have. It always asks first, since it can remove other people's commits from the remote. Of the two, - f is the careful one: it refuses if the remote has something you have not seen. - n only tries, and reports what a push would send.

Tuatara does not ask for passwords itself. With an address that uses ssh, your keys come from the ssh agent of your system. If the server refuses, Tuatara shows git's own words.

The remote menu looks after the remotes themselves: M a adds one and M u gives one a new address. The full menu also renames, removes, and forgets branches that the remote has deleted.

Try it, with a directory standing in for a server

  1. In a terminal, make an empty repository to play the server: git init --bare /tmp/recipes-server.git.
  2. In the status of ~/recipes, press M a. Press RET at the name to take origin, then type /tmp/recipes-server.git and RET for the address.
  3. Press P, then - u, then e. Type origin and RET. The echo area reports the push when it is done, and the status gains a line beginning Upstream:.
  4. Make a small change to a recipe, save, stage and commit it. The second line of the status says 1 ahead and a section lists the commit as not pushed.
  5. Press P p. The section goes, and you are level with the remote again.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does

noneM-x git-remote-addgit-remote-addAdd a remote: a name asked for (origin when nothing is typed and there is none) and its address; its branches are fetched with f e.

15.11 Blame and the file menu

15.11.1 Who changed each line

Blame answers the question "where did this line come from?". M-x git-blame lists the current file a line at a time, and before each line the commit that last changed it, its author and its date. RET or l on a line shows that commit in full, so you can read the message and see what else changed with it. q closes. The name is git's and sounds harsher than the tool is. Most often the answer is yourself, two years ago, with a good reason in the message.

Blame reads the file as saved, so save first.

15.11.2 The file menu

M-x git-file-menu opens a menu of git actions for the file you are in. It works from the file's own buffer, without a visit to the status, and from a file's line in the status.

ModalNon-modalWhat it does
nones, uStages the file, and unstages it.
noneS, UStages the hunk at the cursor, and unstages it.
nonedShows the file's uncommitted changes.
noneLLists the commits that changed the file.
nonebBlame.
nonerGoes back through the file's history (see Rewind below).
nonefPuts the file back to how a revision has it, after asking.
noneRRenames the file, in git and on disk. (Full menu.)
noneDDeletes the file from git and from disk, after asking. (Full menu.)

Renaming a file through git, with R here, keeps its history joined to the new name, and the buffers that visit the file follow it.

If you use the menu often, give it a key in your init file. Chapter 20 shows how.

15.12 Rewind: a file as it was

Rewind shows a file as it stood at each commit that changed it, one step at a time. It is the quickest way to answer "what did this recipe say before I rewrote it?", and to copy a paragraph back out of the past.

Press C-x G in a file. A new buffer shows the file as its latest commit left it, read-only, with the cursor on the line you were on. Then:

ModalNon-modalWhat it does
nonepShows the file one commit older.
nonenShows it one commit newer.
nonerLets you choose a commit from the file's log.
nonecShows the commit that left the file like this.
noneC-c wCopies that commit's short hash.
noneC-x GGoes back to the file as it is now, on the same line.
noneqCloses the buffer.

While you rewind, the mode line says Rewind and the commit's hash in the warning colour, followed by the commit's date and which of how many it is, such as 3/5. You cannot mistake the old text for the file as it is now.

The text is read-only, but you can select and copy from it as from any buffer (chapter 4) and paste into the real file. The history follows the file back through a rename. Changes you have not committed are not part of it, since they are in no commit.

Rewind works on directories too. Press C-x G in a directory listing (chapter

  1. and the listing shows the directory as its latest commit left it, with files

that have since been deleted. p and n step through the commits as before. RET on a file there goes through that file's history from that commit, and q comes back to the directory. Commands that would change files, such as copying or renaming, are refused in such a listing, because the files in it are from the past.

Try it, with the recipes

  1. Open ~/recipes/scones.txt, which by now has several commits. Put the cursor on the flour line.
  2. Press C-x G. The mode line says Rewind and a hash. The text is the file as last committed.
  3. Press p a few times. The flour line changes back through grams and cups. At the oldest commit, the echo area says there is none before it.
  4. Press c to read the commit that made the version you are looking at, then q to close it.
  5. Press n to come forward, then C-x G. You are back in the real file.

noneM-x git-rewind-newergit-rewind-newerShow the file or directory of this history as the commit after left it.
noneM-x git-rewind-togit-rewind-toShow the file or directory of this history as a commit chosen from its log left it, the latest first, by its hash, date, author or subject.

15.13 Repositories you only look at

Git can be told by a repository to run programs: hooks, filters and other helpers named in the repository's own settings. That is fine in a directory of your own and unwise in one a stranger sent you. For this reason the status asks before it first opens a project, and one of the answers is l, look only.

In a look-only repository you can read the status, the log, diffs, blame and rewind as usual. The mode line of every git buffer says Look only. The keys that would change the repository are dimmed in the menus, and pressing one says why it is refused. A repository that holds evidence is always look-only.

Chapter 12 explains the question, how look-only reading works, and M-x trust-project, which asks again when you have changed your mind.

15.14 Less common work

The status has menus for parts of git that most people need seldom or never. They work like the menus above, and C-h in each lists its actions. This section says what each is for, so that you know it is there when the day comes.

15.14.1 Worktrees

A worktree is a second directory that shows another branch of the same repository. With one, you can have main open in one directory and metric in another at the same time, without checking out back and forth. Z opens the menu: Z c makes a worktree for a new branch, Z g shows the status of one, and Z d deletes one.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneZ, C-c Zgit-worktree-menuOpen the worktree menu: make a worktree for a branch, or for a new one, show a worktree's status, move or delete one.
noneM-x git-worktree-branchgit-worktree-branchMake a new branch, asked for, starting at a revision asked for, and a worktree for it in a directory asked for.
noneM-x git-worktree-checkoutgit-worktree-checkoutMake a worktree for a branch asked for, in a directory asked for: the branch checked out there, to work on beside this one.

15.14.2 Bisect: finding the commit that broke something

Suppose the website looked right last month and looks wrong today, and fifty commits lie between. Bisect finds the one at fault by halving. B B asks for a commit that is bad and one that was good. Git checks out a commit in the middle. You look, and say B g for good or B b for bad, and git halves again. After about six answers it names the commit. B r ends the search and returns you to where you were. If a command can tell good from bad, the full menu's B x lets it answer for you.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does

noneM-x git-bisect-goodgit-bisect-goodSay the commit checked out has not the fault: git tries one after it.

noneM-x git-bisect-resetgit-bisect-resetStop looking: HEAD goes back to where it was when the bisection began.

15.14.3 Ignoring files

Some files do not belong in the history: backups, files a program makes as it runs, anything private. The ignore menu, i, adds a file or a pattern such as *.bak to the list of what git leaves alone. i t writes it in the .gitignore file at the top of the repository, which is shared with everyone who has the repository. i p keeps the rule on your computer only. The full menu's i s writes it in the .gitignore of the current directory. Ignored files are listed in the last section of the status.

15.14.4 Notes on commits

A note is a remark attached to a commit after the fact, without changing the commit. T T writes one, for the commit on the cursor's line or one you name.

15.14.5 Patches and bundles

A patch is a commit written out as a file, to send to someone by mail or on a stick. In the patch menu, W c writes commits as patch files and W a applies a patch file to your files. The full menu's W s saves your uncommitted changes as a patch. The menu under w takes patch files in as commits, with their authors and messages: w w starts, and w c and w a go on or stop when one does not fit.

A bundle is a whole repository in a single file, for carrying to a computer that has no network. W b writes one and W v checks one, both in the full menu.

15.14.6 Repositories inside repositories

A submodule is another repository kept in a directory of yours at one exact commit, such as a theme that your website uses and someone else maintains. o opens its menu: o a adds one, and o u checks them all out after you have cloned a repository that has some.

A subtree also brings another repository into a directory, but copies its files into your own history, so that people who clone yours need nothing extra. O opens its menu.

A sparse checkout goes the other way. It shows only some directories of a large repository in your files and leaves the rest in the history. > opens its menu: > s chooses the directories and > d brings everything back.

15.14.7 Any git command

For anything the menus do not have, ! in the status asks for the words you would type after git in a terminal, such as log --oneline -5, runs git with them in the repository and shows what it printed. No shell is involved, so the words go to git exactly as you type them.

Git is one of several things that work on files and text in Tuatara. The next chapter, Data, pictures and PDFs, turns to files that are not plain text.

Data, pictures and PDFs

Looking at files that are more than plain text.

Most of this manual is about text you write yourself. This chapter is about files that come from somewhere else: a table of figures saved from a spreadsheet, a photo from a camera, a form someone scanned and sent as a PDF, a Word document. Tuatara opens all of them with C-x C-f, the same key as for any file, and shows each in the way that suits it. A table gets a colour for each column. A picture and a PDF are drawn. A file that is neither text nor anything Tuatara can draw is shown as the raw numbers it is made of, in the hex view.

The chapter starts with tables of data, because those you can also change: filter, sort and tidy. Pictures, PDFs and Office documents are for looking at only. Nothing in this chapter writes to them.

One reminder about the state keys. i starts INSERT state, and C-g or ESC returns to NORMAL state. The single-letter keys in this chapter are pressed in NORMAL state. Keys that start with C-x or C-c work in both.

16.1 Delimited data: CSV and TSV

A spreadsheet program can save a sheet as plain text. Each row becomes a line, and the cells of the row are written one after another with a comma between them. That is a CSV file, for comma-separated values. A TSV file is the same with a tab between the cells. Banks, shops, membership systems and nearly every program that holds a table can write one. The character between the cells is called the separator, a line is called a record, and a cell is called a field.

Such a file is easy for a program to read and hard for a person. The fields are of different lengths, so the columns do not line up, and by the sixth comma of a long line you no longer know which column you are in. Tuatara helps in two ways. It gives each column its own colour, so that your eye can follow a column down the screen. And the mode line says which column the cursor is in.

A file whose name ends in .csv opens in CSV mode. One that ends in .tsv or .tab opens in TSV mode, which is CSV mode with the tab as the separator. For a file with another ending, M-x csv-mode or M-x tsv-mode turns the mode on by hand. Lines in these modes are never wrapped, because a record cut in two would break the columns. A long record runs off the right edge of the window, and the window scrolls sideways as the cursor moves along it.

16.1.1 Columns are counted from 0

Figure 16.1 shows the membership list of a tramping club. The cursor is on Taupo, in the second column.

The mode line says CSV, then col and the number of the column, then that column's name. The number starts at 0: the first column is col 0, the second is col 1. The name comes from the first line of the file, which Tuatara takes as the header. Wherever this chapter asks you for a column, you can answer with the name or with the number, and the number is the one the mode line shows.

There are eight colours. In a table with more than eight columns, column 8 has the colour of column 0 again, column 9 that of column 1, and so on. If you find the colours too much, M-x rotate-colouring goes on to a plainer style that colours only the separators and the quoted fields, and then to no colour at all. Chapter 13 describes these styles. To choose one for every CSV file, put (set-colouring 'csv-mode :sparse) in your init file.

A field may hold the separator itself. An address such as 12 Lake Road, Wanaka has a comma in it. Programs write such a field between double quotes, and Tuatara reads it as one field. A quoted field may even run over several lines, and the mode line still names the right column on each of them.

16.1.2 Moving in a table

There are no special keys for moving in a table. The keys of chapter 2 work as in any text: h and l move along a record, j and k move from record to record, and a search with C-s goes to a value. What changes is that you always know where you are. Watch the mode line as you move along a line, and the column number and name change each time you pass a separator.

To follow one column down a long table, turn on the highlight for the cursor's column with C-x T c, described in chapter 1. It only helps where the fields above and below are about the same width.

16.1.3 The separator

Tuatara works out the separator from the first line of the file. It counts the commas, semicolons, tabs and pipes (|) there and takes the one there are most of. Semicolons are common in files from countries that write a decimal comma. You do not have to say anything for those files to work.

Now and then the guess is wrong, or the file uses something else, such as a colon. C-c C-s asks for the separator of the buffer you are in. It offers comma, semicolon, tab, pipe, colon and space by name, and detect, which makes the guess again. Any other single character can be typed as itself. The echo area then says, for example, Fields separated by semicolon, and the colours change to match.

If all your files use one separator, set *csv-separator* in your init file, for example to #\; for the semicolon. Tuatara then stops guessing.

16.1.4 The header

The first line of most CSV files names the columns. Tuatara treats it as the header: its names are shown in the mode line and offered when you are asked for a column, a filter never hides it, and a sort leaves it where it is.

In a long table the header scrolls out of sight after the first screen. C-x / L keeps it at the top of the window while the rest scrolls under it, in the same colours as the columns below. Press it again to let the header scroll away. To have every table open that way, set *list-header-lock* to t.

Some files have no header. Their first line is a record like the others, and you do not want it left out of a sort. C-x / t tells Tuatara that the first line of this buffer is a record. The mode line then shows only the column number, and columns are offered by number. Press it again to make the first line the header once more. If none of your files has a header, set *csv-header* to nil.

Try it, with a club's members

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/members.csv and press RET. Press i and type the five lines of figure 16.1, each ended with RET. Press C-g and save with C-x C-s.
  2. The fields took their colours as soon as you typed the first comma. Press M-< (modal: g g) to go to the top. The mode line says col 0 name.
  3. Press j twice, then l until the cursor is on Taupo. The mode line says col 1 town.
  4. Press C-c C-s, type semicolon and press RET. There are no semicolons in the file, so each line is now one field and has one colour.
  5. Press C-c C-s again, type detect and press RET. The echo area says Fields separated by comma and the columns are back.
  6. Press C-x / t. The echo area says the first line is a record like the rest, and the mode line shows col 1 with no name. Press C-x / t again to make it the header.

16.2 Showing only some records

A table is most useful when you can ask it a question. Which members live in Wanaka? What did the shop sell in March? Chapter 6 introduced search filters, which narrow a list to the entries that match a pattern. In a table they do one thing more: they can look at a single column. A search for 2021 in the whole line would also find a phone number that happens to hold those digits. A filter on the joined column finds only the people who joined that year.

C-x / f shows only the records that match. It asks two questions. The first is the column, and each column is offered with the value it has in the first record beside it, so you can see what it holds. The second is the pattern to look for in that column. Records that do not match are hidden. They are still in the file, and saving writes all of them.

You can name the column in several ways.

You typeThe pattern is tried on
a name, such as townThe column the header gives that name.
$1Column 1, the second one. $0 is the first.
$* or nothing at allThe whole record, as C-x / s does.

The pattern follows the rules of search in chapter 6. Small letters match capitals too, unless you type a capital yourself. Quotes around a field are taken off before the pattern is tried, so you never have to type them.

C-x / h is the opposite. It hides the records that match and shows the rest. Use it to get things out of the way, such as the cancelled orders.

While a filter is on, the mode line says by what the table is filtered and how many records are left, as in Filtered by kiwi: 12 of 1,000 records. A second filter narrows what the first left, so you can ask for Wanaka and then, of those, for 2023. C-x / l lists the filters, and d on a line there takes that one away. C-x / r takes them all away and shows the whole table. The header is shown whatever the filters say.

You can edit the records you see. A change that would reach into a hidden record is refused, so a filter never changes what you cannot see.

16.2.1 Deleting records for good

Sometimes you want a smaller file, to send someone only their own town's members. C-x / k asks the same two questions and then deletes every record that does not match, keeping the ones that do. C-x / d deletes the ones that match. Both act on the whole table, or on the lines you have selected if there is a selection. The header always stays. Each is one step for C-/ (modal: u) to undo, and nothing reaches the file until you save.

When you are not sure of a pattern, try it with C-x / f first. You see what would be kept, and nothing is lost if you got it wrong.

The same keys work in other files that hold one record on each line, such as a log. The setting *line-record-modes* names the modes that count. A log has no header until C-x / t makes its first line one, and its columns are its words, apart by spaces.

Try it, with the club's members again

  1. Open ~/members.csv from the last Try it.
  2. Press C-x / f. At the question about the column, type town and press RET. At the next question type wanaka and press RET. Only Aroha and Mere are left under the header, and the mode line says how many of the four records are shown.
  3. Press C-x / f again, answer joined and then 2023. Only Mere is left.
  4. Press C-x / l. Both filters are listed. Press q to close the list.
  5. Press C-x / r. All four members are back.
  6. Press C-x / h, answer $1 and then napier. Hemi is hidden and the other three are shown. Press C-x / r again.

16.3 Sorting a table

The sorting commands of chapter 3 know about tables. In a CSV or TSV file, M-x sort-fields asks which column to sort by, in the same way a filter asks, and then puts the records in the order of that column. Each record moves whole, and the header stays first.

sort-fields compares the values as text. That is right for names and towns. It is wrong for numbers, because as text 100 comes before 25: the comparison looks at the first character and 1 is before 2. For a column of prices, counts or years, use M-x sort-numeric-fields, which reads the number at the start of each value. A value with no number counts as 0.

Both sort from small to large. sort-fields-reverse and sort-numeric-fields-reverse sort from large to small, which is what you want for "the biggest sales first".

Like every sorting command, these act on the lines you have selected and do nothing without a selection. To sort the whole table, select it all first with C-x h. A sort is refused while a filter hides some of the lines, so press C-x / r before you sort. A sort is one step to undo with C-/ (modal: u).

Try it, with a shop's sales

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/sales.csv and press RET. Press i and type these lines, each ended with RET:

       date,item,town,price
   2026-03-02,gumboots,Motueka,89
   2026-03-02,rain jacket,Nelson,240
   2026-03-05,wool socks,Motueka,24
   2026-03-09,thermos,Takaka,55
   2026-03-11,tent pegs,Nelson,9

    Press C-g and save with C-x C-s.

  2. Press C-x h to select everything. Press M-x, type sort-fields and press RET. At the question about the column, type price and RET. The prices are now in the order 24, 240, 55, 89, 9. That is the order of text.
  3. Press C-x h again and run M-x sort-numeric-fields on price. Now the order is 9, 24, 55, 89, 240, and the header is still the first line.
  4. Press C-x h and run M-x sort-numeric-fields-reverse on price. The rain jacket is at the top.
  5. Press C-x / f, answer town and then nelson. The two sales in Nelson are shown, the dearest first. Press C-x / r to see them all again.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x sort-fieldssort-fieldsSort the lines the selection touches by one field of each, as text: fields are separated by spaces and tabs, and the prefix argument names the field (the first by default; a negative one counts from the end of the line).
noneM-x sort-fields-reversesort-fields-reverseSort the lines the selection touches by one field of each, as text, in descending order: as M-x sort-fields, the prefix argument naming the field (a negative one counting from the end of the line).
noneM-x sort-numeric-fieldssort-numeric-fieldsSort the lines the selection touches by the number at the start of one field of each (the prefix argument's, as for sort-fields): 0x and hexadecimal digits, or a number in SORT-NUMERIC-BASE, decimal by default and then with a fraction and exponent; a field without a number counts as 0.

Chapter 11 explains what happens when the table is very large. A filter or a sort of millions of records runs in the background, and you can go on working while it does.

16.4 The hex view

Every file is a row of numbers, each from 0 to 255. Such a number is called an octet, or a byte. In a text file the numbers stand for letters: 97 is a. In a photo or a program they stand for something else, and shown as letters they are nonsense. The hex view shows the numbers themselves. Hex is short for hexadecimal, a way of writing numbers with sixteen digits, 0 to 9 and then a to f, so that every octet is exactly two digits: 97 is written 61.

Few people need the hex view every day. It is there for the times you want to know what is really in a file. Is this file that will not open really a picture, or something else with a picture's name? Why do two lines that look the same compare as different? Is there something invisible at the start of the file?

M-x hex-mode shows the buffer you are in as hex, and the same command shows it as text again. Figure 16.2 shows the start of the club's membership list.

Each row shows sixteen octets. On the left is the offset: how far into the file the row starts, also in hex. In the middle are the sixteen octets. On the right are the characters they make. An octet that is not a letter, digit or sign you could print is shown as a dot. In the figure, the first octet of the second row is 0a, the end of a line, and it shows as a dot on the right.

The motion keys move by octets and rows: h and l one octet, j and k one row. The octet under the cursor is marked in both places at once, in the hex digits and in the text beside them, so you can see which character a number stands for. The mode line shows Hex, the offset of the cursor, and digits or text for the side the cursor is on. TAB moves the cursor from one side to the other. : (non-modal: M-g g) asks for an offset and goes there. Type it in decimal, or with 0x in front for hex.

Only the rows on the screen are worked out, so the hex view of a very large file opens at once.

16.4.1 Searching for octets

A text search cannot find what cannot be typed. M-x hex-search-forward asks for octets in hex, with or without spaces between them, and goes to the next place after the cursor that holds them. ff d8 ff finds the start of a JPEG photo, for example, and 25 50 44 46 finds %PDF, the first four octets of a PDF. The echo area says where it was found, in hex and in decimal. M-x hex-search-backward looks before the cursor.

16.4.2 Changing octets

The hex view can change a file, one octet over another. In INSERT state, with the cursor on the hex side, typing hex digits writes over the octets there. With the cursor on the text side, typing writes characters over them. M-x hex-set-byte asks for one octet in hex and writes it at the cursor, then moves on.

The size of the file never changes in the hex view. The keys that would add or remove text say so and do nothing, because one octet too many would shift everything after it. As always, nothing reaches the file until you save.

A buffer that is narrowed (chapter 7) is not shown in hex. Widen it first with C-x x w.

16.4.3 Files that open in hex by themselves

Tuatara looks at the start of every file it opens. If it finds an octet with the value 0 in the first 64 KB, the file is not text. Programs, archives and disk images have such octets and text does not. A file like that opens in the hex view straight away, where showing it as text would fill the screen with rubbish. If you would sooner see such files as text, set *hex-view-binary-files* to nil.

Try it, with the club's members once more

  1. Open ~/members.csv and press M-< to go to the top. Press M-x, type hex-mode and press RET. The echo area says Hex view on, and the screen looks like figure 16.2.
  2. Press l four times. The cursor is on 2c, and the comma on the right is marked with it. The mode line shows the offset 0x00000004.
  3. Press TAB. The cursor is now on the comma in the text. Press TAB again to go back to the digits.
  4. Press M-x, type hex-search-forward and press RET. Type 57 61 6e 61 6b 61, which spells Wanaka, and press RET. The echo area says Found at 0x1d (29).
  5. Press : (non-modal: M-g g), type 0 and press RET to go back to the start.
  6. Run M-x hex-mode again. The echo area says Hex view off and the table is back in its colours.

16.5 Pictures

Open a picture with C-x C-f and Tuatara draws it. It knows the common kinds, among them PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, TIFF, HEIF and AVIF, and the newer JPEG 2000 and JPEG XL. It tells the kind from what is in the file. A photo that someone named beach.txt is still shown as a photo.

The picture is drawn as large as the window allows and never larger than it really is. A line above it says what it is and how many pixels wide and high. The buffer is read-only and has nothing to save. q closes it.

This is for a quick look: is this the photo I meant, what is on this scan, which of these twelve files is the one with the lake. For more than a look, O hands the picture to the program your desktop uses for pictures, as chapter 9 describes. Chapter 10 shows how a directory listing can preview each picture as you move down the list, which is the fast way through a directory of photos.

Drawing happens in the background. A large photo takes a moment, and in that moment you can go on to something else. The mode line shows that work is going on, and C-x j lists it as Drawing with the file's name. Killing the buffer stops the drawing.

An Org note can show the pictures it links to among its lines, each drawn the same way; chapter 14 describes it under links.

The program that turns the file into a picture runs shut in a sandbox, where it can reach neither the network nor your other files. A picture from a stranger can therefore be looked at without worry. Chapter 12 explains the sandbox.

16.5.1 Pictures in a terminal

In its own window Tuatara always shows pictures. In a terminal it depends on the terminal. Some terminals, such as kitty and Ghostty, can draw pictures, and Tuatara asks the terminal when it starts. The setting *tui-pictures* is :auto as standard, which means "show them where the terminal says it can". Set it to t if your terminal can draw but does not say so, or to nil to have no pictures. Inside tmux or screen, :auto shows none.

Where pictures cannot be shown, a picture opens in the hex view, as the last section of this chapter describes.

16.5.2 Very large pictures

Before it draws anything, Tuatara reads the size the file claims to have and works out how much memory the drawing needs. A picture that needs more than *picture-memory* is not drawn, and the line above says how large it is and what it would take. The standard is 4 GB, enough for a photo of about 85 million pixels. This guards against a small file that claims to be an enormous picture.

Try it, with a holiday photo

  1. Find a photo on your computer, such as one from your phone. This example calls it ~/Pictures/beach.jpg.
  2. Press C-x C-f, type the photo's name and press RET. The photo is drawn. The line above it says it is a JPEG image and gives its size.
  3. Press C-x 3 to split the window. The photo is drawn in both windows, in each as large as fits. Press C-x 1 (modal: F) to go back to one window.
  4. Press M-x, type show-file-metadata and press RET. A new buffer says what the photo keeps of itself: the camera, the time it was taken and, if the camera stored it, the place. Press q to close it.
  5. Press q to close the photo.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneO, C-c Oopen-externallyOpen the file shown, in the desktop's own program for its kind (xdg-open), or the one OPEN-EXTERNALLY-PROGRAMS gives its Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) type, for what Tuatara does not do: printing, forms, playing.

16.6 PDFs

A PDF is a document fixed on its pages: a bank statement, a manual, a form from the council. Open one with C-x C-f and Tuatara shows its pages as they would print. You can turn the pages, make them larger, search the text, and copy from it. You cannot change a PDF or fill in a form in it. For that, O opens it in your desktop's PDF program.

The mode line says PDF, the page you are on and how many there are, and how the page is fitted, as in Page 1 of 2, fit page. Like pictures, the pages are drawn in the background by a program shut in the sandbox. Each page is drawn as other PDF programs show it, trimmed to the part the PDF says is to be seen. The pages near the one you are reading are drawn ahead, so turning a page is quick. q closes the PDF. When you open the same PDF another day, it opens at the page and zoom where you left it.

16.6.1 Turning pages

l goes to the next page and h to the one before, and so do PageDown and PageUp (written <next> and <prior> in the tables). g h goes to the first page and g l to the last. g p asks for a page number and goes there, which is the quick way to page 212 of a manual.

j and k scroll down and up within a page. At the bottom of a page, j goes on to the top of the next, so you can read a whole document with one key. When the whole page fits in the window there is nothing to scroll, and j and k turn a page at a time. The mouse wheel does the same as j and k. g g shows the top of the page and g e its end.

16.6.2 Zoom

A PDF opens with each page fitted whole into the window. That is good for seeing the layout and often too small to read. w fits the width of the page to the window. The text is then as large as it can be without scrolling sideways, and you read down the page with j. p fits the whole page again.

= or + makes the page larger, by a quarter each time, and - makes it smaller. The echo area says the zoom, such as Zoom: 125%. 0 goes back to the fit you chose with p or w. When a page is wider than the window, H and L scroll it left and right.

d shows the pages dark: the white of the paper becomes the background colour of your theme and the black of the text becomes its text colour. It is easier on the eyes at night. It holds for every PDF until you press d again or leave Tuatara. To have it always, set *pdf-view-dark-pages* to t.

16.6.3 Searching, and the text of a PDF

C-s asks for text and searches the PDF from the page you are on. It turns to the page where the text is found, and the echo area shows the page number and the line. C-s and then RET with nothing typed finds the next place. As in every search, small letters match capitals too.

T switches from the pages to the text of the PDF, as plain text in the same buffer, with a line marking where each page starts. There the keys move as in any text. You can search it in every way chapter 6 describes, select a paragraph and copy it with the keys of chapter 4. T goes back to the pages, at the page the cursor was on. PageDown, PageUp and g p go by pages in the text too.

A scanned PDF is a special case. A scanner makes a photo of each page, and a photo of words holds no text. Such a PDF shows its pages like any other, but a search finds nothing and T shows a single line saying that there is no text in it.

16.6.4 What the PDF says of itself, and files inside it

i shows what the PDF says of itself, in a help buffer: its title and author, the programs that made it, when it was made and changed, how many pages it has and their size, whether it is locked with a password, and whether it holds forms or scripts. This is useful when you wonder where a document came from. q closes the help.

A PDF can carry other files inside it, as an email carries attachments. An invoice may hold its own figures as a spreadsheet, for example. a lists the files embedded in the PDF in a buffer beside it. There, n and p move from one to the next, and RET or s saves the one on the line. Tuatara asks where to put it and writes it there as it is. It never opens or runs an embedded file. If the PDF has none, the echo area says so.

To see the raw octets of a PDF, run M-x hex-mode in its pages.

16.6.5 The LaTeX line of a page

For a PDF you made from a LaTeX or Org file with Tuatara, C-c C-v opens that file in the other window at the line that made the part of the page you see. A double click on the page goes to the line of the point you clicked. Chapter 14, "From a line to the PDF and back", says how the two ways work together.

Try it, with a scanned form

  1. Find a PDF of a few pages. A form you scanned is a good one, such as an enrolment form for a school in Timaru. This example calls it ~/Documents/form.pdf.
  2. Press C-x C-f, type its name and press RET. The first page is shown whole, and the mode line ends with Page 1 of and the number of pages.
  3. Press l to go to page 2, then g p, type 1 and press RET to go back.
  4. Press w. The page is now as wide as the window. Press j a few times to read down it.
  5. Press = twice. The echo area says Zoom: 125% and then Zoom: 156%. Press L and H to move across the page. Press 0 and then p to see the whole page again.
  6. Press T. If the form was scanned, a line says there is no text in it. If it was made on a computer, you see its text. Press T to go back to the pages.
  7. Press i to read what the PDF says of itself. A scan often names the scanner as the program that made it. Press q to close the help.
  8. Press a. Most forms have no embedded files, and the echo area says so.
  9. Press q to close the PDF.

16.6.6 Commands and settings for PDFs

16.7 Office documents

Word documents, Excel workbooks and PowerPoint presentations open with C-x C-f too, and so do the OpenDocument files that LibreOffice writes. Tuatara shows them in one of two ways.

If LibreOffice is installed, Tuatara has it draw the pages of the document, shut in the sandbox, and shows them as it shows a PDF. Every key of the PDF section works: l and h turn pages, w fits the width, C-s searches. You see the document as it would print, with its fonts, tables and pictures.

T switches to the document read as text. Tuatara reads the file itself and writes what it finds as an outline: the headings of a Word document, the sheets and cells of a workbook, the slides of a presentation. That is the view for copying a paragraph out, or for searching a workbook for a number. It is read-only. T there goes back to the pages.

Without LibreOffice, the document opens as text straight away, and the echo area says why. You can ask for that always by setting *office-view-pages* to nil, which also means LibreOffice is never run. The older kinds of Office file, from before 2007 (.doc, .xls, .ppt), can only be shown as pages. Without LibreOffice they open as raw octets.

Either way, the document is never changed, and nothing in it is run. Macros stay asleep, and links to the internet are not followed. To edit the document, O opens it in your desktop's program. If that program offers to run the document's macros, say no unless you trust where the file came from.

Two settings keep a document read as text within bounds. A small Office file can stand for a great deal of text. Reading stops at *office-note-size-limit* characters and the text says that the rest is left out. A single cell or formula longer than *office-value-length-limit* characters is cut short and ends in ....

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x office-view-pagesoffice-view-pagesShow the pages of the Office document read as text here, in its place.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*office-view-pages*tt, nilWhether a Word document, an Excel workbook or a PowerPoint presentation (and the older and OpenDocument kinds of them) opens as its pages.
*office-note-size-limit*16777216a whole number, 1 or moreThe most characters a note read from an office file may have.
*office-value-length-limit*2000a whole number, 1 or moreThe most characters of one value an office file's note shows.

16.8 What a file says of itself

Many files carry facts about themselves that you do not see when you look at them. A photo records the camera, the time and often the place where it was taken. A Word document records who wrote it and who saved it last. A PDF records the program that made it. These facts are called metadata.

M-x show-file-metadata shows them in a buffer of their own, which q closes. It works on the file of the buffer you are in, and on the picture or PDF you are looking at. In a directory listing the key is g i, and it reports on the file the cursor is on. With C-u before it, it asks for a file.

The report has two parts. The first is what your computer knows about the file: where it is, what kind of file its contents say it is, its size, who owns it, when it was last changed, and its SHA-256 sum, a long number that is the same for two files only when they are the same octet for octet. The second part is what the file keeps inside itself. What is there depends on the kind of file:

  • a photo: the camera and its settings, the times, the place if it was stored, and whether a small preview picture is kept inside;
  • a PDF: the title, the author, the programs that made it, the dates, and how many times it was saved;
  • a Word, Excel or PowerPoint file: the author, the last person to save it, and the dates;
  • a sound or video file: its tags, such as the title and artist, and its times;
  • an encrypted file: which keys it was encrypted for.

There are everyday reasons to look. Before you put a photo of your house on the internet, check whether it carries the place it was taken. Before you send a document to a customer, check whose name is in it as the author. When two dates disagree, the file's own record of when it was made is often the one to trust over the date in a directory listing, which changes each time the file is copied.

The file is read in the background by Tuatara alone. Nothing in it is run, and the time your computer keeps for when the file was last read is left as it was.

For an encrypted file, the report can also say whose the keys are, by looking them up in your own keyring. That runs the gpg program, so Tuatara asks first. The setting *metadata-look-up-key-owners* says whether it asks every time (:ask, the standard), always looks them up (t) or never does (nil). The file itself is never handed to gpg.

Try it, with the holiday photo and the members

  1. Open ~/members.csv. Press M-x, type show-file-metadata and press RET. A buffer opens with the file's path, kind, size, owner and times. A plain text file keeps nothing more of itself. Press q.
  2. Press C-x C-f, type ~/Pictures/ and press RET to list the directory with your photo in it. Move to the photo with j.
  3. Press g i. The report now has a second part, with what the camera wrote into the photo. Look for the time and for a position.
  4. Press q to close the report, and q again to close the directory.
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneg ishow-file-metadataShow what the file shown is and what it says of itself, in a buffer of its own, which q closes: the file the buffer visits, the entry on the line in a list of a directory, the PDF or picture in its view; with C-u, or where there is none, asked for.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*metadata-look-up-key-owners*:askt, :ask, nilWhether M-x show-file-metadata looks up, in your own GnuPG keyring, whose the keys an encrypted file is for are.

16.9 When a file cannot be drawn

Things go wrong with files. A download stops halfway and leaves half a picture. A file has the name of one kind and the contents of another. A terminal cannot draw pictures. In each case Tuatara tells you what happened in the echo area and shows you what it can.

What you openedWhat you get
A picture that is damaged or too largeIts octets in the hex view.
A picture, where pictures cannot be shownIts octets in the hex view.
A PDF whose pages cannot be drawnIts text.
A PDF, where pictures cannot be shownIts text.
An Office document, without LibreOfficeIts text, or for the kinds from before 2007 its octets.
Any other file that is not textIts octets in the hex view.

When a file falls back to the hex view, it is opened safely, as chapter 12 describes: read-only, with nothing in it acted on. The echo area gives the reason and ends with its octets, opened safely.

The hex view is the right place to land, because it never fails. Every file can be shown as its octets, and the first few often tell you what the file really is. A file that starts with %PDF is a PDF whatever its name says. One that starts with PK is a zip archive, or a Word document, which is a zip archive inside. One whose first row is all zeros is probably a download that never finished. From there M-x show-file-metadata tells you what kind of file the contents say it is, and M-x hex-search-forward finds what you are looking for inside it.

The terminal

A shell inside the editor, with its output kept as text you can search and copy.

Sooner or later you want to run a command while you are writing: check what is in a directory, rename a batch of files, run a script, look at what a program is doing. You can switch to another window on your desktop and back. Tuatara offers another way. M-x terminal runs your shell in a buffer, so the shell sits next to your text and what it prints can be read, searched and copied like any other text.

This chapter shows how to open a terminal and where it appears, how typing there differs from typing in a file, how to look back through what a program printed, how to paste, how to use links and pictures, and what to do with a program that wants a key Tuatara would keep for itself. The last part is about the other direction: Tuatara running inside a terminal, which is how many people start it, and what that changes for you.

A word on names. A shell is the program that reads the commands you type (ls, cd, grep) and runs them. It is bash unless you use another. A terminal in this chapter is a buffer that shows a shell, or any other program, running on a screen of its own. The first part of the chapter is about that. The last part is about the terminal your own desktop gives you, in which Tuatara itself can run.

The state keys from chapter 1 apply as always, with one twist. In a terminal you are typing into a program, so most keys do not mean what they mean in a file. The sections below say which do.

17.1 Opening a terminal

M-x terminal opens one. It starts your shell in the directory of the buffer you came from, in a window across the bottom of the screen, about a third of the screen high. If you were looking at ~/letters/council.txt, the shell starts in ~/letters/. Type ls and you see your letters.

Each M-x terminal opens another terminal, with a name of its own: *terminal*, *terminal*<2>, and so on. When the program ends, for example when you type exit, the buffer and its window go with it. Killing the buffer with C-x k ends the program too, without asking.

A terminal opened from a file you opened safely (chapter 12), or from a directory you listed as safe or as evidence, starts in your home directory instead. The shell's prompt and its helpers then read nothing from that directory, which could hold a hostile .envrc or .git. The echo area says so when it happens.

Figure 17.1 shows the screen with a letter above and a shell below.

The lower window is the terminal. Its mode line says Terminal, and TUATARA[I] says you are in INSERT state, typing into the program. The text after Terminal is the title the shell gave its window, if it gave one (many set user@host:~/dir).

17.1.1 Where it appears

The bottom is the standard place. *terminal-place* says where terminals show: :bottom, :top, :left, :right or :full. The first four give a window along that whole side of the screen. :full uses the window you are in, and when you quit that terminal, the window shows what it showed before.

*terminal-size* is how high the window is at the top or bottom, as a fraction of the screen (0.3) or a number of rows (15). *terminal-width* is how wide it is at the left or right, as a fraction (0.5, half the screen) or a number of columns (80).

Five commands open a terminal in a place of your choosing, whatever *terminal-place* says: terminal-bottom, terminal-top, terminal-left, terminal-right and terminal-full. Use them when you want a terminal beside a long document today, and your usual place is the bottom.

By default the shell is your own: $SHELL, or /bin/sh if that is not set. *terminal-program* names another program with its arguments, for example ("bash" "-l") or ("fish").

17.1.2 Showing and hiding

You often want the terminal for a few seconds. M-x terminal-toggle is made for that. It shows the terminal you opened last and types into it. Run it again from inside the terminal and the window closes. The program goes on while it is hidden, and when you show it again, the screen is as you left it. If there is no terminal yet, it opens one.

terminal-toggle has no key to begin with. If you use a terminal often, give it one in your init file (chapter 20).

Try it, running a command while you write

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/letter.txt and press RET. Press i and type Dear Aroha,. Press C-g and save with C-x C-s.
  2. Run M-x terminal. A window opens across the bottom with a prompt.
  3. Type ls and press RET. Your files are listed, letter.txt among them.
  4. Press C-x o. You are back in the letter. The shell is still there.
  5. Run M-x terminal-toggle. The terminal is selected and you are typing into it again.
  6. Run M-x terminal-toggle once more. The window closes, and the letter has the whole screen.
  7. Run M-x terminal-toggle again. The shell comes back as it was, with your ls still on its screen.
  8. Type exit and press RET. The terminal and its window are gone.

17.2 Typing into a terminal

While you type into a terminal, every key goes to the program. That includes Escape and C-c, which a shell uses to give up on a command, and the arrow keys, which walk back through the commands you have typed. The text you type does not go into the buffer. It goes to the program, and the program prints the result.

A handful of keys stay the editor's, so that you can always leave. The setting *terminal-editor-keys* lists them. As standard they are:

ModalNon-modalWhat it does in a terminal
noneC-xThe same as everywhere: windows, buffers, files and the rest
noneM-xRun a command by name
noneC-gStop typing and look at the history (next section)
noneC-\The same as C-g, and also types into the terminal again
noneC-qSend the next key to the program, whatever it is
noneC-sSearch the terminal's history

Everything else goes to the program. If your program needs one of these keys itself, you have two ways out. C-q sends one key, once. Taking the key out of *terminal-editor-keys* frees it for good. The next sections show both.

Each key is written as you would write it for bind-key in chapter 20: "C-x", "M-x", and so on. Your init file can change the list.

Programs that fill the screen, such as less, htop and nvim, work as they do in any terminal. The mouse works too, when the program asks for it. Hold Shift while you click if you would rather the editor take the mouse.

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*terminal-editor-keys*("C-x" "M-x" "C-g" "C-\\" "C-q" "C-s")a list, each textKeys that stay the editor's while you type into a terminal (M-x terminal).

17.2.1 Sending a key the editor keeps

You are running nano in a terminal, and it uses C-x to exit. Pressing C-x would start an editor key sequence instead. Press C-q first. The echo area says Key for the program:. The next key you press goes to nano, whatever it is. C-q C-x gives nano its C-x. C-q C-g gives the program its C-g, which bash takes as "give up what you were doing" without leaving what you typed.

If a program needs C-g all the time, as another editor does, take it out of the list in your init file:

(setf *terminal-editor-keys*
      (remove "C-g" *terminal-editor-keys* :test #'string=))

C-g then goes to the program, and C-\ alone stops typing.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-qterminal-send-keySend the next key typed to the program in this terminal, whatever it is: one of those that stay the editor's (C-g, C-x, M-x, C-q), say.

17.3 The history view

A program prints more than fits on a screen. A long ls scrolls off the top. A build prints hundreds of lines. In an ordinary terminal you scroll back with the mouse. In Tuatara, press C-g or C-\. The terminal turns into its history view: everything the program printed, including what went up off its screen, shown as plain text with its colours. The program keeps running behind it. The mode line says Terminal history, and the echo area says which key types into it again.

In the history view you have the keys of any text. You can move with j, k, h and l, search with C-s and C-r, and select with V (chapter 3). You press y to copy (chapter 4). Nothing you press goes to the program, so there is no danger of typing a command by accident.

Figure 17.2 shows what you can do, with a build log as the example.

To go back to typing, press i or a, or C-\ again. RET does the same, and copies first whatever you selected, so that what you found is ready to paste.

The history keeps 100,000 lines of what went off the screen as standard. *terminal-scrollback* changes the number. A terminal that has not printed anything for ten seconds has its older history packed away in the background, a little at a time, so that a long history costs a fraction of the memory. Reading it unpacks it again without you noticing. *terminal-compress-after* sets the ten seconds, and nil turns the packing off.

If you scroll the mouse wheel up while a program that does not read the wheel is on the screen, Tuatara shows the history view for you, so that scrolling back works as you expect. A pager such as less gets the wheel as the up and down keys instead.

17.3.1 Searching the history

C-s while you type does not go to the program. It opens the history view and starts a search, back from where the program's cursor is. Look for the line you want, press RET to leave the search, and carry on in the history view. In the history view, C-s and C-r search forward and back as in any text (chapter 3).

This is the quickest way to find an error message in a long build.
