nonea, i, C-\terminal-start-typingType into the terminal again after its history view (M-x terminal-stop-typing): everything typed goes to its program, the screen shown as it is now.
noneRETterminal-copy-and-typeIn a terminal's history view, copy what is selected (as M-w) and type into the terminal again; with nothing selected, type into it again.
noneM-x terminal-searchterminal-searchSearch the terminal's whole history, from where its program's cursor is back (C-r as anywhere): typing there, its history view is shown first and the search starts once it is in; in the history view, search on from point (C-s).
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*terminal-scrollback*100000a whole number, 0 or moreHow many lines a terminal (M-x terminal) keeps that have gone up off its screen.
*terminal-compress-after*10nil, or a number, 0 or moreHow long a terminal's program has printed nothing before its scrollback is compressed, in the background, a little at a time, so that a terminal with a long history holds a fraction of the memory.

Try it, looking back through output

  1. Run M-x terminal. Type ls -l /usr/bin and press RET. Most of the list has gone off the top of the window.
  2. Press C-g. The mode line says Terminal history.
  3. Press k a few times to move up. You are reading the whole list as text, and the lines that went off the top are there.
  4. Press C-r, type bash and press RET. The cursor moves to the nearest line above with bash in it.
  5. Press V to select the line, then RET. The line is copied and you are typing into the shell again.
  6. Type echo and a space, then press C-V (Control, Shift and v). The line is pasted after echo. It is not run. Press C-u to clear the line.

17.4 Pasting

Pasting into a terminal is different from pasting into a file. What you paste goes to a program that may run it. A shell, given three lines, may run all three at once, and a line that holds a hidden command could do harm.

Tuatara pastes carefully. The text is marked as pasted, which a shell such as bash understands. It shows the lines at the prompt and runs none of them until you press RET. Control characters in the text become spaces, so that pasted text cannot send commands to the terminal itself. A program that does not mark pastes would run each line as it arrives, so Tuatara asks first when the text has more than one line.

While you type into the terminal, C-V and S-<insert> paste the text you copied last, in Tuatara or in another program. C-V is Control, Shift and v together, which is the paste key in most terminals. *terminal-paste-keys* lists the keys, and you can change it. In the history view, p and C-y paste and go back to typing. The middle mouse button pastes whatever you selected last in any program, the way it does in a desktop terminal.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
nonep, C-yterminal-pastePaste into the terminal's program the text copied last, in Tuatara or another program (as C-y takes it), and type into the terminal: marked as pasted for a program that asks, so that a shell runs none of its lines until you press RET, and its control characters made spaces, so that pasted text cannot work the terminal.
none<mouse-2>terminal-paste-primaryPaste into the terminal's program the text selected last in any program (the primary selection), as the middle button does, and type into it.

*terminal-paste-keys*("C-V" "S-<insert>")a list, each textKeys that paste into a terminal while you type there (M-x terminal-paste): the text copied last, in Tuatara or another program, marked as pasted for a program that asks (a shell then runs none of its lines until you press RET).

Try it, pasting a command from a note

  1. Open ~/notes.txt, press i and type ls -l ~. Press C-g.
  2. Put the cursor on the line, press V and y to copy it. It says Copied.
  3. Run M-x terminal. Press C-V. The command appears at the prompt. It has not run.
  4. Press RET. The shell lists your home directory.

17.5 Links

Programs print web addresses and file names. A terminal buffer shows them underlined, as :link. Press C-c C-o with the cursor on one, or hold Control and click it with the mouse. Tuatara asks before doing anything, and the question names where the link leads, because a link can show one thing and go to another.

A file on your computer opens in Tuatara, in another window. A web or mail address opens in your desktop's own program. Programs can also write links of their own (ls --hyperlink), and Tuatara follows those the same way.

The history view works the same: put the cursor on a link and press C-c C-o.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-c C-o, C-<down-mouse-1>terminal-open-linkOpen the link under the mouse (C-click) or at point in a terminal: a link a program wrote (ls –hyperlink, OSC 8) or a web or file address written there.
FaceWhat it paints
:linkLinks and URLs.

17.6 Pictures and colours from programs

A program that draws pictures with the kitty graphics protocol, such as timg or kitten icat, can draw them in a terminal buffer, if Tuatara itself can show pictures where it runs (chapter 16). In a window of your desktop it can. In a terminal it can when that terminal can, such as kitty or Ghostty. Where it cannot, such a program draws with text, as it would anywhere else.

Pictures take memory. *terminal-picture-memory* is the most a terminal keeps, 64 MiB as standard. Set it to 0 and programs always draw with text. A file meant to slow a terminal down, by drawing a picture thousands of times, has its pictures dropped when you print it with cat. The text stays.

Programs choose colours and styles, and Tuatara shows them as faces. Bold, italic, underlined, faint and reversed text have a face each, listed below. The sixteen basic colours a program may choose follow your theme, so the output of ls --color looks at home next to your text. Colours beyond those sixteen are shown as the program asked, rounded to the nearest of 4,096.

17.7 The title

Many shells set a title for their window, usually your name, the machine and the directory. Tuatara shows it in the terminal's mode line, after Terminal. It is cut at 40 columns. *terminal-title-limit* changes that, and nil hides the title. When you have several terminals open, the title tells you which is in which directory.

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*terminal-title-limit*40nil, or a whole number, 0 or moreThe most columns of a terminal's title (as the shell gives it, user@host:~/dir in many) the mode line shows.

17.8 Escape, nvim and the shell

Escape is the awkward key. A shell uses it for editing the line, and a full-screen editor such as nvim uses it all the time to leave insert mode. Tuatara, in its own state keys, may use Escape to go back to NORMAL state.

As standard, *escape-quits* is off (chapter 8), and in a terminal Escape goes to the program. In nvim, Escape does what you expect. To stop typing and look at the history, press C-g or C-\.

If you turned *escape-quits* on, Escape stops typing in a terminal, as C-g does, and the program never sees it. Two things then help. C-q followed by Escape sends one Escape to the program. And *terminal-send-escape*, set to t, gives Escape to a full-screen program (one on the alternate screen, such as nvim, less or htop) while a shell at its prompt still lets Escape stop typing. That is usually what you want with both settings on: Escape works inside nvim, and at a shell it takes you to the history. C-g stops typing in either case.

(setf *escape-quits* t
      *terminal-send-escape* t)

M-x terminal-send-escape sends Escape to the program whatever it is, at a shell prompt too. It has no key. If you want one that works while you type, add it to the list of editor keys and bind it for terminals:

(push "C-;" *terminal-editor-keys*)
(bind-key "C-;" 'terminal-send-escape :mode 'terminal)
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x terminal-send-escapeterminal-send-escapeSend Escape to the program in this terminal, at a shell's prompt too, whatever ESCAPE-QUITS and TERMINAL-SEND-ESCAPE say.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*terminal-send-escape*nilt, nilWhether Escape goes to a full-screen program in a terminal (one on the alternate screen: nvim, less, htop) even while ESCAPE-QUITS is on.

Try it, with a program like top

  1. Run M-x terminal. Type top and press RET. The screen fills with the list of programs, updating as you watch.
  2. Press C-g. Typing stops. The mode line says Terminal history, and the screen text stands still to read, while top goes on behind it.
  3. Press i. You are typing into top again and the screen is current.
  4. Press C-q, then q. The echo area asks Key for the program: and the q goes to top, which ends. You are back at the shell.

17.9 The terminal library

The terminal buffer reads what programs print with a library from Ghostty. M-x terminal-version says which version your Tuatara runs on. It is useful when you report a problem. If the library is missing, M-x terminal says so instead of opening a terminal.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x terminal-versionterminal-versionSay which version of the terminal library (libghostty-vt, from Ghostty) M-x terminal runs on.

17.10 Running Tuatara inside a terminal

Many people start Tuatara from the shell of their desktop terminal with tuatara, and edit in that window. It works the same as the window version. A few things depend on the terminal you use.

17.10.1 Keys

Old terminals cannot tell some key presses apart. Escape and the start of an Alt key both send an escape character, so a program has to wait a moment to see whether another character follows. Tab and C-i are the same byte, and so are RET and C-m.

Newer terminals, among them kitty, foot, WezTerm and Ghostty, can send keys whole, using the kitty keyboard protocol. With it, Tuatara knows that Escape is Escape, that M-x is M-x, and nothing waits 25 milliseconds. The setting *kitty-keyboard* decides whether Tuatara uses the protocol. The standard, :auto, asks the terminal when Tuatara starts and uses it if the answer is yes. Set it to t to use it always, or to nil never. You only need the setting if your terminal says it speaks the protocol but does not work with it, or the other way round.

If your terminal does not speak it, everything works, with one small delay after Escape while Tuatara waits to see what follows.

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*kitty-keyboard*:auto:auto, t, nilWhether the terminal frontend reads keys by the kitty keyboard protocol.

17.10.2 Colours and pictures

*tui-colours* says how many colours Tuatara uses. The standard, :auto, goes by what the terminal says. If the COLORTERM variable says truecolor or 24bit, your theme's colours show exactly. Otherwise Tuatara uses as many as TERM allows, and none where NO_COLOR is set. Setting it to :24-bit, 256, 16 or 8 overrides that, which helps when a terminal is wrong about itself, for instance over a remote connection that does not pass COLORTERM on.

Pictures (chapter 16) need a terminal that speaks the kitty graphics protocol. Under tmux or screen they stay off. The setting *tui-pictures* is described in chapter 16.

17.10.3 Terminal inside the terminal

You can run M-x terminal while Tuatara runs in a terminal. A shell in a terminal buffer in Tuatara in a terminal of your desktop is quite normal, and works.

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*tui-colours*:auto:auto, :24-bit, 256, 16, 8, nilHow many colours Tuatara uses in a terminal.

The daemon and other machines

One editor that keeps running, and the screens that show it.

Until now each time you started tuatara you got an editor of its own. Its buffers lived as long as it did. When you closed the terminal they were gone, unless the session setting of chapter 7 brought them back. This chapter shows another way. You start one editor with no screen of its own, and then look at it through as many screens as you like. That editor is called a daemon. It keeps running when you close a screen, so your buffers, your undo history and your searches are still there when you come back.

The same idea reaches further. The daemon can run on another computer, a server, and you can look at it from your own desk. The files, the programs and the work all stay on the server. Your computer draws the screen and sends your keys. This is not the same as opening a single file over ssh, which chapter 9 covers. There the editor runs here and only the file is far away. Here the whole editor is far away.

You will need a terminal for the commands at the start. Everything inside the editor is pressed in NORMAL state unless it starts with C-x or C-c. i starts INSERT state, and C-g or ESC returns to NORMAL state.

18.1 One editor in the background

A daemon is useful when you work on the same things all day and open and close terminals as you go. You start it once, in the morning. Each terminal you open after that shows it. Close the terminal at lunch and the editor does not notice. Open another in the afternoon and everything is as you left it.

18.1.1 The commands you type in a terminal

These are not editor commands. You type them in your shell, the program that reads what you type in a terminal.

  • tuatara --daemon starts the editor in the background and gives you your prompt back once it is ready. It reads your init file and loads your packages first, which can take a moment, and then says that the daemon runs.
  • tuatara --client shows the daemon in this terminal. With file names after it, those files are opened in the daemon. A client reads no init file of its own, because the daemon has already read yours.
  • tuatara --client --start does the same, but starts the daemon first if none is running. Many people use only this one.
  • tuatara --client --gui shows the daemon in a window of its own instead of in the terminal.
  • tuatara --stop stops the daemon. It asks about any change you have not saved, as described under "Stopping the daemon" below.

Words that mean the same as for plain tuatara work after --client too: a line number such as +40 before a file name, --safe and --hex. Chapter 12 explains the safe visit.

A client is one screen showing the daemon, with a frame of its own and buffers of its own. When you close a client, its buffers stay in the daemon. Another client can take them up. A client started while the daemon is still starting waits for it and says so.

18.1.2 Names for several daemons

You can run more than one daemon. Give each a name, made of letters, digits, - and _, at most forty characters long. A daemon with no name is called default.

tuatara --daemon=work
tuatara --client=work
tuatara --stop=work

One daemon for your work and another for your home projects keeps their buffers apart. --start goes with a name as well: tuatara --client=work --start.

18.1.3 Closing a client

C-x C-c in a client closes that client. Its screen goes, your terminal is yours again, and the daemon carries on. Buffers with changes you have not saved stay as they are, ready for the next client. To end the daemon itself, use daemon-quit or tuatara --stop.

A client also closes when its last buffer is closed. If you press C-x k on the only buffer a client has, the client ends as if you had pressed C-x C-c. The scratch buffer that every new client starts with does not count while you have typed nothing in it.

Two clients can have the same buffer, when both opened the same file. C-x k in one of them only takes the buffer from that client: its windows show another of its own buffers, and the other client keeps the buffer with any changes not saved, without a question. When the last client that has it kills it, the buffer goes, asking first about unsaved changes. A client that has ended does not count. D in the buffer list and C-x p k leave a shared buffer in the same way, while C-u C-x p k kills the project's buffers of every client. Letting go of a client's last buffer closes the client, as killing it does.

18.1.4 More than one window of a client

C-x 5 2 opens another frame of the same client, with the same buffers. In a terminal it takes turns with the first in that terminal. In a window of the desktop it is a second window. C-x 5 0 closes the frame you are in. The client ends when its last frame closes.

18.1.5 The D in the mode line

While your editor runs as a daemon, its mode line, and that of each client, shows a D after the other signs. The sign P before it is for work in the background that chapter 11 describes. The D is lit while there is a daemon and faint otherwise, and it never moves, so nothing after it jumps about. The setting *daemon-indicator* is the letter, and nil takes it away. The face :mode-line-sign is what it is drawn in.

18.1.6 Commands, settings and faces for the daemon

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x daemon-quitdaemon-quitStop the editor running in the background (tuatara –daemon), from any of its clients, asked first about every change not saved in it, the clients that ended included, group by group: s saves those of a group, l leaves them unsaved, C-g keeps the daemon running; the saves begun are waited for (C-g there keeps it running too).
noneC-x 5 2make-frameOpen another frame showing the current buffer and work in it: a window of its own on the desktop, or in a terminal a whole screen of its own shown in place of the one before, the frames taking turns on the terminal, the mode line naming the one shown (F1, F2).
noneC-x 5 0delete-frameClose the frame worked in, with its windows; its buffers stay, shown in the other frames as before.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*daemon-indicator*"D"nil, or textWhat the mode line shows for a daemon, last among its signs before [-].
FaceWhat it paints
:mode-line-signThe mode line's signs before [-] while their work goes on: P while a job of the buffer runs or waits its turn (processing-indicator), U while a directory of indexed-directories is being read (indexing-indicator), S while one is searched (searching-indicator), D while the editor runs as a daemon (daemon-indicator); in the theme's warning colour, to stand out.

18.2 Clients in the buffer list

Each client has its own buffers. C-x b offers yours, and the buffers that belong to nobody, such as *Messages*. C-x C-b shows the list of chapter 7 with a section for each client in place of the sections for projects, so you can see what each screen has open.

A buffer you open or make in a client is that client's. The buffers the daemon had before its first client came, such as its *lisp-scratch* and *org-scratch*, are every client's and stay so. You can show them in any client, and they stay in the group Every client's. Each client starts on a scratch buffer of its own instead, numbered when the name is taken (*lisp-scratch*<2>), and M-x org-scratch in a client shows its own *org-scratch*, made for it the first time.

Figure 18.1 shows the list in a client that was started at two o'clock, with one client that has already ended. The client has files of two projects open, so its directory holds a section for each.

Your own client comes first, marked This client, with the directory it was started in. Other running clients follow, folded. The clients that have ended come after them in a faint colour, the last to end first. Their buffers are still in the daemon, and the list keeps them until you take them up or kill them. The last section holds the buffers every client is offered, in one section whatever projects they are in.

Within a client's group, the buffers are in a section for each project, in the order of the list of chapter 7, each heading under the text of the client's and its buffers under the text of its own, as chapter 7 has them. A client whose buffers are all in one project, or all in none, shows them straight under its heading. TAB folds a project's section on its own. Folding the client folds its projects with it, and they come back as they were when you unfold it. D on a project's heading kills that client's buffers of the project, and the other clients keep theirs; D on the client's heading kills its whole group. C-x p k kills your client's buffers of the project you are in, and C-u C-x p k those of every client, as chapter 7 says.

On the heading of a client that has ended, RET takes its buffers up into your client. d there marks every buffer of that group for deletion, and x kills them, asking first about unsaved changes. Starting tuatara --client with no file names does the same as RET for the client that ended last. The face :list-dim is the faint colour of the ended clients.

18.2.1 The client that stays

When the last buffer of a client is closed, the client closes. That would leave a daemon with no screen to show you. So one client may stay open, left on a scratch buffer of its own, made for it when it has none. It never takes a buffer of another client or of the group Every client's. The setting *client-kept-without-buffers* says which:

ValueThe client that stays
:firstthe one opened first of those still running (standard)
:lastonly the last one left
:allevery client
nilnone; every client closes with its last buffer

The heading of the client that stays says (persistent), as in Figure 18.1. To choose another, put the cursor in that client's section of the buffer list and press K. That client stays until it ends. With :all there is nothing to choose.

The buffers of encrypted files are an exception. They close with their client, and what was copied from them goes too, so that their text does not outlive the person who opened them.

18.2.2 Commands and settings for clients

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneK, C-c Kbuffers-keep-clientMake the client whose group the cursor is in, in the buffer list, the one that stays when its last buffer is closed, in place of the one CLIENT-KEPT-WITHOUT-BUFFERS names, until it ends.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*client-kept-without-buffers*:first:first, :last, :all, nilWhich clients of a daemon stay when their last buffer is closed.
FaceWhat it paints
:list-dimWhat is of less interest in a list, set back: help buffers and the headings of clients that ended in the buffer list (C-x C-b), packages not loaded, bookmarks whose file is gone, files ignored in rimu and in a git status, a value missing in the health report (M-x check-health), a line saying more are not shown.

Try it, with one editor kept running all day

  1. In a terminal, type tuatara --client --start ~/notes.txt and press RET. The daemon starts and the file opens. The mode line shows D.
  2. Press i, type buy stamps, then C-g and C-x C-s to save. Press i and type call Hemi without saving. Press C-g.
  3. Press C-x C-c. The terminal is yours again. The editor is still running.
  4. In another terminal, type tuatara --client and press RET. Press C-x C-b. The first client is listed as ended. Put the cursor on its heading and press RET. notes.txt is here with call Hemi still in it.
  5. Press C-x C-c again when you are done. The daemon stays for tomorrow.

18.3 Stopping the daemon

M-x daemon-quit in any client, or tuatara --stop in a terminal, stops the daemon. It asks about every change you have not saved, in every buffer of every client, those of ended clients included, one group at a time. For each group you press one of three keys:

  • s saves the changes of that group.
  • l leaves them unsaved. They are lost.
  • C-g stops the question and keeps the daemon running.

The daemon ends only when the saves you chose have been written. If you press C-g while it waits, it carries on running and says that saves are still under way. Every other client is told that the daemon ends, gives its terminal back and exits.

tuatara --stop typed where there is no terminal, in a script, cannot ask. It stops the daemon only when no change would be lost. It writes unsaved changes as auto-saved copies, if the auto-save setting of chapter 7 allows it. When some change has no copy, the daemon goes on, and the message says how to stop it from a terminal. When the system itself asks the daemon to end, as at logout, there is also no one to ask. It writes its auto-saved copies first and waits up to thirty seconds for saves already begun.

A daemon told to stop always ends. If it has not ended in 60 seconds, or in 90 when there was no terminal to ask, the daemon is ended all the same, so that a new daemon of that name can start. Before it goes, it writes in its log (~/.cache/tuatara/daemon-NAME.log) which threads were running and the calls its editor was waiting in. The log names functions only, never what they were given. Read it when a daemon seems to have stopped late.

18.4 Sessions for each client

The session setting *keep-session* of chapter 7 works for a daemon too. The daemon keeps one session file for each daemon name, written client by client, so the windows of one client are never mixed with another's. If the daemon is started again, each client's group is there as one that ended, and tuatara --client with no file names takes up the one that ended last. Files opened safely are not opened again by themselves. They wait, closed, in their group, and open safely when a client takes the group up.

Try it, with the daemon stopped and started again

  1. Add (setf *keep-session* t) to your init file and restart the daemon with tuatara --stop followed by tuatara --daemon.
  2. Type tuatara --client ~/notes.txt, then press C-x C-c. Type tuatara --stop and answer s if asked.
  3. Start the daemon again and type tuatara --client. The group of the client that ended last is taken up, and notes.txt is open.

18.5 A daemon on another machine

Suppose you have a small server called pinetree, in a cupboard in Taupo, and you keep your notes and a few projects on it. With a daemon there you open your editor from any computer and find it as you left it, with the files next to the programs that build them. Language servers, git and terminal buffers all run on pinetree. Your computer draws the screen.

18.5.1 Starting, using and stopping

Name the server before the daemon's name, with a colon between them:

tuatara --client=pinetree:
tuatara --client=aroha@pinetree.example:work
tuatara --client=pinetree: --start todo.org
tuatara --stop=pinetree:

The first shows the default daemon on pinetree. The second shows the daemon called work there, as the user aroha. The third starts a daemon on pinetree first if none runs, and opens todo.org there. The last stops it.

A name with a dot or an @ in it is taken as a server. A plain name such as --client=work is a daemon on this computer. A server named only by an alias from your ~/.ssh/config file needs a colon after it, as in pinetree:.

The files you name are the server's. A relative name such as notes.org is notes.org in your home directory on pinetree, and /etc/hosts is the file of that name there.

18.5.2 What has to be in place

The connection is made by the ssh program of your system, as if you had typed ssh pinetree, with your keys and your ~/.ssh/config. If ssh needs a passphrase it asks in your terminal first. You need to have connected to the server once before, and checked its host key, because a host whose key is not known is refused. You also need setpriv, a small program from the util-linux package, which ties the connection to the client so that it ends when the client does, even if the client is killed.

On the server you need the same build of Tuatara. If it is older, or not there, the client tells you and exits. If Tuatara is not on the server's PATH, name it in M-x server-list with T, as shown below.

The server has to run OpenSSH. A daemon takes a client from another machine only when OpenSSH's own server carries the connection. It refuses a connection through any other ssh server. The daemon must run under an ordinary account, directly on the server, not as root and not in a container.

If the server removes your runtime directory when you log out, the daemon's socket goes with it. --start says so. On a server run by systemd, the command loginctl enable-linger keeps the directory.

18.5.3 Keys limited with command=

An entry in the server's authorized_keys file may be limited with a command= setting. That does not stop the key from forwarding a connection to the daemon's socket. If you give such a key to someone, add restrict or no-port-forwarding to the same entry.

18.5.4 What a server is given

A server you have not trusted gets the keys you type, the size of your screen and the names of the files you open. Nothing else of your computer reaches it. Pictures are drawn on the server and sent to your window as small pictures of the size shown, so a page of a large scan does not cross the network whole. Whatever your ~/.ssh/config says, ssh is told not to forward X11, Kerberos tickets, or an agent, and not to run local or remote commands.

A client closes with C-x C-c and leaves the daemon on pinetree running. A client that is killed, or whose terminal is closed, takes its ssh connection with it.

18.6 The trusted servers

Some things are useful across the connection: the clipboard, your keys for signing, files dropped on the window. Each is off until you trust a server with it. M-x server-list shows the trusted servers in a buffer called *Servers*, a line for each. A server not on the list is given nothing.

M-x server-trust adds a machine, written as --client takes it. Note that pinetree.example and aroha@pinetree.example are two entries. A new entry has nothing turned on. Each thing is then turned on by a key on its line, after Tuatara asks and says what the server will be given. Turning a thing off asks nothing.

18.6.1 The columns

 M Server            Agent Keys used for  GPG Clipboard Dropped files to Trusted
   aroha@pinetree    yes   github.com     no  yes       Dropped          2026-11-04
   napier.example    no                   no  no        no               2026-11-06
ColumnWhat it says
MA mark (> or D) put on the line.
ServerThe machine, as --client names it.
AgentWhether your ssh agent is forwarded there.
Keys used forThe machines the agent's keys may be used for from there; any when none is named.
GPGWhether gpg-agent is forwarded there.
ClipboardWhether the clipboard is shared with it.
Dropped files toThe directory there that dropped files are sent to, or no.
TrustedThe day you trusted the machine.
Tuatara thereThe program to run there, if not the one on its PATH.

18.6.2 The keys of the list

Each key acts on the servers marked with m, or on the line the cursor is on when none is marked.

ModalNon-modalWhat it does
none+trust another machine, with nothing turned on
noneAforward the ssh agent, or stop
noneHname the machines the agent's keys may be used for from there
noneGforward gpg-agent, or stop
noneCshare the clipboard, or stop
noneFsend dropped files to a directory there, or stop
noneTname the tuatara to run there
noneDforget the server, after asking

The list is kept in a file named ssh-servers in Tuatara's state directory. A line it cannot read gives its server nothing.

18.6.3 The ssh agent

An ssh agent holds your private keys and signs for you, so a program that needs to log in somewhere does not have to ask for your passphrase. With A on for a server, the programs there, git for example, can sign with your keys while a client shows that daemon. Tuatara does not hand over the agent you keep your keys in. The client starts an agent of its own for this connection and puts in it only the keys your ssh configuration names for that server. Each key is added so that every use of it brings up a question on your screen, and nothing is signed until you say yes. If there is no program to ask the question, the client says so and does not connect.

H limits where the keys may be used from the server. With github.com named, the server can use them for github.com and nothing else. Write the names as they appear in your known_hosts file. This needs OpenSSH 8.9 or later on both machines. If the limit cannot be applied, the client refuses to connect. To forward the agent with no limit, name no machine.

The agent reaches only the programs of that client's frames. Another client of the same daemon sees none of it, and it ends with the connection.

18.6.4 The gpg agent

GnuPG is a program for signing and encrypting, and gpg-agent holds its keys. With G on, gpg on the server signs and decrypts with your keys, which stay on your computer. The passphrase is asked here. The forwarded socket cannot export or change your keys, so nothing on the server can take them. While gpg-agent here keeps the passphrase, the server can use that key without asking again.

Two things need setting on the server. gpg there must not start an agent of its own, so put the line no-autostart in gpg.conf in GnuPG's directory there (gpgconf --list-dirs homedir says where it is, usually ~/.gnupg). And the ssh server should remove a leftover socket before forwarding a new one, which means adding StreamLocalBindUnlink yes to /etc/ssh/sshd_config as root. When the client cannot tell whether that is set, it says what to add.

To encrypt a file on the server to someone else, gpg there needs their public key. In the list of your keys (M-x gpg-list-keys), mark the keys with m and run M-x server-copy-keys. It asks for the trusted server and sends the public keys over ssh in the background. Nothing secret is sent.

18.6.5 The clipboard and dropped files

With C on, the clipboard goes both ways while the client's window has the keyboard. What you copy in the daemon reaches the clipboard on your computer, and the daemon may read what you copied here. Text that comes from the server loses its control characters, so that pasting it into a terminal cannot carry a hidden escape sequence. Without C, nothing of the clipboard crosses.

With F on, a file you drop onto the window showing the server's daemon is sent into a directory there, Dropped in your home directory unless you give another name. A name beginning with / is taken from the root. The file is written for you alone under a name nothing else has, and nothing in it is run. Only files are sent, at most 100 MB each.

18.6.6 A language server for a server

A language server runs where the daemon runs. If pinetree has none installed and you cannot install one, M-x server-bring-language-server copies one from your computer, in the background, to a directory of the editor's own on the server. Nothing is fetched from the internet. It must be a program for the server's kind of machine that needs nothing but the usual system libraries. M-x server-remove-language-server takes it away again.

18.6.7 Commands for the trusted servers

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x server-listserver-listList the trusted servers, the machines whose daemons a client here (tuatara –client=HOST) may give more than the keys typed and the size of the screen, each with what it is given: the ssh agent, with the machines its keys may be used for from there; gpg-agent; the clipboard; files dropped on the window, sent to a directory there.
none+, C-c +server-trustTrust a machine asked for in the minibuffer, as tuatara –client= names it (build.example, me@build.example, or an alias of ~/.ssh/config): it goes on the list of trusted servers (M-x server-list) with nothing given yet, each thing then turned on there by itself.
noneA, C-c Aserver-toggle-agentForward your ssh agent to the server on the line, or those marked, or no longer: on, the programs there can sign with your keys while a client shows its daemon, each use asked about here, and only for the machines named by H where OpenSSH can limit them.
noneH, C-c Hserver-agent-destinationsName, in the minibuffer, the machines the keys of your ssh agent may be used for from the server on the line, or those marked, commas between them (github.com, me@git.example); none for any.
noneG, C-c Gserver-toggle-gpgForward gpg-agent to the server on the line, or those marked, or no longer: on, gpg there signs and decrypts with your keys, which stay here, and cannot export or change them.
