noneF, C-c Fserver-toggle-filesSend the files dropped on a window showing the daemon of the server on the line, or those marked, to a directory there, asked for (from the home directory there unless it begins with /), or no longer: on, a file dropped is copied there, its size checked first, and nothing of it run.
noneT, C-c Tserver-tuatara-programName, in the minibuffer, the tuatara to run on the server on the line, or those marked, when it is not the one on the PATH of the commands ssh runs there: /opt/tuatara/bin/tuatara, or a name found on that PATH; empty for the one on that PATH.
noneM-x server-bring-language-serverserver-bring-language-serverCopy a language server installed on this machine to the server on the line of the list of trusted servers, or those marked, chosen in the minibuffer among those the editor knows that are here: nothing is fetched from anywhere.
noneM-x server-remove-language-serverserver-remove-language-serverTake away a language server M-x server-bring-language-server brought to the server on the line of the list of trusted servers, or those marked, chosen in the minibuffer among those it lists there.
noneM-x server-copy-keysserver-copy-keysCopy the public keys marked in the list of GnuPG keys (M-x gpg-list-keys), or the one at the cursor, into gpg's keyring on a trusted server asked for, so that M-x gpg-encrypt-file there can encrypt to them: exported here and imported there over ssh, in the background.

Try it, with a daemon on pinetree

  1. On pinetree, over ssh, type tuatara --daemon. Then leave the ssh session. Check that you can type ssh pinetree without a surprise.
  2. On your own computer, type tuatara --client=pinetree: --start todo.org. The file opens, in the home directory on pinetree. The mode line shows D.
  3. Press C-x C-b. The client is listed with the directory it started in.
  4. Press M-x, type server-trust, press RET, type pinetree and press RET. Answer the question. Press M-x and type server-list.
  5. Put the cursor on the pinetree line and press C. Answer y. The Clipboard column now says yes. Copy a line in the daemon with M-w and paste it into a program of your own computer.
  6. Press C-x C-c. The daemon on pinetree is still running. Type tuatara --stop=pinetree: to end it.

Try it, with a key that may be used for one place only

  1. Open M-x server-list, put the cursor on a trusted server and press H.
  2. Type github.com and press RET. The Keys used for column shows it.
  3. Press A and answer y. The next client of that server forwards your agent, each use confirmed on your screen, for github.com alone.

Packages

Adding to Tuatara what not everyone needs, and keeping it up to date.

Tuatara does a lot by itself, but some things are wanted by only a few people. One person reads Outlook mailboxes, another keeps a calendar in step with a phone, another wants a different set of colours. Putting all of that in the editor would make it larger and slower for everyone. So these things are kept apart, as packages, and you add the ones you want. This chapter explains what a package is, how you name one in your init file, how Tuatara fetches and checks it, and how you update it, switch it off or get rid of it. The end of the chapter describes the packages the project publishes.

The init file is the file where you tell Tuatara how you like things. Chapter 20 covers it. Here you only add a line or two to it, which the steps show. Every key in this chapter is pressed in NORMAL state unless it starts with C-x or C-c, which work in both states.

19.1 What a package is

A package is a directory of Lisp files that adds something to Tuatara: a command, a way of opening a kind of file, a set of colours. Lisp is the language Tuatara is written in. You do not need to read it to use a package, but you can, and Tuatara offers to show it to you before it runs anything.

A package lives in one of two places. Most live in a git repository on the internet, which is a directory of files with a history of every change made to it. Tuatara fetches the version you ask for into a directory of its own. The other kind is a directory on your own disk, which suits something you wrote yourself. Tuatara calls the place a package comes from its source.

A package does three things for you that a loose file of code would not. Tuatara compiles it, which turns the Lisp into a form the computer runs fast, and it does this in the background while you go on typing. It loads the package at every start, in a few thousandths of a second, from the compiled form. And it checks who signed the version it fetched, so that a changed package does not slip in unnoticed.

19.2 Naming a package in your init file

You name a package with a line in your init file. The line says what the package is called and where it comes from:

(load-package "themes"
              :source "https://github.com/Tuatara-Editor/tuatara-themes")

load-package is the whole interface. The name comes first, in quotes, and the rest are keywords, each followed by its value. Only the keywords you need are written. Tuatara reads the init file when it starts, fetches the package the first time, and asks you about it (see "The first load" below).

If you use a source for several packages, give it a short name once with package-source, and use that name after :source:

(package-source "mine" "~/Projects/my-packages/")
(load-package "hello" :source "mine")

An address that begins with https:// or ssh, or a directory on your disk (~/ means your home directory), is accepted. An address that begins with http:// or git:// is refused, because anyone on the way could read it and change what is sent. Section "Sources that are not encrypted" says how to allow one on a network you trust.

19.2.1 The keywords

Table 19.1. What can follow the name in a load-package line.
KeywordWhat it says
:sourceWhere the package comes from: the name given with
package-source, an address, or a directory.
:versionWhich version to fetch: a tag, a branch or a commit.
Left out, or "release", it is the newest tag. With
"latest" it is the newest commit, and it is also the
one taken when the repository has no tag yet. A whole
40-character commit keeps the package at that commit.
:directory, :fileThe package's directory inside the source, and its first
file, when they are not the package's name. The directory
is NAME/, else the top of the source. The file is
NAME.lisp, else load.lisp.
:signersThe fingerprints of the keys that must have signed it.
:plain tAllows an http:// or git:// address.
:disabled tLeaves the whole line out, as if it were not there.
:if FORMLeaves the line out when FORM gives nil. It is how
one init file serves two machines.
:defer tLoads the package once Tuatara has started, not while
the init file is read.
:after "other"Loads it only after the package or group other has.
:commandsLoads it when one of these commands is first run.
:modesLoads it when a buffer first takes one of these modes.
:init, :configForms run before the package loads, and after it. Its
settings and keys go after :config.

A form is a piece of Lisp in brackets, such as (setf *garamond-mode-line* nil). :config takes any number of them, one after another. This is the place for a package's settings, since they exist only once the package has loaded:

(load-package "garamond"
              :source "https://github.com/Tuatara-Editor/tuatara-garamond"
              :config
              (setf *garamond-mode-line* nil))

:defer, :after, :commands and :modes are for starting quickly. A package you use once a week does not have to be ready at the first frame. With :commands or :modes it waits until you ask for it. Even then you do not have to remember to load it: running one of its commands loads it first.

load-package with no :source loads nothing. It groups settings and keys under a name, the way the starter init file does for "keys" and "looks". Tuatara also corrects a misspelt name: a name a letter or two away from a package it knows is an error that names the one it thinks you meant.

19.2.2 The first load

The first time Tuatara meets a package it fetches it, in the background, and asks before it compiles and loads it:

Compile and load the package themes? (y, n or v)

Below the question it shows where the package comes from, who signed it and with which key, when it is signed, and what each answer does. You answer with one key, with no RET. y goes on. n leaves the package unloaded, and Tuatara asks again at the next start. v lists the package's directory so that you can read its source first, opened safely so that nothing in it runs. C-g means "not now" and also asks again next time. Any other key puts Answer y, n or v. before the question and asks again. Keys you typed before the question appeared are thrown away, so a key meant for your text can never answer it.

After y the compiling happens in a second copy of Tuatara that has no window and runs apart from your editor. You can keep working. C-x j lists the job and C-x J stops it. When it is done, the package loads in one step, between two of your commands, so no command ever runs with a package half loaded.

If you trust your sources and want no question, set *package-ask-before-loading* to nil.

19.3 The package manager

M-x package-manager shows the packages your init file loads from a source, one line each, in a buffer called *Packages*. It works as the buffer list of chapter 7 does: you move over the lines, mark some, and act on the marked ones.

The columns are the mark, the name, the version (directory for a directory of your disk), the first letters of the commit, what became of the package this session, who signs its source's versions, and the source. The state is one of loaded, fetching, failed, refused, declined, kept, unloaded, removed and not fetched. A package that is not loaded is drawn in the faint colour, as in the figure. declined means you said no at the question. refused means its code uses a name this Tuatara does not have, because the package is newer than your Tuatara or a newer Tuatara renamed something. A refused package is never run, and the reason shows beside the list where the README would be. The README of the package under the cursor shows beside the list, or below it when the window is narrow. P turns it off and on.

The keys are those of the lists you already know, with a few of its own.

Table 19.2. Keys in the package manager.
ModalNon-modalWhat it does
noneRET, lLists the package's directory, to read its source.
noneoThe same, in another window.
nonen, pGo to the next package, and the one before.
nonem, u, U, tMark, unmark, unmark all, swap the marks.
nonefFetches the marked packages again (see "Updating").
noneLLoads the marked ones.
noneKUnloads the marked ones from the running editor.
noneRRemoves them: unloads them and keeps them from loading.
noned, then xMarks for deletion, then deletes what is kept of them.
noneDDeletes what is kept of the marked ones.
noneh, qCloses the list.

With nothing marked, each of these acts on the package on the cursor's line.

M-x package-scan reads your init file again for load-package lines that have a :source, loads each package that is not loaded, as at a start, and then shows the package manager. It is what you run after adding a line to the init file, when you do not want to restart Tuatara.

Try it, adding the themes package

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/.config/tuatara/init.lisp and press RET. This is your init file.
  2. Press g then e to go to the end. Press o to open a new line and type: (load-package "themes" :source "https://github.com/Tuatara-Editor/tuatara-themes")
  3. Press C-g and then C-x C-s to save.
  4. Run M-x package-scan. *Packages* opens with a line for themes. In a moment the question appears. Press v to look at the source, then q to come back, and answer y. If the line says failed and the echo row says the package is refused because of a signer, your keyring lacks the key that signed it. Import it as described under "Signatures and trust", run M-x package-update and try again.
  5. The echo row says the package is compiled and loaded. The line in the list now says loaded.
  6. Run M-x load-theme. The list now includes fourteen more themes. Choose nord and press RET. The colours change at once.

19.3.1 Commands of the package manager

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x package-managerpackage-managerManage the packages the init file loads from a source (load-package with :source) in a list, as the buffer list (C-x C-b) manages buffers.
noneM-x package-scanpackage-scanLook in the init file for the packages it loads from a source (each load-package with :source), and load each that is not loaded or on its way, as at the start: fetched in the background, asked about before it is compiled, loaded.

19.4 Updating

A package fetched from a repository keeps the version you first took. When its author publishes a newer one, M-x package-update looks again. It asks each repository for the version the load-package line wants (the newest tag, the newest commit, or the tag, branch or commit you named), fetches what is new in the background and, when it is a different commit from the one you have, asks the question of the first load again. Packages that are already up to date are said to be so. When several were fetched, the echo row says once they are all done, and names any that are not loaded. Directories of your own disk are left alone, since you change those yourself.

M-x package-update-marked, or f in the package manager, does the same for only the packages you marked, or for the one on the line.

A package can say, in a comment at the top of its first file, the oldest Tuatara it works with: ;;;; Needs: Tuatara 0.91.0. Tuatara reads that line without running anything. If the newest version needs a newer Tuatara than yours, Tuatara looks back through the earlier versions for the newest that fits, says which one it took, and loads that. If none fits, the version you have stays. A package that says nothing loads in any Tuatara.

Tuatara keeps the version it took and the one before it, each with its compiled files. When a new version fails to load, because it cannot be compiled or uses a name your Tuatara lacks, the one before it is loaded in its place, and a message tells you so once.

Try it, updating everything

  1. Run M-x package-update. The echo row says it is fetching.
  2. Press C-x j to see the job. When it finishes, packages with nothing new are said to be up to date.
  3. If a package has a new commit, the question of the first load appears for it. Press v to read what changed, q to come back, then y.
  4. Open M-x package-manager. The Version and Commit columns show what you have now.
  5. To update only some: press m on two packages, then f. Only those two are fetched again.

19.4.1 Commands for updating

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x package-updatepackage-updateFetch again each package load-package fetched (not the directories of your disk), in the background.
nonef, C-c fpackage-update-markedFetch again the marked packages (>), or with none marked the one on the current line, as M-x package-update does them all.

19.5 Signatures and trust

Code you load runs with all your rights. That is true of any editor's extensions. So Tuatara asks who signed each version, as one way of noticing when something has changed hands.

The author signs a tag or a commit with a key, using GPG or SSH. Tuatara asks git who signed the one it fetched. Git does the checking, with gpg and your keyring for a GPG signature and with ssh-keygen for an SSH one, and nothing in the repository is run to do it. The question at the first load says who signed the version, and your y makes that signer the one Tuatara remembers for the source. The memory is kept in a file called package-trust beside the packages, which you can read. This is called trust on first use: you decide once, and Tuatara holds the source to that decision.

From then on:

  • A version signed by the same key is taken.
  • A version signed by another key, or unsigned when the versions before it were signed, or whose signature does not check out, is refused. The version you have keeps running.
  • A source whose first version was unsigned goes on having unsigned versions taken, since nobody has to sign. The first signed version makes its signer the one remembered.

A refusal says what changed:

The package tally from https://example.org/tally.git is refused: unsigned,
and the versions taken before were signed by Ann Author (key SHA256:...).
The version loaded now is kept; M-x package-trust-again trusts its source
anew, as the first time

Sometimes the change is honest: the author has a new key, or moved the project. Then you decide, as at the first time. M-x package-trust-again asks which package, forgets who signed its source, and fetches it again. The question names the new signer, and your y makes it the one remembered. Think before you press it. If you do not know why the key changed, ask the author.

A version signed with a GPG key your keyring lacks is refused, and Tuatara remembers the key's fingerprint. Import the key with M-x gpg-import-keys and run M-x package-update. Versions signed by that key, or by the key it belongs to, are then taken.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x package-trust-againpackage-trust-againTrust the source of a package asked for anew, as the first time: who signed the versions taken from it is forgotten, and the package is fetched again (M-x package-update); the version found is asked about with who signed it (PACKAGE-ASK-BEFORE-LOADING), and once it is let load, that signer is the one remembered.
noneM-x gpg-import-keysgpg-import-keysImport the keys in a file asked for (armoured or not) into your keyring; say what was imported.

19.5.1 Naming the signers yourself

If you know whose keys you want, say so, and only versions signed by them are taken, from the very first:

(package-source "mine" "https://example.org/my-packages.git"
                :signers '("SHA256:hdVZ5mzqXcO1EQf8N4u9MJvZb7TfsHkLqR2wPaXyC0s"))

An SSH key's fingerprint is what ssh-keygen -lf KEY.pub prints. A GPG key's is the 40 hexadecimal digits that gpg --fingerprint shows. A key's short ID is refused, and so is a signing subkey's fingerprint: give the key's own. load-package takes :signers as well. Names in the init file always decide for their source, and package-trust-again does not change that.

19.5.2 Sources that are not encrypted

A server inside your organisation may speak only http://. You can allow it for one package at a time:

(load-package "tally" :source "http://git.example.org/tally.git" :plain t)

Whoever controls the network between you and that server can hand you an older version of the package than the newest, one with a bug that has since been fixed. A signature does not stop that, because the old version is genuinely signed. Use :plain t only on a network you trust. The Signed by column of the package manager says unencrypted for these sources.

19.5.3 Settings

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*package-check-signatures*tt, nilWhether a package's versions are taken only when signed by a key you trust.

*package-check-signatures* is t, and you should leave it so. Setting it to nil makes every version of every source be taken, signed by anyone or by no one, and nothing is remembered. That is only for a machine whose sources are trusted some other way. M-x check-health says when signatures are not checked.

19.6 Unloading and removing

A package can be taken out of Tuatara in three steps, each going further than the one before.

M-x package-unload (K in the package manager) takes the package out of the running editor: its commands, keys, modes, settings and hooks, and any work it has in the background, which is stopped. A buffer in one of its modes is put in the mode its file calls for, so nothing you typed is lost. The package's code stays on the disk and its load-package line stays in your init file, so it loads again at the next start. Use it for a package that is misbehaving, or to try Tuatara without it for the afternoon.

M-x package-remove (R) unloads it and keeps it from loading at the next start as well, without changing your init file. Tuatara remembers in its state directory that you removed the package, passes the load-package line over at each start and says so once in *Messages*. Its code stays on the disk, so bringing it back is quick.

M-x package-delete (D, or d then x) unloads and removes it and then deletes what Tuatara keeps of it: the versions fetched and their compiled files. For a package from a directory of your own disk only the compiled files go. Your directory is never touched. It asks first, with the size of what goes:

Unload, remove and delete the package hello, 1.2 MB? (y or n, then RET)

M-x package-load (L) goes the other way. It loads a package again by its load-package line, as at the start. That works for one you unloaded, one you removed (it is then no longer removed), and one you deleted (it is fetched again). In the package manager each of these four acts on the packages you marked, or on the one on the line. Elsewhere the commands ask which package.

To stop a package for good, also take its line out of your init file, or put ;; in front of it, or add :disabled t to the line. Unloading alone does not do that. A deleted package that is still named in the init file comes back at the next start.

Try it, removing a package you no longer use

  1. Run M-x package-manager and press j (non-modal: C-n) until the cursor is on kitty.
  2. Press R. The package is unloaded and its state reads removed.
  3. Restart Tuatara and open the package manager again. kitty is still there but is not loaded and was not asked about.
  4. Press L on its line. It loads again.
  5. To free the disk space as well, press D. The question names the size. Answer y and then RET. Remove the load-package line from your init file when you are sure you are done with it.

19.6.1 Commands for unloading and removing

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneK, C-c Kpackage-unloadTake a package out of the running editor: its commands and keys, with their labels, its modes, the places it gave Tuatara's commands, its ways of showing text, its functions on Tuatara's lists of hooks and of work to do now and then, its settings and its work in the background, which is stopped.
noneR, C-c Rpackage-removeUnload a package (M-x package-unload) and take it out of the packages loaded: it is not loaded from now on, nor at the next start, though the init file names it; the init file is left as it is, and Tuatara says in Messages once a session that it passes the package over.
noneM-x package-deletepackage-deleteUnload a package (M-x package-unload), remove it from the packages loaded (M-x package-remove), and delete what Tuatara keeps of it: the versions of it fetched and their compiled files, or for a directory of your disk its compiled files alone, the directory of yours left as it is.
noneL, C-c Lpackage-loadLoad a package the init file loads from a source that is not loaded now, by its load-package there, as at the start: one unloaded (M-x package-unload), removed (M-x package-remove), whose loading failed, or one deleted, fetched again.

19.6.2 Clearing out sources no longer used

Tuatara keeps what it fetches until you say otherwise. When you rename a source or stop using one, the old copies stay in the packages directory. M-x package-remove-unused finds them: every source that no package-source names and no load-package fetches from, and every package of a source you still use that no load-package names. A load-package turned off with :disabled t, or left out by :if, still counts as used.

It lists what would go in *Help*, each with its size, and asks once. Answer n and nothing is touched. Answer y and the directories are deleted in the background. Each is looked at again just before it goes, so a source you name in the meantime stays. Only Tuatara's own packages directory is searched. A directory of your own disk named as a source is never touched. If your init file stopped at an error when Tuatara started, the command does nothing until the file reads through, since everything after the error would look unused.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x package-remove-unusedpackage-remove-unusedDelete the package sources Tuatara keeps that nothing in this session names any more: a source no package-source names and no load-package fetches from, or a package of a source no load-package names; one left out by :disabled or :if counts as named.

19.6.3 Where packages are kept

Tuatara keeps what it fetches in ~/.local/share/tuatara/packages/, or under $XDG_DATA_HOME when you have set that. *packages-directory* puts them somewhere else. It must be a directory you made yourself, and while it is missing nothing is fetched or loaded from it. *package-size-limit* is the most a package may take on the disk while it is fetched, its history and files together. A fetch that grows past it is stopped and its files deleted. The standard is 512 MiB. *package-sources* holds the sources named with package-source. Set them with that function and not by hand.

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*package-sources*nila list, each (NAME . WHERE)The places packages come from (PACKAGE-SOURCE sets them).
*packages-directory*nilnil, or a directory's nameThe directory Tuatara keeps the packages it fetches in.
*package-size-limit*536870912a whole number, 0 or moreThe most octets a package may take on disk while it is fetched, what git keeps of its history and its files together: a fetch that grows past it is ended and its files deleted.
*package-ask-before-loading*tt, nilWhether you are asked before a package is first compiled and loaded: one fetched the first time, and again when an update brings another commit; one of a directory of yours the first time only, what you change in it later being yours.

19.7 What a package needs: check-health

Some packages need a program that is not part of Tuatara. csvdt needs csvdt, outlook needs readpst, kitty needs kitty. Tuatara does not install these. It looks for them, and M-x check-health reports what it found. The report has a section for Tuatara and a section for each package that is loaded, in a buffer called *Health*. A check that passed is drawn in one colour, one that failed in another, and a value that is missing in the faint one. When a package does not work, this is the first place to look: it says that a program is not found and, for some, where to get it.

The check also tells you when signatures are not checked. It runs in the background, so the report comes when it is ready.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x check-healthcheck-healthShow what each language and major mode has here.
FaceWhat it paints
:list-goodA state that is as it should be, in a list: a check that passed in the health report (M-x check-health).
:list-badA state that is not as it should be, in a list: a check that failed in the health report (M-x check-health).
:list-dimWhat is of less interest in a list, set back: help buffers and the headings of clients that ended in the buffer list (C-x C-b), packages not loaded, bookmarks whose file is gone, files ignored in rimu and in a git status, a value missing in the health report (M-x check-health), a line saying more are not shown.

19.8 The packages the project publishes

The project's packages are not part of the editor. Each is a repository of its own, https://github.com/Tuatara-Editor/tuatara-NAME, for the name of the package. You load one with its address as the source, no package-source line needed. Each package's README, in its repository, gives the steps and the settings, and its settings show in C-h v once it is loaded. Every package puts its commands under a prefix of its own, C-c and a letter.

19.8.1 palimpsest

A PDF can be saved over and over, and each save can leave the earlier text in the file. palimpsest takes a PDF apart into every save it holds, from the original to the latest edit, and looks for the signs of editing that examiners of documents know. It reads the file's own bytes and runs nothing in it, and it never changes the file. M-x palimpsest examines the PDF you are looking at, or asks for one. The report is made in the background and lists findings with the strongest first. In the report, C-c p is the prefix for its other commands, such as saving a revision as a PDF of its own.

19.8.2 csvdt

csvdt is a separate program that converts the times and durations in CSV records. The csvdt package runs it on a CSV buffer, a selection or the lines you banked, and shows the result in *csvdt output*. The buffer the records came from is never changed. In a CSV or TSV buffer its commands are under C-c v: C-c v r runs what you chose, and C-c v ? says what a run would cover without running it. You install csvdt yourself.

19.8.3 csv-columns

csv-columns rearranges the columns of every record the way awk's print does. C-c r a asks for the columns, counted from 0, so that $0,$2,$1 swaps the second and third. It needs nothing installed. A large file is done in the background, and each run is one step to undo.

19.8.4 facematch

facematch ranks candidate photos by how probable it is that they show the person in one or more master photos. You mark photos in the directory view, then C-c f f runs the comparison, in the background and shut in Tuatara's sandbox. The comparing engine is a separate program that you download from its release page, check against the list of sums beside it, and name in *facematch-program*. Tuatara never downloads it for you.

19.8.5 garamond

Some writers put two spaces after a full stop, others one. garamond keeps the spacing a document asks for, which the document says in its own Local Variables: block. The mode line shows 2S or 1S, and typing one space after a sentence becomes two where the document wants two. M-x garamond-mode turns it on by hand. It needs nothing installed.

19.8.6 kitty

kitty opens windows of the kitty terminal, which Tuatara starts itself, so that you get its fast drawing, its ligatures and its pictures. M-x kitty opens one in the current directory. M-x kitty-input types the selection or the current line into it, and M-x kitty-text brings its text, scrollback included, into a buffer you can search. You install kitty yourself.

19.8.7 outlook

outlook opens Outlook items (.msg), saved mail (.eml) and mailboxes (.pst, .ost) as messages, read only. It was made for looking at mail as evidence: nothing in a message runs, and attachments open only when you ask, from private copies. In a message, P shows it as it looks, O opens an attachment in the desktop's own program after asking, and C-c o is the prefix for the same commands. In a mailbox, C copies messages out. It needs readpst and WeasyPrint.

19.8.8 caldav

caldav shares Tuatara's agenda with GNOME Calendar, Thunderbird and phones, through a CalDAV server (Radicale, or EteSync through its local bridge). The calendars are kept in one Org file, and only what is under a calendar's heading is synced. The password is never in your init file: it is in the desktop's keyring. In Org files and the agenda its commands are under C-c s, with C-c s s syncing now. Its README sets a server up step by step.

19.8.9 themes

themes adds fourteen colour themes, each a dark or light version of a palette you may know from other editors: catppuccin-mocha, catppuccin-latte, dracula, nord, one-dark, solarized-dark, solarized-light, tokyo-night, tokyo-night-light, rose-pine, rose-pine-dawn, everforest-dark, everforest-light and kanagawa-wave. It needs nothing installed.

M-x load-theme lists every theme, with a description beside each, and applies the one you choose. To have one at every start, put it after the package line:

(load-package "themes"
              :source "https://github.com/Tuatara-Editor/tuatara-themes")
(load-theme 'catppuccin-mocha)

M-x toggle-light-dark-theme switches between a light and a dark theme. The standard pair is Tuatara's own two, and *light-theme* and *dark-theme* name others. If the window follows the desktop's light or dark style, these two are the ones it switches between. Any set-face line in your init file stays on top of a theme.

(setf *dark-theme* 'tokyo-night
      *light-theme* 'tokyo-night-light)
ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x load-themeload-themeChoose a colour theme, with each theme's description beside it.
noneM-x toggle-light-dark-themetoggle-light-dark-themeSwitch between the light and the dark theme: the two ao variants, unless the init file sets light-theme and dark-theme to others.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*light-theme*tuatara.defaults::ao-lighta theme's nameThe light theme toggle-light-dark-theme switches to, and the one used while the desktop is light (FOLLOW-DESKTOP-STYLE).
*dark-theme*tuatara.defaults::ao-darka theme's nameThe dark theme toggle-light-dark-theme switches to, and the one used while the desktop is dark (FOLLOW-DESKTOP-STYLE).

19.9 Writing a package of your own

A package is a directory of Lisp files and can be small: one command in one file is enough. How to write one, which parts of Tuatara it may use, and how to publish it, is the subject of the developer handbook. To try a directory of your own on your disk, name it with package-source and load it as the lines near the start of this chapter show. Tuatara compiles it and asks about it like any other.

Making it your own

Changing Tuatara to suit you, and keeping the changes.

Every chapter so far has said "as standard" about something: the font, the colours, the keys, the way a journal entry is named. This chapter is about changing those. You do it with a small file of your own, called the init file, which Tuatara reads each time it starts. Nothing you put in it is ever overwritten by an update.

The chapter shows what the file is and where Tuatara keeps it, how to change a setting, how to give a key to a command, how to move or turn off the modal states, how to pick a theme and a font, and how to write snippets of your own. Two things that nothing else in the manual covers, the calendar and the journal, have a short section each. The last section holds the odds and ends that have no better home.

You do not need to know Lisp. Every change in this chapter is one line that you copy, with a word or two changed.

20.1 The init file

The init file is a plain text file called init.lisp in a directory of its own, ~/.config/tuatara/. The first time Tuatara runs and finds no file there, it writes one for you. The message Wrote a starter init file says so. After that Tuatara never writes it again. It is yours.

The starter file lists every setting there is. Each one sits in a comment (a line that starts with ;; is a comment, and Tuatara skips it), with a few words saying what the setting does and, after Not set:, what it is when you leave it alone. To use a setting you take away the ;; and the space after it. To go back to the standard, you put them back.

  ;; Two keys typed quickly one after the other in INSERT state leave it for
  ;; NORMAL state, and neither stays in the text. Not set: nil.
  ;; (setf *insert-escape-keys* "jk")

The block above is as the starter file has it. With the last line's ;; taken away, it reads (setf *insert-escape-keys* "jk") and the setting is on. Everything is in groups, each begun by a banner of equals signs. Search for three of them with C-s to jump from one group to the next.

Tuatara reads the file once, from the top, each time it starts. A change you make is therefore there the next time you start. You do not have to start again to try it. Put the cursor just after the closing bracket of the line and press C-x C-e. That runs the line in the editor you are using, and the echo area shows what it returned. The line stays in the file, so the change is still there tomorrow.

If a line in the file is wrong, say a bracket is missing or a name is misspelt, Tuatara tells you on the echo row, with the line, and goes on to read the rest. It always starts. You can open the file and mend it.

To open the file, press C-x C-f, type ~/.config/tuatara/init.lisp and press RET.

Try it, with the init file

  1. Press C-x C-f, type ~/.config/tuatara/init.lisp and press RET.
  2. Press g g (non-modal: M-<), then C-s, type fill-column and press RET. The search stops on the line ;; (setf *fill-column* 72), which has a comment above it about the column that M-q (modal: g Q) fills to.
  3. Press g h (non-modal: C-a) to go to the start of the line, then l until you are on the first ;. Press d three times to take away both semicolons and the space.
  4. Press g l (non-modal: C-e) to go to the end of the line, then C-x C-e. The echo area shows 72.
  5. Press C-h v, type *fill-column* and press RET. The help says the value is 72.
  6. Press C-x C-s to save. Starting Tuatara again keeps the 72.

20.2 Where Tuatara keeps its files

Tuatara keeps what it makes in three places, each with a different job. The division follows the standard that most programs on Linux follow, so a tool that backs up or cleans your home directory already knows about them.

  • The configuration directory, ~/.config/tuatara/, holds what you wrote or chose. This is the init file, your snippets, your note and export templates, and your logos. If you lose it you lose your choices.
  • The state directory, ~/.local/state/tuatara/, holds what Tuatara remembers about how you work: the files you opened lately, where you were in each, your bookmarks, the session, and the copies of unsaved changes. If you lose it nothing you wrote is gone, but Tuatara forgets its habits.
  • The cache directory, ~/.cache/tuatara/, holds things Tuatara can make again: previews, pages drawn from documents, copies of files opened safely, compiled packages and the log of what happened. You can delete it at any time.

Fetched packages are kept in a fourth place, ~/.local/share/tuatara/, described in chapter 19.

Figure 20.1 shows the directories and what each holds.

If your computer sets XDG_CONFIG_HOME, XDG_STATE_HOME, XDG_CACHE_HOME or XDG_DATA_HOME, Tuatara uses a directory called tuatara inside each of them instead of the ones in the figure. You can also set the directories yourself, which is useful when you keep them on an encrypted drive. The three settings below do it. Make the directory first, with mkdir -m 700, so that only you can read it. While the directory is not there, because the drive is not mounted, Tuatara keeps those things in memory and says so.

(setf *state-directory* "/run/media/aroha/Data/tuatara/state/")

*cache-directory* is the same for the cache directory. It is nil, which means ~/.cache/tuatara/ (or tuatara inside XDG_CACHE_HOME), or the name of a directory. Files you open from outside leave copies in the cache, so a cache on an encrypted drive keeps those copies off the plain disk:

(setf *cache-directory* "/run/media/aroha/Data/tuatara/cache/")

20.2.1 What to copy to another computer

To have your Tuatara on another computer, copy the configuration directory, ~/.config/tuatara/, and nothing else. It holds the init file and everything you wrote. Packages are fetched again on the new computer when the init file asks for them.

Copy the state directory as well if you want the new computer to know your recent files and bookmarks. Do not copy the cache. It is rebuilt as you work, and parts of it are only right for the computer that made them.

Paths in the init file, such as a directory for your journal, must exist on the new computer too.

20.2.2 Settings for the directories

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*state-directory*nilnil, or a directory's nameThe directory Tuatara keeps what it remembers between sessions in.
*cache-directory*nilnil, or a directory's nameThe directory Tuatara keeps its cache in.
*packages-directory*nilnil, or a directory's nameThe directory Tuatara keeps the packages it fetches in.

Try it, with the directories

  1. In a terminal, type ls ~/.config/tuatara/ ~/.local/state/tuatara/. The first list holds init.lisp. The second holds files such as bookmarks and recent-files, and the directory auto-save.
  2. In Tuatara, press C-h v, type *state-directory* and press RET. The value is NIL, which means the standard directory of the figure.

20.3 Changing a setting

A setting is a name that holds a value. Its name starts and ends with a star, *fill-column*, so that it is easy to tell from a command. You change one with setf, which means "set to":

(setf *fill-column* 72)

The line reads: set *fill-column* to 72. The value can be a number, a word in quotes, t for yes, nil for no, or a name that starts with a colon, such as :bar. The help of each setting says which it takes.

C-h v asks for a setting's name and shows its value, what it means, and where it was defined. It is the quickest way to find out what you can put after the name. M-: lets you type a line without opening the init file, which is useful to try a value out before you save it.

Some settings hold a list of things, for example the modes that do something. To add to one instead of replacing it, put your item in front of what it holds:

(push "C-;" *terminal-editor-keys*)

A few settings are better said with a function than with setf, because they take a mode and a value. The starter file has these written out, for example (set-tab-width 'c-mode 8). Keep to the form the starter file shows.

Chapter 21 lists every setting and what it is as standard.

20.4 Keys of your own

bind-key gives a key to a command. It is the main command of the init file. You give it the keys and the command's name, which is the name that C-h f and M-x show. Keys are written as the help writes them: C- is Control, M- is Meta (Alt on most keyboards) and S- is Shift. Keys that you press one after the other are separated by a space.

(bind-key "C-c t" 'toggle-light-dark-theme)

After that line, C-c t switches between the light and the dark theme in every buffer and in both states. The mark before the command's name is a single quote, and it belongs there.

Where a key goes depends on the map you name with :map. Table 20.1 lists the forms you will use. In all of them you can put any command in place of the one shown.

Table 20.1. The ways to bind a key.
FormWhat it does
(bind-key "C-c t" 'command)The key works in every buffer and both states
(bind-key "o" 'command :map :leader)SPC o in NORMAL state, and C-x SPC o everywhere
(bind-key "e" 'command :map :normal)e in NORMAL state only
(bind-key "C-c e" 'command :map 'csv-mode)The key in CSV buffers only
(bind-key "m l" 'command :map :leader :mode '(org-mode markdown-mode))SPC m l in Org and Markdown only
(bind-key "t n" '("numbers" . command) :map :leader)SPC t n, shown as "numbers" in the key hints
(bind-key "t" nil :map :leader :label "toggles")The label of a prefix: SPC then shows t +toggles
(unbind-key "C-c t")Takes a key away

Three more things about the table. First, the maps. :global is the standard, every buffer in both states. :normal, :insert and :support are the keys of the NORMAL state, the INSERT state and the buffers that Tuatara makes itself, such as lists and help. :leader is the leader, described in the next section. Other maps are named after one kind of question: :pattern, for instance, is every question that asks for a pattern to search for. A map can also be the name of a major mode, as the CSV line shows. Then the key is only there in buffers of that mode and the modes made from it.

Second, :mode is a quicker way to say the same. It takes one mode or a list. A key bound for a mode never changes what the same key does in other modes, so you can give SPC m l one meaning in Org and another in code without either getting in the other's way.

Third, labels. The key hints (chapter 8) show the name of a command beside each key. A label is a name of your own to show instead. The two ways to give one are in the table: put the label and the command together in a pair, or bind a prefix to nil and give it a label.

Which keys are free? C-h k followed by a key says what the key does now. A key with nothing bound says so. C-c followed by a letter is a good place to start, and C-c t is free as standard. The letters h j k l only ever move the cursor in NORMAL state. Do not give them another job.

Try it, with a key of your own

  1. Open the init file with C-x C-f and go to its end with g e (non-modal: M->).
  2. Press o to open a new line and type this line. (bind-key "C-c t" 'toggle-light-dark-theme)
  3. Press C-g to go back to NORMAL state, then C-x C-e. The echo area shows the name of the command.
  4. Press C-c t. The colours turn light. Press it again and they are dark again.
  5. Press C-x C-s to save. To take the key away again, put (unbind-key "C-c t") under the line, or put ;; in front of it.

20.5 A leader key of your own

The leader is a map of keys that belong to you. As Tuatara comes, nothing is under it, so there is nothing to learn that you did not put there. In NORMAL state, in lists and in the calendar, SPC opens it. C-x SPC opens it in every buffer and state, INSERT state and a session with modal editing off too, so a leader key works wherever you are.

The starter file lists, commented out, a set of leader keys that suit many people: SPC f to find a file, SPC b to go to the other buffer, SPC w for a family of window keys, and so on. Take away the ;; in front of the ones you want, or write your own with :map :leader.

(bind-key "o" 'find-file :map :leader)
(bind-key "t" nil :map :leader :label "toggles")
(bind-key "t l" 'soft-wrap-mode :map :leader)
(bind-key "t h" 'hl-line-mode :map :leader)

The four lines make SPC o open a file. They also make SPC t a prefix with the label "toggles", with SPC t l to wrap long lines and SPC t h to highlight the line the cursor is on. After you press SPC, the key hints show what is under it, so you do not have to remember.

If SPC is a key you would like for something else, move the leader.

(setf *leader-key* ",")

Now the leader is on , in NORMAL state, and SPC is free again. C-x SPC does not move. Chapter 8 lists the leader's settings with the settings for modal editing.

20.6 Modal editing, and turning it off

Tuatara comes with modal editing on. A file opens in NORMAL state, where letters are commands. i starts INSERT state, where letters are typed, and C-g goes back. Chapter 1 introduced it.

Some people would rather type at once and use the keys with Control and Meta for commands, as other editors do. If that is you, turn modal editing off:

(setf *modal-editing* nil)

Every buffer then takes the keys of its mode and the global keys. Typing puts letters in the text. The states are gone from the mode line. Every command is still there, to run with M-x or to bind to a key. The leader stays, under C-x SPC. The commands that selecting, cursors, spelling and replacing have in NORMAL state are under C-z, on the same letters: C-z m f selects the function around the cursor, C-z t adds a cursor below.

Try it, with modal editing off

  1. In the init file, press g e (non-modal: M->) and o, and type (setf *modal-editing* nil). Press C-g, then C-x C-e. The echo area shows NIL.
  2. Open another file with C-x C-f. The mode line no longer shows a state and the letters you type go into the text.
  3. To go back, change the line to (setf *modal-editing* t) and press C-x C-e again. You can also take the line out of the file.

You can keep modal editing and make leaving INSERT state easier. C-g is the key that does it as standard, and so does ESC. If you would rather type two letters, set a pair that hardly ever follows one another in your writing.

(setf *insert-escape-keys* "jk")

Typing j puts a j in the text at once, like any key. If k comes within a fifth of a second, the j is taken out again and you are in NORMAL state. Slower, or with another key between, both letters stay. It works while you type in an ordinary buffer. It does not work in the minibuffer, in a terminal or with several cursors.

Chapter 8 describes *escape-quits*, which makes ESC do all that C-g does.

SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*insert-escape-keys*nilnil, or textTwo keys that leave INSERT state for NORMAL state when typed one right after the other.

20.7 Themes and faces

A theme is a set of colours for everything Tuatara draws. A face is the look of one kind of thing: how a comment is drawn, or the line you are on, or the mode line. A theme gives every face its look.

20.7.1 Choosing a theme

M-x load-theme lists the themes, each with a line saying what it is like, and puts the one you choose in force. There are four.

  • ao-dark is the standard: a deep navy ground with an amber accent.
  • ao-light is the same palette worked for a white ground.
  • terminal uses the sixteen colours of your terminal, so Tuatara follows whatever colours the terminal uses.
  • plain uses no colours at all, only bold, underline, reverse video and dim. It is for terminals that cannot show colour.

The theme you choose with M-x load-theme lasts until you leave. To keep it, put it in the init file:

(load-theme 'ao-light)

In a window of its own, Tuatara follows the desktop. If the desktop turns dark in the evening, Tuatara switches to its dark theme, and back again in the morning. *follow-desktop-style* set to nil stops that and keeps one theme. M-x toggle-light-dark-theme switches between the dark and the light theme by hand. *light-theme* and *dark-theme* say which two themes it, and the desktop, switch between.

(setf *light-theme* 'plain)
(setf *dark-theme* 'terminal)

Try it, with a theme

  1. Press M-x, type load-theme and press RET. Choose ao-light with the arrow keys and RET. The colours turn light.
  2. Press M-x and run toggle-light-dark-theme. They turn dark again.
  3. To keep the light theme, open the init file and add (load-theme 'ao-light) on a line of its own. Press C-g, then C-x C-e and C-x C-s.

20.7.2 Changing one face

M-x list-faces shows every face, each with a sample drawn as the theme in force draws it, and a line saying what it colours. M-x describe-face shows all that is known of one face, including what the theme and your init file set for it. Both are covered in chapter 8.

set-face changes a face. It takes the face's name and then pairs of an attribute and a value:

(set-face :comment :fg :cyan :italic t)
(set-face :hl-line :bg "#1a2a3a")

The first line draws comments in cyan italics. The second gives the line you are on a dark blue ground. A colour is a name such as :red, a number from 0 to 255, or a six-digit code in quotes. The attributes are :fg and :bg for the text and the ground, :bold, :italic, :dim and :reverse, which each take t or nil, and :underline. In a window of its own a face can also have a :font and a :height.

What you set stays on top of any theme. Choose another theme and your comment colour is still yours.

20.7.3 A theme of your own

When a theme is nearly right, define one of your own that changes only what you do not like. Name it, say in a few words what it is, say which theme to start from, and give the colours that differ:

(define-theme my-ao
  "Ao on black."
  :faces-from ao-dark
  :palette ((ground "#000000")))
(load-theme 'my-ao)

The colours of a theme go by role: ground is the background, text the text, comment the comments, blue and green and so on. The palette says what each role is. In the example only ground changes, from navy to black, and everything drawn on the ground follows. After define-theme, M-x load-theme lists my-ao with the others.

20.7.4 The faces

The faces in the table below are the ones the other chapters do not describe. :default is the text and the ground, the face under all others. The next four colour the lines of a log or a message when they say error, warning, information or a hint.

FaceWhat it paints
:defaultText with no other face, and the background: plain, so the terminal's own colours show until a theme sets them.
:errorErrors marked in text, such as the error lines of a log.
:warningWarnings marked in text, such as the warning lines of a log.
:infoInformation marked in text, such as the info lines of a log.
:hintHints and debugging marked in text, such as the debug lines of a log.

Syntax colouring is the colour a language's words get as you write code in it: keywords, strings, numbers, the names of functions and so on. The faces below name the kinds of word a language has. Chapter 13 explains how a file is coloured. A theme gives each of these faces a colour, and you can change any with set-face. Their names are the ones tree-sitter, the parser that finds the words, gives them.

FaceWhat it paints
:attributeAttributes, annotations and decorators.
:constant.character.escapeEscape sequences in strings, captured as tree-sitter names them.
:constant.numericNumbers, captured as tree-sitter names them.

:escapeEscape sequences inside strings.
:function.macroMacros, where defined or called.
:function.methodMethods, where defined or called.
:function.specialSpecial functions, such as preprocessor macros.
:keyword.directivePreprocessor directives and pragmas, captured as tree-sitter names them.

:namespaceNamespaces, modules and packages.
:propertyFields, properties and keys.
:punctuation.specialPunctuation with a meaning of its own, such as string interpolation.

:variable.otherOther variables: fields and members.

Markdown, Org and the other languages for writing text have faces for the parts of a page: headings, emphasis, links, quotations, code and lists.

:markup.headingHeadings in markup, and the marks that make them (the # of Markdown).

:markup.heading.2Headings of the second level in markup.
:markup.heading.3Headings of the third level in markup.

20.8 Fonts

In a window of its own (tuatara --gui), Tuatara draws the text in a font you choose. In a terminal the font is the terminal's own, and these commands say so and change nothing.

To make the text larger or smaller for the moment, press C-x C-+. That makes it a step larger, about a fifth. Each press of + after it goes on. - makes it smaller, and 0 returns to the size it started with. Holding Ctrl and turning the mouse wheel does the same. The size is for this session. When you want a size for good, change the font in the init file.

M-x font-list shows every font installed on the computer, the ones whose letters are all the same width first, each with a sample written in it. Move to a line and press RET to see the window in that font now. Press w to copy the line that chooses it for good. Then paste it into your init file with C-y.

(setf *gui-font* "Adwaita Mono 14")

A font is a family, an optional style and a size in points. The text window works best with a font whose letters are all one width, since the text is laid in columns. M-x set-frame-font is another way to the same change by name: type a family and a size after it. <f11> makes the window fill the screen, and M-<f10> makes it as large as the screen allows with its title bar. Press either again to go back.

Try it, with a bigger font

  1. In a window (tuatara --gui), press C-x C-+. The text grows by a step. Press + twice more, then 0 to go back to the standard size.
  2. Press M-x, type font-list and press RET. Move to a line of a font you like with j and k and press RET. The window changes at once.
  3. Press w. The echo area says the line is copied.
  4. Open the init file, press g e (non-modal: M->), o, and paste with C-y. Change the size in the quotes to 14. Press C-g, C-x C-e, then C-x C-s.

20.8.1 Commands and faces for fonts and the window

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneM-x font-listfont-listList every font installed in Fonts, the fixed-width ones first: each family with its variants, the line of the init file that chooses each, and a sample written in it.
noneRETfont-list-useShow the window in the font on the current line of the list of fonts, for this session; w copies the line that chooses it for good.

noneM-x set-frame-fontset-frame-fontChoose the window's font among the fixed-width fonts installed: a family, with any style and size typed after it (DejaVu Sans Mono Bold 12); without a size, the size in use stays, and so does any scaling by C-x C-+.
noneC-x C-+, C-x C--, C-x C-0text-scale-adjustMake the window's font larger or smaller, by the last key of the keys that ran it: - a step smaller, 0 the size it started with, any other (+, =) a step larger, 1.2 times; with a prefix argument, that many steps.
noneM-x text-scale-increasetext-scale-increaseMake the window's font a step larger (1.2 times), or the prefix argument's worth of steps.
noneM-x text-scale-decreasetext-scale-decreaseMake the window's font a step smaller, or the prefix argument's worth of steps.

noneM-<f10>toggle-frame-maximizedMake the window as large as the screen allows, or go back to its size before.
FaceWhat it paints
:font-list-lineThe line for the init file that chooses a font, in the list of fonts (M-x font-list).
:list-nameThe name of a thing set apart in a list, above what it holds: a font's family over its variants in M-x font-list.

20.9 Your name

Some of what Tuatara writes carries your name: the author line of an exported document, a note template and a snippet. As standard it uses the full name your account has on the computer, or else the login name. To use another, set it:

(setf *user-full-name* "Aroha Smith")

Its table is in chapter 13, with the snippets that use it.

20.10 Snippets of your own

A snippet is a piece of text with places to fill in. You type its short key and press TAB, and the text goes in with the cursor on the first place. Chapter 13 tells all about the places. This section is about making a snippet that no one else has, for something you write often.

A snippet is a file. It lives in ~/.config/tuatara/snippets/, in a directory named for the mode that it is for. fundamental-mode is for every buffer. org-mode is for Org notes. The file starts with three lines: the name, the key you type, and a line with two dashes. Everything after the dashes is the text that goes in. In the text, $1, $2 and so on are places that TAB moves through, $0 is where the cursor ends, and ${1:text} is a place that begins with text you can type over. $AUTHOR is your name, and $CURRENT_DATE, $CURRENT_MONTH and $CURRENT_YEAR are today's date.

C-c y (insert-snippet) chooses one from a list by name. M-x copy-snippet copies one of Tuatara's own into your directory, so that you can change it. Yours then takes its place.

Try it, with a snippet for a letter's greeting

  1. In a terminal, type these two commands.

    mkdir -p ~/.config/tuatara/snippets/fundamental-mode
printf '# name: Greeting\n# key: dear\n# --\nKia ora ${1:Aroha},\n\n$0\n\nKind regards,\n$AUTHOR\n' > ~/.config/tuatara/snippets/fundamental-mode/greeting
  2. In Tuatara, open a new file with C-x C-f and the name ~/letter.txt. Press i, type dear and press TAB. The greeting goes in, with the name ready to type over.
  3. Type Hemi, press TAB, and the cursor moves to the empty line for your letter. Your name is at the bottom.
  4. Press C-g, then u until the text is gone. Delete the snippet file if you do not want it.

20.11 How lines are shown

Tuatara can show the same text in several ways without changing a character of it: the line the cursor is on painted across the window, long lines wrapped onto several rows, a line down the window at the fill column, the column the cursor is in painted down the window, the text in a column in the middle of the window, the characters that draw nothing shown as their codes, and the pictures an Org note links to drawn among its lines. Each is a mode you switch on or off. They all work the same way.

A command with -mode at the end switches the thing for the buffer you are in. That buffer keeps its choice. Most have a key under C-x T, for "toggle". The same command with global- in front switches it for every buffer that has not chosen for itself, while Tuatara runs. A setting in the init file says what every buffer has from the start. A list of modes, such as *soft-wrap-modes*, says it for one kind of buffer, all Org notes or all code, whatever the setting for every buffer says.

A buffer's own choice counts first, then the list of modes, then the setting for every buffer. Each switch says what it did on the echo row. With a count before it, C-u 1, a command switches on whatever it was, and C-u 0 switches it off.

The commands and what they show, with the keys they have, are in the table below. Some of them are shown in other chapters. Here they are together.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneC-x T hhl-line-modeHighlight the line point is on in the current buffer, or stop: every row of it, out to the window's edge, in the :hl-line face, under the syntax colours and the selection, in the selected window.
noneC-x T ccursor-column-modeHighlight the column point is in, down the window, in the current buffer, or stop: in the :cursor-column face (the :hl-line face's colour unless set apart), over the backgrounds of the text (a source block's, the selection's) and under the line point is on, past the end of short lines too, in the selected window.
noneC-x T lsoft-wrap-modeWrap the long lines of the current buffer at a word's edge, or stop: a line longer than the window is shown on as many rows as it needs, at the fill column (C-x f), or the window's edge when that is nearer; the text is not changed.
noneC-x T vvisual-line-modeMark the current buffer's fill column (C-x f) with a line down the window, or stop: the last column a filled line may reach, the 80th for a fill column of 80, painted in the :visual-line face over the text's backgrounds (a source block's, the selection's) and under the line point is on.

noneM-x global-cursor-column-modeglobal-cursor-column-modeHighlight the column point is in, down the window, in every buffer, or stop, while the editor runs (GLOBAL-CURSOR-COLUMN-MODE in the init file keeps it); a buffer that chose with C-x T c, and the modes CURSOR-COLUMN-MODES names, keep theirs; with a count, on when it is positive, off when it is zero or less.

noneM-x global-text-direction-modeglobal-text-direction-modeShow right-to-left text in the order it is read, in every buffer, or stop, while the editor runs (GLOBAL-TEXT-DIRECTION-MODE in the init file keeps it); a buffer that chose with M-x text-direction-mode, and the modes TEXT-DIRECTION-MODES names, keep theirs; with a count, on when it is positive, off when it is zero or less.
noneM-x global-inline-pictures-modeglobal-inline-pictures-modeShow the pictures a buffer links to and its formulas among its lines, in every buffer, or stop, while the editor runs (GLOBAL-INLINE-PICTURES-MODE in the init file keeps it); a buffer that chose with C-x T p, and the modes INLINE-PICTURES-MODES names, keep theirs; with a count, on when it is positive, off when it is zero or less.

Text that is written from right to left, such as Hebrew and Arabic, is shown in the order it is read. text-direction-mode is for the rare text where you want each line's letters in the order they are stored instead.

The settings say the same in the init file. Each mode has a pair: *global-NAME-mode* for every buffer, and *NAME-modes* for the kinds of buffer that differ. The first is t or nil. The second is a list of (MODE . VALUE), where MODE is the name of a major mode, with or without -mode, and VALUE is t or nil. A mode counts for the modes made from it, and the nearest one listed decides. For example, to wrap lines in Org notes and plain text but not in CSV files, whatever the rest do:

(setf *soft-wrap-modes* '((org-mode . t) (text-mode . t) (csv-mode . nil)))

The pairs, each with what it shows:

  • *global-hl-line-mode* and *hl-line-modes* paint the line the cursor is on across the window. It is on for every buffer unless you set the first to nil. To keep it off in CSV files only: (setf *hl-line-modes* '((csv-mode . nil))).
  • *global-soft-wrap-mode* and *soft-wrap-modes* wrap long lines onto several rows. They are off unless set, except in help and the about buffer, which wrap. (setf *global-soft-wrap-mode* t) wraps everywhere.
  • *soft-wrap-at-fill-column* says where a wrapped line breaks. With t, the default, at the fill column or the window's edge, whichever is nearer. With nil always at the window's edge, so on a wide window the lines are long.
  • *global-visual-line-mode* and *visual-line-modes* draw a line down the window after the fill column, the 80th column when it is 80. Nothing wraps. Off unless set: (setf *visual-line-modes* '((prog-mode . t))).
  • *global-centred-text-mode* and *centred-text-modes* show the text in a column in the middle of the window. Off unless set: (setf *centred-text-modes* '((org-mode . t) (text-mode . t))).
  • *centred-text-width* is the width of that column, 80 by default. With (setf *centred-text-width* 70) the text takes 70 columns and the margins are blank.
  • *global-cursor-column-mode* and *cursor-column-modes* paint the column the cursor is in down the window. Off unless set: (setf *cursor-column-modes* '((csv-mode . t))) helps to read a table.
  • *global-invisible-characters-mode* and *invisible-characters-modes* show characters that draw nothing as their codes, such as <FEFF> for a byte-order mark. Off unless set, but always on in a file opened safely. (setf *global-invisible-characters-mode* t) shows them everywhere.
  • *global-text-direction-mode* and *text-direction-modes* say how lines of right-to-left text are shown. They take more than t and nil. The default, :auto, shows the order read, each line starting at the side its first letter is written from. :right-to-left and :left-to-right do the same with every line starting at the side named. nil shows each line's characters in the order stored. A file opened safely is shown in the order stored. (setf *text-direction-modes* '((csv-mode . nil))) keeps CSV files in the order stored.
  • *global-inline-pictures-mode* and *inline-pictures-modes* draw the pictures an Org note links to among its lines, as chapter 14 describes. Off unless set, and never in a file opened safely: (setf *inline-pictures-modes* '((org-mode . t))).

20.12 The calendar

C-x n a shows the calendar in a window below the one you are in: the month of today and the month before and after it, with the cursor on today. C-x n A shows it in the window you are in instead, in place of its buffer. q closes it and brings your buffer back.

The arrow keys, or h l for a day back or on and k j for a week back or on, move through the days. H and L show the month before and after, and J and K move the cursor a month. . goes to today, and g l goes back to where you were before you moved. g d asks for a date and goes to it. You can answer with 2026-12-24, with tomorrow, fri or +3d, or as any date is asked for in Tuatara. o shows the months around one you name, such as jan 27 for January 2027.

Days that have something on them are marked. An agenda entry (chapter 14) marks its day, and a journal entry (the next section) underlines it. RET on a day opens what it is marked for. When a day has both, Tuatara asks which, and each answer is one key. n opens the journal entry for the day at the cursor, or makes it. m marks the days that have agenda entries and u takes the marks off. p d says which day of the year the cursor is on, and p c says the week and the ISO date.

Three settings change how the calendar looks. By default it shows three months and weeks begin on Monday. *calendar-months* set to 12 shows a whole year. *calendar-week-start-day* set to 0 begins weeks on Sunday. *calendar-months-per-row* says how many months stand side by side. It is as many as fit when it is nil.

*calendar-mark-days* says whether the days that have agenda entries are marked as soon as the calendar shows them. It is t by default. With nil the calendar opens without marks and m puts them on when you want them, which is quicker if you have a large agenda:

(setf *calendar-mark-days* nil)

(setf *calendar-week-start-day* 0)
(setf *calendar-months* 12)
(setf *calendar-months-per-row* 3)

20.13 The journal

A journal is a note for each day: what you did, what you thought, what to remember. C-x n j opens today's entry, or makes it when there is none. A new entry is a file with a formatted name (chapter 9), in a directory called journal inside the directory of your notes, with the day as its title, such as Friday 20 March 2026, and the word journal among its keywords. It is saved at once, so there is a file to find later. M-x journal-new-entry always makes a new one, even when there is one for today. With C-u before it, it asks for a date.

When there is more than one entry for the day, Tuatara asks which you want. In the calendar, an entry marks its day, and n opens or makes the entry for the day at the cursor. You can look back through the month and open any day.

The journal is a set of ordinary notes, so you can search them, link to them and export them like any others. Everything about how they are named and written is a setting.

The directory is *journal-directory*. The word that marks an entry, so that entries can be told from your other notes, is *journal-keyword*. An entry lasts a day as standard. *journal-interval* makes it a week, a month or a year. The kind of file is *journal-file-type*, one of :org, :markdown or :text. *journal-title-format* says what the title looks like. It may add the time, or ask each time. *journal-file-name*, when set, gives entries plain names such as 2026-03-20.org in place of formatted ones. *journal-org-header* is the text an Org entry starts with.

(setf *journal-directory* "~/journal/")
(setf *journal-interval* :weekly)
(setf *journal-file-type* :markdown)

The three lines put the entries in ~/journal/, one for each week, as Markdown files.

noneM-x journal-new-entryjournal-new-entryMake a new journal entry for today, whatever entries there are; with C-u, for a date asked for.

20.14 Odds and ends

The rest of the names that belong to this chapter are small. They are grouped by what they do.

20.14.1 Changing case, and what a character is

Three commands change the case of a word or a selection. They act on the selection when there is one, and on the next word when there is not. capitalize-region is the same for a selection alone. delete-trailing-whitespace takes the spaces and tabs from the ends of lines. It works on the selection if there is one and on the whole buffer if not. C-x = says which character the cursor is on, with its code in three bases.

noneM-x downcase-dwimdowncase-dwimPut the region in lower case, or with none the next word, as downcase-word does.
noneM-x capitalize-dwimcapitalize-dwimCapitalise the region, or with none the next word, as capitalize-word does.
noneM-x capitalize-regioncapitalize-regionCapitalise each word of the region.
noneM-x delete-trailing-whitespacedelete-trailing-whitespaceDelete the spaces and tabs at the end of every line, of the selection when there is one, else of the whole buffer (of the part shown of a narrowed one), and then the blank lines at its end too (DELETE-TRAILING-LINES).

20.14.2 Buttons and the mouse

A button is a piece of text that does something when you press RET on it: a link in a help page, a name in a list. TAB goes to the next one in a buffer and S-TAB goes back. Moving past the last goes round to the first. push-button does what the button at the cursor does. It is on RET and l, and on C-c l. Links in Markdown are followed with a command of their own.

The mouse works as in other programs. A click puts the cursor, a drag selects, two clicks select a word and three a line. Letting go of the button makes what you selected the desktop's primary selection, which the middle button pastes in Tuatara and in other programs.

ModalNon-modalCommandWhat it does
noneTABforward-buttonMove point to the next button, from the last round to the first.
noneS-TABbackward-buttonMove point to the button before, from the first round to the last.
nonel, RET, C-c lpush-buttonDo what the button at point does: open what it names.
none<down-mouse-1>push-button-at-clickPut point where the first mouse button went down, as <down-mouse-1> does, and do what a button there does.
noneC-c C-omarkdown-follow-link-at-pointFollow the Markdown link point is on (C-c C-o, and RET in NORMAL state): to the heading a table of contents's link (#an-anchor) leads to, a web or mail address in the desktop's program after asking, or a file, visited.
none<drag-mouse-1>mouse-drag-regionSelect from where the first mouse button went down to where the mouse is now, point following it, in the window it went down in; held above or below that window's text, it scrolls a line at a time.
none<up-mouse-1>mouse-releaseThe first mouse button let go: a drag ends there, what it selected staying selected and becoming the desktop's primary selection, which the middle button pastes in other programs.
none<double-mouse-1>mouse-select-wordSelect the word the first mouse button went down on twice, point at its end: the run of letters, digits and _ there, or of spaces, or of other signs; on a bracket, the bracketed group.
none<triple-mouse-1>mouse-select-lineSelect the line the first mouse button went down on three times, its line break too.

Grammars are what colour and parse a language. Tuatara turns on those of the common languages by itself. For another, a file asks whether to turn its grammar on, and M-x turn-on-grammar does it later. M-x turn-off-grammar stops a language being coloured or parsed, in later sessions too.

20.14.4 Lists and the cursor's popups

When Tuatara lists completions beside the cursor with C-M-i, the faces below say how the list is drawn. In a buffer you can also have the entries of a directory listed as you type a path, after the slash.

*complete-paths* is t by default: type ~/notes/ and the entries of that directory are listed beside the cursor. Typing narrows the list and RET puts the chosen one in. With nil nothing is listed. *complete-paths-modes* says it for kinds of buffer, in the form of the pairs of the section "How lines are shown", and wins over the setting. To list paths in code but not in Org notes:

(setf *complete-paths-modes* '((org-mode . nil) (prog-mode . t)))

When Tuatara lists files to choose from, it shows when each was changed. *relative-age-limit* is how many seconds back that counts as an age such as 5 min ago or 3 days ago. Older files show the date. The default is two weeks (1209600). With 0 every file shows its date:

(setf *relative-age-limit* 0)

*preview-buffers* is nil by default. With t, choosing a buffer with C-x b shows the buffer under the cursor of the list in your window while you choose, and your own buffer comes back if you give up:

(setf *preview-buffers* t)
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes

*complete-paths-modes*nila list, each (MODE . ON)Major modes whose buffers list a path's directory as it is typed, or not, whatever COMPLETE-PATHS says.
*relative-age-limit*1209600a whole number, 0 or moreSeconds within which the last change of a file among completion candidates is shown as an age (5 min ago, 3 days ago); older ones show the date.
*preview-buffers*nilt, nilWhether choosing a buffer shows the selected buffer in the window you are in.
FaceWhat it paints

:popup-barThe scroll bar of the list of completions beside the cursor.
:popup-currentThe chosen completion in the list beside the cursor.
:popup-headingThe first line of the documentation beside the list of completions: the name and its parameters.
:completion-mode-directoryThe d of a directory's permissions beside it among completion candidates.
:completion-mode-linkThe l of a symbolic link's permissions beside it among completion candidates.
:input-method-pendingKeys typed under an input method that wait for the next key to settle them (an a under swedish-postfix, waiting to see whether an a, an e or another key comes), underlined.

Reports and lists, such as the health report of M-x check-health, have faces for the name of a field and for what cannot be changed:

FaceWhat it paints

20.14.5 Limits and safety

Four settings are limits that keep a mistake from filling your computer. Each has a sensible standard, and a reason to change it is rare.

  • *insert-file-limit* is how much of another file M-x insert-formatted-note-template reads. A larger file is refused.
  • *program-output-limit* is how much of what a program writes Tuatara takes. A program that writes more is stopped.
  • *wipe-passes* is how many times a file that you wipe is overwritten with random octets before it is deleted. Once is enough for a drive that writes in place.
  • *markdown-toc-on-save* makes the table of contents of a Markdown file again each time you save, under the heading tagged :TOC:.
SettingDefaultValuesWhat it changes
*insert-file-limit*16777216a whole number, 0 or moreThe most octets M-x insert-formatted-note-template reads from a file that is no note template.
*program-output-limit*67108864a whole number, 1 or moreThe most octets PROGRAM-OUTPUT takes of what a program writes.
*wipe-passes*1a whole number, 1 or moreHow many times a file wiped is overwritten with random octets before it is deleted.
*markdown-toc-on-save*tt, nilWhether a Markdown file's table of contents is made again each time it is saved.

C-c M-m shows what a macro call in Lisp code expands to, which is useful when you write your own functions in the init file. pattern-finish takes what you typed in a question that asks for a pattern, and says why when it cannot.

Every setting

The name, default, values and purpose of every setting you can change.

The earlier chapters describe the settings of each subject where you meet it. This chapter lists them all in one table, in the order of the alphabet, so that you can look one up by name. The table is made from the program each time this manual is made, so it never lists a setting that Tuatara does not have.

A setting is a name that starts and ends with a star, such as *auto-save*. You change one in your init file, as in (setf *auto-save* nil). The table has four columns. The first is the name of the setting. The second is its default, the value Tuatara has until you change it, and a long value is cut short with three dots. The third says which values the setting takes: t, nil for a setting that is on or off, a list of the words it understands, such as :absolute, :relative, nil, or a kind of value, such as a whole number, text or a directory's name. The fourth says what the setting changes. Its full description in the editor says what each value does.

Only the settings that Tuatara promises to keep are listed. A setting that is not here may change from one version to the next, and should not be set in an init file you keep for years.

To find a setting from within the editor, press C-h v and type a few letters of its name. Tuatara shows its value, the values it takes and its full description. M-x check-health lists any setting whose value is not one of those it takes. To find the settings that mention a word, press C-h a and type the word.
